quiz.question: Which statement best describes a flipped classroom?
options: The teacher lectures in class and learners do all exercises alone at home
Learners are taught entirely online and never meet the teacher
Learners are grouped by ability and taught on different days
Learners study new content before class through videos or readings, and class time is used for problem solving and discussion
quiz.explanation: Flipping swaps the usual order: first exposure to content happens at home, and the “homework” (application, discussion, doubt-solving) happens in class with the teacher. The first option is the traditional classroom; the second is fully online learning, not flipping.

lessons.title: Evaluation systems
lessons.summaryHtml: Evaluation is the systematic process of judging how far learning objectives have been achieved; it adds a value judgement to measurement. Its elements form a triangle of objectives, learning experiences and evaluation, and its types are classified by timing and purpose (placement, formative, diagnostic, summative), by the standard of comparison (norm-referenced, criterion-referenced, ipsative) and by the agency (internal, external, self, peer). A good test is valid, reliable, objective and usable, and item analysis (the difficulty and discrimination indices) keeps question banks healthy. Under the Choice Based Credit System, UGC’s 10-point letter grades lead to the credit-weighted SGPA and CGPA, and the NEP-era credit frameworks extend this. Computer-based testing, NTA’s percentile normalisation and innovations such as open-book exams, e-portfolios and rubrics complete the syllabus. Expect terminology matches, statement questions and short numericals on SGPA, CGPA and item analysis.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Measurement puts a number on performance (“she scored 42 out of 50”). Assessment collects evidence of learning by many means, such as tests, assignments, observation and projects. Evaluation goes one step further and makes a judgement: “42 out of 50 means she has mastered this unit and is ready for the next one”. Gronlund’s summary is that evaluation = quantitative description (measurement) + qualitative description + value judgement. An evaluation system is the whole arrangement of these judgements in an institution: when learners are assessed, by whom, with what tools, how the results are graded and recorded, and how they are used.

Why it matters for NET

Evaluation is one of the most regularly tested parts of Teaching Aptitude. Common questions pair evaluation types with their purposes, test statements about formative and summative, or norm- and criterion-referenced, evaluation, and ask about the qualities of a good test. Increasingly, they cover CBCS grading, computer-based testing and new practices such as open-book exams and e-portfolios. Short numericals (SGPA, CGPA, difficulty and discrimination indices) also appear, and they are easy marks for anyone who knows the formula.

Elements of evaluation

Evaluation is tied to teaching through a triangle of three elements that shape one another: educational objectives (what learners should achieve), learning experiences (the teaching–learning activities) and evaluation (evidence of whether the objectives were achieved). Evaluation checks the objectives and also improves the learning experiences, so the arrows run both ways. The process has a fixed order: formulate objectives → define them as observable behaviours → select or construct tools → administer the tools → interpret the results and judge → use the feedback. Evaluation is therefore continuous (not a one-time event), comprehensive (cognitive, affective and psychomotor domains), objective-based and diagnostic and remedial.

Types of evaluation

BasisTypesKey idea
Timing and purpose (Airasian and Madaus)Placement, formative, diagnostic, summativeBefore instruction (entry position); during (feedback); during, for persistent difficulties (causes, then remedial teaching); at the end (certify and grade)
Standard of comparisonNorm-referenced, criterion-referenced, ipsativeAgainst a group (percentile, rank); against a pre-set standard (mastery; Glaser, 1963); against the learner’s own earlier performance
AgencyInternal, external, self, peer, 360-degreeOwn teacher; outside examiner; the learner; classmates; many sources together
ModeOral, written, practical, computer-basedViva voce; pen-and-paper; performance; on screen
FormalityFormal, informalScheduled tests; observation and questioning in class
Role (Lorna Earl)Assessment of, for and as learningSummative; formative; the learner monitors his or her own learning (metacognition)

Formative and summative were named by Michael Scriven (1967) in the context of curriculum evaluation, and Bloom later applied them to student learning. Formative results are not usually used for final grades; summative results are. Continuous and Comprehensive Evaluation (CCE) means regular (continuous) assessment covering both scholastic and co-scholastic areas (comprehensive). The Right to Education Act, 2009 calls for comprehensive and continuous evaluation in elementary education.

Tools and techniques

  • Tests: essay type (organisation and expression, but subjective scoring), short answer, and objective type (multiple choice, true/false, matching, completion: wide coverage and high scorer reliability).
  • Observation tools: rating scale (the degree of a trait, for example on 5 points), checklist (presence or absence, yes/no), anecdotal record (a factual note of a significant incident), cumulative record (a progressive record of a learner over the years).
  • Others: portfolio or e-portfolio (a purposeful collection of work showing growth), rubric (criteria with described performance levels), project, interview, questionnaire, sociometry (J.L. Moreno: mapping peer relations).
  • Blueprint (table of specifications): a chart that spreads the marks across content areas, objectives (for example Bloom’s levels) and question types, so the paper has content validity.

Qualities of a good test

Validity (does it measure what it claims to?) is the most important. Its types are content validity (covers the syllabus adequately), criterion-related validity (concurrent: agrees with a present criterion; predictive: forecasts future performance), construct validity (measures a theoretical trait such as intelligence) and face validity (looks suitable to the people taking it). Reliability (consistency) is estimated by test–retest (same test, twice), parallel forms (two equivalent forms), split-half (odd and even items, corrected with Spearman–Brown), Kuder–Richardson KR-20 and Cronbach’s alpha (internal consistency), and inter-rater agreement. Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. Objectivity means that different examiners give the same score. Usability (practicability) covers cost, time and ease of administration. Discriminating power is the ability to separate able from less able learners.

Spearman–Brown (doubling): rfull = 2rhalf ÷ (1 + rhalf). Because a longer test samples more behaviour, it is more reliable.

Item analysis

Arrange the answer scripts from the highest to the lowest score and take the top and bottom groups (Kelley’s 27% each is standard). For each item, count the correct answers in the upper group (RU) and the lower group (RL); let n be the size of one group.

  • Difficulty index P = (RU + RL) ÷ 2n, or, for the whole class, the number correct ÷ the number who attempted. A higher P means an easier item. Items near 0.5 leave the most room for discrimination; very easy and very hard items are usually revised.
  • Discrimination index D = (RU − RL) ÷ n, ranging from −1 to +1. By Ebel’s guideline, 0.40 and above is very good, 0.30–0.39 reasonably good, 0.20–0.29 marginal and below 0.20 poor. A negative D (the weak do better than the strong) signals a faulty item or a wrong key.
  • Distractor analysis: a good distractor attracts more lower-group than upper-group students; a distractor that no one chooses is useless.

Scores and grading

A raw score means little alone. A percentile rank gives the percentage of the group at or below the score. The z-score is z = (X − mean) ÷ SD, and the T-score is T = 50 + 10z, which removes negatives and decimals. Absolute grading uses fixed mark ranges (criterion-referenced); relative grading depends on the distribution of the group (norm-referenced). Direct grading awards grades straight from performance; indirect grading first gives marks and then converts them to grades.

Evaluation in CBCS

UGC asked universities to adopt the Choice Based Credit System from the 2015–16 session. Its main features are these.

  • Semester and credit: a semester has 15–18 weeks, about 90 teaching days. One credit = one hour of lecture or tutorial, or two hours of practical or field work, per week.
  • Course types: Core; Elective (Discipline Specific Elective, Generic Elective from an unrelated discipline, Dissertation or Project); Ability Enhancement Courses (AECC: Environmental Science and English/MIL Communication; SEC: Skill Enhancement Courses). In the UGC template an Honours programme needs about 140 credits and a Programme (general) degree about 120.
  • Assessment: continuous internal assessment plus an end-semester examination. Grading may be absolute or relative.
  • 10-point scale: O (Outstanding) 10, A+ (Excellent) 9, A (Very Good) 8, B+ (Good) 7, B (Above Average) 6, C (Average) 5, P (Pass) 4, F (Fail) 0, Ab (Absent) 0. Non-credit courses are marked Satisfactory or Unsatisfactory and are left out of the averages.
  • SGPA = Σ(Ci × Gi) ÷ ΣCi over the courses of a semester. CGPA = Σ(Cj × Sj) ÷ ΣCj over the semesters, where Cj is the total credits of semester j and Sj its SGPA. Both are rounded to 2 decimal places and shown on the transcript.

NEP-era frameworks. UGC’s Curriculum and Credit Framework for Undergraduate Programmes (under NEP 2020) keeps the credit and grade logic. One credit of theory or tutorial = 1 hour a week (15 hours in a semester of at least 15 weeks); one credit of practicum = 2 hours a week (30 hours). Exits are a UG Certificate at 40 credits, a UG Diploma at 80, a 3-year degree at 120 and a 4-year Honours degree at 160. The research stream in the fourth year is open to students with 75% marks or more in the first six semesters. Evaluation is continuous: sessional work and the terminal examination both count towards the final grade. The Academic Bank of Credits stores earned credits so that they can be carried across institutions.

Computer-based testing

In computer-based testing (CBT) the candidate reads and answers on a computer at a test centre. NTA was approved by the Cabinet on 10 November 2017 as a society under the Societies Registration Act, 1860, to run entrance and eligibility tests online, and it has conducted UGC-NET in CBT mode since December 2018. The advantages of CBT are fast and error-free scoring, the shuffling of questions and options, multiple sessions, rich item types, immediate analytics and less paper handling. Its limitations are the need for infrastructure and power, a digital divide for rural candidates, technical glitches and security risks. Linear CBT gives everyone a fixed form; computer adaptive testing picks each item according to the earlier responses. When an exam runs in several shifts, NTA converts raw scores into percentiles within each session: percentile = 100 × (candidates in the session with a raw score equal to or less than the candidate’s) ÷ (total candidates in the session). The percentile is computed to 7 decimal places to reduce ties.

Innovations in evaluation

  • Structural: semesters, credits and grades (CBCS), internal assessment, credit transfer and the Academic Bank of Credits, digital certificates (National Academic Depository, DigiLocker).
  • Tools: question banks and item banking, blueprints, rubrics, e-portfolios, peer and self-assessment, projects and presentations.
  • Modes: open-book and take-home exams (which test application rather than recall), online and remotely proctored exams, on-demand examinations (such as the NIOS On-Demand Examination System), on-screen marking of scanned scripts, OMR and CBT.
  • Policy: UGC’s evaluation-reform guidance calls for continuous and comprehensive evaluation over one high-stakes exam, criterion-based grading and outcome-based education. NEP 2020 proposes PARAKH (Performance Assessment, Review, and Analysis of Knowledge for Holistic Development) as a national assessment centre and a 360-degree, multidimensional holistic progress card, and it calls for a shift from rote learning to competency-based assessment.

Worked examples

Example 1. SGPA. Credits 4, 4, 3, 3, 2 with grades O, B, A+, A, B+.

Step 1: grade points 10, 6, 9, 8, 7. Step 2: credit points 40, 24, 27, 24, 14, total 129. Step 3: total credits 16. Step 4: SGPA = 129 ÷ 16 = 8.0625, reported as 8.06. The unweighted mean of the grade points is 40 ÷ 5 = 8.00; it is wrong because it gives a 2-credit course the same weight as a 4-credit course.

Example 2. SGPA with a fail. Credits 4, 4, 4, 2 with grades A, F, B+, O.

Step 1: credit points 32, 0, 28, 20, total 80. Step 2: the F course still counts in the credits taken, so the credits are 14. Step 3: SGPA = 80 ÷ 14 = 5.714, reported as 5.71. The trap is to drop the F course and divide 80 by 10, giving 8.00.

Example 3. CGPA. Four semesters with credits 20, 22, 24, 22 and SGPAs 7.2, 8.1, 6.9, 7.6.

Step 1: 20 × 7.2 = 144.0; 22 × 8.1 = 178.2; 24 × 6.9 = 165.6; 22 × 7.6 = 167.2. Step 2: the total is 655.0 over 88 credits. Step 3: CGPA = 655 ÷ 88 = 7.443…, reported as 7.44. The simple average of the SGPAs, 29.8 ÷ 4 = 7.45, is the trap.

Example 4. Item analysis. With upper and lower groups of 25 each, an item is answered correctly by 18 in the upper group and 6 in the lower group.

Step 1: P = (18 + 6) ÷ 50 = 0.48, a moderate difficulty. Step 2: D = (18 − 6) ÷ 25 = 0.48, which is very good (above 0.40). Keep the item. If RU were 6 and RL 12 with n = 30, D = −0.20: the item or its key is faulty.

Example 5. Standard scores and percentile. A score of 72 in a test with mean 60 and SD 8 gives z = (72 − 60) ÷ 8 = 1.5 and T = 50 + 10 × 1.5 = 65. In an NTA session of 2,000 candidates, if 1,640 candidates (including the candidate) have a raw score equal to or less than the candidate’s, the percentile is 100 × 1,640 ÷ 2,000 = 82.

Example 6. Spearman–Brown. If the correlation between the two halves is 0.80, the whole-test reliability = 1.60 ÷ 1.80 = 0.889 ≈ 0.89. This is always higher than the half-test value for any positive r below 1.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFormula or fact
EvaluationMeasurement + qualitative description + value judgement (Gronlund)
Types by timingPlacement (before), formative (during), diagnostic (during, persistent difficulty), summative (end)
Formative and summativeMichael Scriven, 1967
Criterion-referencedRobert Glaser, 1963; compare with a standard. Norm-referenced: compare with a group
Difficulty indexP = (RU + RL) ÷ 2n; higher P = easier
Discrimination indexD = (RU − RL) ÷ n; −1 to +1; 0.40 and above very good; negative = faulty
Spearman–Brown2r ÷ (1 + r)
z and Tz = (X − mean) ÷ SD; T = 50 + 10z
UGC 10-point scaleO 10, A+ 9, A 8, B+ 7, B 6, C 5, P 4, F 0, Ab 0
SGPA, CGPAΣ(credits × grade point) ÷ Σ credits; Σ(semester credits × SGPA) ÷ Σ credits; 2 decimals
CBCS course typesCore; DSE, GE, Dissertation or Project; AECC (EVS, English/MIL); SEC
UG credit framework1 credit = 15 h theory or 30 h practicum; exits at 40, 80, 120 and 160 credits; research stream with 75%
NTAApproved 10 Nov 2017; society (1860 Act); UGC-NET in CBT since December 2018; percentile to 7 decimals

NTA traps

  • Formative versus diagnostic. Wrong: “diagnostic evaluation is just formative evaluation”. Fix: both happen during instruction, but diagnostic goes deeper into the causes of persistent difficulties and leads to remedial teaching.
  • Reliability versus validity. Wrong: “a reliable test must be valid”. Fix: reliability is necessary but not sufficient; a valid test must be reliable.
  • Difficulty index direction. Wrong: “P = 0.9 means a very difficult item”. Fix: P is the proportion correct, so 0.9 is very easy.
  • Dividing by the wrong n. Wrong: D = (RU − RL) ÷ total class. Fix: divide by the size of one group.
  • Unweighted averages. Wrong: averaging grade points or SGPAs directly. Fix: weight by credits.
  • Dropping F. Wrong: excluding failed courses from the credits. Fix: under UGC’s definition the SGPA uses the credits of the courses taken, so F (0 points) still adds its credits.
  • Grade names. Wrong: B+ = “Above Average”. Fix: B+ is Good (7); B is Above Average (6); C is Average (5).
  • CAT versus linear CBT. Wrong: “every CBT is adaptive”. Fix: most Indian CBTs, including UGC-NET, are linear; only CAT picks items from the responses.
  • Open-book means easy. Wrong: “no preparation needed”. Fix: it tests application and analysis, which need deeper preparation.

How NTA asks this

Formats. Matching types of evaluation with purposes, and tools with descriptions (rating scale, checklist, anecdotal or cumulative record); statement pairs on norm- and criterion-referenced testing, or on reliability and validity; “which are correct” on CBCS or CBT features; ordering the evaluation process or the grade letters; and short numericals on SGPA, CGPA, P and D, and Spearman–Brown.

Mini Assertion–Reason. A: Diagnostic evaluation is usually followed by remedial teaching. R: Diagnostic evaluation identifies the specific causes of a learner’s difficulties. Both are true, and knowing the cause is exactly what makes a targeted remedy possible, so R explains A (option 1).

Elimination tricks. For a type-of-evaluation match, anchor the time word: “before” means placement and “end” means summative; then split the two “during” types by “feedback” (formative) or “causes” (diagnostic). For SGPA or CGPA options, compute the unweighted average first; if it appears among the options, it is usually the trap, unless the credits are all equal. For P and D, note that P can never be negative, so a negative option must be a D value.

terms.definition: A continuous, systematic process of judging the extent to which objectives are achieved: measurement (quantitative) plus qualitative description plus a value judgement.
Evaluation during instruction to give feedback and improve learning; the term was introduced by Michael Scriven (1967). Also called assessment for learning.
Evaluation at the end of a unit, course or programme to grade, certify or promote; assessment of learning.
Evaluation that finds the causes of persistent learning difficulties, followed by remedial teaching.
A test that compares a learner’s performance with a pre-set standard (criterion), not with other learners; the idea was set out by Robert Glaser (1963).
The consistency of scores: the same learners get similar scores on repeated or equivalent measurement.
The extent to which a test measures what it claims to measure; the most important quality of a test.
D = (R<sub>U</sub> − R<sub>L</sub>) ÷ n: how well an item separates the high scorers from the low scorers; it ranges from −1 to +1.
Credit-weighted averages of grade points: SGPA for one semester, CGPA across all the semesters so far, rounded to 2 decimal places.
Computer-based testing in which the next item is chosen according to the candidate’s responses so far: a correct answer usually brings a harder item.

lessons.examTip: For SGPA and CGPA, always weight by credits: multiply each grade point by its credits, add, and divide by the total credits. The trap option is the simple (unweighted) average of the grade points, so compute it too and make sure you avoid it.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each; numericals need slightly longer than recall questions).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 8 minutes. For every SGPA or CGPA problem, write the credit × grade-point column and its total before dividing.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (unweighted average, F dropped, D divided by 2n or by the class size, checklist and rating scale swapped).
Write from memory: the UGC 10-point scale, the four timing types of evaluation with one example each, the four validity types and five reliability methods, and the P and D formulas.
Make up two SGPA problems of your own with unequal credits, solve them both weighted and unweighted, and note how far apart the two answers are.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 45–75 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Every SGPA, CGPA and item-analysis numerical correct, each within 90 seconds.
The UGC 10-point scale (letter, meaning, grade point) written from memory without error.
Placement, formative, diagnostic and summative told apart correctly in every statement question.

quiz.question: Which of the following best describes formative evaluation?
options: Evaluation at the end of a course to award grades and certificates
Evaluation before instruction to place learners in suitable groups
Evaluation during instruction to give feedback and improve learning
Evaluation that ranks learners against a national norm group
quiz.explanation: Formative evaluation happens while teaching is still going on; its purpose is feedback to improve learning and teaching (assessment for learning). The first option is summative, the second is placement, and the fourth describes norm-referenced testing.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Placement decides the starting position before teaching (A-III). Formative monitors and gives feedback during teaching (B-IV). Diagnostic finds the causes of persistent difficulties (C-I). Summative certifies at the end (D-II). The most common distractor swaps formative and diagnostic, because both happen during instruction.

b: I. Finding the causes of persistent learning difficulties
II. Certifying or grading achievement at the end
III. Deciding the entry position of learners before instruction
IV. Monitoring progress and giving feedback during instruction

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: A student takes five courses with credits 4, 4, 3, 3 and 2 and earns grades O, B, A+, A and B+ respectively on the UGC 10-point scale. What is the SGPA?
quiz.explanation: Grade points: O = 10, B = 6, A+ = 9, A = 8, B+ = 7. Credit points: 4×10 + 4×6 + 3×9 + 3×8 + 2×7 = 40 + 24 + 27 + 24 + 14 = 129. Total credits = 16. SGPA = 129 ÷ 16 = 8.0625, reported as 8.06. The trap 8.00 is the unweighted mean of the grade points, (10 + 6 + 9 + 8 + 7) ÷ 5.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A: a weighing scale that always reads 2 kg too high is consistent (reliable) but not accurate (valid). Because consistency and accuracy are different properties, reliability does not guarantee validity. The reverse fails: an unreliable test cannot be valid.

stmts: Assertion (A): A test can be highly reliable and yet not valid.
Reason (R): Reliability concerns the consistency of scores, while validity concerns whether the test measures what it is meant to measure.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is the definition of norm-referenced testing (percentile ranks, relative grading). Statement II is false: a criterion-referenced test checks whether each learner has reached a pre-set standard (mastery), whatever the others score; ranking is the norm-referenced purpose.

stmts: Statement I: A norm-referenced test interprets a learner’s score by comparing it with the scores of a reference group.
Statement II: A criterion-referenced test was designed mainly to rank learners against their classmates.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In a class of 100 students, the upper 27 and the lower 27 scorers are taken for item analysis. An item is answered correctly by 20 students of the upper group and 8 of the lower group. What is its discrimination index?
quiz.explanation: D = (R_U − R_L) ÷ n, where n is the size of one group. D = (20 − 8) ÷ 27 = 12 ÷ 27 = 0.444 ≈ 0.44. 0.52 is the difficulty index (20 + 8) ÷ 54 = 0.519; 0.12 divides 12 by 100 (the whole class), and 0.28 divides 28 by 100.

quiz.question: Which of the following are features of the Choice Based Credit System (CBCS) as recommended by UGC?
options: A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: CBCS uses semesters and credits (A), offers choice across course types (B), grades with SGPA and CGPA (C) and allows credits to be transferred (E). D is false: CBCS relies on continuous internal assessment together with end-semester examinations.

stmts: A. A semester system with courses measured in credits
B. Choice among core, elective and ability or skill enhancement courses
C. Letter grades with SGPA and CGPA
D. No internal or continuous assessment at all
E. Mobility of learners through the transfer of credits

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of the evaluation process in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: Objectives are first formulated (B) and then stated as observable behaviours (D). Tools are then chosen to match those behaviours (A), administered (E), and the results interpreted to make judgements and give feedback (C). Tools cannot be selected before the behaviours to be measured are defined.

stmts: A. Selecting or constructing evaluation tools
B. Formulating educational objectives
C. Interpreting results and making judgements
D. Defining objectives in terms of expected behaviour
E. Administering the tools and collecting evidence
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In computer adaptive testing (CAT),
options: every candidate answers the same items in the same order
the paper is printed and marked by OMR
the next item is selected on the basis of the candidate’s responses to earlier items
only essay-type items can be used
quiz.explanation: CAT tailors the test: a correct answer usually brings a harder item and a wrong answer an easier one, so ability is estimated with fewer items. A fixed common sequence describes a linear test; OMR is paper-based; CAT mostly uses objective items.

quiz.question: The reliability coefficient between the two halves (odd and even items) of a test is 0.60. Using the Spearman–Brown formula, what is the reliability of the whole test?
quiz.explanation: Spearman–Brown for doubling the length: r = 2r_h ÷ (1 + r_h) = (2 × 0.60) ÷ 1.60 = 1.20 ÷ 1.60 = 0.75. Leaving 0.60 as it is ignores that the whole test is twice as long; 0.36 squares it; 0.80 is not given by the formula.

domains.name: Research Aptitude
domains.blurb: Types and methods of research, steps, thesis writing, ICT in research and ethics.

lessons.title: Research: meaning, types and methods
lessons.summaryHtml: Research is a systematic, controlled, empirical and critical search for new knowledge or for answers to a defined problem. It has recognisable features: it is systematic, logical, empirical, replicable, objective and self-correcting. Research is classified by purpose (fundamental, applied, action, evaluation), by objective (exploratory, descriptive, diagnostic, explanatory), by approach (quantitative, qualitative, mixed), by time (cross-sectional, longitudinal) and by the control the researcher has (experimental, quasi-experimental, ex post facto). Behind every method is a paradigm: positivism (Comte) seeks general laws through objective measurement, post-positivism (Popper, Kuhn, critical realism) accepts that knowledge is fallible and probabilistic, and interpretivism seeks the meanings people give to their actions. NTA tests this unit through thinker–idea matches, “identify the type of research” scenarios, method features and Assertion–Reason pairs on paradigms.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Everyone asks questions, but research answers them in a disciplined way. A researcher defines a clear problem, collects evidence with a planned procedure, analyses it honestly and reaches a conclusion that someone else could check by repeating the work. Kerlinger’s well-known description calls scientific research systematic, controlled, empirical and critical. Older textbook definitions (quoted in Kothari) say the same in steps: define the problem, form hypotheses, collect and organise data, draw deductions and test the conclusions. The word itself suggests “search again”: research re-examines what we think we know.

Two further ideas make this unit easy. First, research is classified in several independent ways (by purpose, objective, approach, time and control), so one study can be “applied, descriptive, quantitative and cross-sectional” at the same time. Second, every method rests on a paradigm: a set of beliefs about what reality is (ontology), how we can know it (epistemology) and what role values play (axiology).

Why it matters for NET

Research Aptitude is one of the ten units of Paper 1, and this lesson is its foundation. Questions recur on the meaning and characteristics of research, identifying the type of a described study, positivism versus post-positivism versus interpretivism, thinker–idea matches (Comte, Popper, Kuhn, Weber, Lewin), the features of experimental, descriptive, historical, qualitative and quantitative methods, and Assertion–Reason pairs about causality and generalisation. These are low-calculation, high-accuracy marks: a clear table in your head settles most of them in under a minute.

Concepts in depth: characteristics and objectives

Good research is:

  • Systematic and logical: it follows planned steps, and its reasoning (inductive or deductive) can be checked.
  • Empirical: it rests on observation and evidence, not on authority, tradition or intuition.
  • Controlled: it tries to rule out rival explanations by holding other factors constant.
  • Replicable and verifiable: the procedure is reported so that others can repeat it.
  • Objective and critical: conclusions follow the evidence, and the method is open to criticism.
  • Self-correcting and cyclical: findings are revised when new evidence appears, and each answer raises new questions.
  • Generalisable (in quantitative research): results apply beyond the sample when sampling is sound.

Kothari lists four broad objectives, which give four kinds of study: to gain familiarity with a phenomenon (exploratory or formulative), to portray the characteristics of a group or situation accurately (descriptive), to find how often something occurs or what it is associated with (diagnostic), and to test a causal hypothesis (hypothesis-testing or experimental).

Research reasons in two directions. Deduction moves from a general theory to a specific, testable prediction (theory → hypothesis → observation). Induction moves from specific observations to a general pattern (observation → pattern → theory). Quantitative, hypothesis-testing research is mainly deductive; grounded theory and much qualitative work are mainly inductive. John Dewey’s account of reflective thinking gives five steps that textbooks call the scientific method: a felt difficulty, its location and definition, a suggested solution, reasoning out its implications, and testing by further observation or experiment.

Concepts in depth: types of research

BasisTypesClue words in a question
Purpose (use)Fundamental (basic, pure); applied; action; evaluationtheory, principles / practical problem / own practice, cycles / worth of a programme
ObjectiveExploratory; descriptive; diagnostic; explanatory (causal)little known, insight / what is / how often, associated with / why, cause
ApproachQuantitative; qualitative; mixed methodsnumbers, statistics / meanings, words / both, sequenced
TimeCross-sectional (one time); longitudinal (trend, cohort, panel)at one point / same group followed over years
ControlExperimental; quasi-experimental; ex post facto (causal-comparative)manipulated, random assignment / intact groups / already happened
SettingLaboratory; field; simulationcontrolled room / natural setting / model
Nature of dataConceptual (ideas, theory); empirical (experience, observation)philosophical analysis / data-based

Kothari also contrasts descriptive research, which describes the state of affairs as it exists, with analytical research, which uses facts already available and evaluates them critically. Action research was named by the social psychologist Kurt Lewin in the 1940s and brought into schools by Stephen Corey; it is local, collaborative and cyclical (plan, act, observe, reflect), and it aims at improvement, not generalisation. Evaluation research judges a programme: formative evaluation improves it while it runs, and summative evaluation judges its overall worth at the end.

Concepts in depth: paradigms

Positivism. Auguste Comte coined the terms “positivism” and “sociology”. His law of three stages says human thought passes from the theological to the metaphysical to the positive (scientific) stage. Positivism holds that only knowledge verified through observation is genuine. It seeks general, law-like (nomothetic) explanations; it favours hypotheses, measurement, experiments, large samples and statistics; and the researcher stays detached and value-free. In the 1920s and 1930s the Vienna Circle developed logical positivism, with its verification principle: a statement is meaningful only if it can be verified empirically (or is true by definition).

Post-positivism. Karl Popper argued that no number of confirming cases can prove a universal theory, but a single sound counter-case can refute it. So falsifiability, not verification, marks a theory as scientific. Thomas Kuhn (The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 1962) showed that science works within paradigms: periods of normal science end in revolutions or paradigm shifts. Critical realism (Roy Bhaskar) holds that reality exists independently of us, but our knowledge of it is fallible. Post-positivists therefore still measure and test, but they treat findings as probabilistic, admit that observation is theory-laden, and use triangulation (several methods, sources or investigators) to reduce bias. Objectivity becomes an ideal to approach, not a certainty.

Interpretivism and constructivism. Max Weber (and Dilthey before him) argued that social action must be understood from the actor’s point of view: Verstehen. Reality is seen as socially constructed; the aim is deep, idiographic understanding of particular cases. Related traditions are phenomenology (Husserl: lived experience), hermeneutics (interpretation of texts), symbolic interactionism and ethnomethodology. The critical paradigm (the Frankfurt School) adds the aim of exposing power and changing society, and pragmatism (Peirce, James, Dewey) judges methods by what works, which is why it underlies mixed methods.

QuestionPositivismPost-positivismInterpretivism
Reality (ontology)Objective, knowableObjective, known imperfectlySocially constructed, multiple
Knowledge (epistemology)Verified observation, certaintyProbabilistic, falsificationMeanings, understanding
ResearcherDetached, value-freeAims at objectivity, admits biasInvolved, reflexive
Typical methodsExperiments, surveys, statisticsSame, plus triangulation, multiple methodsEthnography, case study, in-depth interviews
LogicDeductive, nomotheticDeductive, hypothesis testingInductive, idiographic

Concepts in depth: methods

Experimental method. The researcher manipulates an independent variable, controls other variables, and ideally assigns participants to groups at random, then measures the effect on the dependent variable. Campbell and Stanley (1963) grouped designs into three families. Pre-experimental designs have no proper control: the one-shot case study, the one-group pretest–posttest design and the static-group comparison. True experimental designs use random assignment: the pretest–posttest control group design, the posttest-only control group design and the Solomon four-group design (four groups, two of them pretested, two of them treated, so the effect of the pretest itself can be separated). Quasi-experimental designs manipulate the treatment but use intact groups, such as the non-equivalent control group design and the time-series design.

Internal validity asks whether the treatment really caused the change. Campbell and Stanley listed threats such as history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression, selection, experimental mortality (drop-out) and selection–maturation interaction. External validity asks whether results generalise to other people, settings and times. Participant effects also matter: the Hawthorne effect (behaviour changes because people know they are being studied), the John Henry effect (the control group works harder to compete) and the Pygmalion effect (expectations shape performance).

Descriptive method. It describes “what is”: surveys (the normative survey), case studies, developmental studies (longitudinal or cross-sectional), correlational studies, and causal-comparative or ex post facto studies, in which the cause has already occurred (for example, comparing the achievement of students who did and did not attend pre-school). Correlation shows association, not causation.

Historical method. It reconstructs the past from primary sources (original documents, eyewitness accounts, relics) and secondary sources (accounts by people who were not present). Every source is tested by external criticism (is it genuine?) and internal criticism (is its content accurate and credible?).

Qualitative and quantitative approaches.

FeatureQuantitativeQualitative
AimMeasure, test hypotheses, generaliseUnderstand meanings and context
DataNumbersWords, images, observations
SampleLarge, usually probabilitySmall, purposive, until saturation
InstrumentTests, structured questionnairesThe researcher, in-depth interviews, participant observation
DesignFixed in advanceEmergent, flexible
ExamplesExperiment, survey, correlational studyEthnography, phenomenology, grounded theory, narrative, case study

Qualitative terms that NTA uses: emic (insider view) and etic (outsider, analytical view), thick description (Geertz: behaviour described with its context and meaning), grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss, 1967: theory built from data through constant comparison), saturation (stop sampling when new data add nothing new). Mixed methods (Creswell) combine both: convergent parallel (both at once), explanatory sequential (quantitative first, then qualitative to explain it) and exploratory sequential (qualitative first, then a quantitative phase).

Worked examples

Example 1: classify the study. A lecturer notices that her students skip the weekly quiz. She changes the quiz timing, observes attendance for four weeks, reflects with colleagues and plans a second change.

  1. Who does the research? The practitioner herself, on her own practice.
  2. Aim? To improve that practice, not to build a general theory.
  3. Pattern? Plan, act, observe, reflect, then plan again.

Answer: action research. It is not applied research in the usual sense, because an outside researcher solving a practical problem for others does not work in cycles on her own practice.

Example 2: experiment or not? Three studies on computer-assisted learning (CAL):

  1. Students are randomly split; one group gets CAL for a term, and both are tested. This is a true experiment (manipulation plus random assignment).
  2. Two existing sections are used; section A gets CAL and section B does not. This is quasi-experimental (manipulation, but intact groups).
  3. Last year’s marks of students who chose CAL are compared with those who did not. This is ex post facto: the “treatment” happened before the study and students selected themselves, so motivation could explain the difference.

Example 3: identify the paradigm. Statement: “We tested the hypothesis at the 5% level. The result supports it, but it remains provisional and could be overturned by better evidence; we triangulated with interviews to reduce bias.”

The hypothesis test shows a scientific, measuring approach, so it is not interpretivism. But the claim is treated as provisional and bias is reduced by triangulation, which classic positivism’s certainty does not allow. Answer: post-positivism.

Example 4: Solomon four-group design. Groups: G1 pretest–treatment–posttest; G2 pretest–posttest; G3 treatment–posttest; G4 posttest only (all randomly assigned).

  1. Groups pretested: G1 and G2, so 2.
  2. Groups treated: G1 and G3, so 2.
  3. Groups post-tested: all 4.
  4. Why? Comparing G1 with G3 shows whether taking the pretest changed the treatment’s effect (the “testing” threat to validity).

Example 5: an Assertion–Reason on causality. A: A strong positive correlation between hours of television and aggression proves that television causes aggression. R: Correlation measures the strength of association between two variables.

R is true. A is false: association does not show direction (aggressive children may choose violent programmes) or rule out a third variable (home environment). Answer: (A) is false but (R) is true.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact to remember

ComtePositivism, sociology; law of three stages: theological → metaphysical → positive
Vienna CircleLogical positivism; verification principle
PopperFalsifiability; The Logic of Scientific Discovery (German 1934, English 1959)
KuhnParadigm, normal science, scientific revolution (1962)
WeberVerstehen; interpretive sociology
Kurt LewinCoined “action research” (1940s); Stephen Corey took it into schools
Glaser and StraussGrounded theory (1967)
Campbell and StanleyPre-experimental, true experimental, quasi-experimental designs; threats to internal validity (1963)
Solomon four-group4 groups, 2 pretested, 2 treated; separates the pretest effect
Historical criticismExternal = authenticity of the source; internal = credibility of its content
Nomothetic / idiographicGeneral laws / the particular case
Emic / eticInsider view / outsider view
Mixed methods (Creswell)Convergent parallel; explanatory sequential (QUAN → qual); exploratory sequential (QUAL → quan)

NTA traps

  • Applied vs action research. Wrong: “any study that solves a practical problem is action research.” Fix: action research is done by the practitioner on her own practice, in cycles; applied research solves a practical problem, often for others, with wider relevance.
  • External vs internal criticism. Wrong: “external criticism checks whether the facts are true.” Fix: external criticism checks whether the document is genuine; internal criticism checks the truth of what it says.
  • Ex post facto as experimental. Wrong: “comparing smokers and non-smokers is an experiment.” Fix: nobody assigned smoking, so it is ex post facto (causal-comparative).
  • Positivism vs post-positivism. Wrong: “post-positivism rejects measurement.” Fix: post-positivism keeps measurement and hypothesis testing but treats knowledge as fallible.
  • Verification vs falsification. Wrong: “Popper held that a theory is scientific if it can be verified.” Fix: verification belongs to logical positivism; Popper’s criterion is falsifiability.
  • Quasi-experiment. Wrong: “no manipulation.” Fix: there is manipulation; what is missing is random assignment.
  • Correlation as cause. A correlation, however strong, does not by itself establish cause and effect.
  • Qualitative means non-rigorous. Wrong. Qualitative research has its own rigour: purposive sampling, saturation, thick description, triangulation and member checking.

How NTA asks this

  • Scenario MCQ: a study is described and you name its type or method. Look for the clue words in the types table.
  • Match the following: thinkers with ideas; methods with features; types of research with examples; designs with families.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: causality in ex post facto studies, aims of action research, claims of positivism and post-positivism, generalisation in case studies.
  • Multiple select: characteristics of research, features of a paradigm, threats to internal validity, qualitative approaches.
  • Sequence: steps of historical research, Dewey’s steps of reflective thinking, the order of the mixed-methods phases, or the chronology of major works.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. Fundamental research, B. Applied research, C. Action research, D. Evaluation research. List II: I. A teacher improving homework completion in her own class, II. Judging whether a scholarship scheme raised enrolment, III. A theory of how children acquire grammar, IV. Designing a remedial reading programme for a district. Answer: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II. Fix the easiest pair first (the teacher in her own class is action research), then strike every option that disagrees.

Elimination trick: in paradigm questions, the words “verify”, “law” and “value-free” point to positivism; “falsify”, “probabilistic” and “triangulate” point to post-positivism; “meaning”, “Verstehen” and “socially constructed” point to interpretivism.
Watch out: one study can belong to several types at once (for example applied, quantitative and cross-sectional). If an option pair seems to conflict, check whether the two labels come from different bases of classification.

terms.definition: A systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation that seeks new knowledge or the answer to a defined problem, using a planned procedure that others can repeat.
Research aimed at building or extending theory and general principles, without an immediate practical application in view.
Research aimed at solving a practical, immediate problem of society, industry or an institution; it uses the principles that fundamental research discovers.

Research carried out by practitioners (for example a teacher) on their own practice, in cycles of plan–act–observe–reflect, to improve that practice. The term was introduced by Kurt Lewin in the 1940s.
“After the fact” research: the independent variable has already occurred, so the researcher studies it without manipulating it and cannot establish cause and effect firmly.
The paradigm, named by Auguste Comte, that treats only observable, verifiable facts as genuine knowledge and seeks general laws through objective, quantitative, value-free inquiry.

The paradigm that accepts an objective reality but holds that it can be known only imperfectly and probabilistically; theories are tested by attempts at falsification (Popper) and results are cross-checked by triangulation.
The paradigm that seeks to understand social action through the meanings people attach to it (Weber’s Verstehen); it favours qualitative, context-rich methods.
In historical research, external criticism tests whether a source is genuine (authenticity); internal criticism tests whether its content is accurate and credible.
A longitudinal study follows the same units over time; a cross-sectional study collects data from different units at one point in time.

lessons.examTip: In “identify the type of research” questions, ask three quick questions in order: Is the goal theory or a practical fix (fundamental vs applied)? Does the researcher manipulate the cause (experimental) or study a cause that has already happened (ex post facto)? Is the practitioner studying her own practice to improve it (action research)?

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 9 minutes. For each scenario, write the one clue word that decided the type of research.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (applied vs action, external vs internal criticism, verification vs falsification, quasi vs ex post facto).
Rebuild from memory the thinker–idea table (Comte, Vienna Circle, Popper, Kuhn, Weber, Lewin, Glaser and Strauss, Bhaskar) and the three Campbell–Stanley design families.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours, without looking at the solutions.
Finish with the lesson quiz and the bank questions at about 60 seconds each.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 15 problems done within 19 minutes.
Every thinker–idea pair in the fact sheet recalled without notes.
Any “identify the type of research” scenario classified in under 45 seconds.

quiz.question: Research that is conducted mainly to extend the frontiers of knowledge and to build theory, without an immediate practical use in view, is called:
quiz.explanation: Fundamental (basic or pure) research aims at theory and general principles. Applied research uses those principles to solve an immediate practical problem, action research is done by practitioners to improve their own practice, and evaluation research judges the worth of a programme or policy. The clue is “without an immediate practical use”.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Comte named positivism and proposed the law of three stages (III). Popper made falsifiability the line between science and non-science (IV). Kuhn described normal science interrupted by revolutions or paradigm shifts (I). Weber argued for Verstehen, understanding action through its meaning to the actor (II). Each distractor swaps one pair: Comte with Popper, Kuhn with Weber, or Popper with Kuhn.

a: A. The term “positivism” and the law of three stages
B. Falsifiability as the criterion of science
C. Normal science and paradigm shifts
b: I. Thomas Kuhn
II. Max Weber
III. Auguste Comte
IV. Karl Popper

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true. Causal claims need control over the cause and randomisation to rule out other explanations. Because the cause has already happened, the researcher has neither, so rival explanations (self-selection, third variables) remain open. R is exactly why A is true, so option 1.

quiz.explanation: Statement I is the core of post-positivism (critical realism): reality is real, but our knowledge of it is fallible, so claims are probabilistic. Statement II is false: post-positivists still use quantitative methods, hypotheses and statistics; they simply treat results as provisional and add triangulation and falsification. Rejecting quantification is closer to a strong interpretivist position.

options: A, B, D and E only
A, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: Research is empirical (A), replicable (B), systematic (D) and self-correcting (E). Authority (C) is exactly the non-scientific source of knowledge that research replaces: a conclusion is accepted because of evidence and method, not because of who states it. Option 1 misses self-correction, and options 3 and 4 include C.

quiz.question: In historical research, checking whether a letter is genuine, for example whether its paper, ink, handwriting and signature fit the date it claims, is called:
quiz.explanation: External criticism asks whether the source itself is authentic (who wrote it, when, is it a forgery). Internal criticism then asks whether what the genuine document says is accurate and credible. Content analysis is a systematic coding of message content, and triangulation is cross-checking with several sources or methods.

quiz.question: A researcher collects data on the reading habits of the same group of 200 first-generation learners every year from Class 6 to Class 12. This design is best described as:

A cross-sectional design would compare different students in Classes 6 to 12 at one time. lessons.title: Steps of research, sampling and tools
lessons.summaryHtml: Every research project follows a recognisable sequence: formulate the problem, review the literature, develop hypotheses, prepare the research design and the sample design, collect data, analyse it, test the hypotheses, interpret and generalise, and write the report. A hypothesis is a testable, tentative statement about the relation between variables; the null hypothesis is the one a statistical test tries to reject, with a known risk of Type I and Type II errors. Variables are independent, dependent, extraneous, intervening or moderating, and they are measured on nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio scales. Samples are drawn by probability methods (simple random, systematic, stratified, cluster, multi-stage) or non-probability methods (convenience, purposive, quota, snowball), and data are collected with questionnaires, schedules, interviews, observation, rating and attitude scales and projective techniques. Reliability asks whether a tool measures consistently; validity asks whether it measures what it should. NTA asks the order of steps, sampling scenarios, scale–originator matches, reliability and validity types, and short numericals such as the sampling interval or the Spearman–Brown correction.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Research is a journey with fixed stations. You choose a problem, read what is already known, guess an answer (the hypothesis), plan how to test it (the research design), decide whom to study (the sample), collect and analyse data, and write up what you found. The quality of the answer depends on three choices made along the way: whom you study (sampling), how you collect data (tools), and whether those tools measure consistently (reliability) and correctly (validity).

Why it matters for NET

This is the most procedural part of Research Aptitude, and NTA likes it because it is easy to test in sequence and matching formats. Expect questions on the order of the research steps, features of a good hypothesis, Type I and Type II errors, kinds of variables and levels of measurement, identifying a sampling method from a scenario, questionnaire versus schedule, attitude scales and their originators, and the types of reliability and validity. Short numericals (sampling interval, proportional allocation, Spearman–Brown) appear occasionally and are quick marks if you know the formula.

Concepts in depth: the steps of research

Kothari presents the research process as eleven steps. Learn them in order, because sequence questions pick five of them and shuffle them.

  1. Formulating the research problem.
  2. Extensive literature survey.
  3. Developing the working hypotheses.
  4. Preparing the research design.
  5. Determining the sample design.
  6. Collecting the data.
  7. Execution of the project.
  8. Analysis of data.
  9. Hypothesis testing.
  10. Generalisations and interpretation.
  11. Preparation of the report or thesis.

In practice the steps overlap and feed back: the literature survey often reshapes the problem, and a pilot study may change the tools. A good research problem is significant, novel, researchable with available data, time and money, within the researcher’s competence and interest, and ethically acceptable. The research design is the blueprint: it states what data are needed, from whom, how, and how they will be analysed. R. A. Fisher’s three principles of experimental design are replication, randomisation and local control.

Concepts in depth: hypotheses

Kerlinger calls a hypothesis a conjectural statement of the relation between two or more variables. A good hypothesis is testable (it can be supported or refuted by data), clear and specific, states a relationship between variables, is consistent with known facts and theory, is as simple as possible (parsimony), and is limited in scope. Hypotheses come from theory, earlier studies, observation, analogy and intuition. Exploratory studies often have no hypothesis; they generate hypotheses for later research.

TypeMeaningExample
Null (H₀)No difference or no relationshipMean scores of the online and offline groups do not differ.
Alternative (H₁)A difference or relationship existsMean scores of the two groups differ.
DirectionalStates which way the difference goes; one-tailed testThe online group scores higher.
Non-directionalStates a difference without direction; two-tailed testThe two groups score differently.
Research (working)The researcher’s expectation, in wordsPeer tutoring improves reading fluency.
StatisticalStated about population parametersH₀: μ₁ = μ₂

A test never “proves” a hypothesis. It asks how likely the data would be if H₀ were true. If that probability (the p-value) is below the level of significance α (commonly 0.05 or 0.01), H₀ is rejected. Two errors are possible:

DecisionH₀ actually trueH₀ actually false
Reject H₀Type I error (probability α)Correct decision (power = 1 − β)
Do not reject H₀Correct decision (1 − α)Type II error (probability β)

Lowering α (say from 0.05 to 0.01) reduces Type I errors but, for the same sample size, increases Type II errors. Increasing the sample size reduces both.

Concepts in depth: variables and measurement

The independent variable is the presumed cause; the dependent variable is the measured effect. An extraneous variable is any other variable that could affect the dependent variable; when it varies together with the independent variable it becomes a confounding variable, and when it is held constant it is a control variable. An intervening (mediating) variable is an unobserved process between cause and effect. A moderator changes the strength or direction of the relationship. Attribute (organismic) variables such as age or gender cannot be manipulated, only selected.

S. S. Stevens (1946) gave four levels of measurement. Each level has all the properties of the ones above it.

LevelPropertyExampleTypical statistics
NominalCategories onlyGender, religion, jersey numberMode, frequency, chi-square
OrdinalOrder, unequal gapsClass rank, grades, Likert itemMedian, percentiles, rank correlation
IntervalEqual gaps, arbitrary zeroTemperature in °C, calendar yearMean, SD, Pearson r
RatioEqual gaps, true zeroIncome, age, weight, marks out of 100All, including ratios and CV

Concepts in depth: sampling

The population (universe) is the whole group of interest; the sampling frame is the list from which units are drawn; the sample is the part actually studied. A value describing the population is a parameter; the corresponding value from the sample is a statistic. Sampling error is the chance difference between them and shrinks as the sample grows (the standard error of the mean is σ ÷ √n, so halving it needs four times the sample). Non-sampling errors (a faulty frame, non-response, biased questions, recording mistakes) do not shrink with sample size.

MethodHow units are chosenKind
Simple randomEvery unit equally likely (lottery, random numbers)Probability
SystematicRandom start, then every kth unit; k = N ÷ nProbability
StratifiedHomogeneous strata; random sample from each (proportionate or disproportionate)Probability
ClusterWhole natural groups (schools, villages) chosen at randomProbability
Multi-stageClusters chosen in stages (districts → blocks → villages → households)Probability
Convenience (accidental)Whoever is easy to reachNon-probability
Purposive (judgement)Chosen deliberately for relevance or expertiseNon-probability
QuotaFixed numbers per category, filled by the interviewer’s choiceNon-probability
Snowball (chain referral)Each respondent refers others; for hidden populationsNon-probability

Strata should be homogeneous within and different from each other; clusters should ideally be heterogeneous within, each a mini-population. Stratified sampling improves precision; cluster sampling saves cost and travel. The required sample size grows with the variability of the population, the confidence wanted and the precision wanted. For a proportion, Cochran’s formula is n₀ = z²p(1 − p) ÷ e², and for a finite population n = n₀ ÷ (1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N).

Concepts in depth: tools of data collection

Primary data are collected afresh by the researcher; secondary data already exist (census reports, published statistics, records). The main tools are:

  • Questionnaire (filled in by the respondent; cheap, wide reach, low response when mailed) and schedule (filled in by the enumerator; works with non-literate respondents). Questions may be closed (fixed options) or open.
  • Interview: structured (fixed wording and order), semi-structured, unstructured (in-depth), focused interview (Merton), clinical and telephone interviews; the focus group is a moderated group discussion.
  • Observation: participant or non-participant, structured or unstructured, controlled or uncontrolled.
  • Rating scales and checklists, and inventories of interests or personality.
  • Attitude scales: Bogardus social distance scale (1925); Thurstone’s method of equal-appearing intervals (1928); Likert’s summated rating scale (1932); Guttman’s cumulative scale or scalogram (1944); Osgood’s semantic differential with bipolar adjectives (1957).
  • Sociometry (J. L. Moreno): mapping choices within a group as a sociogram.
  • Projective techniques: Rorschach inkblot test, Thematic Apperception Test (TAT), word association and sentence completion.
  • Delphi technique: anonymous rounds of expert opinion with controlled feedback, moving towards consensus.

Concepts in depth: reliability and validity

Reliability typeWhat it showsHow
Test–retestStability over timeSame test, same group, two occasions; correlate
Parallel (alternate) formsEquivalenceTwo equivalent forms; correlate
Split-halfInternal consistencyCorrelate odd and even halves; correct with Spearman–Brown 2r ÷ (1 + r)
Kuder–Richardson (KR-20, KR-21)Internal consistency, right/wrong itemsFrom item difficulties
Cronbach’s alpha (1951)Internal consistency, any item typeα = k ÷ (k − 1) × (1 − Σ item variances ÷ total variance)
Inter-raterAgreement between observersPercentage agreement, Cohen’s kappa κ = (pₒ − pₑ) ÷ (1 − pₑ)
Validity typeQuestion it answers
Face validityDoes the test look as if it measures the trait? (Not a technical proof.)
Content validityDo the items represent the whole domain or syllabus? Judged by experts and a blueprint.
Concurrent validityDo scores agree with a criterion measured at the same time?
Predictive validityDo scores predict a later criterion, such as later performance?
Construct validityDoes the test behave as the theory of the trait predicts? Convergent and discriminant evidence (Campbell and Fiske’s multitrait–multimethod matrix).

Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity. A validity coefficient cannot exceed the square root of the reliability coefficient (the index of reliability). For a study as a whole, internal validity means the design supports the causal claim, and external validity means the results generalise. Qualitative researchers use parallel ideas: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability (Lincoln and Guba’s trustworthiness criteria).

Worked examples

Example 1: proportional stratified allocation. A college has 600 arts, 300 science and 100 commerce students (N = 1,000). A sample of 80 is drawn in proportion to stratum size.

  1. Sampling fraction f = 80 ÷ 1,000 = 0.08.
  2. Arts: 600 × 0.08 = 48. Science: 300 × 0.08 = 24. Commerce: 100 × 0.08 = 8.
  3. Check: 48 + 24 + 8 = 80.

Example 2: Cronbach’s alpha. A 4-item scale has item variances whose sum is 6, and the variance of the total score is 16.

  1. α = k ÷ (k − 1) × (1 − Σσᵢ² ÷ σₜ²) = 4 ÷ 3 × (1 − 6 ÷ 16).
  2. 1 − 0.375 = 0.625; 4 ÷ 3 × 0.625 = 0.833.
  3. α ≈ 0.83, usually read as good internal consistency.

Example 3: sample size for a proportion. 95% confidence (z = 1.96), margin of error ±5% (e = 0.05), unknown proportion so p = 0.5.

  1. n₀ = 1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05² = 3.8416 × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 384.16, so 385 after rounding up.
  2. If the population is only N = 2,000: n = 384.16 ÷ (1 + 383.16 ÷ 2,000) = 384.16 ÷ 1.1916 ≈ 322.4, so 323.

Example 4: Cohen’s kappa. Two observers classify 100 classroom episodes as “on task” or “off task”. Both say on task in 40, both say off task in 30; A says on and B says off in 20; A says off and B says on in 10.

  1. Observed agreement pₒ = (40 + 30) ÷ 100 = 0.70.
  2. A says “on” 60 times, B says “on” 50 times. Chance agreement pₑ = 0.6 × 0.5 + 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.50.
  3. κ = (0.70 − 0.50) ÷ (1 − 0.50) = 0.40: only moderate agreement once chance is removed, although raw agreement looked like 70%.

Example 5: name the variables. “The effect of activity-based teaching on the science achievement of Class 8 pupils, and whether the effect differs for rural and urban pupils.” Independent variable: teaching method. Dependent variable: science achievement. Moderator: locality (rural or urban). Intervening variable: the pupils’ understanding (learning) that the method produces. Possible extraneous variable: prior achievement, to be controlled.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFormula or fact
Systematic intervalk = N ÷ n; units r, r + k, r + 2k, …
Proportional allocationnₕ = n × Nₕ ÷ N
Standard error of the meanσ ÷ √n (4 × sample to halve it)
Cochran (proportion)n₀ = z²p(1 − p) ÷ e²; 95%, ±5%, p = 0.5 gives 384.16 → 385
Finite population correctionn = n₀ ÷ (1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N)
Spearman–BrownDoubling: 2r ÷ (1 + r); k times: kr ÷ (1 + (k − 1)r)
Cronbach’s alphak ÷ (k − 1) × (1 − Σσᵢ² ÷ σₜ²)
Cohen’s kappa(pₒ − pₑ) ÷ (1 − pₑ)
ErrorsType I = reject true H₀ (α); Type II = retain false H₀ (β); power = 1 − β
Fisher’s principlesReplication, randomisation, local control
Scales and originatorsBogardus 1925, Thurstone 1928, Likert 1932, Guttman 1944, Osgood 1957
Levels (Stevens 1946)Nominal, ordinal, interval, ratio

NTA traps

  • Quota as probability sampling. Wrong: “quota is stratified sampling.” Fix: quotas are filled by the interviewer’s choice, so selection probabilities are unknown: non-probability.
  • Strata vs clusters. Wrong: “both should be homogeneous.” Fix: strata are homogeneous within; clusters should be heterogeneous within.
  • Type I vs Type II. Wrong: “Type I is accepting a false H₀.” Fix: Type I rejects a true H₀; think “I = innocent convicted”.
  • Power. Wrong: power = 1 − α. Fix: power = 1 − β.
  • “Proving” a hypothesis. Wrong: “the hypothesis was proved.” Fix: data support or fail to support; H₀ is rejected or not rejected.
  • Reliability and validity. Wrong: “a reliable test is valid.” Fix: reliable does not imply valid; valid implies reliable.
  • Questionnaire vs schedule. The respondent fills a questionnaire; the enumerator fills a schedule.
  • Split-half without correction. The half-test correlation understates the full test’s reliability; apply Spearman–Brown.
  • Larger samples remove all error. They reduce sampling error only; non-sampling error may even rise with a larger, less carefully supervised survey.

How NTA asks this

  • Sequence: five of the eleven research steps, the steps of hypothesis testing, or the chronology of attitude scales.
  • Match the following: sampling methods with descriptions, scales with originators, reliability or validity types with procedures, variables with descriptions, levels of measurement with examples.
  • Scenario MCQ: identify the sampling method, the tool or the variable type from a short description.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: Type I/II errors and power, reliability versus validity, stratified versus cluster sampling, questionnaire versus schedule.
  • Numerical: sampling interval, proportional allocation, Spearman–Brown, occasionally alpha or sample size.

Mini-example (A-R). A: Stratified random sampling usually gives more precise estimates than a simple random sample of the same size. R: In stratified sampling the population is divided into strata that are internally homogeneous. Both are true, and R explains A: with homogeneous strata the variation inside each stratum is small, so the combined estimate varies less. Answer: option 1.

Elimination trick: in a multi-select on sampling, first strike every option that includes quota, snowball, convenience or purposive when the question asks for probability methods. Usually only one option survives.
Watch out: “random” in everyday language is not random sampling. Stopping “random people” in a market is convenience sampling, because nobody’s chance of selection is known.

terms.definition: A tentative, testable statement about the relation between two or more variables, formulated before data are collected and then tested against evidence.
The hypothesis of no difference or no relationship; a statistical test calculates how likely the data are if H₀ is true and rejects H₀ when that probability is below the level of significance.

terms.term: Type I and Type II errors
terms.definition: A Type I error rejects a true H₀ (probability α, the level of significance); a Type II error fails to reject a false H₀ (probability β). The power of a test is 1 − β.
An unobserved process that links the independent and dependent variables, such as “learning” between teaching method and test score; it is inferred, not measured directly.
A variable that changes the strength or direction of the relation between the independent and dependent variables, such as gender changing the effect of a teaching method.
The actual list (register, directory, map) from which the sample is drawn; a poor frame causes errors that a larger sample cannot remove.
Dividing the population into internally homogeneous strata and drawing a random sample from each, often in proportion to stratum size.
A form of questions that an enumerator or interviewer fills in while asking the respondent; unlike a questionnaire, it can be used with respondents who cannot read.
The consistency of a measuring tool: stability over time (test–retest), equivalence of forms (parallel forms), internal consistency (split-half, KR-20, Cronbach’s alpha) and agreement between raters.
The extent to which a tool measures what it claims to measure: content validity, criterion-related validity (concurrent, predictive) and construct validity.

lessons.examTip: Sampling questions hinge on one word. “Every kth” is systematic; “homogeneous subgroups, sample from each” is stratified; “select whole groups” is cluster; “fixed numbers per category, not random” is quota; “respondents refer others” is snowball. And remember: a reliable test need not be valid, but a valid test must be reliable.

quiz.question: Arrange the following steps of the research process in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: The problem is formulated first (B) and sharpened by an extensive literature survey (D); only then can a research design be prepared (A), data collected (C) and analysed (E). Option 3 starts with the literature survey, which is done after at least a broad problem area is chosen, and option 4 collects data before designing the study.

stmts: A. Preparing the research design
B. Formulating the research problem

quiz.question: A researcher needs a systematic sample of 60 students from a list of 1,200. The random start chosen from the first interval is 7. Which roll number is the fifth student selected?
quiz.explanation: Sampling interval k = N ÷ n = 1,200 ÷ 60 = 20. The selected numbers are 7, 27, 47, 67, 87, …, so the fifth is 7 + 4 × 20 = 87. 67 is the fourth, 107 the sixth, and 80 comes from 4 × 20 without the random start.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: The independent variable is the presumed cause (III) and the dependent variable the measured outcome (I). An intervening variable is the unobserved link, such as learning (IV). A moderator, such as gender or age, changes how strongly or in which direction the cause acts (II). The distractors swap the independent and dependent variables, or the intervening and moderator variables.

b: I. The outcome that is measured to see the effect
II. Changes the strength or direction of the relation between cause and effect
III. The presumed cause, manipulated or selected by the researcher
IV. An unobserved process that links the cause to the effect

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: A is the standard definition of H₀. R is false: a hypothesis is formulated before data collection and guides it. Stating a hypothesis after seeing the results and presenting it as if it had been planned is a questionable practice called HARKing (hypothesising after the results are known).

stmts: Assertion (A): A null hypothesis states that there is no difference or no relationship between the variables.
Reason (R): Hypotheses are normally formulated after the data have been collected and analysed.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is correct: rejecting a true H₀ is a Type I error, whose probability is α. Statement II is false: power is 1 − β, the probability of rejecting H₀ when it is actually false. 1 − α is the probability of correctly retaining a true H₀ (the confidence level).

stmts: Statement I: A Type I error occurs when a true null hypothesis is rejected.
Statement II: The power of a statistical test is equal to 1 − α.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: The correlation between the two halves of a test is 0.60. Using the Spearman–Brown formula, the estimated reliability of the full test is:
quiz.explanation: Split-half correlation gives the reliability of a half-length test. Spearman–Brown for doubling: r = 2r½ ÷ (1 + r½) = 2 × 0.60 ÷ 1.60 = 0.75. 0.60 forgets the correction, and 1.20 (simply doubling) is impossible because a reliability coefficient cannot exceed 1.

quiz.question: Which of the following are probability sampling methods?
options: A, B, C and E only
quiz.explanation: In systematic (A), cluster (C) and stratified random (E) sampling, every unit has a known, non-zero chance of selection. Quota sampling (B) resembles stratified sampling but the interviewer chooses who fills each quota, and snowball sampling (D) grows through referrals; both are non-probability methods.

stmts: A. Systematic sampling
B. Quota sampling
C. Cluster sampling
D. Snowball sampling
E. Stratified random sampling
