quiz.question: A set of questions that an enumerator carries to each respondent and fills in personally while asking the questions face to face is called a:
quiz.explanation: A schedule is filled in by the enumerator; a questionnaire is filled in by the respondent (often sent by post or online). Because the enumerator reads the questions, a schedule works with respondents who cannot read, and it has a higher response rate, but it costs more and can suffer from interviewer bias.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Because reliability is only about consistency, a tool can give the same wrong answer every time: a bathroom scale that always reads 2 kg heavy is reliable but not valid. The converse fails: a valid test must be reliable.

stmts: Assertion (A): A test can be highly reliable and yet not valid.
Reason (R): Reliability concerns the consistency of measurement, whereas validity concerns whether the test measures what it is intended to measure.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Temperature measured in degrees Celsius is an example of which level of measurement?
quiz.explanation: Celsius has equal intervals (the difference between 10° and 20° equals that between 30° and 40°) but its zero is arbitrary, not an absence of heat, so 20 °C is not “twice as hot” as 10 °C. That is the interval scale. Kelvin, with a true zero, would be ratio.

lessons.title: Thesis writing, ICT in research and ethics
lessons.summaryHtml: A thesis moves from preliminary pages (title page, declaration, certificate, acknowledgements, contents, abstract) through the main chapters (introduction, review of literature, methodology, results, discussion, conclusions) to the reference matter (references or bibliography, appendices). A journal article follows the IMRaD pattern: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion. Sources are acknowledged in a referencing style: APA 7 (author–date, social sciences and education), MLA 9 (author–page, language and literature) or Chicago 17 (notes–bibliography for history and the humanities, or author–date). ICT supports every stage: databases and INFLIBNET services (Shodhganga, Shodhgangotri, ShodhShuddhi), reference managers, statistical and qualitative software, persistent identifiers (DOI, ORCID) and research metrics (impact factor, h-index, i10-index). Research ethics forbids fabrication, falsification and plagiarism, requires honest authorship and informed consent, and in India is backed by the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, with similarity levels 0 to 3 and graded penalties. NTA asks style-feature matches, similarity-level penalties, misconduct definitions, h-index numericals and the structure of a thesis.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Research is not finished until it is written up and shared honestly. A thesis reports a whole research programme; an article reports one study to a journal. Both must show where every borrowed idea came from, using a referencing style: a fixed set of rules for citing sources in the text and listing them at the end. Today every stage uses ICT, from searching databases to checking similarity. And every stage is governed by research ethics: do not invent or twist data, do not take credit for others’ work, list authors honestly, and protect the people you study.

Why it matters for NET

This lesson closes the Research Aptitude unit, and its questions are among the most predictable in Paper 1. Expect matches of referencing styles with features or disciplines, the correct format of a citation, Latin abbreviations (ibid., op. cit., loc. cit.), the order of thesis chapters, INFLIBNET services, identifiers and metrics (DOI, ORCID, impact factor, h-index), definitions of fabrication, falsification and plagiarism, authorship rules and the UGC 2018 plagiarism regulations with their levels and penalties. Several of these are pure recall, so a clean fact sheet converts directly into marks.

Concepts in depth: thesis and article writing

PartContents
Preliminary pagesTitle page, declaration by the scholar, certificate by the supervisor, acknowledgements, table of contents, lists of tables, figures and abbreviations, abstract
Main body1. Introduction (problem, objectives, hypotheses, significance, scope); 2. Review of literature; 3. Research methodology (design, sample, tools, procedure, analysis); 4. Results and analysis; 5. Discussion; 6. Summary, conclusions, recommendations and suggestions for further research
Reference matterReferences or bibliography, appendices (questionnaires, raw tables), index (if any)

In India, “thesis” usually means the PhD report and “dissertation” the Master’s or MPhil report (the usage is reversed in the USA). A journal article follows IMRaD: Introduction (why), Methods (how), Results (what was found), and Discussion (what it means). It opens with a title, an abstract (a short summary, commonly 150–250 words, sometimes structured under headings) and keywords, and ends with references. Methods and results are usually written in the past tense, and established knowledge in the present tense. Article types include original research articles, review articles, short communications, case reports and letters. Before publication, peer review may be single-blind (reviewers know the authors), double-blind (neither knows the other) or open.

Latin abbreviations used with footnotes: ibid. (ibidem, “in the same place”: the same source as the immediately preceding note); op. cit. (opere citato, “in the work cited”: a work cited earlier, usually a different page); loc. cit. (loco citato, “in the place cited”: the same page of a work cited earlier); et al. (and others); cf. (compare); viz. (namely); sic (thus, an error in the original); passim (here and there throughout). Chicago 17 discourages ibid. in favour of shortened notes, and APA and MLA do not use these abbreviations at all.

Concepts in depth: referencing styles

FeatureAPA 7 (2019)MLA 9 (2021)Chicago 17 (2017)
Main fieldsPsychology, education, social sciencesLanguage, literature, humanitiesHistory, humanities (notes); sciences (author–date)
In-text(Sharma & Iyer, 2021, p. 45)(Sharma and Iyer 45)Superscript note number; or (Sharma and Iyer 2021, 45)
Three or more authors in textFirst author et al. from the first citationFirst author et al.All names up to three; et al. for four or more (notes and author–date)
End listReferencesWorks CitedBibliography (notes) or References (author–date)
Date positionAfter the authors, in parenthesesNear the end, among the publication detailsEnd of the entry (notes); after the authors (author–date)
Title capitalisationSentence case for books and articlesTitle caseTitle case
Place of publicationOmittedOmittedIncluded for books (made optional in the 18th edition)
Authors in the end listUp to 20; beyond that, 19, an ellipsis, then the lastTwo in full; three or more as first author, et al.Up to ten; more than ten, first seven then et al.

One book (two authors, second edition) in each style:

  • APA 7: Sharma, R. K., & Iyer, M. (2021). Research methods in education: A practical guide (2nd ed.). Orient Press.
  • MLA 9: Sharma, Ravi K., and Meera Iyer. Research Methods in Education: A Practical Guide. 2nd ed., Orient Press, 2021.
  • Chicago 17 bibliography: Sharma, Ravi K., and Meera Iyer. Research Methods in Education: A Practical Guide. 2nd ed. New Delhi: Orient Press, 2021.
  • Chicago 17 first note: 1. Ravi K. Sharma and Meera Iyer, Research Methods in Education: A Practical Guide, 2nd ed. (New Delhi: Orient Press, 2021), 45. A later note is shortened: 2. Sharma and Iyer, Research Methods, 52.

One journal article (three authors):

  • APA 7: Nair, A., Das, P., & Khan, S. (2022). Digital divide and online learning in rural Kerala. Journal of Indian Education, 48(2), 115–130. https://doi.org/10.xxxx/jie.2022.0482
  • MLA 9: Nair, Anil, et al. “Digital Divide and Online Learning in Rural Kerala.” Journal of Indian Education, vol. 48, no. 2, 2022, pp. 115–30.
  • Chicago 17 bibliography: Nair, Anil, Priya Das, and Salim Khan. “Digital Divide and Online Learning in Rural Kerala.” Journal of Indian Education 48, no. 2 (2022): 115–30. https://doi.org/10.xxxx/jie.2022.0482.

(The sources and DOI are invented for illustration.) Notice the markers: APA puts the year in parentheses right after the authors, uses “&”, italicises the journal and volume, and gives the DOI as a URL. MLA reverses only the first author’s name, puts the article title in quotation marks and labels “vol.”, “no.” and “pp.”. MLA 9 organises every entry by core elements: author, title of source, title of container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, publication date, location. Other styles: Harvard (a generic author–date style), Vancouver (numbered, medicine) and IEEE (numbers in square brackets, engineering and computing).

Edition check: the Chicago Manual of Style 18th edition was published in 2024 (for example, it lists up to six authors in the bibliography and makes the place of publication optional). Unless a question names the 18th edition, answer by the 17th edition rules above.

Concepts in depth: ICT in research

StageTools and services
Searching literatureScopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, PubMed, ERIC, JSTOR; INFLIBNET’s e-ShodhSindhu consortium; One Nation One Subscription (approved by the Union Cabinet in November 2024, implemented through INFLIBNET)
Theses and proposalsShodhganga (Indian electronic theses and dissertations), Shodhgangotri (synopses of research proposals)
Managing referencesZotero (free, open source), Mendeley, EndNote, JabRef (BibTeX)
Collecting dataGoogle Forms, SurveyMonkey, KoBoToolbox, online interviews
Analysing dataSPSS, R, SAS, Stata, Excel, Python (quantitative); NVivo, ATLAS.ti, MAXQDA (qualitative)
WritingWord processors, LaTeX and Overleaf
Checking similarityShodhShuddhi (launched in 2019; it provided Ouriginal/Urkund and moved to DrillBit in 2023), Turnitin, iThenticate
Identifying works and peopleDOI (persistent identifier of a digital object such as an article), ORCID (16-digit researcher identifier), ISSN (8 digits, serials), ISBN (13 digits, books)

Research metrics. The Journal Impact Factor (Eugene Garfield’s idea, published by Clarivate in the Journal Citation Reports) for year Y = citations in Y to items published in Y − 1 and Y − 2 ÷ citable items published in Y − 1 and Y − 2. Scopus’s CiteScore uses a four-year window. For individuals, the h-index (Hirsch, 2005) is the largest h such that h papers have at least h citations each; the g-index (Egghe, 2006) is the largest g such that the top g papers together have at least g² citations; the i10-index (Google Scholar) counts papers with at least 10 citations. Altmetrics track attention on social media and news. Open access comes as gold (free to read on the publisher’s site, often with a fee to authors), green (a version self-archived in a repository), hybrid (open articles in a subscription journal) and diamond (free to both readers and authors). Beware predatory journals, which take fees without real peer review.

Concepts in depth: research ethics

The core misconduct is FFP. Fabrication is making up data or results. Falsification is manipulating materials, equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data, so that the record is not accurate (for example, deleting inconvenient observations or retouching images). Plagiarism is using another person’s ideas, processes, results or words without due credit. Plagiarism has several forms: verbatim copying, mosaic plagiarism or patchwriting, paraphrasing without citation, translation plagiarism, idea plagiarism and self-plagiarism (text recycling).

Other questionable or unethical practices: duplicate (redundant) publication; salami slicing (splitting one study into several minimal papers); gift or honorary authorship (naming someone who did not contribute) and ghost authorship (leaving out someone who did); coercive citation and citation cartels; undisclosed conflicts of interest; p-hacking; and HARKing (presenting a hypothesis formed after seeing the results as if it had been planned). The ICMJE lists four authorship criteria, and every author must meet all four: a substantial contribution, drafting or critical revision, final approval, and accountability. Others are acknowledged. The Committee on Publication Ethics (COPE), founded in 1997, gives journals guidance on handling misconduct.

With human participants, researchers need informed consent (voluntary, with an understanding of the purpose, risks and the right to withdraw), protection of privacy (anonymity: even the researcher cannot link data to a person; confidentiality: the researcher can, but does not disclose it) and approval from an institutional ethics committee. Landmark documents are the Nuremberg Code (1947), the World Medical Association’s Declaration of Helsinki (1964) and the Belmont Report (1979: respect for persons, beneficence and justice). In India, the ICMR’s National Ethical Guidelines (2017) govern biomedical and health research. For animal research the principle is the 3Rs: replacement, reduction and refinement.

Concepts in depth: UGC regulations

The UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018 were notified on 23 July 2018. Key points:

Level (similarity)Student thesis or dissertationFaculty or researcher publication
Level 0: up to 10%Minor similarity, no penaltyNo penalty
Level 1: above 10% to 40%Submit a revised script within a period not exceeding 6 monthsWithdraw the manuscript
Level 2: above 40% to 60%Debarred from submitting a revised script for 1 yearWithdraw; denied one annual increment; no new Master’s, MPhil or PhD supervision for 2 years
Level 3: above 60%Registration for the programme cancelledWithdraw; denied two successive increments; no new supervision for 3 years
  • A repeated offence is punished at the next higher level; repeating Level 3 can lead to suspension or termination of a faculty member as per service rules.
  • Excluded from the similarity calculation: quoted work used with permission or attribution; references, bibliography, table of contents, preface and acknowledgements; generic terms, laws, standard symbols and standard equations. Common knowledge up to 14 consecutive words is also excluded.
  • The core work (abstract, summary, hypothesis, observations, results, conclusions and recommendations) must be original and should not have any similarity.
  • Cases go to a Departmental Academic Integrity Panel (DAIP), chaired by the head of department, and then to an Institutional Academic Integrity Panel (IAIP), chaired by a Pro-VC or Dean; the DAIP must complete its inquiry within 45 days.
  • Scholars submit an undertaking that the work is original, and institutions deposit soft copies of theses and dissertations with INFLIBNET within a month of the award of the degree.

Other UGC measures: a two-credit (30-hour) course on Research and Publication Ethics was made compulsory in PhD coursework by a UGC circular of December 2019; its six units cover philosophy and ethics, scientific conduct, publication ethics, open access publishing, publication misconduct, and databases and research metrics. The UGC-CARE list of journals was introduced in 2019; in February 2025 UGC announced that it would no longer maintain the list and issued suggestive parameters for choosing peer-reviewed journals. The UGC PhD Regulations, 2022 (notified 7 November 2022) dropped the requirement to publish papers before submitting the thesis and ask scholars to train in teaching or writing. Check ugc.gov.in for later changes.

Worked examples

Example 1: h-, g- and i10-index. Citations of ten papers: 30, 17, 10, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0, 0, 0.

  1. h-index: rank 4 has 6 citations (6 ≥ 4), rank 5 has 4 (4 < 5). h = 4.
  2. g-index: running totals 30, 47, 57, 63, 67, 69, 70, 70, 70, 70. Compare with g²: at g = 8, 70 ≥ 64; at g = 9, 70 < 81. g = 8.
  3. i10-index: papers with at least 10 citations are 30, 17 and 10, so i10 = 3.

The g-index is never smaller than the h-index, because it gives credit for very highly cited papers.

Example 2: Journal Impact Factor. A journal published 120 citable items in 2022 and 130 in 2023. In 2024 those items were cited 300 and 450 times respectively.

  1. Numerator: citations in 2024 to 2022–23 items = 300 + 450 = 750.
  2. Denominator: citable items in 2022–23 = 120 + 130 = 250.
  3. 2024 Impact Factor = 750 ÷ 250 = 3.0. Citations to 2024 items, or to items older than two years, do not count.

Example 3: applying the UGC 2018 ladder.

  1. A dissertation shows 8% similarity: Level 0, no penalty.
  2. A thesis shows 52%: Level 2, the scholar is debarred from submitting a revised script for one year.
  3. A faculty member’s paper shows 45%: Level 2, withdraw the paper, lose one annual increment and supervise no new Master’s, MPhil or PhD students for two years.
  4. A thesis shows exactly 40%: “above 10% to 40%” includes 40, so Level 1.

Example 4: who is an author? A study has five contributors. P designed it and wrote the draft; Q analysed the data and revised the draft; R, the head of department, only arranged the lab; S collected questionnaires but did not see the manuscript; T provided funding. P and Q both approve the final version and accept accountability.

Only P and Q meet all four ICMJE criteria. R (gift authorship if listed), S (no drafting or approval) and T (funding alone) should be acknowledged, not listed as authors.

Example 5: which footnote abbreviation? Notes: 1. Sharma, Research Methods, 45. 2. Same book, page 45. 3. Kumar, Sampling, 12. 4. Sharma again, page 80. 5. Sharma again, page 80.

Note 2 is ibid. (the immediately preceding source, same page). Note 4 is op. cit., p. 80 (Sharma cited earlier, a different page). Note 5 is ibid. again, because note 4 is Sharma. Had note 4 cited Sharma page 45, the traditional form would be loc. cit.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact to remember
Article structureIMRaD: Introduction, Methods, Results, and Discussion
APA 7 in-text(Author, Year, p. x); “&” inside parentheses; et al. for 3+ authors from the first citation
MLA 9 in-text(Author page), no comma, no “p.”; et al. for 3+ authors; list called Works Cited
Chicago 17Notes–bibliography or author–date; notes use et al. for 4+ authors; 18th edition in 2024
Impact Factor (year Y)Citations in Y to items of Y − 1 and Y − 2 ÷ citable items of Y − 1 and Y − 2
h / g / i10h papers with ≥ h citations / top g papers with ≥ g² citations in total / papers with ≥ 10 citations
IdentifiersDOI (article), ORCID (16 digits, person), ISSN (8 digits, serial), ISBN (13 digits, book)
INFLIBNETShodhganga (theses), Shodhgangotri (synopses), ShodhShuddhi (plagiarism software, 2019), e-ShodhSindhu (e-resources)
MisconductFFP; duplicate publication, salami slicing, gift and ghost authorship, HARKing
ICMJE authorshipAll four: contribution, drafting or revision, final approval, accountability
Ethics documentsNuremberg 1947, Helsinki 1964, Belmont 1979, COPE 1997, ICMR guidelines 2017
UGC 2018 levels0: ≤ 10%, 1: > 10–40%, 2: > 40–60%, 3: > 60%
UGC RPE course2 credits, compulsory in PhD coursework (circular of December 2019)

NTA traps

  • Ibid. vs op. cit. Wrong: “op. cit. = the immediately preceding source.” Fix: that is ibid.; op. cit. refers back to a work cited earlier, and loc. cit. to the same page of it.
  • APA vs MLA in-text. APA has a comma and the year: (Nair et al., 2022, p. 59). MLA has neither: (Nair et al. 59).
  • APA 6 rules in APA 7 questions. APA 7 omits the publisher location, uses et al. for three or more authors from the first citation and lists up to 20 authors in the reference list.
  • Bibliography vs references. A reference list contains only cited works; a bibliography may include works consulted.
  • Level boundaries. “Up to 10%” is Level 0, and 40% exactly is still Level 1. Student and faculty penalties differ: do not give a student “withdraw the manuscript”.
  • Exclusions. References, bibliography and properly quoted, attributed text are excluded from similarity; results and conclusions are not.
  • Gift authorship is acceptable. Wrong. A position, funding or supervision alone does not qualify anyone as an author under ICMJE.
  • Shodh names. Ganga = theses, Gangotri = synopses, Shuddhi = plagiarism check.
  • Anonymity = confidentiality. Wrong. Anonymous data cannot be linked to a person by anyone; confidential data can be, but are not disclosed.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: styles with fields or features, Latin abbreviations with meanings, INFLIBNET services with functions, identifiers with objects, UGC levels with penalties.
  • Sequence: chapters of a thesis, the IMRaD order, or the chronology of ethics documents and style editions.
  • Assertion–Reason and Statement I/II: self-plagiarism, exclusions from similarity, authorship criteria, open-access types, impact factor windows.
  • Multiple select: ICMJE criteria, forms of misconduct, exclusions from the similarity check, elements of a reference.
  • Numerical: h-index, g-index, i10-index or impact factor from a short list.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. Level 0, B. Level 1, C. Level 2, D. Level 3 (student thesis). List II: I. Registration cancelled, II. No penalty, III. Revised script within six months, IV. Debarred from resubmission for one year. Answer: A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I. Fix Level 0 first (no penalty), and most options fall away.

Elimination trick: in citation-format questions, look first for the year. A year in parentheses right after the author means APA (or Chicago author–date); no year at all in the parentheses means MLA; a superscript number means Chicago notes.
Watch out: policy facts change (UGC-CARE, PhD regulations, national subscriptions). If an option refers to a very recent change, check the current position on ugc.gov.in before the exam.

terms.definition: The standard structure of a research article: Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion, preceded by a title and abstract and followed by references.
A reference list contains only the works cited in the text (APA “References”, MLA “Works Cited”); a bibliography may also include works consulted but not cited.
American Psychological Association style, 7th edition (2019): author–date citations such as (Nair et al., 2022, p. 118); used in psychology, education and the social sciences.
Modern Language Association style, 9th edition (2021): author–page citations such as (Nair et al. 118) and a Works Cited list built from core elements and containers; used in language and literature.

The Chicago Manual of Style, 17th edition (2017): a notes–bibliography system with numbered footnotes or endnotes (history, humanities) and an author–date system (sciences). An 18th edition appeared in 2024.

Fabrication (making up data), falsification (manipulating data, materials or processes, or omitting results) and plagiarism (using another person’s ideas, results or words without credit): the three core forms of research misconduct.
The largest number h such that h of a researcher’s papers have at least h citations each (J. E. Hirsch, 2005).

Citations received in a year by items a journal published in the previous two years, divided by the number of citable items it published in those two years; published by Clarivate in the Journal Citation Reports.

The UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018: similarity Level 0 up to 10%, Level 1 above 10% to 40%, Level 2 above 40% to 60%, Level 3 above 60%, with graded penalties.
An INFLIBNET initiative of the Ministry of Education (launched in 2019) that gives universities access to plagiarism detection software.

lessons.examTip: For UGC similarity questions, memorise the ladder 10–40–60 and the two penalty columns. Student theses: revise within 6 months, debarred 1 year, registration cancelled. Faculty publications: withdraw; withdraw + 1 increment + 2 years no new supervision; withdraw + 2 increments + 3 years no new supervision.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 11 minutes without notes (about 80 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. For each metric problem, write the sorted citation list and mark the h (or g) cut-off before choosing.
Check every answer with solutions.md and log each mistake with its trap (ibid. vs op. cit., APA vs MLA punctuation, student vs faculty penalties, fabrication vs falsification).
Write one book and one journal article in APA 7, MLA 9 and Chicago 17 from memory, then compare with the lesson.
Recite the UGC 2018 ladder (10–40–60) with both penalty columns, then redo the wrong problems after 24 hours.
Finish with the lesson quiz and the bank questions at about 60 seconds each.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Every UGC similarity question answered with the correct level and the correct penalty column.
The h-index and impact factor problems each solved within 60 seconds.
One source correctly formatted in APA 7, MLA 9 and Chicago 17 without notes.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: APA is author–date and dominates psychology, education and the social sciences (IV). MLA uses author and page, as in (Nair et al. 118), for language and literature (II). Chicago notes–bibliography uses superscript note numbers with footnotes or endnotes, typical of history (I). Vancouver numbers the sources in order of first citation and is used in medicine (III). The distractors swap APA with MLA, Chicago with Vancouver, or MLA with Chicago.

b: I. Numbered footnotes or endnotes with a bibliography; history and humanities
II. Author–page in-text citation; language and literature
III. Numbered citations in order of first appearance; medicine and biomedical sciences
IV. Author–date in-text citation; psychology, education and social sciences

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: APA 7 dropped the publisher location, so Statement I is true. It also changed the rule for in-text citations: for three or more authors, use the first author’s surname and “et al.” from the very first citation, as in (Nair et al., 2022). Listing all names at first citation was the APA 6 rule for three to five authors, so Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: In APA 7, the publisher’s location (city) is omitted from a book reference.
Statement II: In APA 7, a work by three authors is cited in the text with all three surnames the first time it is cited.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: A researcher’s nine papers have been cited 25, 18, 12, 9, 7, 6, 3, 1 and 0 times. What is her h-index?
quiz.explanation: Sort the citations in descending order and find the last rank r whose paper has at least r citations: rank 6 has 6 citations (6 ≥ 6), rank 7 has 3 (3 < 7). So h = 6. 9 is the number of papers, and 7 is the rank where the condition first fails.

quiz.question: Under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, a PhD thesis with a similarity of 38% (after the permitted exclusions) leads to which consequence for the scholar?
options: No penalty, as it is a minor similarity
Debarment from submitting a revised script for one year
Cancellation of registration for the programme
Submission of a revised script within a period not exceeding six months
quiz.explanation: 38% lies in Level 1 (above 10% up to 40%). For students, Level 1 requires a revised script within a stipulated time not exceeding six months. One-year debarment is the Level 2 penalty (above 40% to 60%), cancellation of registration is Level 3 (above 60%), and no penalty applies only up to 10% (Level 0).

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. Fabrication invents data; falsification manipulates or omits data or processes. Either way the published record no longer matches reality, and other researchers build on false findings. That is why they are among the gravest forms of misconduct.

stmts: Assertion (A): Fabrication and falsification are treated as serious research misconduct.
Reason (R): Both corrupt the research record by reporting data or results that do not reflect what was actually done or observed.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: According to the ICMJE (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors) recommendations, which of the following are criteria that every author must meet?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, D and E only
quiz.explanation: ICMJE lists four criteria, and an author must meet all four: a substantial contribution (A), drafting or critical revision (B), final approval (D) and accountability (E). Holding a position such as head of department (C) does not justify authorship; adding such a person is gift or honorary authorship. Contributors who do not meet all four criteria are acknowledged instead.

stmts: A. Substantial contribution to the conception or design of the work, or to the acquisition, analysis or interpretation of data
B. Drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content
C. Being the head of the department where the work was done
D. Final approval of the version to be published
E. Agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Arrange the following parts of a PhD thesis in the order in which they usually appear.
quiz.explanation: The abstract is in the preliminary pages (B). In the main body, the review of literature (A) comes before the methodology (D), which comes before the results (C). Appendices belong to the reference matter at the end (E). So B, A, D, C, E.

stmts: A. Review of literature
B. Abstract
C. Results and analysis
D. Research methodology
E. Appendices
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Shodhganga, maintained by INFLIBNET, is best described as:
options: A plagiarism detection service for universities
A repository of synopses of ongoing research proposals
A reservoir of Indian electronic theses and dissertations
A database of Indian experts and their profiles
quiz.explanation: Shodhganga is the repository of Indian electronic theses and dissertations deposited by universities. Shodhgangotri holds synopses of research proposals, ShodhShuddhi provides plagiarism detection software, and VIDWAN is the expert database. The similar names are the trap.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: A is true: undisclosed text recycling, or self-plagiarism, presents old work as new and can breach duplicate-publication rules. R is false: authors often transfer copyright or grant exclusive licences to publishers, and in any case the ethical duty to disclose earlier publication does not depend on who owns the copyright.

stmts: Assertion (A): Re-using large parts of one’s own published paper in a new paper without citing it can amount to research misconduct.
Reason (R): An author is always free to reuse his own published text in any way, because he remains its sole copyright owner in every case.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In MLA 9, how is page 59 of an article by Anil Nair, Priya Das and Salim Khan (2022) cited in parentheses in the text?
quiz.explanation: MLA uses author and page only, with no comma and no “p.”, and uses “et al.” for three or more authors: (Nair et al. 59). Option 1 is APA 7 style, option 4 is Chicago author–date style (which in the 17th edition would name all three authors), and option 2 lists all three names, which MLA does only for two authors.

lessons.title: Reading comprehension
lessons.summaryHtml: Unit 3 of Paper 1 tests comprehension through an unseen passage followed by a set of questions; in recent papers this has usually been one passage with five questions, so the unit is worth about 10 marks. The passages are drawn from education, society, environment, philosophy, science, economics and culture, and they are usually 350–500 words long. The questions ask for the main idea or title, specific details, inferences, the meaning of a word or phrase in context, the author's tone or attitude, and statements that are or are not supported. The skill being tested is disciplined reading: every answer must be justified by the text, not by your general knowledge or opinion. This lesson gives you a repeatable method (skim, map, read the stems, answer with evidence), the vocabulary of tone, the four classic wrong-option traps, and five full passage sets to practise at exam speed.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Reading comprehension checks whether you can read an unfamiliar passage and answer questions using only what the passage says. It is not a test of your knowledge of the topic. A candidate who knows a great deal about climate change can lose marks on a climate passage by answering from memory, while a candidate who knows nothing about the topic can score full marks by reading carefully. The whole skill comes down to one habit: every answer must be justified by words in the passage.

Think of yourself as a careful witness in court. You may report what the passage says (detail), what it clearly implies (inference) and how it says it (tone), but you may not add evidence of your own.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 3 is usually tested through one unseen passage followed by five questions, so it carries about 10 marks, and it can be the most reliable 10 marks of Paper 1. There is no syllabus to memorise and no negative marking, and the answers are in front of you. Recent passages have been drawn from education, social issues, environment and development, philosophy and ethics, science and technology, economics and culture, usually in a formal, essay-like style. Main-idea, detail and inference questions dominate; tone, title and vocabulary-in-context questions appear regularly. Check ugcnet.nta.ac.in for the current pattern.

The unit also matters beyond its own marks. Every Paper 1 unit uses long stems, statements and assertion–reason pairs, so accurate reading improves your score everywhere.

Concepts in depth

1. The kinds of questions

TypeTypical stemWhere the answer livesHow to confirm it
Main idea / title“The central idea is …”, “The most suitable title is …”The whole passage, often the first and last paragraphsThe option must cover every paragraph and go no further
Detail“According to the passage …”One or two sentencesScan for the key word and read the whole sentence
Inference“It can be inferred / concluded …”, “The author implies …”Between the lines, but anchored to specific sentencesIt must follow without any outside assumption
Vocabulary in context“As used in the passage, the word X means …”The sentence containing X and its neighboursSubstitute the option into the sentence
Tone / attitude“The author’s attitude towards X is …”Adjectives, qualifiers, contrastsLook for balance words (yet, but, however)
Purpose of a part“The example of the physician is given to …”The sentence before the exampleAsk what claim the example supports
NOT / EXCEPT“Which is NOT supported / mentioned …”Every paragraphTick off the three supported options; the one left is the answer
Assumption“The argument assumes that …”The gap between evidence and conclusionNegate the option: if the argument collapses, it is the assumption

2. Fact, inference, assumption and opinion

These four ideas are the grammar of comprehension, and NTA often builds options that blur them.

  • Fact (explicit statement): the passage says it. “Multiple-choice papers can be scored by machines within hours.”
  • Inference: not said, but follows. From “the numbers rise while the understanding … may stay the same” we infer that higher scores alone do not prove better learning.
  • Assumption: not said, but needed. “I trust the pharmacist because the system that certified her works” assumes that certification systems are reliable.
  • Opinion or judgement: a value claim (“the best reform”, “a disastrous policy”). It becomes a correct answer only in questions about the author’s view, and only if the author holds it.

The negation test separates an assumption from a merely related statement. Negate the option; if the argument no longer works, the option is an assumption. The must-be-true test separates a sound inference from a possible one: if you can imagine the passage being true and the option false, the option is not a safe inference.

3. Tone vocabulary

Tone options use a fairly fixed vocabulary. Know these precisely:

WordMeaningWordMeaning
Analyticalexamines causes and parts, neutralDidacticintended to teach or moralise
Criticalpoints out faults, with reasonsCynicaldistrusts motives, assumes the worst
Ironicsays one thing, means anotherSardonicgrimly mocking
Ambivalentholds mixed or conflicting feelingsApathetic / indifferentshows no interest or concern
LaudatorypraisingNostalgiclonging for the past
Cautionarywarns of a dangerPolemicalaggressively argues one side
Objectivefree of personal feelingPessimisticexpects the worst outcome

Academic passages chosen for NET are almost never apathetic, abusive or sentimental. Most are analytical, balanced, critical-but-fair or cautionary. A tone option that is extreme in feeling is usually a distractor.

4. A method that works under time pressure

  1. Skim (1–2 minutes). Read the first paragraph fully, the first sentence of each middle paragraph and the last paragraph fully. Note the topic and the author’s stance.
  2. Map. Write a few words per paragraph: “P1 backwash defined; P2 reliable vs valid; P3 formative; P4 exams = samples”. This map finds details in seconds.
  3. Read the stems (not the options) so that your full reading is purposeful.
  4. Read closely, marking signal words: however, but, yet (contrast); therefore, thus (conclusion); for example (illustration).
  5. Answer detail and vocabulary questions first by going back to the line. Answer main-idea and tone questions last, when you have the whole picture.
  6. Eliminate using the four traps below, and confirm your final choice with a quotation.

The combined sitting is 3 hours for 150 questions (about 72 seconds per question on average). A passage set of five questions deserves 7–9 minutes including reading, which is still close to the average rate because the reading time is shared across five questions.

5. The four classic traps

TrapWhat it looks likeHow to catch it
Too narrowTrue, but covers one paragraph or exampleMain-idea options must fit every paragraph
Too broad / out of scopeGoes beyond the topic or adds world knowledgeAsk: where does the passage say this?
Extremealways, never, all, only, proves, completelyCompare with the author’s hedges (may, often, some)
Distortion / reversalUses passage words but flips cause and effect or the comparisonRe-read the sentence the words came from

Worked examples

Example 1: main idea by elimination (Passage 1)

Options: (a) exams should be replaced by continuous assessment; (b) the form of an exam shapes learning, so exams should be designed as samples of understanding; (c) MCQs are more valid than essays; (d) formative assessment lowers anxiety.

Step 1. Map: P1 backwash; P2 reliable vs valid; P3 formative vs summative; P4 exams needed but are samples.

Step 2. (a) is contradicted by P4 (“None of this means that final examinations should be abolished”): extreme. (c) reverses P2: MCQs are more reliable, less valid. (d) is true but lives in one sentence of P3: too narrow.

Step 3. (b) touches P1, P2 and P4 and adds nothing new. Answer: (b).

Example 2: inference versus possibility (Passage 2)

Text: “the trader behaved well partly because a single act of cheating would be remembered by everyone whose goodwill he needed.”

Candidate inferences: (i) in the village, fear of losing reputation checked dishonesty; (ii) village traders were more honest than city shopkeepers; (iii) all village traders were honest.

Working. (i) must be true: the sentence gives reputation as one reason for good behaviour. (ii) compares two groups the passage never compares: out of scope. (iii) turns “partly” and a typical case into “all”: extreme. Only (i) survives the must-be-true test.

Example 3: finding an assumption with the negation test (Passage 2)

Argument: “I trust the pharmacist not because I know her but because I believe that the system which trained, certified and inspects her works.”

Option: “Certification and inspection are, on the whole, carried out properly.” Negate it: “Certification and inspection are not carried out properly.” The writer’s reason for trusting the pharmacist disappears, so the option is an assumption. By contrast, “Pharmacists are more honest than traders” can be negated without affecting the argument, so it is not an assumption.

Example 4: tone from qualifiers (Passage 3)

Clues: “Some economists therefore propose …”, “Supporters argue …”, “Critics reply …”, “Both sides agree on one point …”, “The practical lesson is modest but important.”

Working. The author reports two sides fairly (not polemical), explains causes (analytical) and ends by warning decision-makers about hidden costs (cautionary). Words like “modest” rule out enthusiasm. Best description: analytical and cautionary. “Sentimental”, “sarcastic” and “indifferent” have no support.

Example 5: timing a passage set

A 420-word passage read at 210 words per minute takes 420 ÷ 210 = 2 minutes. Five questions at 45 seconds each take 225 seconds. Total 120 + 225 = 345 seconds = 5 min 45 s. With a partial re-read of 25% (105 words = 30 seconds), the total is 6 min 15 s. So a 7–9 minute budget leaves room for checking.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule to remember
WeightUsually one passage with 5 questions (about 10 marks); check ugcnet.nta.ac.in
Reading timewords ÷ reading speed (words per minute)
Set budget7–9 minutes: 2 skim, 2–3 read, 3–4 answer
Main ideaCovers all paragraphs; not narrower, not broader
DetailGo back to the line; the answer is usually a paraphrase
InferenceMust be true given the passage; no outside facts
AssumptionNegation test: negate it and the argument collapses
ToneBalanced and analytical is common; extreme feelings are rare
NOT questionsFind the three supported options; the leftover is the answer
Signal wordshowever, yet, but = turn; therefore, thus = conclusion
No negative markingNever leave a passage question blank

NTA traps

  • Answering from knowledge. Wrong reasoning: “Wetlands store carbon, I studied that, so this must be right.” Fix: the passage must say or imply it. An option that is true in the world but absent from the passage is wrong.
  • The true-but-narrow title. Wrong reasoning: “Formative assessment lowers anxiety is stated, so it is the main idea.” Fix: a title must cover the whole passage.
  • Missing a reversal. Wrong reasoning: “Reliable and valid both appear in the option, so it matches.” Fix: check the direction. The passage says MCQs are more reliable but less valid.
  • Treating a reported view as the author’s view. Wrong reasoning: “Critics reply that nature cannot be priced, so the author thinks so.” Fix: “Critics reply” reports a view; look for where the author speaks in their own voice.
  • Extreme inference. Wrong reasoning: “Replication failed for many studies, so most science is false.” Fix: the passage says “a worrying proportion” in some fields; “most” and “all sciences” are extreme.
  • Dictionary meaning in a vocabulary question. Wrong reasoning: choosing the common meaning of a word. Fix: substitute each option into the sentence; the contextual meaning wins (in “qualified promises”, qualified means limited by conditions).

How NTA asks this

Most Unit 3 questions are plain multiple choice built on the passage. A few formats recur:

  • “Which of the following is/are correct according to the passage?” with statements A–D. Test each statement against the text separately.
  • “Which is NOT supported?” Look for the reversal or the outside fact.
  • Title and tone questions with one balanced option and three extreme ones.
  • Purpose of an example (“the physician and judge are mentioned to …”).

Mini-example: a statement question on Passage 5

Statement I: Peer reviewers usually repeat the experiment before accepting a paper. Statement II: Failed replications weaken a claim even if it was published in a prestigious journal.

The passage says reviewers “rarely repeat the experiment themselves”, so I is false. It says a claim is weakened “however prestigious the journal that printed it”, so II is true. Answer: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

Elimination tricks. Strike out any option with an extreme word the passage does not use; strike out any option you cannot locate; in main-idea questions, compare the two survivors by asking which one also fits the last paragraph.

terms.definition: The single claim the whole passage supports. A correct main-idea option covers all the paragraphs, not just one example, and does not go beyond the text.
Information stated directly in the passage. Detail questions are answered by returning to the line, not by memory.
A conclusion that is not stated but must be true (or is very strongly supported) given what the passage says, without adding outside assumptions.
An unstated premise the author takes for granted and that the argument needs in order to work. If it were false, the argument would collapse.
The author’s attitude towards the subject or audience, shown through word choice, qualification and emphasis: analytical, critical, ironic, ambivalent, laudatory and so on.
Fast reading for the gist and structure of a text: first and last paragraphs, topic sentences and signal words.
Searching a text quickly for a specific word, name, number or phrase, without reading everything.
An option that may be true in the real world but is neither stated nor implied in the passage. In comprehension it is wrong.
An option with words such as always, never, all, only or proves, where the passage makes a limited or qualified claim.
Connectives that reveal structure: however, yet, but (contrast); therefore, thus, so (conclusion); for example (illustration); moreover (addition).

lessons.examTip: Before choosing any option, point to the sentence that proves it. If you cannot put your finger on supporting words in the passage, the option is out of scope, too extreme or a distortion, however true it sounds.

steps: Read Passage 6 in practice-set.md once for the gist (about 2 minutes), write a one-line main idea, then answer problems 1–5 in 5 minutes.
Attempt the strategy drills, problems 6–15, in 10 minutes without notes.
Check with solutions.md. For every wrong answer, write the trap you fell for (too broad, too narrow, extreme, distortion, out of scope, reversal) in your error log.
For every inference question you got right, underline the exact words in the passage that justify it. If you cannot, count it as a lucky guess.
Do the five passage sets of the lesson quiz and bank at 8–10 minutes per set, including reading.
Redo the questions you got wrong after 24 hours, reading only the relevant paragraph.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
Each passage set (5 questions plus reading) finished within 9 minutes.
At least 23 of the 25 passage questions in the quiz and bank correct.
For every answer, you can quote the line of the passage that supports it.

quiz.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Examinations should be replaced by continuous classroom assessment.
The form of an examination shapes how students learn, so tests should be designed as samples of genuine understanding.
Multiple-choice tests are more valid than essays because machines can mark them.
Formative assessment lowers the anxiety of students.
quiz.explanation: The passage moves from the backwash effect (tests shape learning), through the reliability–validity tension and formative assessment, to the conclusion that examinations are samples of learning, not its purpose. Option 2 covers all of this. Option 1 is contradicted by the last paragraph (“None of this means that final examinations should be abolished”). Option 3 reverses the passage: machine-marked papers are more reliable, not more valid. Option 4 is true but covers only one sentence of paragraph 3, so it is too narrow.

stem.passage:
Every examination teaches something, though not always what its designers intended. When a test rewards the reproduction of memorised answers, students quickly learn that the safest route to success is to memorise; when it rewards the application of ideas to unfamiliar problems, they learn to think. Educational researchers call this the backwash effect: the form of assessment flows backwards into the classroom and reshapes teaching and learning long before the examination is held.

The effect is neither good nor bad in itself. A well-designed test can pull teaching towards understanding just as a poorly designed one can push it towards rote learning. The difficulty is that tests which measure deep understanding are harder and costlier to build and to mark. Multiple-choice papers can be scored by machines within hours, and they are consistent: two examiners cannot disagree about which option was ticked. Essay answers and projects capture more of what we value, but marking them takes time, and different examiners may award different marks to the same script. Large systems, which must assess millions of candidates fairly and quickly, are therefore drawn towards formats that are reliable even when they are less valid.

This tension has led many teachers to distinguish between assessment of learning and assessment for learning. The first is summative: it certifies, at the end of a course, what a learner has achieved. The second is formative: it happens during the course, and its purpose is to show both teacher and learner what should happen next. A short quiz whose marks never enter the final record, a draft essay returned with comments, or a question asked in class to discover a common misconception are all examples. Because nothing depends on them, such exercises lower anxiety and invite honest mistakes, and mistakes, properly examined, are among the most efficient teachers.

None of this means that final examinations should be abolished. Societies need some way of certifying competence, and a doctor or an engineer who has never been tested would inspire little confidence. The point is rather that examinations should be treated as samples of learning, not as its purpose. When the sample becomes the target, the numbers rise while the understanding they were meant to indicate may stay the same. A system that remembers this will spend as much effort on the quality of its questions as on the security of its question papers.
stem.passageTitle: Passage 1 · Education: what examinations teach

quiz.question: According to the passage, why are large examination systems drawn towards formats such as multiple-choice papers?
options: Such formats measure deep understanding better than essays.
Examiners are unwilling to mark essays and projects.
Such formats remove the backwash effect from classrooms.
They can be marked quickly and consistently, even though they capture less of what is valued.
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 2: multiple-choice papers “can be scored by machines within hours, and they are consistent”, and large systems are “drawn towards formats that are reliable even when they are less valid”. Option 1 reverses the claim. Option 2 is not stated: the problem is time and consistency, not unwillingness. Option 3 is wrong because every format has a backwash effect (“Every examination teaches something”).

quiz.question: As used in the passage, the “backwash effect” refers to:
options: the influence that the form of an assessment has on teaching and learning before the test is held
the anxiety students feel after their results are declared
the fall in marks that follows a change in the syllabus
the practice of returning draft essays with comments
quiz.explanation: The passage defines it directly: “the form of assessment flows backwards into the classroom and reshapes teaching and learning long before the examination is held.” The other options use ideas from the passage (anxiety, drafts) or outside ideas (syllabus change) but not this definition. Definition questions reward those who go back to the sentence instead of guessing from the word itself.

quiz.question: Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
options: Doctors and engineers are usually certified through essay examinations.
Marks from formative quizzes should count towards the final grade to motivate students.
A rise in examination scores does not by itself show that understanding has improved.

quiz.question: The attitude of the author towards final examinations can best be described as:
options: hostile: they damage learning and should go
balanced: they are necessary, but must not be treated as the goal of learning
indifferent: their design makes little difference to learning
uncritically enthusiastic: they are the best measure of competence
quiz.explanation: The author says societies “need some way of certifying competence” (so not hostile) but warns that examinations should be “samples of learning, not … its purpose” (so not uncritical). The whole passage argues that design matters a great deal, which rules out indifference. Balanced, qualified positions are very common in NTA passages; extreme tone options are usually wrong.

stem.passage:
Every examination teaches something, though not always what its designers intended. When a test rewards the reproduction of memorised answers, students quickly learn that the safest route to success is to memorise; when it rewards the application of ideas to unfamiliar problems, they learn to think. Educational researchers call this the backwash effect: the form of assessment flows backwards into the classroom and reshapes teaching and learning long before the examination is held.

The effect is neither good nor bad in itself. A well-designed test can pull teaching towards understanding just as a poorly designed one can push it towards rote learning. The difficulty is that tests which measure deep understanding are harder and costlier to build and to mark. Multiple-choice papers can be scored by machines within hours, and they are consistent: two examiners cannot disagree about which option was ticked. Essay answers and projects capture more of what we value, but marking them takes time, and different examiners may award different marks to the same script. Large systems, which must assess millions of candidates fairly and quickly, are therefore drawn towards formats that are reliable even when they are less valid.

This tension has led many teachers to distinguish between assessment of learning and assessment for learning. The first is summative: it certifies, at the end of a course, what a learner has achieved. The second is formative: it happens during the course, and its purpose is to show both teacher and learner what should happen next. A short quiz whose marks never enter the final record, a draft essay returned with comments, or a question asked in class to discover a common misconception are all examples. Because nothing depends on them, such exercises lower anxiety and invite honest mistakes, and mistakes, properly examined, are among the most efficient teachers.

None of this means that final examinations should be abolished. Societies need some way of certifying competence, and a doctor or an engineer who has never been tested would inspire little confidence. The point is rather that examinations should be treated as samples of learning, not as its purpose. When the sample becomes the target, the numbers rise while the understanding they were meant to indicate may stay the same. A system that remembers this will spend as much effort on the quality of its questions as on the security of its question papers.

quiz.question: A candidate reads at 225 words per minute. She reads a 450-word passage once, then re-reads 30% of it while answering, and spends 40 seconds on each of the 5 questions. How long does the passage set take her in all?
quiz.explanation: First reading: 450 ÷ 225 = 2 min = 120 s. Re-reading: 30% of 450 = 135 words, 135 ÷ 225 = 0.6 min = 36 s. Answering: 5 × 40 = 200 s. Total = 120 + 36 + 200 = 356 s = 5 min 56 s. Leaving out the re-reading gives 5 min 20 s; leaving out the first reading gives 3 min 56 s. A budget of 6–8 minutes per passage set is realistic.

lessons.title: Communication: meaning, types and barriers
lessons.summaryHtml: Communication is the process of creating shared meaning: a sender encodes an idea into symbols, sends it through a channel, and a receiver decodes it and responds with feedback, all in a context and against a background of noise. The word comes from the Latin communis, “common”. Communication can be classified by level (intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public, mass), by code (verbal and non-verbal), by formality (formal channels and the grapevine) and by direction (downward, upward, horizontal, diagonal). Effective communication depends on clarity, feedback and listening, and it becomes harder across cultures, in groups and in classrooms, where the teacher must manage many receivers at once. Barriers can be physical, physiological, semantic, psychological, cultural or organisational, and NTA questions ask you to identify them from short scenarios. This lesson covers the concepts, the names and terms NTA pairs in match questions (Hall, Mehrabian, Watzlawick, Tuckman, Flanders, the Johari window) and the traps built on them.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Communication is the process by which people create shared meaning. A sender has an idea, turns it into words or signs, sends it, and a receiver interprets it and responds. When the meaning in the receiver’s mind is close to the meaning in the sender’s mind, communication has succeeded. The word comes from the Latin communis, “common”: to communicate is to make something common between two minds.

Most failures are not failures of speaking but of shared meaning: the words were heard, but understood differently. That is why the syllabus puts “barriers” next to “types”. You will be asked to spot where and why meaning breaks down.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 4 (Communication) usually yields around five questions in Paper 1, and this lesson covers most of the conceptual ones: the elements of the process, characteristics, types, non-verbal codes, inter-cultural, group and classroom communication, and barriers. Match-the-list questions (term with meaning, theorist with concept, direction with example) and statement or assertion–reason questions dominate; scenario questions ask you to classify a barrier. The other lesson of this unit, on mass media and society, covers models and media theories. Check ugcnet.nta.ac.in for the current syllabus.

Concepts in depth

1. Elements of the communication process

ElementMeaningClassroom example
Sender (source)Originates the messageThe teacher
IdeationForming the idea to be sharedDeciding to explain photosynthesis
EncodingConverting the idea into symbolsChoosing words, a diagram, gestures
MessageThe encoded contentThe explanation itself
Channel / mediumThe path the message travelsSpeech, whiteboard, LMS, e-mail
ReceiverThe person for whom the message is meantThe students
DecodingInterpreting the symbolsStudents making sense of the diagram
FeedbackThe receiver’s responseA question, a puzzled look, a quiz answer
NoiseAnything that distorts the messageA noisy fan, unfamiliar terms, anxiety
ContextThe setting: physical, social, cultural, temporalAn examination week, a rural classroom

The sequence is: ideation → encoding → transmission through a channel → decoding → feedback. Noise can enter at any stage, not only in the channel.

2. Characteristics of communication

  • A process: continuous and dynamic, not a single act.
  • Two-way when feedback exists; one-way when it does not (a notice board, a recorded lecture).
  • Irreversible: a received message cannot be withdrawn.
  • Inevitable: Paul Watzlawick and his colleagues (1967) argued that “one cannot not communicate”. Silence, posture and absence also send messages.
  • Contextual: the same words mean different things in different settings.
  • Both content and relationship: every message says something and also signals how the speakers relate (another of Watzlawick’s axioms).
  • Intentional or unintentional: a yawn during a lecture communicates, whether or not the student meant it to.

3. Types of communication

By level: intrapersonal (within oneself: thinking, reflecting, self-talk), interpersonal (between two or a few people), group (small groups, typically 3 to about 15), public (one speaker to an audience) and mass (through media to a large, heterogeneous, anonymous audience with delayed feedback).

By code: verbal communication uses words, oral (lecture, discussion, telephone) or written (letters, reports, e-mail). Non-verbal communication uses everything else.

By formality: formal communication follows the official structure (circulars, minutes, reports). Informal communication, the grapevine, arises from social relations; it is fast, but it can carry rumour. Keith Davis described four grapevine patterns: single strand, gossip, probability and cluster, of which the cluster chain is the most common (a few people pass the message to selected others).

By direction: downward (superior to subordinate: instructions, circulars), upward (subordinate to superior: reports, grievances, suggestions), horizontal or lateral (between peers at the same level: coordination) and diagonal or cross-wise (across both levels and departments: saves time, but can bypass authority).

4. Non-verbal communication

CodeConcerned withName to remember
KinesicsGestures, facial expression, posture, body movementRay Birdwhistell
ProxemicsSpace and distanceEdward T. Hall
HapticsTouch
ChronemicsTime: punctuality, waiting, pace
OculesicsEye contact and gaze
Paralanguage (vocalics)Tone, pitch, volume, rate, pausesGeorge Trager
ArtifacticsClothing, jewellery, objects, décor
OlfacticsSmell

Paul Ekman and Wallace Friesen classified body movements into emblems (gestures with a direct verbal translation, such as a thumbs-up), illustrators (movements that accompany and depict speech), affect displays (facial expressions of emotion), regulators (nods and glances that manage turn-taking) and adaptors (self-touching, such as rubbing the hands when anxious).

Hall’s proxemic zones (for North American middle-class adults, in his original study):

ZoneApproximate distanceTypical use
Intimateup to about 18 inches (0.46 m)close family, comforting
Personalabout 1.5 to 4 feet (0.46–1.2 m)friends, informal talk
Socialabout 4 to 12 feet (1.2–3.7 m)business, office, seminar
Publicabout 12 feet (3.7 m) and beyondlectures, speeches

Mehrabian’s 7–38–55. In experiments on messages about feelings and attitudes where the words conflicted with the voice or face, listeners’ judgements of liking were explained 7% by the words, 38% by the tone of voice and 55% by facial expression (7 + 38 + 55 = 100). The finding does not mean that words carry 7% of the meaning of all communication; a lecture on thermodynamics is carried mostly by its words.

5. Effective communication

The 7 Cs are a standard checklist: clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous (some lists use considerate or credible). Effective communication also needs listening. Hearing is physiological, the reception of sound; listening is psychological: attending, understanding, evaluating and responding. Active listening means giving full attention, paraphrasing, asking clarifying questions and withholding judgement, not planning your reply while the other person is still speaking.

6. Inter-cultural communication

  • High-context vs low-context (Edward T. Hall): in high-context communication, meaning lies in the setting, relationships and non-verbal cues, and much is implied; in low-context communication, meaning is made explicit in words, rules and contracts.
  • Monochronic vs polychronic time (Hall): monochronic cultures treat time as linear and do one thing at a time with fixed schedules; polychronic cultures handle several things at once and put relationships before schedules.
  • Hofstede’s dimensions: power distance, individualism vs collectivism, masculinity vs femininity, uncertainty avoidance, long-term orientation and indulgence vs restraint.
  • Barriers: ethnocentrism (judging others by one’s own culture’s standards), stereotyping, language differences, different norms for gestures, eye contact, touch and time. The remedy is cultural sensitivity and relativism: interpreting behaviour in its own cultural context.

7. Group communication

Tuckman’s stages (1965): forming → storming → norming → performing, with adjourning added in 1977. Groupthink (Irving Janis) is the tendency of a cohesive group to seek agreement so strongly that it stops appraising alternatives realistically.

NetworkStructureProperties
Wheel (star)All messages pass through one central personMost centralised; fastest and most accurate for simple tasks; central person satisfied, others least satisfied
ChainA line; each member linked to the nextHierarchical; slow; distortion over many links
YA chain that branches at one endFairly centralised
CircleEach member talks to two neighbours in a loopDecentralised; slower; higher satisfaction
All-channel (comcon)Everyone talks to everyoneLeast centralised; best for complex tasks; highest satisfaction; n(n − 1)/2 channels

8. Classroom communication

Classroom communication is mostly face-to-face group communication with one dominant sender. It is effective when it is two-way: the teacher reads feedback (questions, answers, expressions) and adjusts. Ned Flanders’ Interaction Analysis Categories (FIAC) code classroom talk every few seconds into ten categories:

GroupCategories
Teacher talk: indirect influence1 Accepts feeling, 2 Praises or encourages, 3 Accepts or uses ideas of students, 4 Asks questions
Teacher talk: direct influence5 Lecturing, 6 Giving directions, 7 Criticising or justifying authority
Student talk8 Response, 9 Initiation
Other10 Silence or confusion

The I/D ratio = (tallies in categories 1–4) ÷ (tallies in 5–7). A higher ratio means a more indirect, student-centred style.

The Johari window (Joseph Luft and Harrington Ingham) helps teachers and students understand self-disclosure: open area (known to self and others), blind area (known to others, not to self), hidden area (known to self, not to others) and unknown area (known to neither). Feedback from others reduces the blind area; self-disclosure reduces the hidden area; both enlarge the open area.

9. Barriers to effective communication

BarrierWhere the distortion arisesExampleRemedy
Physical / environmentalSurroundings, distance, equipmentTraffic noise, poor acoustics, weak networkControl the environment; check the equipment
PhysiologicalThe body of sender or receiverHearing loss, fatigue, illnessAccommodate; use multiple channels
Semantic / languageWords and symbolsJargon, ambiguity, poor translationPlain language; define terms; examples
Psychological / perceptualMind and emotionsPrejudice, anxiety, selective perception, premature evaluationEmpathy; active listening; a safe climate
CulturalNorms and valuesDifferent meaning of gestures or eye contact; ethnocentrismCultural sensitivity
Organisational / structuralHierarchy and rulesFiltering through many levels, rigid channels, status gapsFlatter structures; open-door policy
Technological / channelWrong or overloaded mediumA complex policy sent as a text message; information overloadMatch the medium to the message

Worked examples

Example 1: classifying barriers in a scenario

A guest lecturer uses the term “heuristics” without explaining it; the hall’s fan is loud; a student who failed the last test assumes every comment is aimed at her; the head of department’s instruction reaches the students only after passing through three coordinators, who each shorten it.

Working. Unexplained term = semantic. Fan = physical. Student’s assumption = psychological (selective perception). Shortened instruction = organisational (filtering through levels).

Example 2: counting channels in networks

A department of 7 teachers moves from a wheel (the head linked to each of the other 6) to an all-channel network. How many extra two-way channels appear?

Step 1. Wheel: 6 channels, one from the centre to each member.

Step 2. All-channel: C(7, 2) = 7 × 6 ÷ 2 = 21 channels.

Step 3. Increase = 21 − 6 = 15. This is why an all-channel network is richer but slower to coordinate in large groups.

Example 3: the I/D ratio from FIAC tallies

A 10-minute observation gives tallies: category 1: 4, 2: 10, 3: 6, 4: 20, 5: 60, 6: 15, 7: 5, 8: 30, 9: 10, 10: 10.

Step 1. Indirect teacher talk (1–4) = 4 + 10 + 6 + 20 = 40.

Step 2. Direct teacher talk (5–7) = 60 + 15 + 5 = 80.

Step 3. I/D ratio = 40 ÷ 80 = 0.5: the teacher uses twice as much direct influence as indirect.

Step 4. Total tallies = 170; teacher talk = 120, so teacher talk is 120 ÷ 170 ≈ 70.6% of the lesson, and student talk (8–9) is 40 ÷ 170 ≈ 23.5%.

Example 4: reading Mehrabian correctly

Claim in an option: “Mehrabian proved that 93% of all communication is non-verbal.”

Working. 38 + 55 = 93 is where the figure comes from, but the experiments concerned single words spoken with a conflicting tone or face, judged for feelings and attitudes. The general claim is an over-generalisation. The correct statement is conditional: when verbal and non-verbal cues about feelings conflict, receivers rely more on the non-verbal cues.

Example 5: using the Johari window

A new lecturer does not realise that she speaks too fast; her students notice it. After a mid-semester feedback form tells her so, she slows down.

Working. The fast speech was in her blind area (known to others, not to her). Feedback moved it into the open area. If she had known it but hidden it, it would have been in the hidden area, which shrinks through self-disclosure.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
EtymologyLatin communis, “common”
Process orderIdeation → encoding → channel → decoding → feedback (noise at any stage)
LevelsIntrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public, mass
DirectionsDownward, upward, horizontal (lateral), diagonal (cross-wise)
“One cannot not communicate”Watzlawick and colleagues (1967)
Kinesics / proxemicsBirdwhistell / Edward T. Hall
Hall’s zonesIntimate < 18 in, personal 1.5–4 ft, social 4–12 ft, public > 12 ft
Mehrabian7% words, 38% tone, 55% face, for conflicting messages about feelings only
High / low contextImplicit, relationship-based / explicit, word-based (Hall)
TuckmanForming, storming, norming, performing, adjourning
All-channel channelsn(n − 1)/2; wheel has n − 1
GrapevineInformal; most common pattern is the cluster chain (Keith Davis)
FIAC1–4 indirect, 5–7 direct, 8–9 student talk, 10 silence; I/D = (1–4) ÷ (5–7)
Johari windowOpen, blind, hidden, unknown (Luft and Ingham)

NTA traps

  • Mehrabian over-generalised. Wrong reasoning: “words carry 7% of all meaning.” Fix: only for conflicting messages about feelings and attitudes.
  • Proxemics versus kinesics. Wrong reasoning: “posture is about space.” Fix: posture and gesture are kinesics; distance and territory are proxemics.
  • Grapevine as formal. Wrong reasoning: “it is part of every organisation, so it is official.” Fix: it is informal, even though it is universal and often fast and accurate.
  • Noise only in the channel. Wrong reasoning: “noise is sound on the line.” Fix: semantic and psychological noise arise at encoding and decoding.
  • Diagonal versus horizontal. Wrong reasoning: “different departments means diagonal.” Fix: same level, different departments is horizontal; diagonal needs a different level as well.
  • Storming and norming swapped. Fix: conflict comes before cohesion: forming, storming, norming, performing.
  • Hearing equals listening. Fix: hearing is physiological; listening is active interpretation.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the lists: non-verbal code with meaning, direction with example, network with property, theorist with concept, Johari quadrant with description.
  • Scenario classification: which barrier, which direction, which network.
  • Statements and assertion–reason on characteristics (irreversible, inevitable, contextual) and on Mehrabian or Hall.
  • Sequence: stages of the process, Tuckman’s stages, proxemic zones by distance.

Mini-example: assertion–reason

(A) Feedback turns one-way communication into two-way communication. (R) Feedback is always verbal.

A is true: feedback carries the receiver’s response back to the sender. R is false: a frown, silence or a raised hand is feedback too. Answer: (A) is true but (R) is false.

Elimination tricks. In a match question, fix the pair you are surest of (for example chronemics = time) and strike out every option that disagrees; usually two options remain, and one more certain pair decides. In barrier questions, locate the distortion (environment, body, words, mind, structure, culture) before reading the options.

terms.definition: Encoding is turning an idea into symbols (words, gestures, images); decoding is the receiver turning those symbols back into meaning.
The receiver’s response, which tells the sender how the message was understood and turns one-way communication into two-way communication.
Anything that distorts or interrupts a message at any stage: physical (sound), physiological (hearing loss), semantic (ambiguous words) or psychological (prejudice).
The study of body movements, gestures, facial expressions and posture as communication; associated with Ray Birdwhistell.
The study of how people use space and distance when communicating; the term was introduced by the anthropologist Edward T. Hall.
The vocal but non-verbal part of speech: tone, pitch, volume, rate, pauses and fillers.
The informal communication network of an organisation. It is fast and flexible but can carry rumour; the cluster chain is its most common pattern.
A culture (in Hall’s sense) where much of the meaning is carried by the situation, relationships and non-verbal cues rather than by explicit words.
A model of self-awareness with four areas: open (known to self and others), blind, hidden and unknown. Feedback shrinks the blind area; self-disclosure shrinks the hidden area.
A barrier arising from words and symbols: jargon, words with several meanings, poor translation, unfamiliar abbreviations.

lessons.examTip: In barrier questions, ask where the distortion happens. If it is in the environment it is physical; in the body, physiological; in the words, semantic; in the mind (emotion, prejudice, selective perception), psychological; in the structure (hierarchy, filtering), organisational; in norms and values, cultural.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 9 minutes, writing a one-word reason (the barrier type, the network, the quadrant) beside each answer.
Check with solutions.md and write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (for example, Mehrabian over-generalised, proxemics confused with kinesics, grapevine called formal).

Make a one-page sheet: the elements of the process, the five non-verbal codes, Hall’s four zones, the four directions, the five networks, Tuckman’s stages, the Johari quadrants and the ten Flanders categories.
Redo the problems you got wrong after 24 hours.
Finish with the lesson quiz and bank at 60 seconds per question.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 15 problems finished within 19 minutes.
Every match question in the quiz and bank answered by fixing one certain pair first, in under 60 seconds.
Any barrier scenario classified correctly with its location (environment, body, words, mind, structure, culture).

quiz.question: The word “communication” is derived from the Latin word communis, which means:
quiz.explanation: Communis means common or shared. The idea is that communication creates a commonness of meaning between sender and receiver. “To transmit” describes only the mechanical part and is a common distractor.

b: I. Use of time, such as punctuality and waiting
II. Touch
III. Body movements, gestures and posture
IV. Use of space and distance

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about Albert Mehrabian’s “7–38–55” finding is correct?
options: Words carry only 7% of the meaning in all communication.

It was derived from experiments on messages about feelings and attitudes, where words and non-verbal cues were inconsistent.
It shows that written communication is less effective than oral communication.
quiz.explanation: Mehrabian studied how listeners judge a speaker’s liking or attitude when the words conflict with tone or facial expression: in that setting the words contributed 7%, tone of voice 38% and facial expression 55%. quiz.question: In what Edward T. Hall called a high-context culture, the meaning of a message is carried mainly by:
options: the literal words used, stated as directly as possible
the situation, relationships and non-verbal cues shared by the communicators
quiz.explanation: In high-context communication much is left unsaid because the communicators share history, status cues and relationships; the context carries the meaning. Options 1–3 describe low-context communication, where meaning is made explicit in words and documents.
