lessons.title: Mass media and society
lessons.summaryHtml: Mass communication is communication from an organised source, through a technology, to a large, mixed and largely anonymous audience, with limited and delayed feedback. Mass media include print, broadcast (radio and television), film, new or digital media and India’s traditional folk media. Their functions were classically listed as surveillance, correlation and transmission of culture (Lasswell), with entertainment added by Wright, and they have dysfunctions too, such as the “narcotising” effect named by Lazarsfeld and Merton. Models of communication moved from linear (Aristotle, Lasswell, Shannon–Weaver, Berlo) to interactive (Osgood–Schramm) and transactional (Barnlund, Dance), and India has its own Sadharanikaran model. Theories of media effects run from the hypodermic needle, through two-step flow and uses and gratifications, to agenda setting, cultivation and the spiral of silence. New media add interactivity, convergence and user-generated content, and bring new problems: the digital divide, filter bubbles and misinformation. NTA asks these as theorist–theory matches, chronology sequences and assertion–reason pairs.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Mass media are the technologies and institutions through which a few senders reach very many receivers: newspapers, magazines, radio, television, film and, today, the internet and social platforms. They inform us about events we cannot see for ourselves, shape which issues seem important, entertain us, sell to us and connect us. Because so much of what people know about the world comes through them, societies argue constantly about how powerful the media are, who controls them and how they should be regulated.

This lesson has four parts: what mass communication is and what it does; the models that describe communication; the theories of media effects; and the new media, with the Indian landscape of institutions and laws.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 4 usually yields around five questions, and mass media, models and theories supply a large share of them. NTA repeatedly tests theorist–theory matches (McLuhan, Lasswell, Gerbner, Noelle-Neumann, McCombs and Shaw), chronological order of models, McLuhan’s hot and cool media, functions and dysfunctions, and Indian media milestones. Questions on new media, the digital divide and misinformation have become more common. Check ugcnet.nta.ac.in for the current syllabus.

Concepts in depth

1. What makes communication “mass”

  • The source is an organisation (a newspaper, a channel, a platform), not an individual acting alone.
  • The audience is large, heterogeneous (mixed in age, class, education) and anonymous to the sender.
  • Feedback is delayed and indirect (ratings, letters, comments, analytics).
  • Messages pass through gatekeepers (editors, producers, algorithms) and are produced for simultaneous or near-simultaneous reception.
  • Communication is largely one-to-many; new media blur this with many-to-many exchange.

2. Types of mass media

TypeExamplesStrengthsLimits
PrintNewspapers, magazines, booksPermanent, detailed, re-readableNeeds literacy; slower
Broadcast / electronicRadio, televisionReach, immediacy; radio works without literacy or electricity grid (battery sets)Transient, time-bound, limited feedback
FilmCinema, documentaryEmotional power, audiovisualCostly to produce
New / digital mediaWebsites, social media, OTT, podcastsInteractive, on demand, user-generatedMisinformation, digital divide
Traditional / folk mediaPuppetry, folk theatre, balladsTrusted, local idiom, participatoryLimited reach

Folk forms NTA pairs with states: Yakshagana (Karnataka), Tamasha (Maharashtra), Nautanki (Uttar Pradesh), Jatra (West Bengal and Odisha), Bhavai (Gujarat), Burrakatha (Andhra Pradesh), Therukoothu (Tamil Nadu), Pandavani (Chhattisgarh).

3. Functions and dysfunctions

  • Harold Lasswell (1948): surveillance of the environment (news), correlation of the parts of society (interpretation and editorial comment), transmission of the social heritage (education and socialisation).
  • Charles Wright (1960) added entertainment.
  • Lazarsfeld and Merton (1948): status conferral (coverage confers prestige), enforcement of social norms (exposure of deviance) and the narcotising dysfunction: people mistake knowing about an issue for doing something about it.
  • Denis McQuail: information, correlation, continuity, entertainment and mobilisation.
  • Development role: Wilbur Schramm’s Mass Media and National Development (1964) argued for media in the service of development. India’s Satellite Instructional Television Experiment (SITE, 1975–76) beamed educational and development programmes to villages.

4. Models of communication

Model (year)TypeKey idea
Aristotle (classical)Linear, speaker-centredSpeaker, speech, occasion, audience, effect; persuasion through ethos, pathos, logos
Lasswell (1948)Linear, verbalWho says what in which channel to whom with what effect; no feedback
Shannon–Weaver (1949)Linear, mathematicalInformation source → transmitter → channel → receiver → destination, with a noise source; built for telephone engineering; Weaver named technical, semantic and effectiveness problems
Newcomb (1953)Triangular (ABX)Two people (A, B) and an object (X) tend towards symmetry of attitudes
Osgood–Schramm (1954)Circular, interactiveBoth parties encode, interpret and decode; communication as a cycle
Schramm (1954)InteractiveCommunication works where the fields of experience of sender and receiver overlap
Gerbner (1956)GeneralPerception and production of messages; reality versus its representation
Westley–MacLean (1957)Mass communicationA (advocate), B (audience), C (gatekeeper channel), X (events); feedback
Berlo SMCR (1960)LinearSource and receiver (skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system, culture), message (content, elements, treatment, structure, code), channel (five senses)
Dance (1967)HelicalCommunication grows like a helix, shaped by what went before
Barnlund (1970)TransactionalParticipants send and receive simultaneously; meaning is co-created
Sadharanikaran (Nirmala Mani Adhikary)Indian, non-linearRooted in Bharata’s Natyashastra; sahridayas (sender and receiver) reach sahridayata (commonness) through bhava, abhivyanjana, sandesha, sarani, rasaswadana, with doshas (noise), sandarbha (context) and pratikriya (feedback)

Roman Jakobson’s six functions of language (1960) are also matched: emotive (addresser), conative (addressee), referential (context), poetic (message), phatic (contact) and metalingual (code).

5. Theories of media effects

TheoryPeopleCore claim
Hypodermic needle / magic bulletInter-war propaganda studiesStrong, direct, uniform effects on a passive mass audience
Two-step flowLazarsfeld, Berelson, Gaudet (1944); Katz and Lazarsfeld (1955)Media → opinion leaders → wider public; limited direct effects
GatekeepingKurt Lewin; David Manning White (1950)Editors select and filter news
Knowledge gapTichenor, Donohue and Olien (1970)More information widens the gap between better-off and worse-off groups
Agenda settingMcCombs and Shaw (1972)Media set the salience of issues: what to think about
Uses and gratificationsBlumler and Katz (1974)Active audience chooses media to satisfy needs
Spiral of silenceNoelle-Neumann (1974)Fear of isolation silences perceived minorities
CultivationGeorge GerbnerLong-term heavy TV viewing shapes the perceived world (mean world syndrome)
Media dependencyBall-Rokeach and DeFleur (1976)The more people depend on media, the greater the media’s influence
FramingGoffman (1974), later media scholarsHow an issue is presented shapes how it is understood
Diffusion of innovationsEverett Rogers (1962)Adopters: innovators 2.5%, early adopters 13.5%, early majority 34%, late majority 34%, laggards 16%

Normative theories of the press. Four Theories of the Press (Siebert, Peterson and Schramm, 1956) described authoritarian, libertarian, social responsibility (linked to the Hutchins Commission, 1947) and Soviet communist theories. Denis McQuail later added development media theory and democratic-participant theory.

6. Media and society: critical ideas

  • Marshall McLuhan, Understanding Media (1964): “the medium is the message” (the form of a medium changes society more than its content), the “global village”, hot and cool media. His view is often called technological determinism.
  • Jürgen Habermas: the public sphere, a space where citizens debate public matters.
  • Adorno and Horkheimer (Frankfurt School): the culture industry, standardised mass culture that produces passive consumers.
  • Herman and Chomsky, Manufacturing Consent (1988): the propaganda model, with five filters (ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, and an ideological “common enemy” filter).
  • MacBride Commission (UNESCO, Many Voices, One World, 1980): imbalance in global information flows and the call for a New World Information and Communication Order.

7. New media

New media are digital, networked, interactive and hypertextual; content is modular and can be changed and recombined. Lev Manovich named five principles: numerical representation, modularity, automation, variability and transcoding. Key ideas: convergence (Henry Jenkins, 2006), the prosumer who both produces and consumes (Alvin Toffler, 1980), the network society (Manuel Castells), Web 1.0 (read), Web 2.0 (read–write, participatory) and Web 3.0 (semantic or decentralised), citizen journalism and user-generated content.

Problems: the digital divide (in access, in skills and in outcomes); the filter bubble (Eli Pariser, 2011) and echo chambers, where personalisation narrows exposure; and information disorder: misinformation (false, shared without intent to harm), disinformation (false and deliberately deceptive) and malinformation (genuine information used to harm). Deepfakes make audiovisual evidence less trustworthy, so media literacy matters more than ever.

8. The Indian landscape

YearMilestone
1780Hicky’s Bengal Gazette, the first newspaper printed in India
1930 / 1936Indian State Broadcasting Service set up (1930); renamed All India Radio (1936)
1959Television begins in Delhi; Doordarshan separated from AIR in 1976
1966Press Council of India first set up (Press Council Act, 1965); abolished in the Emergency and re-established in 1979 under the Press Council Act, 1978
1975–76SITE: satellite television for rural education and development
1990 / 1997Prasar Bharati Act passed (1990); Prasar Bharati comes into existence on 23 November 1997
1995Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act
2002 / 2006Community radio permitted for educational institutions (2002); extended to NGOs and other non-profits (2006). Anna FM (2004) was the first campus community radio station
2021IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules: a code of ethics and a three-tier grievance mechanism for digital news publishers and OTT platforms
2023 / 2024Press and Registration of Periodicals Act, 2023 replaces the Press and Registration of Books Act, 1867 (in force from March 2024)

The Press Council is a statutory, quasi-judicial body for the print media, usually chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge; it does not regulate television or OTT. Regulations change, so check the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting and pib.gov.in for current rules.

Worked examples

Example 1: identifying the theory from a scenario

(a) After a week of front-page coverage of water scarcity, a survey finds that water has become the issue citizens rank most important. (b) In a village, most farmers adopt a new seed only after the progressive farmer who reads agricultural magazines recommends it. (c) Heavy television viewers overestimate the risk of crime in their city. (d) Students who oppose a popular campus policy stop voicing their view online because they think they are alone.

Working. (a) Agenda setting: salience transferred from media to public. (b) Two-step flow: media → opinion leader → others. (c) Cultivation: mean world syndrome. (d) Spiral of silence: fear of isolation.

Example 2: diffusion of innovations numerical

A university introduces a new learning platform to 2,000 teachers. Using Rogers’ adopter categories, how many are expected to be early adopters or early majority?

Step 1. Early adopters 13.5% + early majority 34% = 47.5%.

Step 2. 47.5% of 2,000 = 950 teachers.

Check. Innovators 50, early adopters 270, early majority 680, late majority 680, laggards 320: total 2,000.

Example 3: sequencing models

Arrange: Berlo, Barnlund, Lasswell, Osgood–Schramm, Shannon–Weaver.

Working. Recall the anchor years: Lasswell 1948, Shannon–Weaver 1949, Osgood–Schramm 1954, Berlo 1960, Barnlund 1970. A useful memory line: linear models first (late 1940s), then circular (1950s), then SMCR (1960), then transactional (1970).

Example 4: McLuhan’s hot and cool media

Classify: radio, telephone, film, television, photograph, cartoon.

Working. Hot (high definition, low participation): radio, film, photograph. Cool (low definition, high participation): telephone, television, cartoon. Note the counter-intuitive pair: radio is hot, television is cool.

Example 5: separating functions from dysfunctions

Items: surveillance, narcotising effect, entertainment, status conferral, transmission of culture.

Working. Functions of Lasswell and Wright: surveillance, entertainment, transmission of culture. Status conferral is a function named by Lazarsfeld and Merton. The narcotising effect is their dysfunction: people substitute being informed for acting.

NTA traps

  • Hot and cool reversed. Wrong reasoning: “TV has pictures and sound, so it is high definition and hot.” Fix: McLuhan called TV cool (the low-resolution image of his time demanded participation) and radio hot.
  • Press Council dated to 1978. Fix: first set up in 1966 under the 1965 Act; the 1978 Act re-established it in 1979.
  • Prasar Bharati dated to 1990. Fix: the Act is of 1990; the corporation came into existence in 1997.
  • Agenda setting versus framing. Fix: agenda setting is about which issues seem important; framing is about how an issue is presented and interpreted.
  • Narcotising effect listed as a function. Fix: it is a dysfunction (Lazarsfeld and Merton).
  • Shannon–Weaver with feedback. Fix: the original model is linear; feedback came with interactive models (and Wiener’s cybernetics).
  • Two-step flow with a passive audience. Fix: it is a limited-effects theory that gives opinion leaders an active role.

How NTA asks this

  • Match theory with proponent, model with type, folk form with state, press theory with description.
  • Sequence models or Indian media milestones.
  • Assertion–reason on the mechanism of a theory (why the magic bullet assumes passivity; why TV is cool).
  • Which is NOT: not a Manovich principle, not a Lasswell function, not a filter of the propaganda model.

Mini-example: a match question solved by anchors

List I: A. Agenda setting, B. Spiral of silence, C. Cultivation, D. Uses and gratifications. List II: I. Gerbner, II. Blumler and Katz, III. McCombs and Shaw, IV. Noelle-Neumann.

Anchor the certain pair: agenda setting = McCombs and Shaw (A-III). Strike every option without A-III. Next certain pair: cultivation = Gerbner (C-I). Usually only one option remains: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Elimination tricks. In chronology questions, place the earliest and the latest items first (for models, Lasswell and Barnlund), then check the middle. In Indian media questions, separate the year of an Act from the year an institution began.

terms.definition: Communication by an organised source through a medium to a large, heterogeneous, anonymous audience, with delayed and limited feedback.
Selection and filtering of information by editors and other intermediaries before it reaches the audience (Kurt Lewin; applied to news by David Manning White).
The media’s power to decide which issues people think about and how important they seem; they tell us “what to think about” rather than “what to think” (McCombs and Shaw).
Katz and Lazarsfeld’s idea that media influence often passes through opinion leaders, who pass it on to less active members of the public.
An approach that treats the audience as active and asks what people do with media to meet their needs (Blumler and Katz).
George Gerbner’s theory that long-term heavy television viewing shapes viewers’ perception of reality, as in the “mean world syndrome”.
Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann’s theory that people who believe their opinion is in the minority tend to stay silent, which makes the majority view seem stronger.
Marshall McLuhan’s term for a world in which electronic media make distant events immediate and shared, as if in a single village.
The coming together of media industries, technologies and content on digital platforms, and of producer and audience roles (Henry Jenkins).
Unequal access to digital technologies and unequal skills and benefits in using them, between regions, classes, genders and generations.

lessons.examTip: For every theory, learn a triple: the name, the people, and the one-line idea (for example, agenda setting – McCombs and Shaw – what to think about). Most match and assertion–reason questions in this lesson are built from exactly those triples.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes.
Attempt problems 9–15 in 9 minutes. For every theory question, write the name–people–idea triple beside your answer.
Check with solutions.md and log each mistake with its trap (hot and cool swapped, Press Council year confused with the 1978 Act, agenda setting confused with framing, and so on).
Make a timeline card: models (1948–1970), effects theories (1920s–1970s), and the Indian media milestones from 1780 to 2024.
Redo wrong problems after 24 hours.
Finish with the lesson quiz and bank at 60 seconds per question.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
Every model and effects theory placed correctly on your timeline from memory.
The hot/cool classification of radio, film, television and telephone recalled without error.
All 15 problems finished within 19 minutes.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: SMCR (Source–Message–Channel–Receiver) is Berlo’s (1960). The mathematical model, with its noise source, is Shannon and Weaver’s (1949). The circular model is Osgood and Schramm’s (1954). The helix, showing communication growing and building on the past, is Frank Dance’s (1967).

b: I. Frank Dance
II. David Berlo
III. Claude Shannon and Warren Weaver
IV. Charles Osgood and Wilbur Schramm

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Arrange the following models of communication in chronological order, using the years conventionally given in communication textbooks (Shannon–Weaver dated by the 1949 book).
quiz.explanation: Lasswell 1948, Shannon–Weaver 1949, Osgood–Schramm 1954, Berlo 1960, Barnlund 1970: B, D, C, A, E. The usual trap is putting Shannon–Weaver before Lasswell; Shannon’s technical paper appeared in 1948, but the book with Weaver that became the model came in 1949, and Lasswell’s formula is conventionally dated 1948.

stmts: A. Berlo’s SMCR model
B. Lasswell’s verbal model
C. Osgood–Schramm circular model
D. Shannon–Weaver mathematical model
E. Barnlund’s transactional model
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Both are true and R explains A: if messages act like an injection with uniform effects, the audience has no active role. Later research (two-step flow, uses and gratifications) rejected both claims.

stmts: Assertion (A): The hypodermic needle (magic bullet) theory assumes a passive audience.
Reason (R): It holds that media messages are “injected” directly into audiences and produce strong, uniform effects.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I paraphrases the classic formulation behind McCombs and Shaw’s agenda-setting study (the phrase goes back to Bernard Cohen). Statement II is correct: Noelle-Neumann proposed the spiral of silence in the 1970s. Both are true.

stmts: Statement I: Agenda-setting theory holds that the media are more successful in telling people what to think about than what to think.
Statement II: The spiral of silence theory was proposed by Elisabeth Noelle-Neumann.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In Lasswell’s formula “Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect”, the element “in which channel” corresponds to which area of communication research?
quiz.explanation: Who → control analysis; says what → content analysis; in which channel → media analysis; to whom → audience analysis; with what effect → effect analysis. The model is linear and has no explicit feedback.

quiz.question: Which of the following are functions of mass communication as listed by Harold Lasswell and Charles Wright?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, B, D and E only
B, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: Lasswell (1948) named surveillance, correlation and transmission of the social heritage; Wright (1960) added entertainment. The narcotising dysfunction (information replacing action) was described by Lazarsfeld and Merton, and it is a dysfunction, not a function.

stmts: A. Surveillance of the environment
B. Correlation of the parts of society
C. Transmission of the social heritage
D. Entertainment
E. Narcotising dysfunction
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: According to Marshall McLuhan, which of the following is a “cool” medium?
quiz.explanation: McLuhan called a medium hot if it is high in definition and leaves little for the audience to fill in (radio, film, photograph, print), and cool if it is low in definition and demands participation (telephone, television, cartoons, speech). His classification of television as cool is the most frequently tested item.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Yakshagana is the dance-drama of coastal Karnataka (III); Tamasha is Maharashtra’s folk theatre (I); Burrakatha is a narrative ballad form of Andhra Pradesh (IV); Nautanki is the operatic folk theatre of Uttar Pradesh (II). Folk media have been used for health and development messages because they are trusted and use local idiom.

b: I. Maharashtra
II. Uttar Pradesh
III. Karnataka
IV. Andhra Pradesh

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT one of Lev Manovich’s five principles of new media?
quiz.explanation: In The Language of New Media (2001), Manovich listed numerical representation, modularity, automation, variability and transcoding. Linearity is a property of old media such as a film reel or a printed book read from start to finish; new media are non-linear.

quiz.question: Prasar Bharati, India’s public service broadcaster, came into existence in 1997 under an Act passed in:
quiz.explanation: The Prasar Bharati (Broadcasting Corporation of India) Act was passed in 1990, and Prasar Bharati came into existence on 23 November 1997, taking over All India Radio (Akashvani) and Doordarshan. 1995 is the year of the Cable Television Networks (Regulation) Act, a common distractor.

domains.name: Mathematical Reasoning and Aptitude
domains.blurb: Series, codes, relationships and quantitative aptitude.

lessons.title: Reasoning: series, codes and relationships
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers the “reasoning” half of Unit 5: the types of reasoning, number series, letter series, coding–decoding and relationships (blood relations, direction sense and ranking). Every one of these questions hides a single rule, and the whole skill is finding that rule quickly. For number series you test differences, ratios, squares and cubes, and interleaved (alternating) series in a fixed order. For letters and codes you work with position values (A = 1 … Z = 26), the reverse value 27 − n and the EJOTY anchors. For relationships you draw a small family tree or a direction sketch instead of reasoning in your head. With these routines, most questions take under a minute.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Reasoning questions give you a pattern and ask you to extend, decode or apply it. A series is a list of numbers or letters built by a hidden rule. A code turns one word into another by a fixed rule. A relationship question describes family links, positions or directions in words, and you rebuild the picture. You need only a fixed checking routine, a few memorised tables and a quick sketch.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 5 of Paper 1 usually contributes a few questions, and its reasoning part gives some of the most reliable marks in the paper: the answers are exact and each question takes under a minute with practice. Recurring sub-topics: number series (next, missing or wrong term), letter series, coding–decoding, blood relations (plain and coded) and directions. Types of reasoning link this unit to Unit 6.

Concepts in depth: types of reasoning

TypeDirectionStrength of conclusionExample
DeductiveGeneral rule → particular caseCertain, if valid with true premisesAll primes above 2 are odd; so 17 is odd
InductiveObserved cases → general ruleProbable only; new data can overturn it2, 4, 8, 16 … so the rule is “double each time”
AbductiveObservation → best explanationPlausible; the most likely hypothesisThe road is wet, so it probably rained
AnalogicalSimilar case → this caseAs strong as the similarity is relevantThe heart is like a pump, so it can fail like one

Validity is about form, truth about content: a valid argument can have false premises; a sound argument is valid with true premises. Solving a series is inductive, so test your rule on every term.

Concepts in depth: number series

Run these tests in order; stop at the first that fits every term.

  1. Growth check. Slow growth points to differences, doubling or tripling to multiplication, rise-and-fall to an alternating series.
  2. First differences. Constant differences give an arithmetic series; differences forming a simple series (odd numbers, multiples of 7, powers of 2, primes) are the commonest NTA pattern.
  3. Second differences. If the second differences are constant, the terms follow a quadratic rule such as an² + bn + c.
  4. Ratios and mixed rules. Try × k, then × k ± c, then growing rules (× 2, × 3, × 4 … or × 2 + 1, × 2 + 2 …).
  5. Known families. Compare with n², n³, n² ± 1, n³ ± n², n(n + 1), 2ⁿ, primes and Fibonacci numbers; memorise squares to 30, cubes to 15 and primes to 100.
  6. Alternating series. Solve odd and even positions separately.

For a wrong term, find the rule from the terms that agree and check each term; only one breaks it. For a missing term in the middle, the rule must work across the gap.

Concepts in depth: letters, positions and letter series

Convert letters to numbers and the question becomes a number series. Use A = 1 to Z = 26 and the anchors E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25 (EJOTY). The opposite letter of value n has value 27 − n: AZ, BY, CX, DW, EV, FU, GT, HS, IR, JQ, KP, LO, MN. The n-th letter from the right is the (27 − n)-th from the left; past Z, subtract 26. In clusters such as AZ, CX, EV, each position forms its own series (+2 and −2 here).

Concepts in depth: coding and decoding

Code typeHow to spot itExample
Fixed shift (+k or −k)Every letter moves the same number of placesCAT → DBU (+1)
Growing shiftShifts of +1, +2, +3, … along the wordBOOK → CQRO
Opposite letterEach code letter adds to 27 with the originalCAT → XZG
ReversalSame letters in reverse order (sometimes then shifted)CAT → TAC
Position valuesThe code is a number built from letter values (a sum, product or list)CAT → 3 + 1 + 20 = 24
Sentence codesCodes for whole wordssee the method below

Write the word and its code one above the other with position values and read the change letter by letter. For sentence codes, compare two sentences at a time: the common word takes the common code, and words that appear once are settled last by elimination.

Concepts in depth: blood relations

Draw a small tree: one level per generation, males and females marked, couples joined with “=”. Three rules prevent most errors. (1) Never assume a gender: a name or “child” does not fix it; if the gender matters and is not given, the answer is “cannot be determined”. (2) Decode long chains from the innermost phrase: “the only son of my grandfather” first (my father, if the grandfather is paternal), then “his son” (my brother). (3) Count generations: grandparent +2, parent +1, sibling and cousin 0, child −1, grandchild −2; the relation name must match the generation. In coded relations (A + B means A is the father of B, and so on), turn each symbol into a link on the tree first.

Concepts in depth: direction sense and ranking

Use a grid with north up. A right turn is 90° clockwise (N → E → S → W) and a left turn 90° anticlockwise. Track the net east–west movement x and north–south movement y: the distance is √(x² + y²) and the signs give the direction (x > 0, y < 0 is south-east). Shadows: the morning sun is in the east, so shadows fall west; evening shadows fall east. Rows: left position + right position − 1 = total.

Worked examples

Example 1 (difference method). Find the next term: 4, 11, 25, 46, 74, ?

First differences: 7, 14, 21, 28. These are multiples of 7, so the next difference is 35 and the next term is 74 + 35 = 109.

Example 2 (wrong term). Find the wrong term: 3, 7, 16, 35, 72, 153.

3 × 2 + 1 = 7, 7 × 2 + 2 = 16, 16 × 2 + 3 = 35, then 35 × 2 + 4 = 74, and 74 × 2 + 5 = 153 fits the last term. The wrong term is 72 (it should be 74).

Example 3 (letter series and clusters). (a) D, G, K, P, ? (b) BDF, HJL, NPR, ?

(a) Values 4, 7, 11, 16; gaps 3, 4, 5; the next gap 6 gives 22 = V. (b) Each cluster is three letters two apart, starting at B (2), H (8), N (14): the next starts at 20 = T, giving TVX.

Example 4 (coding). PAPER is coded as QCSIW. How is BOOK coded? In the same language LAMP = 42; what is NOTE?

P → Q (+1), A → C (+2), P → S (+3), E → I (+4), R → W (+5): a growing shift, so BOOK → CQRO. LAMP = 12 + 1 + 13 + 16 = 42 is a sum of position values, so NOTE = 14 + 15 + 20 + 5 = 54.

Example 5 (blood relation). Pointing to a boy, Meena says, “He is the son of the only daughter of my father’s father.” How is the boy related to Meena?

“My father’s father” is Meena’s paternal grandfather; his only daughter is Meena’s father’s sister, her aunt. The aunt’s son is Meena’s cousin. Generation check: grandfather +2, aunt +1, her son 0.

Example 6 (coded relation). A + B means A is the father of B; A − B means A is the wife of B; A ÷ B means A is the daughter of B. If M ÷ N − O + P, how is M related to P?

M is the daughter of N; N is the wife of O; O is the father of P. So N and O are the parents of both M and P, and M, being a daughter, is P’s sister. Reverse the question (how is P related to M?) and the answer becomes “cannot be determined”, because P’s gender is never given.

Example 7 (direction and distance). Anita walks 5 km east, turns left and walks 4 km, turns left and walks 8 km, then turns left and walks 8 km. Where is she now?

step  facing  move   position (x, y)
1     East    5 km   (5, 0)
2     North   4 km   (5, 4)
3     West    8 km   (-3, 4)
4     South   8 km   (-3, -4)

Distance = √(3² + 4²) = 5 km; x < 0 and y < 0, so she is south-west of the start.

Example 8 (ranking). Kiran is 14th from the left and 20th from the right. The row has 14 + 20 − 1 = 33. If one student joins at the right end, Kiran becomes 34 − 14 + 1 = 21st from the right.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule or value
Letter anchorsE = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25; opposite letter = 27 − n
n-th letter from the right(27 − n)-th from the left; wrap past Z by subtracting 26
Quadratic seriesconstant second differences (e.g. n², n² + 1, n(n + 1))
Common familiessquares 1, 4, 9, 16 …; cubes 1, 8, 27, 64 …; primes 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 …; 2ⁿ − 1: 1, 3, 7, 15 …; factorials 1, 2, 6, 24, 120
Turnsright = 90° clockwise, left = 90° anticlockwise; 180° reverses the direction
Distance√(x² + y²) with x = net east–west, y = net north–south
Shadowsmorning: shadow to the west; evening: shadow to the east
Row rankingtotal = left + right − 1; right = total − left + 1
Generationsgrandparent +2, parent +1, sibling or cousin 0, child −1, grandchild −2

NTA traps

  • Stopping after two terms. Wrong: “3 to 8 is +5, so add 5.” Fix: 3, 8, 15, 24 has differences 5, 7, 9; test every term.
  • Missing an alternating series. Wrong: forcing one rule on 1, 20, 3, 17, 5, 14. Fix: split odd and even positions.
  • Off-by-one letter counts. Wrong: “the 12th from the right is 26 − 12 = N”. Fix: use 27 − n, so it is O (15).
  • Assuming gender. Wrong: “S is R’s sibling, so S is a brother.” Fix: without a word such as “son”, “wife” or “sister”, the answer is “cannot be determined”.
  • Confusing path and displacement. Wrong: adding all the walks (26 km). Fix: net x and net y, then √(x² + y²).
  • Turning from a south-facing walk. Wrong: “left means west”. Fix: left from south is east.
  • Calling a valid argument true. Wrong: “valid means the conclusion is true.” Fix: validity is about form; only a sound argument guarantees a true conclusion.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct items: next, missing or wrong term; letter position; coded word; relation; distance.
  • Match: series with next terms, coding rules with codes, relation phrases with names, turns with directions.
  • Statement I/II and A–R: a computed fact paired with a rule or a claim about reasoning.
  • Multi and sequence: “which series follow × 2 + 1?”, facts from a family description, west-to-east or dictionary order.

Mini-example (match). A. Father’s sister, B. Brother’s wife, C. Mother’s father, D. Son’s daughter; I. Granddaughter, II. Maternal grandfather, III. Sister-in-law, IV. Aunt. Answer: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I. Fix the surest pair first, then strike out options.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The 20th letter from the right is G. R: The n-th letter from the right is the (27 − n)-th from the left. 27 − 20 = 7 = G, so both are true and R explains A: option 1.

Elimination trick: if the differences are growing, any option below last term + last difference is out at once. In direction questions, the signs of x and y alone usually remove two options.
Watch out: “only son”, “only daughter” and “only child” carry information: they often reveal that the person is the speaker’s own parent.

terms.definition: Reasoning from general premises to a conclusion that must be true if the premises are true and the form is valid. It moves from the general to the particular.
Reasoning from observed cases to a general conclusion that is probable, not certain. Finding the rule of a number series is inductive.
Write the gaps between consecutive terms (first differences), then the gaps between those (second differences), until a clear pattern appears.
Two independent series interleaved: terms 1, 3, 5, … follow one rule and terms 2, 4, 6, … another. Suspect it when the terms go up and down.
The rank of a letter in the alphabet: A = 1, B = 2, …, Z = 26. The anchors E = 5, J = 10, O = 15, T = 20, Y = 25 (EJOTY) make lookups instant.
The letter whose position value adds up to 27 with the given one: A–Z, B–Y, C–X, …, M–N. The n-th letter from the right is the (27 − n)-th from the left.
A rule that turns a word or number into a code, such as a fixed or growing letter shift, the opposite letter, reversal or a position-value sum.
Square or + for male, circle or − for female, a double line (=) for a married couple, a vertical line for parent to child and a horizontal line for siblings.
The straight-line distance from start to finish: add all east–west moves and all north–south moves separately, then use √(x² + y²).
If a person is p-th from one end and q-th from the other end of a row, the row has p + q − 1 people.

lessons.examTip: Before any calculation, look at how fast the series grows. Slow, steady growth means differences; fast growth means multiplication, squares, cubes or powers; up-and-down movement means two alternating series. Choosing the right test first saves most of the time.

Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. Write the rule, the difference row, the family tree or the direction sketch beside each problem.

From memory, write A–Z with position values and opposite letters, squares to 30, cubes to 15, powers of 2 to 2¹² and primes to 100; check them against the fact sheet.
Make up three series of your own (one difference, one ratio, one alternating) and one coded-relation chain, and solve them the next day.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 45–60 seconds per question.

quiz.question: What is the next term of the series 3, 8, 15, 24, 35, ?
quiz.explanation: The differences are 5, 7, 9, 11, so the next difference is 13 and 35 + 13 = 48. Another view: the terms are n² − 1 for n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, so the next is 7² − 1 = 48. Choosing 49 gives n² instead of n² − 1; 46 adds 11 again instead of the next odd number.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: A is n(n + 1): 2, 6, 12, 20, 30, then 6 × 7 = 42 (IV). B is the cubes, so 5³ = 125 (II). C is the primes, so the next prime after 11 is 13 (III). D is “× 2 + 1”: 47 × 2 + 1 = 95 (I). The distractors swap one or two pairs.

b: III. 13
IV. 42

quiz.question: What comes next in the letter series B, E, I, N, ?
quiz.explanation: Position values are 2, 5, 9, 14. The gaps are 3, 4, 5, so the next gap is 6: 14 + 6 = 20 = T (the EJOTY anchor T = 20). S (19) comes from repeating the gap 5.

quiz.question: In a certain code COMPUTER is written as DPNQVUFS. How is KEYBOARD written in that code?
quiz.explanation: Each letter moves one place forward: C → D, O → P, M → N and so on. So K → L, E → F, Y → Z, B → C, O → P, A → B, R → S, D → E, giving LFZCPBSE. JDXANZQC moves each letter back instead; the other two options change one letter wrongly.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Opposite letters add up to 27. G (7) → 20 = T, O (15) → 12 = L, L (12) → 15 = O, D (4) → 23 = W, so GOLD → TLOW and Statement I is true. The 12th letter from the right is the (27 − 12) = 15th from the left, which is O, so Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: If every letter is replaced by its opposite letter (A ↔ Z, B ↔ Y, and so on), the word GOLD becomes TLOW.
Statement II: The 12th letter from the right end of the English alphabet is O.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Pointing to a man, Reena says, “He is the son of the only son of my grandfather.” How is the man related to Reena? (Assume the grandfather is Reena’s father’s father.)
quiz.explanation: The only son of Reena’s paternal grandfather must be Reena’s father. The son of Reena’s father is Reena’s brother. “Cousin” would need the son of an uncle or aunt, but the grandfather has only one son.

quiz.question: Ravi walks 6 km north, turns right and walks 8 km, then turns right again and walks 12 km. How far is he from the starting point, and in which direction?
quiz.explanation: Take the start as (0, 0). North 6 → (0, 6). A right turn from north faces east: 8 km → (8, 6). A right turn from east faces south: 12 km → (8, −6). Distance = √(8² + 6²) = 10 km. He is east and south of the start, so the direction is south-east. 26 km is the total path, not the displacement.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: The terms are 1² + 1, 2² + 1, 3² + 1, 4² + 1, 5² + 1, so R is true, and the sixth term is 6² + 1 = 37, so A is true. A follows directly from R, so R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The next term of the series 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, … is 37.
Reason (R): The n-th term of the series is n² + 1.

quiz.question: Which of the following statements about types of reasoning are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
A, B, C, D and E
quiz.explanation: A, B, C and E describe deduction, induction, abduction and analogy correctly. D is false: validity is about form only. “All fish can fly; a sparrow is a fish; so a sparrow can fly” is valid but has false premises. A valid argument with true premises is called sound.

B. The conclusion of an inductive argument is probable rather than certain.

lessons.title: Mathematical aptitude
lessons.summaryHtml: Mathematical aptitude in Paper 1 covers fractions, percentages, ratio and proportion, profit and loss, simple and compound interest with discounting, averages, and time and distance. The arithmetic is school level, but the exam rewards speed, so this lesson teaches each topic twice: the standard method, and the shortcut that gets the answer in a few seconds. The key idea is the multiplying factor: a 20% rise multiplies by 1.2, a 15% discount by 0.85, and successive changes simply multiply. Add a fraction–percentage table, the average-speed formula 2xy/(x + y), the CI–SI difference formulas and the alligation rule, and almost every question becomes one line of working.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This unit is everyday arithmetic done fast. A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100; a ratio compares two quantities; profit and loss compare selling price with cost price; interest is the price of borrowed money; an average spreads a total equally; and time and distance links speed, time and distance. Most questions reduce to one idea: find the base, turn the change into a factor, multiply.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 5 usually gives a few aptitude questions, and the same skills drive Unit 7 (Data Interpretation), so this lesson earns marks in two units. Percentages, profit and discount, simple versus compound interest, average speed and ratio sharing are the most frequent patterns. No calculator is allowed, so the shortcuts matter as much as the methods.

Concepts in depth: fractions and percentages

To compare fractions, cross-multiply: a/b > c/d exactly when ad > bc (b, d positive). Memorise this conversion table; most exam fractions are built from it.

Fraction%Fraction%
1/2501/812.5
1/333.331/911.11
1/4251/119.09
1/5201/128.33
1/616.671/156.67
1/714.291/166.25

Key percentage rules. (1) An increase of r% multiplies by (1 + r/100) and a decrease by (1 − r/100); successive changes multiply, so two changes a% and b% give a + b + ab/100. (2) If A is x% more than B, then B is x/(100 + x) × 100 % less than A; if A is x% less than B, B is x/(100 − x) × 100 % more. (3) If a price rises by r%, consumption must fall by r/(100 + r) × 100 % to keep spending the same.

Concepts in depth: ratio and proportion

To combine A : B and B : C, make B equal using the LCM. To divide an amount in the ratio a : b : c, one part is amount/(a + b + c). In a proportion a : b = c : d, the product of the extremes equals the product of the means (ad = bc). The fourth proportional to a, b, c is bc/a; the third proportional to a and b is b²/a; the mean proportional of a and b is √(ab). The duplicate ratio of a : b is a² : b². For mixtures, the alligation rule gives the quantities: cheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c), where m is the mean price.

Concepts in depth: profit, loss and discount

Profit % = (SP − CP)/CP × 100 and loss % = (CP − SP)/CP × 100: always on the cost price. Discount % = (MP − SP)/MP × 100: always on the marked price. With a mark-up of m% and a discount of d%, SP/CP = (1 + m/100)(1 − d/100). Successive discounts d₁ and d₂ equal one discount of d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100. If the cost price of n articles equals the selling price of k articles, the profit % is (n − k)/k × 100. A dishonest dealer who gives g grams for every 1000 grams charged gains (1000 − g)/g × 100 % when selling at cost price. Selling two articles at the same price, one at x% profit and the other at x% loss, always gives an overall loss of x²/100 %.

Concepts in depth: interest and discounting

Simple interest: SI = PRT/100 and A = P + SI; a sum doubles in 100/R years. Compound interest: A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ. For half-yearly compounding, use R/2 per half-year and 2n periods; for quarterly, R/4 and 4n. Two shortcuts: the CI for 2 years is the successive change R + R + R²/100 per cent of P; and CI − SI = P(R/100)² for 2 years and P(R/100)²(3 + R/100) for 3 years. If the amounts after n and n + 1 years are known, their ratio is (1 + R/100).

Discounting works backwards from a sum A due in the future. Its present worth PW is the sum that grows to A at simple interest: PW = 100A/(100 + RT). The true discount is TD = A − PW = A·RT/(100 + RT), which is simply the interest on PW. A banker instead charges interest on the full amount: banker’s discount BD = A·RT/100. The difference, the banker’s gain, is BG = BD − TD = TD²/PW, the interest on TD.

Concepts in depth: averages

Always work with sums: sum = average × count. When a new value joins and the average rises by k, the new value is old average + k × (new count). When a value is replaced and the average of n values rises by k, the new value exceeds the old one by n·k. A weighted average is Σ(wᵢxᵢ)/Σwᵢ. The average of an arithmetic sequence equals the average of its first and last terms.

Concepts in depth: time and distance

Distance = speed × time. Convert km/h to m/s by × 5/18 and m/s to km/h by × 18/5. For equal distances at x and y, the average speed is 2xy/(x + y). With distance fixed, speed and time are inversely proportional: at a/b of the usual speed, the time becomes b/a of the usual time. Relative speed is the difference of speeds for objects moving the same way and the sum for opposite directions. A train crossing a pole or a person covers its own length; crossing a platform, bridge or another train it covers the sum of the lengths. For boats: downstream speed = b + s, upstream = b − s, so b = (down + up)/2 and s = (down − up)/2.

Worked examples

Example 1 (percentage). The price of sugar rises 25%. By what percentage must a family cut consumption to keep its spending the same? And what is the net effect of a 25% rise followed by a 20% fall?

Cut = 25/125 × 100 = 20%. Net factor 1.25 × 0.8 = 1, so no change: this is exactly why the 20% cut works.

Example 2 (mark-up, discounts and false weights). (a) Goods marked 40% above cost are sold at a 15% discount. (b) What single discount equals 20% and 10%? (c) A dealer sells at 10% above cost but gives 800 g for every kilogram.

(a) 1.4 × 0.85 = 1.19: 19% profit. (b) 20 + 10 − 200/100 = 28%. (c) He receives 1.1 × CP for goods costing 0.8 × CP: 1.1/0.8 = 1.375, a gain of 37.5%.

Example 3 (SI and CI). P = ₹ 12,000, R = 10% per annum, 3 years.

SI = 12000 × 10 × 3/100 = ₹ 3,600. A = 12000 × 1.1³ = 15,972, so CI = ₹ 3,972. Check with the shortcut: CI − SI = 12000 × (0.1)² × (3 + 0.1) = ₹ 372 = 3,972 − 3,600.

Example 4 (discounting). ₹ 5,600 is due in 3 years at 4% simple interest. Find PW, TD, BD and BG.

RT = 12. PW = 100 × 5600/112 = ₹ 5,000; TD = 5600 − 5000 = ₹ 600; BD = 5600 × 12/100 = ₹ 672; BG = 672 − 600 = ₹ 72, and indeed TD²/PW = 360000/5000 = 72.

Example 5 (averages). The average of 11 numbers is 36. The average of the first six is 32 and of the last six is 41. Find the sixth number.

The sixth number is counted in both groups: 6 × 32 + 6 × 41 − 11 × 36 = 192 + 246 − 396 = 42.

Example 6 (trains and boats). (a) A 240 m train at 72 km/h crosses a 360 m bridge. (b) A boat goes 20 km downstream in 2 hours and 12 km upstream in 2 hours.

(a) 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s; distance 240 + 360 = 600 m; time = 30 s. (b) Down 10 km/h, up 6 km/h: boat = (10 + 6)/2 = 8 km/h, stream = (10 − 6)/2 = 2 km/h.

Example 7 (ratio and alligation). (a) A : B = 3 : 4 and B : C = 6 : 7; share ₹ 7,000 in the ratio A : B : C. (b) Rice at ₹ 30/kg and ₹ 45/kg is mixed to cost ₹ 36/kg.

(a) LCM of 4 and 6 is 12: A : B : C = 9 : 12 : 14, 35 parts of ₹ 200: ₹ 1,800, ₹ 2,400, ₹ 2,800. (b) Cheaper : dearer = (45 − 36) : (36 − 30) = 9 : 6 = 3 : 2.

Formula and fact sheet

TopicFormula or shortcut
Successive changea + b + ab/100 (decreases negative)
x% more / lessother is x/(100 + x) × 100 % less / x/(100 − x) × 100 % more
Profit, losson CP; SP = CP × (1 ± r/100)
Discounton MP; two discounts d₁ + d₂ − d₁d₂/100
Same SP, x% profit and x% lossoverall loss x²/100 %
SIPRT/100; doubles in 100/R years
CIP(1 + R/100)ⁿ − P; half-yearly R/2, 2n
CI − SI2 years PR²/100²; 3 years PR²(300 + R)/100³
Present worth, TDPW = 100A/(100 + RT); TD = A − PW
BD, BGBD = ART/100; BG = BD − TD = TD²/PW
Proportionalsfourth bc/a; third b²/a; mean √(ab)
Alligationcheaper : dearer = (d − m) : (m − c)
Speed unitskm/h × 5/18 = m/s
Average speedequal distances: 2xy/(x + y)
Relative speedsame direction difference; opposite sum
Boatsb = (D + U)/2; s = (D − U)/2

NTA traps

  • Wrong base. Wrong: “A is 25% more than B, so B is 25% less than A.” Fix: the base changes; B is 20% less.
  • Adding successive percentages. Wrong: 10% and 10% discounts = 20%. Fix: 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81, a 19% discount.
  • Profit on SP or discount on CP. Fix: profit and loss on CP, discount on MP, unless stated otherwise.
  • Arithmetic mean of speeds. Wrong: (40 + 60)/2 = 50. Fix: equal distances need 2xy/(x + y) = 48.
  • SI for CI. Wrong: 10% for 2 years = 20%. Fix: compounding gives 21%; check whether the question says “compounded”.
  • Half-yearly compounding. Wrong: keeping R and n. Fix: use R/2 and 2n.
  • Units in train questions. Wrong: dividing metres by km/h. Fix: convert first (× 5/18), and add the lengths of both objects.
  • “Equal profit and loss cancel.” Wrong: 20% profit and 20% loss at the same SP give no net change. Fix: overall loss of 20²/100 = 4%.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct numericals: most items, with the trap answer among the options (50 for 48, 20% for 19%).
  • Match: fractions with percentages, proportionals with values, speed conversions with results.
  • Statement I/II and A–R: a claimed result (“two 10% discounts equal 20%”) paired with a rule.
  • Multi and sequence: true statements about averages or discounts; ordering fractions or investment returns.
  • DI-style sets: a small table of prices or sales with five linked questions, as in Unit 7.

Mini-example (match). A. 72 km/h in m/s, B. 15 m/s in km/h, C. average of 40 and 60 km/h over equal distances, D. relative speed of 50 and 30 km/h in opposite directions; I. 80, II. 48, III. 54, IV. 20. Answer: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I.

Mini-example (A-R). A: At the same rate, CI and SI for the first year are equal (annual compounding). R: In year 1 both methods charge interest on the principal only. Both true, R explains A: option 1.

Elimination trick: estimate first. CI exceeds SI after year 1; average speed lies below the arithmetic mean; successive discounts total less than their sum.
Watch out: “compounded half-yearly” or “quarterly” changes both the rate per period and the number of periods.

terms.definition: The number a quantity is multiplied by for a percentage change: an increase of r% gives 1 + r/100, a decrease of r% gives 1 − r/100.
Two changes of a% and b% give a net change of a + b + ab/100 per cent (use negative values for decreases).
(SP − CP)/CP × 100. Profit and loss per cent are always on the cost price unless stated otherwise.
The reduction from the marked (list) price: discount % = (MP − SP)/MP × 100. Discount is always on the marked price.
SI = P × R × T/100: interest is earned only on the principal, so it grows linearly with time.
A = P(1 + R/100)ⁿ: interest is added to the principal each period, so it grows geometrically. CI = A − P.
For an amount A due after T years at R% simple interest, the present worth is PW = 100A/(100 + RT) and the true discount is TD = A − PW.
Sum of the values ÷ number of values. Adding a constant to every value adds it to the average.
Total distance ÷ total time. For two equal distances at x and y, it is the harmonic mean 2xy/(x + y), which is less than (x + y)/2 unless x = y.
For two ingredients at prices c (cheaper) and d (dearer) mixed to a mean m, the quantities are in the ratio (d − m) : (m − c).

lessons.examTip: Turn every percentage into a multiplying factor and multiply. “Up 20% then down 20%” is 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% fall; “marked up 40%, discount 15%” is 1.4 × 0.85 = 1.19, a 19% profit. One line, no base value needed.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without a calculator (about 75 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. Write the multiplying factor or formula you used beside each answer.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (wrong base, added successive percentages, arithmetic mean of speeds, SI instead of CI, forgot to convert km/h).
Write the fraction–percentage table and the formula sheet from memory; compare with the lesson and fix every gap.
For three problems, solve once by the long method and once by the shortcut, and note the time saved.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions (including the five-question DI set) at 60–75 seconds per question.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 15 problems finished within 20 minutes without a calculator.
Any fraction from 1/2 to 1/16 converted to a percentage in under 3 seconds.
Every successive-percentage and CI question solved in one line with multiplying factors.

quiz.question: The price of an article is first increased by 20% and then decreased by 20%. What is the net change in its price?
quiz.explanation: Factor = 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a 4% decrease. With the formula a + b + ab/100 = 20 − 20 − 400/100 = −4. “No change” forgets that the decrease acts on a larger base.

quiz.question: A car goes from town A to town B at 40 km/h and returns along the same road at 60 km/h. What is its average speed for the whole journey?
quiz.explanation: For equal distances, average speed = 2xy/(x + y) = 2 × 40 × 60/100 = 48 km/h. Check with 120 km each way: 3 h + 2 h = 5 h for 240 km, 48 km/h. The answer 50 is the arithmetic mean, the classic trap.

quiz.question: What is the simple interest on ₹ 8,000 at 5% per annum for 3 years?
quiz.explanation: SI = PRT/100 = 8000 × 5 × 3/100 = ₹ 1,200. ₹ 1,261 is the compound interest for the same data (8000 × 1.05³ − 8000), a common mix-up.

quiz.question: What is the compound interest on ₹ 10,000 at 10% per annum for 2 years, compounded annually?
quiz.explanation: A = 10000 × 1.1² = 12,100, so CI = ₹ 2,100. Shortcut: two successive 10% rises give 10 + 10 + 100/100 = 21%, and 21% of 10,000 = 2,100. ₹ 2,000 is the simple interest.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false

lessons.title: Arguments and deductive/inductive reasoning
lessons.summaryHtml: An argument is a set of statements in which some (the premises) are offered as reasons for another (the conclusion). Deductive arguments claim that the conclusion follows with necessity and are judged valid or invalid; inductive arguments claim only probability and are judged strong or weak. Much of this unit rests on categorical propositions (A, E, I, O), the distribution of terms, the classical square of opposition and the immediate inferences (conversion, obversion, contraposition). Categorical syllogisms are named by mood and figure, and their validity is settled by a handful of rules whose breaches have names: undistributed middle, illicit major, illicit minor, exclusive premises. The lesson also covers formal and informal fallacies, the uses of language, and connotation versus denotation, all of which NTA tests through match-the-list and statement questions.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

An argument is not a quarrel. It is a group of statements in which some statements, the premises, are offered as reasons for another statement, the conclusion. Logic asks one question about an argument: do the premises really support the conclusion? A deductive argument claims that its conclusion follows with necessity, so it is judged valid or invalid. An inductive argument claims only that its conclusion is probable, so it is judged strong or weak. Most Paper 1 questions in this unit work with categorical statements such as “All teachers are learners” or “Some policies are not effective”, and ask what follows from them, how they are related, or what has gone wrong in a piece of reasoning.

Why it matters for NET

Logical Reasoning is one of the most reliable scoring units of Paper 1, because its answers are fixed by rules rather than opinion. Questions from this lesson usually come as match-the-list items (square-of-opposition relations, fallacies with examples, mood–figure names, uses of language), Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason items on validity, soundness and distribution, and short “what follows” problems on the square of opposition and immediate inferences. The underlying source is standard introductory logic of the kind found in Copi’s Introduction to Logic. Once the rules are memorised, most of these questions take well under a minute.

Concepts in depth: the structure of an argument

Indicator words help locate the parts. Conclusion indicators: therefore, hence, so, thus, consequently, it follows that. Premise indicators: since, because, for, given that, as shown by. A passage with no claim that one statement supports another is not an argument; it may be a report, an illustration or an explanation. In an explanation the conclusion-like statement is already accepted (“The ground is wet because it rained”); in an argument it is being established.

PremisesConclusionCan the argument be valid?
All trueTrueYes (sound if valid)
All trueFalseNo, never
At least one falseTrueYes
At least one falseFalseYes

So validity is about form: whenever the premises are true, the conclusion must be true. Soundness adds the actual truth of every premise. For inductive arguments the parallel terms are strong/weak (how much the premises raise the probability of the conclusion) and cogent (strong with true premises). Unlike validity, inductive strength can change when new premises are added.

Argument forms in propositional shape recur in every paper: modus ponens (if p then q; p; so q), modus tollens (if p then q; not q; so not p), hypothetical syllogism (if p then q; if q then r; so if p then r), disjunctive syllogism (p or q; not p; so q) and the dilemmas. Their invalid look-alikes are affirming the consequent (if p then q; q; so p) and denying the antecedent (if p then q; not p; so not q).

Concepts in depth: categorical propositions

A standard-form categorical proposition has a quantifier (all, no, some), a subject term, a copula (are, are not) and a predicate term. Its quantity is universal or particular; its quality is affirmative or negative. The four letters come from the Latin AffIrmo and nEgO.

TypeFormQuantity, qualityDistributesBoolean reading
AAll S are Puniversal affirmativeS onlyS ∩ P̄ = ∅
ENo S is Puniversal negativeS and PS ∩ P = ∅
ISome S are Pparticular affirmativeneitherS ∩ P ≠ ∅
OSome S are not Pparticular negativeP onlyS ∩ P̄ ≠ ∅

A quick memory aid for distribution: universals distribute the subject, negatives distribute the predicate. Non-standard sentences must be translated first: “Only graduates are eligible” becomes “All eligible persons are graduates”; “None but the brave deserve the fair” becomes “All who deserve the fair are brave”; “Not all S are P” is the O proposition; “A few S are P” is I; singular statements such as “Socrates is wise” are treated as A.

Existential import. In the traditional (Aristotelian) view every term refers to an existing class. In the modern (Boolean) view only the particular propositions I and O assert existence; A and E merely deny that a region is occupied. This single difference decides which inferences survive.

Concepts in depth: the square of opposition

A ----- contraries ----- E
|  \                 /  |
|   contradictories     |
|  /                 \  |
I --- subcontraries --- O
(each vertical side: subalternation, A to I and E to O)
  • Contradictories (A–O, E–I): always opposite truth values.
  • Contraries (A–E): cannot both be true; can both be false.
  • Subcontraries (I–O): cannot both be false; can both be true.
  • Subalternation (A→I, E→O): truth flows down from the universal to the particular; falsity flows up from the particular to the universal.
GivenAEIO
A trueTFTF
A falseF??T
E trueFTFT
E false?FT?
I true?FT?
I falseFTFT
O trueF??T
O falseTFTF

Pattern: a true universal or a false particular settles all four; a false universal or a true particular settles only its contradictory. In the modern square, without existential import, only the contradictory relations remain.

Concepts in depth: immediate inferences

OperationHowValid for
Conversionswap S and PE and I; A only “by limitation” (All S are P ⇒ Some P are S); never O
Obversionchange quality and replace P by non-Pall four: A ⇒ No S is non-P; E ⇒ All S are non-P; I ⇒ Some S are not non-P; O ⇒ Some S are non-P
Contrapositionswap S and P and replace both by complementsA and O; E only by limitation; never I

Conversion and contraposition mirror each other: conversion works for E and I, contraposition for A and O.

Concepts in depth: categorical syllogisms, mood and figure

A categorical syllogism has exactly three terms, each used twice. The major term (P) is the predicate of the conclusion, the minor term (S) is its subject, and the middle term (M) appears in both premises only. The premise with P is the major premise and is written first. The mood lists the letters of the major premise, minor premise and conclusion; the figure is fixed by where M stands.

FigureMajor premiseMinor premiseMiddle term is…
1M – PS – Msubject then predicate
2P – MS – Mpredicate of both
3M – PM – Ssubject of both
4P – MM – Spredicate then subject

There are 4 × 4 × 4 = 64 moods and 64 × 4 = 256 forms. Only 15 are valid under the Boolean view: Barbara (AAA-1), Celarent (EAE-1), Darii (AII-1), Ferio (EIO-1); Cesare (EAE-2), Camestres (AEE-2), Festino (EIO-2), Baroco (AOO-2); Datisi (AII-3), Disamis (IAI-3), Ferison (EIO-3), Bocardo (OAO-3); Camenes (AEE-4), Dimaris (IAI-4), Fresison (EIO-4). Nine more become valid when an existence assumption is added, giving the traditional 24: AAI-1, EAO-1 and EAO-2, AEO-2 and AEO-4 (need S to exist); AAI-3, EAO-3, EAO-4 (need M); AAI-4 (needs P). Each figure then has exactly six valid forms.

The rules (a form is valid in the Boolean sense exactly when it breaks none):

  1. The middle term must be distributed at least once (else undistributed middle).
  2. A term distributed in the conclusion must be distributed in its premise (else illicit major or illicit minor).
  3. Two negative premises give no conclusion (exclusive premises).
  4. A negative premise requires a negative conclusion, and a negative conclusion requires a negative premise.
  5. Two universal premises cannot yield a particular conclusion (existential fallacy, Boolean view only).

Using more than three terms, often by an ambiguous middle term, is the fallacy of four terms. Corollaries worth remembering: two particular premises give no conclusion; if one premise is particular, the conclusion must be particular.

Concepts in depth: fallacies

A formal fallacy is a defect of form, visible after replacing the content with letters: undistributed middle, illicit process, exclusive premises, affirming the consequent, denying the antecedent. An informal fallacy is found only by looking at the content.

GroupFallacyWhat goes wrong
RelevanceAd hominemattacks the arguer instead of the argument (abusive, circumstantial, tu quoque)
Ad baculumappeal to force or threat
Ad misericordiamappeal to pity
Ad populumappeal to the crowd or popularity
Straw manrefutes a distorted version of the opponent’s view
Red herringdiverts attention to another issue
Ignoratio elenchiproves a different conclusion (missing the point)
Defective inductionAd ignorantiamsomething is true because it has not been proved false (or the reverse)
Ad verecundiamappeal to an authority outside its field
False causepost hoc ergo propter hoc: after this, therefore because of this
Hasty generalisationa general rule from too few or atypical cases
PresumptionPetitio principiibegging the question: the conclusion is hidden in a premise
Complex questiona question presupposes an unproved answer
Accidenta general rule applied to an exceptional case
False dilemmaonly two options offered when more exist
AmbiguityEquivocationone word used in two senses
Amphibolyambiguous grammar or sentence structure
Accentmeaning shifted by emphasis or quoting out of context
Compositionwhat is true of the parts is claimed of the whole
Divisionwhat is true of the whole is claimed of the parts

Textbooks differ slightly in grouping (older editions of Copi place ad ignorantiam and ad verecundiam under relevance), so NTA options usually use the uncontroversial members of each group.

Concepts in depth: uses of language, connotation and denotation

Language has three basic uses: informative (to state facts, true or false), expressive (to express or arouse feelings), and directive (to cause or prevent action: commands, requests). Two further uses are often added: ceremonial (greetings, rituals, mixing expressive and directive) and performative (the utterance itself does the act: “I apologise”, “I hereby declare the session open”). Words also carry emotive meaning alongside cognitive (literal) meaning; “bureaucrat” and “public servant” may name the same person with different feelings.

A general term has denotation (extension: the objects it applies to) and connotation (intension: the attributes an object must have to be included). As attributes are added the class usually shrinks, so an ordered series of terms in increasing intension is in decreasing (strictly, non-increasing) extension. Terms with the same denotation can have different connotations (“equilateral triangle” and “equiangular triangle”), and a term such as “unicorn” has connotation but an empty denotation. Definitions are classified by purpose: lexical (reports usage), stipulative (assigns a new meaning), precising (removes vagueness), theoretical and persuasive; and by technique: denotative (by examples) or connotative (genus and difference).

Concepts in depth: deductive and inductive reasoning

FeatureDeductiveInductive
Claimconclusion follows necessarilyconclusion is probable
Assessmentvalid/invalid; sound/unsoundstrong/weak; cogent/uncogent
New premisescannot make a valid argument invalidcan strengthen or weaken it
Contentconclusion unpacks what the premises containconclusion goes beyond the premises
Typical formssyllogisms, modus ponens, mathematicsgeneralisation, analogy, causal and statistical reasoning, prediction

“General to particular” versus “particular to general” is a rough guide only: “All swans observed so far are white, so the next swan will be white” is inductive though it ends in a particular. For causal induction, Mill’s methods are: agreement (the one factor common to all cases of the effect), difference (the one factor present when the effect occurs and absent when it does not), the joint method, residues (subtract known causes from a complex effect) and concomitant variation (the effect varies as the factor varies).

Worked examples

Example 1: mood, figure and validity. “No saints are liars. Some priests are liars. Therefore, some priests are not saints.”

  1. Conclusion: Some priests (S) are not saints (P). Major term = saints, minor term = priests, middle term = liars.
  2. Major premise (contains P): No saints are liars, E, form P–M. Minor premise: Some priests are liars, I, form S–M.
  3. Mood EIO; M is the predicate of both premises: figure 2. EIO-2 is Festino.
  4. Check the rules: M is distributed in the E premise; P is distributed in the conclusion (O distributes its predicate) and also in the E premise; one negative premise and a negative conclusion. Valid.

Example 2: naming the broken rule. “All metals are elements. No acids are metals. Therefore, no acids are elements.”

  1. Conclusion: No acids (S) are elements (P). Major premise: All metals are elements (A, M–P). Minor premise: No acids are metals (E, S–M). Form AEE-1.
  2. Middle term “metals” is distributed (subject of A). Good.
  3. The conclusion is E, so it distributes “elements”; in the major premise “elements” is the predicate of an A proposition and is undistributed. The argument goes beyond its evidence about P: illicit major.
  4. Counter-example with the same form: “All dogs are animals. No cats are dogs. Therefore, no cats are animals.” True premises, false conclusion, so the form is invalid even though the original conclusion happens to be true.

Example 3: the square in use. Suppose “Some researchers are not ethical” is false. Decide the other three propositions with the same terms.

  1. O false, so its contradictory A, “All researchers are ethical”, is true.
  2. A true: its contrary E, “No researchers are ethical”, is false.
  3. A true: its subaltern I, “Some researchers are ethical”, is true.

All three are determined: A true, E false, I true. Compare: if O were given true, only A (false) would be determined.

Example 4: immediate inferences. Start from “No students are absent.”

  • Converse: “No absent persons are students” (valid for E).
  • Obverse: “All students are non-absent” (change quality, complement the predicate).
  • Contrapositive: “No non-absent persons are non-students” is not valid; only by limitation “Some non-absent persons are not non-students” follows, and only under existential import.

Then from “Some students are not punctual” (O): the converse “Some punctual persons are not students” does not follow; the obverse “Some students are non-punctual” and the contrapositive “Some non-punctual persons are not non-students” do.

Example 5: classify the reasoning and the fallacy.

  1. “Every student I met from this college was polite, so all its students are polite.” Inductive generalisation; if the sample is tiny, hasty generalisation.
  2. “Since the new principal arrived, results improved; the principal caused the improvement.” False cause (post hoc).
  3. “Either we ban mobile phones completely or discipline will collapse.” False dilemma.
  4. “This textbook is reliable because this textbook says it is reliable.” Petitio principii.
  5. “Each brick is light, so the wall is light.” Composition.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
DistributionA: S; E: S and P; I: none; O: P
ContradictoriesA–O, E–I: opposite truth values always
Contraries / subcontrariesA–E not both true; I–O not both false
SubalternationA ⇒ I, E ⇒ O (truth down, falsity up)
ConversionE, I simply; A by limitation; O never
Obversionall four
ContrapositionA, O simply; E by limitation; I never
Figures1: M-P, S-M; 2: P-M, S-M; 3: M-P, M-S; 4: P-M, M-S
Counts64 moods, 256 forms, 15 valid (Boolean), 24 valid (traditional), 6 per figure
Rulesmiddle distributed once; no illicit process; not two negatives; negative ⇔ negative; no particular from two universals (Boolean)
Uses of languageinformative, expressive, directive (+ ceremonial, performative)
Intension and extensionvary inversely along a chain of genus and species
Mill’s methodsagreement, difference, joint, residues, concomitant variation

NTA traps

  • Not reordering the premises. Wrong: reading the mood in the order the premises are printed. Fix: find the major term from the conclusion’s predicate and put its premise first.
  • O distributes its subject. Wrong: “Some S are not P” is about all S. Fix: O distributes only P.
  • Contraries for contradictories. Wrong: “If A is false, E is true.” Fix: A and E can both be false; only O is fixed.
  • Converting A simply. Wrong: “All teachers are graduates, so all graduates are teachers.” Fix: only “Some graduates are teachers” (by limitation).
  • Valid means true. Wrong: a valid argument has a true conclusion. Fix: only a sound one does.
  • Illicit major versus undistributed middle. Check the middle term first, then the end terms; name the first broken rule that the question offers.
  • Composition versus hasty generalisation. Composition moves from parts to the whole of one object; hasty generalisation moves from some members to all members of a class.
  • “Only” reverses the terms. Wrong: “Only S are P” means All S are P. Fix: it means All P are S.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: square relations with pairs, fallacies with examples, sentences with uses of language, named moods with mood–figure codes.
  • Statement I/II and A-R: validity versus soundness, distribution, existential import, conversion rules.
  • Multiple select: which fallacies are formal, which inferences are valid, which pairs cannot both be true.
  • Order: terms by connotation or denotation.
  • Direct MCQ: the mood and figure of a syllogism, the rule it breaks, the truth values given one proposition.

Mini-example (A-R). A: “Some S are P” and “Some S are not P” can both be true. R: I and O cannot both be false. Both are true, but R speaks about both being false, so it does not explain A: option 2.

Mini-example (match). Pairs A–O, A–E, I–O, E–O against contradictories, contraries, subcontraries, subalternation. Fix the contradictory pair first (A–O), then eliminate every option that disagrees; usually one more pair settles the question.

Elimination trick: in any syllogism question, a form with two negative premises or two particular premises is invalid at once; a form with a negative premise and an affirmative conclusion is invalid at once. These three checks remove most distractors without drawing anything.
Watch out: square-of-opposition questions follow the traditional square unless the question says Boolean or modern. Mood–figure validity questions usually expect the 24 traditional forms; if the question says “unconditionally valid”, use the 15.

terms.definition: A group of statements in which one (the conclusion) is claimed to follow from the others (the premises).
A deductive argument is valid when it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. Validity depends on form, not on the actual truth of the statements.
A deductive argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are actually true; a sound argument always has a true conclusion.
A statement relating two classes: A (All S are P), E (No S is P), I (Some S are P), O (Some S are not P).
A term is distributed when the proposition says something about every member of its class. A distributes S; E distributes S and P; I distributes neither; O distributes P.
The chart of relations among A, E, I and O with the same terms: contradictories, contraries, subcontraries and subalternation.
Mood is the sequence of proposition types (major premise, minor premise, conclusion), e.g. AAA. Figure (1–4) is fixed by the position of the middle term in the premises.
The term that occurs in both premises but not in the conclusion; it must be distributed at least once.
An error in the content or context of reasoning (relevance, presumption, ambiguity), as opposed to a formal fallacy, which lies in the form.
Connotation (intension) is the set of attributes a term implies; denotation (extension) is the set of objects it applies to. More connotation usually means less denotation.

lessons.examTip: For any categorical syllogism, first rewrite it in standard order (major premise, minor premise, conclusion), then mark the distributed terms with the rule “A: subject; E: both; I: none; O: predicate”. Four checks settle almost every question: middle distributed once, no term distributed in the conclusion that is undistributed in its premise, not two negatives, and a negative conclusion exactly when one premise is negative.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every syllogism, write the major, minor and middle terms, the mood, the figure and the distributed terms in the margin before choosing an option.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (premises not reordered, O taken to distribute its subject, contraries read as contradictories, conversion of A taken as simple).
Draw the square of opposition from memory and fill in the eight-row “given one, what of the other three” table; compare with the fact sheet.
List the 15 unconditionally valid forms by name, grouped by figure, and mark the 9 conditional forms with the term that must exist.
Write one original example for each of twelve named informal fallacies, then redo the wrong problems after 24 hours and take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds each.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Mood and figure of any syllogism written in under 45 seconds, including reordering.
The square-of-opposition table reproduced from memory with no errors.

Option 3 swaps contraries and contradictories, the commonest slip.

quiz.question: In the traditional square of opposition, if “All S are P” is false, which of the following is correct?
options: “Some S are not P” is true, while “No S is P” and “Some S are P” are undetermined
