quiz.question: “We should ignore Dr Rao’s findings on plastic pollution; he was once fined for parking in a no-parking zone.” This commits which fallacy?
quiz.explanation: The argument rejects a claim by attacking the person who made it (abusive ad hominem); the parking fine is irrelevant to the evidence on pollution. Ad ignorantiam argues from lack of proof, hasty generalisation from too few cases, and petitio principii assumes its conclusion.

quiz.question: Which of the following is an inductive argument?
options: All metals conduct electricity; copper is a metal; so copper conducts electricity.
If the switch is on, the lamp glows; the switch is on; so the lamp glows.
Either the key is in the bag or in the drawer; it is not in the bag; so it is in the drawer.
Every sample of this alloy tested so far resisted corrosion; so the next sample will also resist corrosion.
quiz.explanation: The last argument generalises from observed cases to an unobserved one, so its conclusion is only probable however many samples were tested: induction. The first is Barbara, the second modus ponens, the third disjunctive syllogism, all deductive forms whose conclusions follow with necessity.

lessons.title: Analogies, Venn diagrams and syllogisms
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson turns the theory of the previous one into fast exam technique. Analogies test whether you can name the exact relation between two words, numbers or letters and find the pair with the same relation; analogical arguments are also judged for strength. Venn diagrams show classes as circles: they help pick the diagram that fits three classes, solve counting problems with the inclusion–exclusion formula, and test syllogisms for validity by shading empty regions and marking occupied ones with an X. The last part covers statement–conclusion syllogism questions: the standard conclusion for each pair of premises, the “either–or” case for complementary pairs, and possibility conclusions. Every such problem can be settled by trying to draw one diagram in which the premises are true and the conclusion is false.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This lesson is about three tools that make reasoning visible. An analogy says that two pairs are related in the same way: “hand is to glove as foot is to sock”. A Venn diagram draws classes as circles so that you can see which combinations of classes are empty and which are occupied. A syllogism question gives two or three statements and asks which conclusions must follow. All three reward the same habit: state the relation exactly, then check it against every option instead of trusting a first impression.

Why it matters for NET

Paper 1 regularly sets short statement–conclusion syllogisms, questions on choosing or reading Venn diagrams, counting problems on overlapping groups, and analogy items, alongside the more theoretical questions from the previous lesson. These are some of the quickest marks on the paper once the method is automatic, and they reappear inside Data Interpretation and Mathematical Reasoning in disguise, for instance as survey data on people using several services.

Concepts in depth: analogies

An analogy question has the form A : B :: C : ?. The skill is to name the relation in A : B precisely enough that only one option fits. Write a bridge sentence (“a sculptor shapes stone with a chisel”) and test each option with it. If more than one option fits, make the sentence more specific.

RelationExampleBridge sentence
SynonymsBrave : Courageousmeans the same as
AntonymsTimid : Boldmeans the opposite of
Part and wholePetal : Floweris part of
Worker and toolCarpenter : Sawworks with
Worker and productAuthor : Novelcreates
Cause and effectDrought : Faminecan cause
Raw material and productCotton : Clothis made into
Creature and dwellingBee : Hivelives in
Individual and groupCow : Herdforms a group called
DegreeWarm : Hotis a milder form of
Study and subjectOrnithology : Birdsis the study of
Unit and larger unitMinute : Houris a smaller unit of

Keep the order of the pair: Flower : Petal is whole to part, the reverse of Petal : Flower, and NTA includes reversed pairs as distractors. Also keep the same part of speech and the same degree.

Number and letter analogies hide an arithmetic rule. Try, in order: squares and cubes and their neighbours (n² ± 1, n³ ± 1, n³ − n), multiples, digit sums and products, and primes. For letters, write the alphabet positions (A = 1 … Z = 26); common rules are a constant shift (ACE : BDF moves each letter by 1), skipping by 2, and the “opposite letter” rule, where a letter and its opposite have positions adding to 27 (A–Z, B–Y, C–X).

Analogical arguments. In logic, an analogy is also a kind of inductive argument: “Drug X and drug Y share structure and side effects; X lowers blood pressure; so Y probably does too.” Its strength depends on: the number of analogues (more is stronger), the variety among the analogues (cases that differ in other ways but still agree make it stronger), the number and relevance of the shared similarities, the number of relevant disanalogies (these weaken it), and the modesty of the conclusion (a weaker claim is easier to support). Relevance matters most: one relevant similarity outweighs many irrelevant ones.

Concepts in depth: Venn diagrams for classes

Two classes can stand in only five relations (these are Gergonne’s relations): identical, the first inside the second, the second inside the first, overlapping, and disjoint. For three classes, first fix each pair, then draw.

ClassesRelationsDiagram
Earth, Solar system, Universeeach inside the nextthree nested circles
Pens, Pencils, Stationerypens and pencils disjoint, both inside stationerytwo separate circles inside a third
Mothers, Women, Teachersmothers inside women; teachers overlap bothone circle inside another, a third overlapping both
Doctors, Women, Indiansevery pair overlapsthree mutually overlapping circles
Rivers, Chairs, Planetsno overlaps at allthree separate circles

Concepts in depth: counting with Venn diagrams

For two sets, n(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B), and the number in neither is N − n(A ∪ B). For three sets, the union is n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C). Let S₁ = sum of the single totals, S₂ = sum of the pairwise totals and S₃ = the triple total. Then:

  • Exactly three = S₃.
  • Exactly two = S₂ − 3S₃ (each pairwise total includes the triple region once).
  • At least two = S₂ − 2S₃.
  • Exactly one = S₁ − 2S₂ + 3S₃.
  • Only A = n(A) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).

Always fill a three-circle diagram from the centre outwards: triple region first, then the “only two” regions, then the “only one” regions. The bounds for two sets are also tested: with n(A) = a, n(B) = b in a group of N, the overlap is at least a + b − N (if positive) and at most the smaller of a and b.

Concepts in depth: testing syllogisms with Venn diagrams

Draw three overlapping circles for S (minor term), P (major term) and M (middle term). They create 8 regions, written here by membership (a bar means “not”):

RegionIn S?In P?In M?
S P Myesyesyes
S P M̄yesyesno
S P̄ Myesnoyes
S P̄ M̄yesnono
S̄ P Mnoyesyes
S̄ P M̄noyesno
S̄ P̄ Mnonoyes
S̄ P̄ M̄nonono (outside all circles)
  1. “All X are Y” shades the part of X outside Y. “No X is Y” shades the overlap of X and Y.
  2. “Some X are Y” puts an X in the overlap of X and Y; “Some X are not Y” puts an X in the part of X outside Y.
  3. Diagram universal premises first. If the particular premise’s area is split by a third circle and neither part is shaded, place the X on the line: it means “at least one of these two regions is occupied, we do not know which”.
  4. Do not draw the conclusion. The syllogism is valid (Boolean) exactly when the diagram of the premises already shows the conclusion: the required region is fully shaded, or contains an X that is not sitting on a line.

A form such as AAI-3 fails this test, because two universal premises only shade. To test it traditionally, add the existence assumption as an X in the only unshaded part of the class assumed to exist; if that forces the conclusion, the form is conditionally valid.

Concepts in depth: statement–conclusion syllogisms

Test-setters follow three conventions: every class named has at least one member; “Some” means “at least one, possibly all”; and a conclusion “follows” only if it is true in every situation allowed by the statements. The standard results for a chain A–B, B–C are:

Statement 1Statement 2Definite conclusion about A and C
All A are BAll B are CAll A are C (and so Some C are A)
All A are BNo B is CNo A is C
Some A are BAll B are CSome A are C
Some A are BNo B is CSome A are not C
No A is BAll B are CSome C are not A (reversed)
No A is BSome B are CSome C are not A (reversed)
All A are BSome B are Cnone
Some + Some, No + No, All A are B + No C is A…check with a diagram; often none

Besides the chain conclusion, each statement gives its own immediate conclusions: “All A are B” gives “Some A are B” and “Some B are A”; “Some A are B” gives “Some B are A”; “No A is B” gives “No B is A” and “Some A are not B” and “Some B are not A”. “Some A are not B” gives no converse.

Either–or. Choose “Either I or II follows” only when (i) neither conclusion follows definitely, (ii) both have the same subject and predicate, and (iii) they are a complementary pair: Some/No (I–E) or All/Some-not (A–O). “Some A are C” and “Some A are not C” are not complementary, because both can be true.

Possibility. “All A being C is a possibility” follows if at least one diagram consistent with the statements makes it true, and fails if the statements rule it out (for example, if “No A is C” follows definitely).

Worked examples

Example 1: a number analogy. 7 : 50 :: 9 : ?

50 = 7² + 1, so the rule is n → n² + 1. For 9: 81 + 1 = 82. Before answering, check whether another rule also fits: 7 × 8 − 6 = 50 would give 9 × 10 − 6 = 84. When two rules fit, prefer the simpler one and look at the options, which normally contain only one of the candidates.

Example 2: three-set counting. In a survey of 200 teachers, 110 read a newspaper (N), 90 watch TV news (T) and 60 listen to radio news (R); 40 use N and T, 30 use N and R, 25 use T and R, and 10 use all three.

  1. Union = 110 + 90 + 60 − 40 − 30 − 25 + 10 = 175, so 200 − 175 = 25 use none.
  2. Exactly two = (40 + 30 + 25) − 3 × 10 = 65; at least two = 95 − 20 = 75.
  3. Only N = 110 − 40 − 30 + 10 = 50; only T = 90 − 40 − 25 + 10 = 35; only R = 60 − 30 − 25 + 10 = 15; exactly one = 100.
  4. Check: 100 + 65 + 10 = 175.

Example 3: Venn test of a valid form. All M are P; some S are M; therefore some S are P (Darii, AII-1).

  1. “All M are P”: shade the part of M outside P, the regions S P̄ M and S̄ P̄ M.
  2. “Some S are M”: the overlap of S and M consists of S P M and S P̄ M; the second is shaded, so the X goes in S P M.
  3. The conclusion needs an X in the overlap of S and P, and S P M has one. Valid.

Example 4: Venn test of invalid forms.

(a) All P are M; all S are M; therefore all S are P (AAA-2). Shading gives S P M̄, S̄ P M̄ (from the first premise) and S P̄ M̄ (from the second). The conclusion needs the whole of S outside P shaded, that is S P̄ M̄ and S P̄ M; the region S P̄ M is not shaded. Invalid (undistributed middle).

(b) Some M are P; all S are M; therefore some S are P (IAI-1). Shade S P M̄ and S P̄ M̄. The X for “Some M are P” may be in S P M or S̄ P M, both unshaded, so it sits on the line of S. Nothing guarantees an X inside S. Invalid, again undistributed middle.

Example 5: statement–conclusion with either–or. Statements: All A are B. Some B are C. Conclusions: I. Some A are C. II. No A is C.

  1. Try to falsify I: put the C’s only in the part of B outside A. Both statements hold and I is false.
  2. Try to falsify II: let C overlap A. Both statements hold and II is false.
  3. Neither follows, but they have the same terms and are an I–E pair, so exactly one is true in every situation: either I or II follows.

Example 6: possibility and three statements. Statements: All cats are dogs. Some dogs are birds. No bird is a rat.

  • “Some dogs are cats” follows (converse by limitation of the first statement).
  • “Some dogs are not rats” follows: the dogs that are birds cannot be rats.
  • “No cat is a rat” does not follow: cats may be dogs outside the birds, and such dogs may be rats. But “Some cats being rats is a possibility” is true.
  • “Some cats are birds” does not follow; it is only possible.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Two setsn(A ∪ B) = n(A) + n(B) − n(A ∩ B); overlap between max(0, a + b − N) and min(a, b)
Three setsunion = S₁ − S₂ + S₃
Exactly two / at least two / exactly oneS₂ − 3S₃ / S₂ − 2S₃ / S₁ − 2S₂ + 3S₃
Regions3 circles: 8 regions (7 inside); n general sets: 2^n
Venn testshade universals first; X on a line when undecided; valid if conclusion is already shown
Chain resultsAll+All = All; All+No = No; Some+All = Some; Some+No = Some-not; No+All = Some-not (reversed)
No definite conclusionAll A are B + Some B are C; Some + Some; No + No
Complementary pairsSome–No (I–E), All–Some-not (A–O), same terms
Letter positionsA = 1 … Z = 26; opposite letters add to 27
Analogical strengthmore analogues, more variety, more relevant similarities, fewer disanalogies, modest conclusion

NTA traps

  • “Some” as “not all”. Wrong: “Some A are B” implies “Some A are not B”. Fix: “Some” allows “all”.
  • Converting A simply. Wrong: “All A are B” gives “All B are A”. Fix: only “Some B are A”.
  • Either–or for any undecided pair. Fix: only for a complementary pair with the same subject and predicate.
  • Reversed analogy pairs. Wrong: choosing Hive : Bee for Bird : Nest. Fix: keep the order of the first pair.
  • Pairwise totals as “exactly two”. A pairwise total includes the people in all three; subtract them.
  • X placed before shading. Leads to an X in a region that should have been empty.
  • Relying on real-world truth. “All pens are fruits” is to be accepted as given; judge only what follows.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct MCQ: “Statements … Conclusions I, II”, with the five standard options; “which diagram best represents…”; analogy completion.
  • Numerical: counts from a three-set survey; minimum or maximum overlap.
  • Match the following: analogy pairs with relations; class triples with diagram shapes; premise pairs with conclusions.
  • Multiple select: which conclusions follow from given statements.
  • A-R / Statement I-II: rules of the Venn method, complementary pairs, strength of analogical arguments.

Mini-example (match). A. All A are B; All B are C. B. All A are B; No B is C. C. Some A are B; No B is C. D. All A are B; Some B are C. Against: I. Some A are not C, II. All A are C, III. No definite conclusion, IV. No A is C. Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III. Settle D first: “All + Some” is the classic “no conclusion” pair.

Speed trick: a conclusion can only follow if the middle term is distributed in some statement and the conclusion is particular whenever a statement is particular. Checking these two points eliminates most wrong conclusions without drawing.
Watch out: questions on syllogism validity in the logic sense may use the Boolean view (no existential import), while statement–conclusion questions assume every class has members. Read which one the question means.

terms.definition: A comparison of two pairs that share the same relation (A : B :: C : D); in argument, an inference that because two things are alike in known respects they are alike in a further respect.
A short sentence that states the exact relation in the first pair (“a carpenter uses a saw”) and is then tested on each option.
A diagram of overlapping circles in which each region stands for a combination of class memberships; three circles give 8 regions including the outside.
In a Venn test, marking a region as empty; universal propositions (A and E) are drawn by shading.
In a Venn test, a particular premise whose X could go in either of two unshaded regions is placed on the line between them, meaning “at least one of these”.
n(A ∪ B ∪ C) = n(A) + n(B) + n(C) − n(A ∩ B) − n(A ∩ C) − n(B ∩ C) + n(A ∩ B ∩ C).
Two conclusions with the same terms such that exactly one must be true, e.g. “Some A are C” and “No A is C”; if neither follows definitely, the answer is “either I or II”.
A conclusion such as “All A being C is a possibility”; it follows if at least one diagram consistent with the statements makes it true.
The convention that every class named in a syllogism question has at least one member.

lessons.examTip: In a statement–conclusion question, never ask “does this look true?” Ask “can I draw one diagram where every statement is true and this conclusion is false?” If you can, the conclusion does not follow. Then check the leftover conclusions for a complementary pair.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).

Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every syllogism, draw the minimal diagram and one counter-diagram per conclusion; for every counting problem, fill the three-circle diagram from the centre outwards.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (“Some” read as “not all”, A converted simply, either–or used for a non-complementary pair, pairwise totals taken as “exactly two”, a reversed analogy pair).
Write the chain-results table (All+All, All+No, Some+All, Some+No, No+All, No+Some, All+Some) from memory and check it against the fact sheet.
Test five syllogistic forms of your choice (at least two invalid) with a three-circle Venn diagram, shading before marking any X.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Any two-statement syllogism question answered in under 60 seconds, with the either–or case recognised correctly.
A three-set counting problem completed with a full region-by-region diagram that adds up to the total.

quiz.question: Author : Novel :: Composer : ?
quiz.explanation: Bridge sentence: “an author creates a novel”. A composer creates a symphony. An orchestra performs it, an instrument is a tool for playing it, and an audience hears it: each is related to a composer, but not by “creates”.
28 = 3³ + 1, so the rule is n → n³ + 1. For 5: 5³ + 1 = 125 + 1 = 126. 125 forgets the “+ 1”, and 216 is 6³.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: A carpenter works with a saw (worker and tool). A petal is part of a flower (part and whole). A drought can cause a famine (cause and effect). Timid and bold are opposites (antonyms). The first option swaps the last two relations.

quiz.question: Which diagram best represents the classes Mothers, Women and Teachers?
options: One circle inside another, and a third circle overlapping both
Two separate circles inside a third circle
quiz.explanation: Every mother is a woman, so the Mothers circle lies inside the Women circle. Some teachers are women and some are not; some teachers are mothers and some are not; so the Teachers circle overlaps both. Nested circles would make every woman a teacher or every teacher a woman.

quiz.question: Of 120 researchers, 70 use SPSS, 55 use R and 40 use Python; 25 use SPSS and R, 20 use SPSS and Python, 15 use R and Python, and 8 use all three. How many use exactly one of the three tools?
quiz.explanation: Only SPSS = 70 − 25 − 20 + 8 = 33. Only R = 55 − 25 − 15 + 8 = 23. Only Python = 40 − 20 − 15 + 8 = 13. Exactly one = 33 + 23 + 13 = 69. Check: exactly two = (25 + 20 + 15) − 3 × 8 = 36, all three = 8, and 69 + 36 + 8 = 113 = the number using at least one; 120 − 113 = 7 use none. 113 is the union and 44 is “at least two”.

quiz.question:
Statements: All A are B. Some B are C.
Conclusions: I. Some A are C. II. Some C are B.
options: Either conclusion I or II follows
Neither conclusion I nor II follows
quiz.explanation: II is the converse of “Some B are C”, and I propositions convert simply, so II follows. I does not: the B’s that are C may all lie outside A (draw A inside B and C overlapping only the part of B outside A). “All + Some” gives no definite conclusion between A and C.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: If the X is placed first, it may have to sit on a line between two regions; shading one of them later then forces the X into the other, which is easy to overlook. Shading first shows directly where the X must go. R is exactly the reason for the rule.

stmts: Assertion (A): In testing a syllogism with a Venn diagram, a universal premise should be diagrammed before a particular premise.
Reason (R): Shading the empty regions first may leave only one possible region for the X of the particular premise.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: I and E propositions with the same terms are contradictories, so Statement I is true. The premises give “All A are C” and its converse by limitation “Some C are A”, but not “All C are A”: C may be much larger than A. Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: “Some A are C” and “No A is C” form a complementary pair: in every situation exactly one of them is true.
Statement II: From “All A are B” and “All B are C”, the conclusion “All C are A” follows.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question:
Statements: No A is B. All B are C.
Which of the following conclusions definitely follow?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: B has members, all of them are C and none are A, so those members are C that are not A (A). “All B are C” gives “Some C are B” by limitation (C). “No A is B” converts to “No B is A”, which gives “Some B are not A” (D). B fails: A may overlap the part of C outside B. E is the invalid simple converse of an A proposition.

stmts: A. Some C are not A
B. No A is C
C. Some C are B
D. Some B are not A
E. All C are B

quiz.question: Arrange the steps of testing a categorical syllogism by the Venn diagram method in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: The diagram comes first (A). Universal premises are shaded before particular ones are marked (B before C). The conclusion is never drawn; you inspect whether it is already there (D), and the verdict follows (E). Option 2 puts the X before the shading, the usual error.

lessons.title: Indian logic
lessons.summaryHtml: Indian logic studies pramāṇa, the valid means of knowledge, and above all anumāna, inference. The classical list has six pramāṇas: pratyakṣa (perception), anumāna (inference), upamāna (comparison), śabda (verbal testimony), arthāpatti (postulation) and anupalabdhi (non-apprehension); schools differ on how many they accept, from one for the Cārvāka to all six for Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita Vedānta. An inference has three terms: pakṣa (the subject, like the hill), sādhya (what is proved, like fire) and hetu (the reason, like smoke), joined by vyāpti, the invariable concomitance of hetu and sādhya. The Nyāya school sets out an inference for others in five members and lists five hetvābhāsas, the fallacies that arise when the hetu is defective. NTA asks these as match-the-list, order and statement questions, so exact names and their meanings matter.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Classical Indian philosophy asks two linked questions: how do we come to know anything, and how can we tell that what we know is valid? The means of valid knowledge is called pramāṇa. Four words go together: pramātā (the knower), prameya (the object known), pramāṇa (the means) and pramā (the valid knowledge that results). Memory, doubt (saṃśaya), error (viparyaya) and hypothetical reasoning (tarka) are not pramā in Nyāya. Among the pramāṇas, inference (anumāna) received the most careful analysis, especially in the Nyāya school founded on the Nyāya Sūtra of Gautama (Akṣapāda). The unit tests which pramāṇas each school accepts, how an inference is built, and how it goes wrong.

Why it matters for NET

Indian logic is named explicitly in the Paper 1 syllabus under Logical Reasoning, and it is a regular source of questions. The favourite formats are match-the-list (pramāṇa with meaning, school with number of pramāṇas, hetvābhāsa with example), order questions on the five members of an inference, and multiple-select or statement questions on hetvābhāsas and the terms pakṣa, sādhya, hetu and vyāpti. Everything is factual and finite, so a clear table in memory is worth several marks.

Concepts in depth: the six pramāṇas

PramāṇaEnglishWhat it givesStock example
Pratyakṣaperceptionknowledge from sense–object contactseeing a pot
Anumānainferenceknowledge through a mark invariably connected with what is inferredfire on the hill from smoke
Upamānacomparisonknowledge of the relation between a name and its object, through similarityrecognising a gavaya (wild ox) from the description “it is like a cow”
Śabdaverbal testimonyknowledge from the statement of a reliable person (āpta)learning a fact from an expert
Arthāpattipostulation, presumptionassuming a fact without which known facts cannot be reconciledfat Devadatta who does not eat by day eats at night
Anupalabdhinon-apprehensiondirect knowledge of an absence“there is no jar on this floor”

Pratyakṣa. The Nyāya Sūtra defines perception as knowledge arising from contact of sense and object (indriyārtha-sannikarṣa) that is not verbal, not erroneous and definite. Nyāya divides it in two ways. By content: nirvikalpaka (indeterminate: the bare grasp of an object before naming or qualifying it) and savikalpaka (determinate: “this is a pot”). By kind of contact: laukika (ordinary: external through the five senses, internal through manas) and alaukika (extraordinary), of three kinds: sāmānyalakṣaṇa (perceiving a whole class through its universal, as in knowing all smoke through smokeness), jñānalakṣaṇa (a past cognition brings a quality into present perception, as when distant sandalwood is “seen” as fragrant), and yogaja (the intuition of yogins). Ordinary contact (sannikarṣa) is of six kinds, from simple conjunction (eye and pot) to the special relation (viśeṣaṇatā) through which Nyāya says we perceive absence.

Upamāna. A city dweller is told by a forester that a gavaya is an animal like a cow. Later, in the forest, he sees such an animal and knows “this is what is called gavaya”. The result (upamiti) is knowledge of the relation between a name and the thing named (saṃjñā–saṃjñi-sambandha). Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā and Advaita accept it; Vaiśeṣika and Sāṅkhya reduce it to inference, and the Buddhists reject it.

Śabda. Nyāya defines it as the instructive statement of a trustworthy person (āptopadeśa). Testimony is divided into laukika (secular) and vaidika (scriptural), or into that about perceptible and imperceptible matters. A sentence yields knowledge only if it satisfies four conditions: ākāṅkṣā (expectancy: the words need one another to complete the sense), yogyatā (compatibility: “he wets the plants with fire” fails), sannidhi or āsatti (proximity: the words are uttered close together in time), and tātparya (the speaker’s intention).

Arthāpatti. When two known facts seem to conflict, we postulate a third that removes the conflict: a man known to be alive is not at home, so he must be somewhere outside. Mīmāṃsā and Advaita treat this as a separate pramāṇa; Nyāya treats it as a negative (purely vyatirekī) inference.

Anupalabdhi. The Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas and Advaitins hold that the absence of a jar on a well-lit floor is known neither by perception (no sense contact with an absence) nor by inference, but by the non-apprehension of something that would have been perceived if present (yogya-anupalabdhi). Non-perception of things that could not be perceived anyway, such as atoms, proves nothing. Nyāya says absence is perceived; Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā rejects anupalabdhi.

Concepts in depth: which school accepts what

SchoolNumberPramāṇas accepted
Cārvāka (Lokāyata)1pratyakṣa
Buddhist (Dignāga, Dharmakīrti)2pratyakṣa, anumāna
Vaiśeṣika2pratyakṣa, anumāna
Sāṅkhya, Yoga3pratyakṣa, anumāna, śabda
Jaina (as usually charted)3pratyakṣa, anumāna, śabda (āgama)
Nyāya4pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, śabda
Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā5the four of Nyāya + arthāpatti
Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā, Advaita Vedānta6the five + anupalabdhi

Two refinements are worth knowing. The Buddhists link their two pramāṇas to two kinds of object: perception grasps the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa), inference the general feature (sāmānyalakṣaṇa). The Jainas themselves divide pramāṇa into pratyakṣa and parokṣa (indirect), placing memory, recognition, tarka, inference and scripture under parokṣa; exam charts usually count them as accepting three. Standard textbooks also summarise the debate on how validity is known: Nyāya holds that both validity and invalidity are known extrinsically (parataḥ), while Mīmāṃsā holds that validity is intrinsic (svataḥ) and invalidity extrinsic.

Concepts in depth: anumāna and vyāpti

Anu means “after” and māna means “knowledge”: inference is knowledge that follows other knowledge. It has three terms:

TermMeaningIn the stock exampleAristotelian parallel
Pakṣasubject of the inferencethe hillminor term
Sādhyawhat is to be proved of the pakṣafiremajor term
Hetu (liṅga, sādhana)reason or marksmokemiddle term

Vyāpti is the invariable concomitance of hetu and sādhya. The hetu is the vyāpya (the pervaded) and the sādhya the vyāpaka (the pervader): wherever smoke is, fire is, but not the other way round (a red-hot iron ball has fire without smoke). When the two terms have unequal extension the vyāpti is viṣama (non-equipollent); when they coincide, as in “whatever is produced is non-eternal” and “whatever is non-eternal is produced”, it is sama (equipollent). The positive form “wherever smoke, there fire” is anvaya vyāpti; the negative form “wherever no fire, there no smoke” is vyatireka vyāpti.

Nyāya lists the ways vyāpti is established: observing agreement in presence (anvaya) and in absence (vyatireka), never observing a contrary case (vyabhicāra-agraha), eliminating hidden conditions (upādhi-nirāsa), indirect proof by tarka, and sāmānyalakṣaṇa perception of the universal. An upādhi is a hidden condition on which an apparent concomitance depends: fire produces smoke only with wet fuel, so “wherever there is fire, there is smoke” is not a vyāpti. The Cārvākas deny that vyāpti can ever be established, and so reject inference.

How an inference arises. One sees smoke on the hill; recalls the vyāpti “wherever smoke, there fire”; forms the parāmarśa (liṅga-parāmarśa) “this hill has smoke, which is pervaded by fire”; and then has the inferential cognition (anumiti) “the hill has fire”. Anumiti is the cognition produced by parāmarśa. (Texts differ on what counts as the karaṇa: Keśava Miśra’s Tarkabhāṣā calls liṅga-parāmarśa itself anumāna, while Annambhaṭṭa’s Tarkasaṃgraha makes knowledge of vyāpti the karaṇa and parāmarśa its operation, vyāpāra. Exam questions test the sequence, not this debate.)

Five marks of a valid hetu. (1) Pakṣadharmatā: it is present in the pakṣa. (2) Sapakṣasattva: it is present in sapakṣas, cases where the sādhya is known to be present (the kitchen). (3) Vipakṣāsattva: it is absent from vipakṣas, cases where the sādhya is known to be absent (a lake). (4) Abādhitaviṣayatva: its conclusion is not contradicted by a stronger pramāṇa. (5) Asatpratipakṣatva: there is no equally strong counter-reason. The Buddhist logicians use the first three as the “three marks” (trairūpya) of a good reason.

Concepts in depth: kinds of anumāna

BasisKindsMeaning and example
Purposesvārthānumānainference for oneself; no formal statement needed
parārthānumānainference for others, set out in the five members
Nyāya Sūtrapūrvavatfrom a perceived cause to an unperceived effect: dark clouds, so rain will come
śeṣavatfrom a perceived effect to its cause: a river in flood, so rain has fallen upstream
sāmānyatodṛṣṭafrom a general uniformity that is not causal: the sun’s change of place, so it moves
Navya-Nyāya (form of vyāpti)kevalānvayīonly positive vyāpti, no vipakṣa exists: “the pot is nameable because it is knowable”
kevalavyatirekīonly negative vyāpti, no sapakṣa exists: “earth differs from the other elements because it has smell”
anvaya-vyatirekīboth positive and negative vyāpti: the smoke–fire inference

Commentators give more than one reading of pūrvavat, śeṣavat and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa; the cause-to-effect and effect-to-cause reading above is the one most textbooks and exam keys use.

Concepts in depth: the five-membered inference

MemberNameStock example
1Pratijñā (proposition, thesis)The hill has fire.
2Hetu (reason)Because it has smoke.
3Udāharaṇa (example)Whatever has smoke has fire, as in a kitchen.
4Upanaya (application)This hill has smoke that is pervaded by fire.
5Nigamana (conclusion)Therefore the hill has fire.

Compared with Aristotle’s syllogism, the Nyāya form states the conclusion first and last, and its third member combines a universal rule with a concrete example, so it is at once deductive (it applies a universal) and inductive (the rule rests on observed cases). The Mīmāṃsakas and Vedāntins hold that three members are enough (either the first three or the last three), and the Buddhists reduce it to two (udāharaṇa and upanaya).

Concepts in depth: hetvābhāsas

HetvābhāsaOther nameWhat is wrongCondition brokenExample
Savyabhicāraanaikāntika (irregular)the hetu is not invariably tied to the sādhyavipakṣāsattvathe hill has fire because it is knowable
Viruddhacontradictorythe hetu proves the absence of the sādhyasapakṣasattva (found only in vipakṣa)sound is eternal because it is produced
Satpratipakṣaprakaraṇasama (counterbalanced)an equally strong reason proves the oppositeasatpratipakṣatva“sound is eternal because audible” against “sound is non-eternal because produced”
Asiddhasādhyasama (unproved)the hetu itself is not establishedpakṣadharmatā (or a sound vyāpti)sound is a quality because it is visible
Bādhitakālātīta, kālātyayāpadiṣṭa (contradicted)the sādhya is disproved by a stronger pramāṇaabādhitaviṣayatvafire is cold because it is a substance

Savyabhicāra has three kinds: sādhāraṇa (too wide, found in sapakṣa and vipakṣa alike, as “knowable” above), asādhāraṇa (too narrow, found only in the pakṣa: “sound is eternal because it has soundness (śabdatva)”, since soundness belongs to sound alone), and anupasaṃhārī (non-conclusive because the pakṣa includes everything, leaving no sapakṣa or vipakṣa: “all things are non-eternal because they are knowable”). Asiddha also has three: āśrayāsiddha (the pakṣa does not exist: “the sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus”), svarūpāsiddha (the hetu is not in the pakṣa: “sound is a quality because it is visible”), and vyāpyatvāsiddha (the supposed vyāpti depends on an upādhi: “the hill has smoke because it has fire”).

Worked examples

Example 1: name the pramāṇa.

  1. A student who was told “a zebra looks like a striped horse” sees one at the zoo and knows “this is a zebra”: upamāna.
  2. You know your friend was in Delhi at noon and is in Mumbai at 3 p.m.; you conclude he must have flown: arthāpatti (for Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta; Nyāya calls it inference).
  3. Entering a well-lit room, you know there is no laptop on the desk: anupalabdhi (Bhāṭṭa, Advaita); perception of absence for Nyāya.
  4. You learn the boiling point of ethanol from a chemistry professor: śabda.

Example 2: identify the terms and the kind. “There has been heavy rain in the hills, because the river here is in flood.”

  1. Pakṣa: the hills (the place about which something is inferred). Sādhya: recent heavy rain. Hetu: the flood in the river below.
  2. Vyāpti: whenever this river floods in this way, there has been heavy rain upstream; a sapakṣa is last monsoon’s flood after known rain.
  3. The inference goes from a perceived effect to an unperceived cause, so it is śeṣavat.
  4. A careful reasoner checks for an upādhi: if a dam upstream released water, the flood would not prove rain.

Example 3: write the five members. Thesis: the kettle is hot.

  1. Pratijñā: The kettle is hot.
  2. Hetu: Because steam is coming out of it.
  3. Udāharaṇa: Whatever gives out steam is hot, as a pressure cooker on the stove.
  4. Upanaya: This kettle gives out steam, which is pervaded by heat.
  5. Nigamana: Therefore the kettle is hot.

Example 4: diagnose the hetvābhāsa.

  1. “The lake has fire, because it has smoke.” The hetu (smoke) is not present in the pakṣa (lake): asiddha, of the svarūpāsiddha kind.
  2. “The hill has fire, because it is a physical object.” Physical objects include lakes, which lack fire: the hetu occurs in a vipakṣa, so savyabhicāra (sādhāraṇa).
  3. “Ice is hot, because it is a substance.” Touch directly shows that ice is cold: bādhita.
  4. “The mind is eternal, because it is produced.” Produced things are non-eternal: viruddha.

NTA traps

  • Swapping the last two pramāṇas. Wrong: Prābhākara accepts anupalabdhi. Fix: arthāpatti is the fifth (Prābhākara), anupalabdhi the sixth (Bhāṭṭa, Advaita).
  • Pakṣa and sādhya reversed. The hill is the pakṣa; fire, what is proved about it, is the sādhya.
  • Viruddha versus bādhita. Viruddha: the reason itself proves the opposite. Bādhita: the reason may look fine, but another pramāṇa (usually perception) contradicts the conclusion.
  • Savyabhicāra versus satpratipakṣa. One reason pointing both ways is savyabhicāra; two different reasons pointing opposite ways is satpratipakṣa.
  • Conditions counted as fallacies. Pakṣadharmatā and vyāpti appear as distractors in “which are hetvābhāsas”.
  • Order of members. Udāharaṇa (the universal rule with example) comes before upanaya (its application).
  • Nyāya’s count. Nyāya accepts four pramāṇas; Vaiśeṣika, its sister school, accepts two.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: pramāṇa and meaning; school and number; hetvābhāsa and example; members and content.
  • Order: the five members, or schools by number of pramāṇas.
  • Multiple select: which are hetvābhāsas, which schools accept a given pramāṇa, which are kinds of perception.
  • A-R / Statement I-II: Cārvāka’s rejection of inference, Nyāya’s treatment of arthāpatti, definitions of vyāpti and parāmarśa.

Mini-example (order). Arrange schools by increasing number of pramāṇas: Nyāya, Cārvāka, Advaita, Sāṅkhya, Buddhist. Answer: Cārvāka (1), Buddhist (2), Sāṅkhya (3), Nyāya (4), Advaita (6).

Mini-example (A-R). A: The Cārvākas reject anumāna. R: They hold that vyāpti cannot be known with certainty, since perception reaches only particular cases. Both true, and R explains A: option 1.

Memory aid: the hetvābhāsas in the Nyāya Sūtra order are “S-V-P-S-K”: savyabhicāra, viruddha, prakaraṇasama (satpratipakṣa), sādhyasama (asiddha), kālātīta (bādhita).
Watch out: spellings vary between books (upaman/upamāna, savyabhichara/savyabhicāra, satpratipaksha/sat-pratipakṣa). Read the options for the idea, not the diacritics.

terms.definition: A means of valid knowledge (the special cause of pramā). Pramātā is the knower, prameya the object known, pramā the valid knowledge.
Perception: knowledge produced by contact of a sense organ with its object; divided into nirvikalpaka (indeterminate) and savikalpaka (determinate).
Inference: knowledge that follows other knowledge, reached through a mark (liṅga or hetu) known to be invariably connected with what is inferred.
Invariable concomitance: the universal relation “wherever there is smoke, there is fire” between hetu (the pervaded) and sādhya (the pervader).
The subject of inference (hill), the property to be proved (fire) and the reason (smoke); roughly the minor, major and middle terms.
The consideration that the pakṣa has a hetu pervaded by the sādhya (“this hill has smoke, which is pervaded by fire”); in Nyāya the immediate cause of the inference.
The five-membered inference for others: pratijñā, hetu, udāharaṇa, upanaya, nigamana.
A fallacious reason that looks like a hetu: savyabhicāra, viruddha, satpratipakṣa, asiddha and bādhita.
Comparison: knowledge of the relation between a name and the thing named, gained by seeing a similarity described earlier (the gavaya example).
Non-apprehension: the direct knowledge of an absence, such as “there is no jar on this floor”, accepted as a separate pramāṇa by Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita Vedānta.

lessons.examTip: Learn the school–pramāṇa ladder as a single line: Cārvāka 1; Buddhist and Vaiśeṣika 2; Sāṅkhya, Yoga (and Jaina, as usually charted) 3; Nyāya 4 (adds upamāna); Prābhākara 5 (adds arthāpatti); Bhāṭṭa and Advaita 6 (adds anupalabdhi). Each step adds exactly one pramāṇa, in that order.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every hetvābhāsa or kind-of-inference problem, write the pakṣa, sādhya and hetu before answering.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (fifth and sixth pramāṇas swapped, pakṣa and sādhya reversed, viruddha taken for bādhita, a condition taken for a fallacy).
From memory, write the school–pramāṇa ladder, the five members with the smoke–fire example, and the five hetvābhāsas with their sūtra names; compare with the fact sheet.
Make up one original example for each pramāṇa and for each hetvābhāsa (with its subtype), and state which condition of a valid hetu it breaks.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
The number of pramāṇas for any school stated instantly, with the added pramāṇa named.
Any hetvābhāsa example classified, with its subtype, in under 45 seconds.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Upamāna is knowledge by comparison (IV). Arthāpatti is postulation or presumption of a fact that explains an apparent conflict (III). Anupalabdhi is non-apprehension, the means of knowing an absence (II). Śabda is verbal testimony of a reliable person (I). The first option swaps arthāpatti and anupalabdhi, the two pramāṇas most often confused.

b: I. Verbal testimony
II. Non-apprehension
III. Postulation (presumption)
IV. Comparison

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following schools accepts all six pramāṇas, including arthāpatti and anupalabdhi?
quiz.explanation: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā and Advaita Vedānta accept all six. Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts five, rejecting anupalabdhi. Nyāya accepts four (perception, inference, comparison, testimony), and Sāṅkhya three.

quiz.question: Arrange the members of the Nyāya five-membered inference (pañcāvayava) in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: The hill has fire (pratijñā); because it has smoke (hetu); whatever has smoke has fire, as in a kitchen (udāharaṇa); this hill has smoke that is pervaded by fire (upanaya); therefore the hill has fire (nigamana): B, D, E, A, C. The thesis comes first and is restated as the conclusion at the end.

stmts: A. Upanaya (application)
B. Pratijñā (proposition)
C. Nigamana (conclusion)
D. Hetu (reason)
E. Udāharaṇa (example with the universal rule)
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In the inference “The hill has fire, because it has smoke”, which of the following is the pakṣa?
quiz.explanation: The pakṣa is the subject about which something is inferred: the hill. Fire is the sādhya (what is to be proved), smoke is the hetu (the reason), and the kitchen is a sapakṣa, a familiar case where smoke and fire are seen together.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Savyabhicāra means “irregular” or “straying”: the hetu is not invariably connected with the sādhya. In its common form (sādhāraṇa), the hetu occurs in both sapakṣa and vipakṣa, as in “the hill has fire because it is knowable”; it points to both sides, which is exactly what anaikāntika means. R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The savyabhicāra hetu is also called anaikāntika (“not one-sided”).
Reason (R): Such a hetu is found both where the sādhya is present and where it is absent, so it does not lead to one conclusion only.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: The Cārvāka (Lokāyata) materialists accept only pratyakṣa and reject inference because, they argue, vyāpti can never be established. Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts five pramāṇas and rejects anupalabdhi; it is the Bhāṭṭa school and Advaita Vedānta that add it.

stmts: Statement I: The Cārvāka school accepts perception as the only valid means of knowledge.
Statement II: Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts anupalabdhi as an independent pramāṇa.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following are hetvābhāsas (fallacies of inference) in Nyāya?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: The five hetvābhāsas are savyabhicāra, viruddha, satpratipakṣa, asiddha and bādhita. Pakṣadharmatā (presence of the hetu in the pakṣa) is a condition of a valid hetu, not a fallacy, and vyāpti is the invariable concomitance on which every valid inference rests.

stmts: A. Asiddha
B. Pakṣadharmatā
C. Viruddha
D. Satpratipakṣa
E. Vyāpti
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: “Sound is eternal, because it is produced.” Which hetvābhāsa does this inference commit?
quiz.explanation: Whatever is produced is non-eternal, so the reason “produced” proves the opposite of the sādhya “eternal”: the contradictory reason, viruddha. It is not asiddha, because sound really is produced (the hetu is present in the pakṣa).

quiz.question: “Devadatta is fat, yet he does not eat during the day; so he must eat at night.” According to the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta schools, this knowledge is obtained by:
quiz.explanation: Two known facts (he is fat; he does not eat by day) seem to conflict, and the only way to reconcile them is to postulate a third (he eats at night). This postulation is arthāpatti. Nyāya does not accept it as a separate pramāṇa; it treats it as a form of inference.

quiz.question: In Indian logic, vyāpti means:
options: The presence of the hetu in the pakṣa
The invariable concomitance between the hetu and the sādhya
A familiar example in which the hetu and sādhya are seen together
The counterbalancing of one reason by another
quiz.explanation: Vyāpti is the universal, invariable relation “wherever there is smoke, there is fire”. Presence of the hetu in the pakṣa is pakṣadharmatā; a familiar example is a sapakṣa used in the udāharaṇa; counterbalancing reasons produce satpratipakṣa.

domains.name: Data Interpretation
domains.blurb: Data sources and types, charts and full DI sets.

lessons.title: Data: sources, classification and representation
lessons.summaryHtml: Data are recorded facts: counts, measurements, categories and ranks. Before you can read a table or a chart in the exam, you must know where data come from (primary or secondary sources), how they are collected (observation, interview, questionnaire, schedule, experiment, records, sensors) and what kind they are (qualitative or quantitative, discrete or continuous, nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio). Raw data are then classified, tabulated into frequency distributions and shown as bar charts, histograms, pie charts, line charts or maps, and each form suits one purpose. Governments now treat data as a public asset, so the syllabus also asks about open data, statistical agencies and data protection. NTA tests this unit through matching (chart to purpose, scale to example, map to use), statement pairs and small numericals such as a pie-chart angle or a histogram height.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Data are recorded observations: marks, home districts, the rank of a college. Statistics begins with three questions. Where did they come from? What kind are they, so which arithmetic is allowed? How should they be arranged and drawn? Lesson 7.2 then applies the answers at exam speed.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 7 usually gives a five-question DI set plus one or two theory questions from this lesson, nearly always matching or statement pairs: chart with purpose, level of measurement with example, map with use, source with type. Small numericals (pie angle, class boundary, histogram height, grouped median) and occasional data-governance facts complete the unit.

Concepts in depth: sources and acquisition of data

Primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator for the study at hand. Secondary data were collected by someone else, for another purpose, and are reused. The same figures can be both: Census counts are primary for the Census office and secondary for a researcher who downloads them. Primary data fit the purpose exactly but cost time and money; secondary data are cheap and quick, but you must check their suitability (same definitions and units?), adequacy (enough coverage?) and reliability (who collected them and how?).

Method of collecting primary dataHow it worksBest for
Direct personal investigation / observationThe investigator observes or asks personallySmall, local, intensive studies
Questionnaire by post or onlineRespondents fill in the form themselvesLarge, literate, scattered groups; cheap; low response rate
Schedule through enumeratorsA trained enumerator asks the questions and fills the formLarge surveys, including respondents who cannot read, as in the Census
ExperimentThe researcher controls conditions and measures the effectCause-and-effect questions

Key secondary sources in India: the Census (Office of the Registrar General), National Sample Survey reports, RBI publications and data.gov.in. A census covers every unit of the population; a sample survey covers a chosen part and generalises. A sample is cheaper and faster; a census has no sampling error but still has non-sampling errors (wrong answers, recording slips).

Concepts in depth: kinds of data and levels of measurement

  • Qualitative data (attributes) name a category: gender, mother tongue, blood group, a Good/Fair/Poor rating. They can be counted, not measured.
  • Quantitative data (variables) are numbers. Discrete variables move in steps (number of books, children, accidents). Continuous variables can take any value in a range (height, weight, time, income).
  • By time: time-series data follow one unit over several periods (India’s GDP from 2015 to 2025); cross-sectional data compare many units at one time (GDP of all states in 2024); panel data follow the same units over time.
Level (Stevens)What it tells youAllowed operationsExamplesSuitable average
NominalNames or labels only= and ≠, countingBlood group, roll number, PIN codeMode
OrdinalOrder, but gaps are not equal< and > as wellRank, grade A/B/C, Likert ratingMedian (and mode)
IntervalEqual gaps, but zero is arbitrary+ and − as wellTemperature in °C or °F, calendar year, IQ scoreMean (and the others)
RatioEqual gaps and a true zero× and ÷ as wellHeight, weight, income, age, temperature in kelvinAll, including geometric mean

The test for ratio versus interval is the sentence “twice as much”. A 40 kg bag is twice as heavy as a 20 kg bag, so weight is on a ratio scale. A day at 30 °C is not “twice as hot” as a day at 15 °C, because 0 °C is not the absence of temperature, so Celsius is an interval scale.

Concepts in depth: classification and tabulation

Classification puts data into groups by a common feature. The four bases are geographical (by place), chronological (by time), qualitative (by attribute, for example literate and illiterate) and quantitative (by class intervals of a variable, such as marks 0–10, 10–20). A good classification is exhaustive and mutually exclusive.

Tabulation sets classified data in rows and columns. The parts of a table are: table number and title (what, where, when); stub (the row headings); caption or box-head (the column headings); body (the figures); head note (units, such as “₹ crore”); footnote (explains a special entry); and source note (where the data came from).

A frequency distribution groups a variable into classes. Key terms: class limits (lower and upper); class mark = (lower + upper) ÷ 2; class width = upper boundary − lower boundary; exclusive classes (0–10, 10–20: the upper limit belongs to the next class) and inclusive classes (0–9, 10–19). To make inclusive classes continuous, subtract half the gap from each lower limit and add it to each upper limit: 10–19 becomes 9.5–19.5. Cumulative frequency adds the frequencies up to a class (less-than type) or from a class onwards (more-than type).

Concepts in depth: graphical representation

DiagramWhat it showsKey rule
Simple bar chartOne variable across separate categories or yearsEqual widths and gaps; only the height matters
Multiple (grouped) bar chartTwo or more variables side by side (boys and girls, by year)A legend is needed
Subdivided (component) barA total and its partsEach part stacked in the same order in every bar
Percentage bar chartThe share of each part, when totals differEvery bar has height 100
HistogramA continuous frequency distributionAdjacent rectangles; area ∝ frequency; unequal widths need frequency density
Frequency polygonThe same distribution as a lineJoin the mid-points of the tops of the histogram bars; close at both ends
OgiveCumulative frequencyPlot against upper boundaries (less-than) or lower boundaries (more-than); they cross at the median
Pie chartParts of one wholeAngle = share × 360°; percentage × 3.6 = degrees
Line chart (time-series graph)Change over time, trendsTime on the x-axis; a broken axis must be marked
Scatter diagramThe relation between two variablesEach point is one pair (x, y); the pattern shows correlation
PictogramCounts shown by small picturesOne picture = a fixed quantity; parts of a picture for fractions
Table chartExact values in rows and columnsBest when precise figures matter more than the visual pattern

In a histogram the area of a bar carries the frequency. With equal classes the height can be the frequency; with unequal classes use frequency density = frequency ÷ class width. A bar chart, in contrast, shows separate categories with gaps, and bar width means nothing.

Concepts in depth: mapping of data

When the data are tied to places, a thematic map works better than a chart. A choropleth map shades whole areas by a ratio or rate (literacy rate by state). A dot map places dots, each worth a fixed number (one dot = 10,000 people), to show distribution. An isopleth map joins points of equal value with lines (isotherms for temperature, isobars for pressure, contours for height). A flow map shows movement, such as migration or trade, with lines whose width is proportional to the volume. GIS software stores such data in layers linked to coordinates and draws these maps.

Concepts in depth: data and governance

  • Official statistics. The Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI) runs the national statistical system. In 2019 the Central Statistics Office and the National Sample Survey Office were merged to form the National Statistical Office (NSO).
  • Open data. The Union Cabinet approved the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (NDSAP) in 2012 so that non-sensitive government data are shared in human-readable and machine-readable forms. The Open Government Data platform data.gov.in publishes these datasets.
  • Personal data. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs how personal data in digital form are processed, based on consent and purpose limitation; its Rules were notified in November 2025 with phased compliance. Check commencement dates at official sources.
  • Good data governance means quality (accurate, complete, timely data), metadata (data about data: who, when, how, units), privacy and security, and open standards for reuse.

Worked examples

Example 1: pie-chart angles. A university spends its budget as follows: salaries 45%, equipment 15%, library 10%, research 20%, maintenance 10%. Find each central angle.

Degrees = percentage × 3.6. Salaries 45 × 3.6 = 162°; equipment 15 × 3.6 = 54°; library 36°; research 72°; maintenance 36°. Check: 162 + 54 + 36 + 72 + 36 = 360°. If the budget were given in rupees, first divide each item by the total, or directly use (item ÷ total) × 360°.

Example 2: histogram with unequal classes. The frequencies are: 0–10: 5, 10–20: 12, 20–40: 30, 40–70: 27, 70–100: 9. Find the height of each bar.

Frequency density = frequency ÷ width: 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5; 12 ÷ 10 = 1.2; 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5; 27 ÷ 30 = 0.9; 9 ÷ 30 = 0.3. Taking width 10 as the standard, the adjusted heights are 5, 12, 15, 9 and 3. Drawing raw frequencies (30 and 27) would make the wide classes look far more crowded; once widths are allowed for, 40–70 falls below 10–20.

Example 3: median and mean from a grouped table. Daily wages (₹) of 60 workers: 100–200: 8, 200–300: 14, 300–400: 20, 400–500: 10, 500–600: 8.

Cumulative frequencies: 8, 22, 42, 52, 60. N/2 = 30 falls in 300–400 (cf before it = 22, f = 20, h = 100). Median = L + ((N/2 − cf) ÷ f) × h = 300 + (8 ÷ 20) × 100 = 340. This is where the two ogives would cross.

Mean: class marks 150, 250, 350, 450, 550. Σfx = 1200 + 3500 + 7000 + 4500 + 4400 = 20600, so mean = 20600 ÷ 60 ≈ 343.33.

Example 4: choosing the diagram. (a) Share of each source in a state’s electricity: pie chart or percentage bar. (b) Enrolment of boys and girls in five years: multiple bar chart. (c) India’s monthly inflation over 36 months: line chart. (d) Heights of 200 students in classes of 5 cm: histogram. (e) Hours studied against marks for 50 students: scatter diagram. (f) District-wise sex ratio: choropleth map.

Mapping of data in more depth

“Mapping of data” in the syllabus means showing data on maps, so that the spatial pattern becomes visible. The first skill NTA tests is choosing the right map for the data.

Kind of dataMapExample
A rate, ratio or density for each areaChoropleth (areas shaded by class)Literacy rate by district
Counts at placesDot map, or proportional symbol map (circles sized by value)Population of cities
Values measured at points on a continuous surfaceIsopleth (lines of equal value)Isotherms (temperature), isohyets (rainfall), isobars (pressure), contours (height)
Movement between placesFlow map (line width ∝ volume)Commuters, migration, trade
A value made visible by resizing areasCartogramStates drawn in proportion to population

Two rules behind the traps. First, a choropleth should show rates or densities, not raw totals: a large district looks prominent whatever its value, so shading total population misleads. Second, in a proportional symbol map the area of the circle is proportional to the value, so the radius is proportional to the square root of the value. A city with 9 times the population gets a circle with 3 times the radius.

Map essentials and scale. Every map needs a title, a legend (key), a scale, a north direction and the source. A scale written as a representative fraction, such as 1:50,000, means 1 unit on the map stands for 50,000 of the same units on the ground: 1 cm on the map is 50,000 cm, or 0.5 km.

Example: scale and circles. (a) On a 1:50,000 map two villages are 7 cm apart. Ground distance = 7 × 50,000 cm = 350,000 cm = 3.5 km. (b) City P has 90,000 people and city Q has 10,000. Circle area ∝ population, so radius ∝ √population: √(90,000 ÷ 10,000) = √9 = 3. P’s circle has 3 times Q’s radius (and 9 times its area).

GIS. A geographic information system stores data in layers tied to coordinates. Vector layers hold points, lines and polygons (wells, roads, district boundaries); raster layers hold grids of cells (satellite images, elevation). Overlaying layers answers questions such as “which villages lie within 5 km of a health centre?”. In India the Survey of India, set up in 1767, is the national mapping agency, and ISRO’s Bhuvan geoportal publishes satellite-based map layers. In data management the same phrase, data mapping, also means matching the fields of one dataset to another before merging them (for example “DOB” to “date_of_birth”).

Table charts and choosing a presentation

A table chart (a table) presents exact figures in rows and columns. It is the best choice when readers need precise values or when many variables must be shown together, and it is the most common form of NET data-interpretation sets. Its weakness is that a trend or pattern is not visible at a glance. A quick rule for choosing: exact values, a table; parts of one whole, a pie chart; comparison across categories, a bar chart; change over time, a line chart; a continuous frequency distribution, a histogram; a spatial pattern, a map.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemRule
Pie sector angle(value ÷ total) × 360° = percentage × 3.6
Class mark(lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2
Inclusive to exclusiveSubtract half the gap from lower limits, add it to upper limits
Frequency densityfrequency ÷ class width (histogram height for unequal classes)
Grouped medianL + ((N/2 − cf) ÷ f) × h
Grouped meanΣ f x ÷ Σ f, with x = class mark
OgivesLess-than against upper boundaries, more-than against lower boundaries; cross at the median
LevelsNominal → ordinal → interval → ratio; only ratio has a true zero
MapsChoropleth: shaded areas; dot: counts; isopleth: equal-value lines; flow: movement
InstitutionsNSO (2019, CSO + NSSO) under MoSPI; NDSAP 2012; data.gov.in; DPDP Act 2023
Map scale 1:n1 map unit = n ground units; 1:50,000 → 1 cm = 0.5 km
Proportional circlesarea ∝ value, so radius ∝ √value
Choosing a maprates by area: choropleth; counts: dot or proportional symbol; point values on a surface: isopleth; movement: flow map

NTA traps

  • “Government data are primary.” Wrong: primary or secondary depends on who collected the data for which purpose, not on the publisher.
  • Celsius as a ratio scale. Wrong: 0 °C is not zero heat. Celsius and Fahrenheit are interval; kelvin is ratio.
  • Histogram height = frequency with unequal classes. Area carries the frequency; use frequency density.
  • Pie chart for a time trend. A pie shows one whole at one moment. A trend needs a line chart.
  • Percentage as degrees. 25% is 90°, not 25°. Multiply by 3.6.

How NTA asks this

Match the lists is the favourite format: chart with purpose, scale with example, map with use, part of a table with its content. Statement pairs test one fact and one trap each (for example, “histogram bars touch” is true, “height is always frequency” is false). Numericals are one-step: sector angle, class mark, boundary, frequency density.

Mini example (Assertion–Reason). A: Temperature measured in °C is on an interval scale. R: The Celsius scale has equal intervals but its zero point is arbitrary. Both are true and R is exactly the reason, so the answer is option 1. If R had said “Celsius has a true zero”, the answer would be option 3.
Elimination trick: in a matching question, first fix the pair you are surest of (for example, pie = parts of a whole). Usually only two options survive; then check one more pair to decide.

terms.definition: Data collected first-hand by the investigator for the current purpose, for example through a survey or an experiment. Original, but costly and slow.
Data already collected by someone else for another purpose, such as the Census, NSS reports or RBI publications. Cheap and quick, but must be checked for suitability.
Data that name a category or quality (an attribute): mother tongue, blood group, satisfaction level. They can be counted but not measured.
Numerical measurements or counts (a variable): height, income, number of children. Discrete if countable in steps, continuous if any value in a range is possible.
Nominal (names only), ordinal (order), interval (equal gaps, no true zero), ratio (equal gaps and a true zero). Each higher level allows more arithmetic.
A table that groups observations into classes and records how many fall in each. Class mark = (lower limit + upper limit) ÷ 2.
Adjacent rectangles for a continuous frequency distribution. Area, not height, represents frequency, so unequal classes need frequency density.
A circle cut into sectors that show parts of a whole. Sector angle = (component ÷ total) × 360°.
The cumulative frequency curve. The less-than and more-than ogives cross at the median.
A thematic map that shades whole areas (states, districts) according to a ratio or rate, such as literacy rate or population density.

lessons.examTip: Link every chart to its one job: pie for parts of a whole, bar for comparing separate categories, histogram for a continuous frequency distribution, line for change over time, scatter for the relation between two variables, choropleth for rates by area. Most matching questions in this unit are decided by that list.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For each matching problem, fix the pair you are surest of first and strike out the options that contradict it.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (primary vs secondary by publisher, interval vs ratio, histogram height with unequal widths, percent read as degrees).
For problems 5–7, redo the working with a different class width or total and confirm that your formula still gives a sensible answer.
Write the fact sheet from memory: four levels of measurement, twelve diagrams with their use, four map types and the three data-governance facts.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and the bank questions at about 60 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Problems 9–15 solved within 12 minutes.
Any pie-chart angle or percentage converted in under 20 seconds (× 3.6 or ÷ 3.6).
All four matching problems in the bank answered correctly on the first attempt.

quiz.question: A researcher studying literacy uses district-wise figures published in the Census of India. For this researcher, the Census figures are:
options: Primary data, because they come from a government source
Secondary data, because they were collected by another agency for another purpose
Qualitative data, because literacy is an attribute
Experimental data, because they were measured
quiz.explanation: Data are primary or secondary relative to the user. The Census office collected them first-hand (primary for the Census), but this researcher reuses them, so they are secondary data. A government source does not make data primary. Literacy rate is a numerical (quantitative) figure, and no experiment was involved.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Blood group only names a category (nominal, III). A rank has order but unequal gaps (ordinal, IV). Celsius temperature has equal gaps but 0 °C is not “no temperature” (interval, I). Weight has a true zero, so 80 kg is twice 40 kg (ratio, II). The distractors swap interval with ratio, or nominal with ordinal, which are the classic confusions.

b: I. Temperature in degrees Celsius
II. Weight of a student in kilograms
III. Blood group of a patient
IV. Rank of a college in a national ranking

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: A college spent ₹4,500 on sports out of a total budget of ₹18,000. In a pie chart of the budget, the central angle of the sports sector is:
quiz.explanation: Sector angle = (4500 ÷ 18000) × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. 25° mistakes the percentage (25%) for degrees. 45° halves the right answer, and 72° is the angle for 20%.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is true: the classes of a continuous variable meet at the class boundaries, so the bars touch. Statement II is false: in a histogram the area represents frequency, so with unequal widths the height must be frequency density (frequency ÷ class width) or an adjusted frequency. Using raw frequencies makes wide classes look too large.

stmts: Statement I: In a histogram the rectangles are drawn without gaps because the class intervals are continuous.
Statement II: When class widths are unequal, the height of each rectangle in a histogram should equal the frequency of that class.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Rainfall over 60 months is a time series, and a line chart is the standard way to show a trend. R states exactly why: time runs along the x-axis and the slope of each segment shows how fast the value rises or falls. So both are true and R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): A line chart is the most suitable diagram for showing the monthly trend of rainfall in a city over five years.
Reason (R): In a line chart, time is taken on the horizontal axis and the joined points show the direction and rate of change between successive periods.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Which of the following are qualitative (categorical) variables?
options: A, C, D and E only
quiz.explanation: A, C and E record categories (E is an ordered category, so it is qualitative data on an ordinal scale). Income (B) is continuous quantitative data and the number of children (D) is discrete quantitative data. Option 4 wrongly treats a count as qualitative; option 2 forgets that ordered categories are still qualitative.

stmts: A. Blood group of a patient
B. Monthly income of a household
C. Mother tongue of a student
D. Number of children in a family
E. Customer rating recorded as Good, Fair or Poor
