quiz.question: Arrange the following stages of a statistical investigation in the correct order.
quiz.explanation: An investigation first defines what is to be studied (B), then collects the data (A), edits, classifies and tabulates them (E), presents them in tables and charts (D) and finally analyses and interprets them (C). Option 1 collects before planning; option 2 presents before organising; option 4 organises data that have not been collected yet.

stmts: A. Collection of data
B. Planning: defining the objective, scope and units
C. Analysis and interpretation
D. Presentation through tables and diagrams
E. Organisation: editing, classification and tabulation
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: In an inclusive frequency distribution of integer marks (10–19, 20–29, 30–39, …), what is the upper class boundary of the class 20–29?
quiz.explanation: The gap between consecutive inclusive classes is 1 (29 to 30), so half the gap, 0.5, is added to each upper limit and subtracted from each lower limit. The class 20–29 becomes 19.5–29.5, so the upper boundary is 29.5. 29 is the upper limit, not the boundary; 24.5 is the class mark.

quiz.question: The less-than ogive and the more-than ogive of a frequency distribution are drawn on the same graph. The x-coordinate of their point of intersection gives the:
quiz.explanation: At the crossing point the number of observations below a value equals the number above it, each being N/2. That value is the median by definition. The mode is read from a histogram (the tallest bar), and the mean is not read from ogives.

quiz.question: A map of India shades each state in darker tones of one colour as its literacy rate increases. This type of map is called a:
quiz.explanation: A choropleth map shades whole administrative areas according to a ratio or rate, such as literacy rate or density. A dot map places dots that each stand for a fixed count; an isopleth map joins places of equal value with lines (isotherms, isobars); a flow map shows movement with lines of varying width.

lessons.title: Data interpretation practice
lessons.summaryHtml: Data interpretation (DI) gives you a table, a bar chart, a pie chart or a line graph and asks five questions on it. The arithmetic is simple, but the time is short, so the marks go to the student who reads the data carefully and calculates only as precisely as the options demand. This lesson teaches a fixed reading method, then the speed tools: percentage–fraction equivalents, percentage change and percentage points, successive change, ratio comparison without division, averages by deviation, and quick estimates of compound annual growth (CAGR). Six full DI sets of five questions cover tables, bar charts, pie charts written as percentage tables, time-series lines and mixed data. Every answer has been recomputed by code.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A DI set gives you a small table or chart and five questions on it. Each question is really a sentence to translate into one calculation: “what percentage of”, “by what percentage more than”, “the ratio of”, “the average of”, “in which year the growth was highest”. You do not need advanced mathematics. You need three habits: read the data (title, units, notes) before the questions; translate each question into the correct formula with the correct base; and calculate only as precisely as the options require. This lesson gives you those habits and the arithmetic shortcuts that make them fast.

Why it matters for NET

Paper 1 usually has one DI set of five questions. That is 10 marks for a single table, so it is worth the most practice per minute in the whole paper. The set can be a table, a bar chart, a pie chart, a line graph or a mix (for example a pie chart of totals and a table of percentages). The questions are dominated by percentages and percentage change, ratios, averages, shares of a total and year-on-year growth, and they sometimes include a question on overall or compound growth. Other units also hide DI arithmetic, for example mathematical aptitude (lesson 5.2).

Concepts in depth: the interpretation method

  1. Read the frame first (20 seconds). Title, units (thousands, lakh, crore, %), the period, and the notes. Many wrong answers come from missing “in ₹ lakh” or “percentage of total”.
  2. Scan the data. Note totals, the largest and smallest values and any obvious trend. If totals are not given, and more than one question needs them, write them down once.
  3. Translate the question. Write the formula with the base: “A is what % of B” is A ÷ B; “A is what % more than B” is (A − B) ÷ B; “change from 2022 to 2024” uses the 2022 value as the base.
  4. Look at the options before calculating. Far apart → estimate. Close together → calculate exactly, and only the parts that separate them.
  5. Sanity-check. A share cannot exceed 100%, a pie cannot exceed 360°, and a growth rate should match the direction of the data.

Concepts in depth: percentages at speed

Fraction%Fraction%
1/2501/1010
1/333.331/119.09
1/4251/128.33
1/5201/137.69
1/616.671/156.67
1/714.291/166.25
1/812.51/205
1/911.111/254
  • Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100. An increase from 300 to 480 is 180/300 = 3/5 = 60%.
  • Percentage points versus per cent. From 20% to 25% is +5 percentage points but a 25% relative increase. When the data are already percentages, read the question word carefully.
  • “More than” and “less than” are not symmetric. If A is 25% more than B (A = 1.25B), then B is 25/125 = 20% less than A. General rule: r% more ⇒ r/(100 + r) × 100% less.
  • Successive change. a% then b% gives a + b + ab/100. +10% then +20% = 32%; +20% then −20% = −4%.
  • Building percentages. 1% of 2900 is 29, so 10% is 290 and 23.8% is about 690. Build any percentage from 50%, 10%, 5% and 1% pieces.

Concepts in depth: ratios, averages and shares

  • Compare fractions without dividing. To compare a/b with c/d, compare a × d with b × c. Is 17/23 bigger than 11/15? 17 × 15 = 255 and 23 × 11 = 253, so yes, just. Or compare each to a benchmark: 29/41 is below 0.71, 43/59 is about 0.73.
  • Average by deviation. Pick a round working mean and average the deviations. For 480, 520, 560, 630: take 550, deviations −70, −30, +10, +80, sum −10, mean = 550 − 2.5 = 547.5.
  • Weighted averages. An average of percentages must be weighted. If 40 students average 60 and 60 students average 70, the overall mean is (40×60 + 60×70)/100 = 66, not 65.
  • Pie charts. Percentage × 3.6 = degrees; percentage × total ÷ 100 = amount. Ratios of two sectors do not need the total at all: 20% : 10% = 2 : 1.
  • Line graphs. The steepest segment shows the largest absolute change, not necessarily the largest percentage change: a rise of 30 on 156 (19.2%) beats a rise of 24 on 132 (18.2%) only narrowly, and a small base can make a smaller rise the biggest in percentage terms.

Concepts in depth: growth over several years (CAGR)

If a value goes from S to E in n years, CAGR = (E ÷ S)1/n − 1. NTA options are usually far enough apart that you can estimate it from a few memorised powers instead of taking roots.

Growth factorValueGrowth factorValue
1.055≈ 1.281.105≈ 1.61
1.085≈ 1.471.125≈ 1.76
1.1021.211.155≈ 2.01
1.1031.3311.204≈ 2.07
1.2021.441.0710≈ 1.97
  • Rule of 72: doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ r. So doubling in 4 years means about 18% a year (exact: 21/4 − 1 ≈ 18.9%), and doubling in 10 years means about 7%.
  • Small rates: (1 + r)n ≈ 1 + nr + n(n − 1)r²/2. For 5% over 5 years: 1 + 0.25 + 0.025 = 1.275.
  • CAGR is below the simple average. Total growth ÷ years (simple average) always overstates the compound rate: 100% growth in 4 years is 25% “simple” but only 18.9% compound. Options often include the simple figure as a trap.

Worked examples

Example 1: a complete mini DI set. Quarterly sales (₹ lakh) of two products: X = 50, 60, 75, 90 and Y = 80, 72, 81, 96 for Q1 to Q4.

(a) Growth of X from Q1 to Q4: (90 − 50) ÷ 50 = 80%.
(b) Combined sales: 130, 132, 156, 186. The largest absolute rise is Q4 (+30). The largest percentage rise: Q3 = 24/132 ≈ 2/11 ≈ 18.2%, Q4 = 30/156 ≈ 19.2%, so Q4, but only just; this is where you calculate rather than estimate.
(c) X’s share of combined sales in Q4: 90/186 ≈ 48.4% (just under half, since 93 would be half).
(d) Average quarterly sales of X: 275 ÷ 4 = 68.75.

Example 2: estimate a CAGR. Exports rose from 200 to 322 (₹ thousand crore) in five years. Ratio 322/200 = 1.61. From the table, 1.105 ≈ 1.61, so CAGR ≈ 10%. The simple average (61% ÷ 5 = 12.2%) is the trap option.

Example 3: order four ratios fast. 17/23, 29/41, 43/59, 11/15. Benchmarks: 29/41 ≈ 0.707; 43/59 ≈ 0.729; 11/15 = 0.733; 17/23 ≈ 0.739. Increasing order: 29/41, 43/59, 11/15, 17/23. Cross-multiplication settles the closest pair (11/15 vs 17/23: 253 < 255).

Example 4: mixed pie and table. A company of 2,400 employees has 30% in Sales, and 40% of Sales staff are women. Women in Sales = 2400 × 0.30 × 0.40 = 288. Multiply the chain of percentages once; do not round in between.

Example 5: keep spending constant. If the price of a commodity rises by 25%, by how much must consumption fall to keep spending unchanged? 25/125 = 20%. The trap answer is 25%.

Formula and fact sheet

Question wordingCalculation
A is what % of BA ÷ B × 100
A is what % more (less) than B(A − B) ÷ B × 100
Percentage change from year 1 to year 2(Y2 − Y1) ÷ Y1 × 100
Change in a percentagePercentage points = P2 − P1; relative % = (P2 − P1) ÷ P1 × 100
Successive changes a%, b%a + b + ab/100
r% more ⇒ how much lessr ÷ (100 + r) × 100
Pie sector% × 3.6 = degrees; % × total ÷ 100 = amount
Weighted averageΣ(n × mean) ÷ Σ n
CAGR(E ÷ S)1/n − 1; doubling time ≈ 72 ÷ r
Compare a/b and c/dCompare a·d with b·c

NTA traps

  • Wrong base. “Increase from 300 to 480” divided by 480 gives 37.5% instead of 60%. The base is the “from” value, or the value after “than”.
  • Percent versus percentage points. When data are percentages, the difference is in points; the relative change is a different number.
  • Plain average of percentages. Averaging 60%, 40%, 20%, 50%, 30% (women in five departments) gives 40%, but the true share, weighted by department size, can be quite different (35.5% in the bank set).
  • Largest absolute change taken as largest percentage change. Check both when a question says “percentage”.
  • Simple average as CAGR. Growth of 100% in 4 years is not 25% a year compounded.
  • Boundary words. “More than 30” excludes 30; “at least” includes it. Count carefully in “in how many years” questions.
  • Units and scales. Thousands, lakh and crore; percentages of different totals cannot be added.

How NTA asks this

The DI set is five direct questions on one data source: usually one percentage, one ratio, one average, one “which year/which item” comparison and one growth or share question. Separate questions test the techniques themselves: successive change, percent versus points, CAGR against simple growth, and fraction equivalents in a matching format.

Mini example (Assertion–Reason). A: A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall leaves a price 25% lower. R: The second change is calculated on the new, higher value. Check: 100 → 150 → 75, so A is true, and R is exactly why. Answer: option 1.
Elimination trick: when options differ by more than about 5% of their size, round every figure to two significant digits and estimate. When two options are within 1% of each other, compute only the one quantity that separates them, exactly.

terms.definition: (New − Old) ÷ Old × 100. The base is always the earlier or reference value.
The plain difference between two percentages. A rise from 20% to 25% is 5 percentage points, but a 25% increase.
Two changes a% and b% in a row give a net change of a + b + ab/100 per cent (use negative signs for decreases).
Part ÷ total × 100. In a pie chart, share × 3.6 gives the central angle in degrees.
A comparison of two quantities by division, written a : b and reduced by the HCF. It has no unit.
Compound annual growth rate: (End ÷ Start)^(1/n) − 1. It is never more than the simple average of the yearly growth rates.
A quantity growing at r% a year doubles in about 72 ÷ r years.
Σ(value × weight) ÷ Σ weight. An average of percentages must be weighted by the group sizes, not taken plainly.
Rounding figures to two or three significant digits to pick an option quickly, when the options are far enough apart.

lessons.examTip: Before calculating, look at the options. If they are far apart, round the data boldly and estimate; if they are close, calculate exactly but only for the options that survive. And always check the base of a percentage: “of”, “more than” and “as a percentage of” each point to a different denominator.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each, the real exam pace).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. For every percentage, underline the base (the value after “of”, “than” or “from”) before calculating.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (wrong base, percent vs percentage points, plain average of percentages, “times as much” vs “increase”).
Learn the fraction–percentage table from 1/2 to 1/20 and the growth-factor table (1.1ⁿ, 1.2ⁿ); test yourself until each takes under two seconds.
Take the six DI sets of the quiz and the bank at 7 minutes per set. Note which question type (percentage, ratio, average, growth, share) costs you the most time.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then repeat one DI set against the clock.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Each five-question DI set finished within 7 minutes.
Any CAGR over 2–5 years estimated to the nearest option in under 60 seconds.
No wrong answer caused by the wrong base in the last two practice rounds.

lessons.title: ICT: basics and terminology
lessons.summaryHtml: Information and Communication Technology (ICT) is the combined use of computers, software, networks and telecommunication to create, store, send and use information. This lesson covers the vocabulary NTA tests every cycle: hardware and software, memory and storage, the units used to measure data, and conversion between binary, octal, decimal and hexadecimal. It then explains the internet, intranet and extranet, how e-mail moves (SMTP to send, POP3 or IMAP to read, CC and BCC), and how audio and video conferencing work. A large table of abbreviations gives you quick marks in match-the-list questions. Most questions here are one-line recall or a small conversion, so accuracy and speed matter more than depth. Learn the traps (1 KB is 1024 bytes in the binary convention, WWW is not the internet, BCC recipients are hidden) and this unit becomes a reliable scoring area.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

ICT (Information and Communication Technology) means using computers, software, networks and telecommunication together to create, store, send and use information. The computer stores and processes data; networks and the internet move it between people. When a teacher records a lecture, uploads it to a portal and students watch it on their phones, every step is ICT. This lesson gives you the vocabulary: hardware, software, storage units, number systems, the internet, e-mail and conferencing.

Why it matters for NET

The ICT unit usually gives a handful of questions in every Paper 1, and they are among the fastest marks in the exam. The common patterns are abbreviations (often as match-the-list), storage units and their order, small number-system conversions, internet versus intranet versus extranet, e-mail terms (CC, BCC, protocols), and hardware and software classification. Little calculation is needed, but the options are built on exact traps such as 1000 versus 1024 or bits versus bytes.

Concepts in depth: hardware

A computer follows the input → process → output cycle, with storage to keep data. The CPU is the processor: its ALU does arithmetic and comparisons, its CU (control unit) fetches instructions and directs the other parts, and its registers are tiny, very fast storage cells.

CategoryExamples
InputKeyboard, mouse, scanner, microphone, webcam, joystick, light pen, barcode reader, OMR, OCR, MICR, biometric reader
OutputMonitor, printer, plotter, speaker, projector
BothTouch screen, modem, network card
StorageHard disk (HDD), solid-state drive (SSD), pen drive, memory card, CD/DVD, magnetic tape

Memory hierarchy, fastest and smallest first: registers → cache → main memory (RAM) → secondary storage (SSD, HDD) → offline storage (tape, optical discs). RAM is volatile read/write memory: SRAM is fast and used for cache, DRAM must be refreshed and is used for main memory. ROM is non-volatile and holds start-up firmware such as the BIOS. Its variants are PROM (written once), EPROM (erased by ultraviolet light) and EEPROM (erased electrically; flash memory is a kind of EEPROM).

Concepts in depth: software

  • System software runs the machine: operating systems (Windows, Linux, macOS, Android), device drivers, utilities (antivirus, backup, compression) and language translators.
  • Application software does users’ tasks: word processors, spreadsheets, browsers, media players.
  • Translators: a compiler translates the whole program at once into object code; an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time; an assembler translates assembly language. A linker joins object files and a loader places the program in memory.
  • Firmware is software stored permanently in hardware, such as the BIOS.
  • Licensing: proprietary (closed source, paid: MS Office), open source (source available and modifiable: Linux, LibreOffice, Firefox, Moodle), freeware (free to use, usually closed source), shareware (free trial, then pay).

Concepts in depth: storage units and number systems

A bit is 0 or 1; a nibble is 4 bits; a byte is 8 bits. In the binary convention used in most Paper 1 questions, each step up is × 1024 = 210: KB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB. Disk makers and network speeds use the decimal (SI) convention, × 1000 per step; the IEC names KiB, MiB and GiB mean the binary sizes. In 2022 the SI added ronna (1027) and quetta (1030) after yotta (1024).

UnitBinary conventionDecimal (SI)
1 KB210 = 1024 bytes103 bytes
1 MB220 = 1,048,576 bytes106
1 GB230 = 1,073,741,824 bytes109
1 TB, 1 PB, 1 EB240, 250, 2601012, 1015, 1018

Number systems. Binary is base 2, octal base 8, decimal base 10 and hexadecimal base 16 (digits 0–9, then A = 10 to F = 15). To convert to decimal, multiply each digit by its place value and add. To convert a decimal integer to base b, divide by b repeatedly and read the remainders from bottom to top. Between binary and octal, group bits in threes from the right; for hexadecimal, group in fours. With n bits you can represent 2n values, 0 to 2n − 1. ASCII uses 7 bits (128 characters); Unicode covers all the world’s scripts, including Indian ones, and its encoding UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per character.

Concepts in depth: internet, intranet and extranet

The internet is the global network of networks that uses the TCP/IP protocols. It grew from ARPANET (1969). The World Wide Web, proposed by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in 1989, is one service that runs on the internet: linked pages identified by URLs and fetched with HTTP. E-mail, file transfer and video calls are other services.

  • IP address: IPv4 is 32 bits (about 4.3 billion addresses); IPv6 is 128 bits.
  • DNS translates names such as ugcnet.nta.ac.in into IP addresses, like a telephone directory.
  • URL: protocol://domain/path, for example https://www.example.ac.in/notes/unit8.html.
  • A browser (Chrome, Firefox, Safari) displays pages; a search engine (Google Search, Bing) is a website that finds them. HTTPS is HTTP encrypted with TLS.
  • Bandwidth is measured in bits per second (kbps, Mbps, Gbps), in decimal units.
FeatureInternetIntranetExtranet
Who can use itAnyoneOnly the organisation’s membersMembers plus selected outsiders
TechnologyTCP/IP, webSameSame, with controlled log-in
ExamplePublic websitesA university staff portalA company’s supplier portal

Networks by area: PAN (a few metres, Bluetooth), LAN (building or campus), MAN (city), WAN (countries; the internet is the largest). A modem converts digital data to line signals and back, a switch joins devices in a LAN, and a router forwards packets between networks.

Concepts in depth: e-mail

An address has the form username@domain; Ray Tomlinson sent the first networked e-mail on ARPANET in 1971 and chose the @ sign. Mail is sent with SMTP and read with POP3 (downloads to one device, usually removing it from the server) or IMAP (keeps it on the server, synchronised across devices). MIME lets mail carry attachments and non-English text.

  • CC (carbon copy) recipients are visible to all; BCC (blind carbon copy) recipients are hidden from everyone else, which protects privacy in mass mail.
  • Reply goes to the sender only; Reply All goes to the sender and the To and CC recipients, never to hidden BCC recipients. Forward sends the message and its attachments to someone new.
  • Spam is unsolicited bulk mail; phishing pretends to be a trusted sender to steal passwords or money.

Concepts in depth: audio and video conferencing

Audio conferencing links three or more people by voice; video conferencing adds live video and needs a camera, microphone, display and more bandwidth. Both are synchronous (everyone at the same time), unlike e-mail, forums or recorded lectures, which are asynchronous. Internet calls use VoIP, which sends speech as data packets, and a codec compresses the audio and video. Quality depends on bandwidth, latency (delay), jitter and packet loss. A webinar is a web seminar where a few presenters address a large audience that mostly listens; a podcast is recorded audio that people play later.

Worked examples

Example 1 (storage units). How many bytes are in 2 MB, and how many bits in 2 KB (binary convention)?

  1. 1 MB = 220 = 1,048,576 bytes, so 2 MB = 2,097,152 bytes.
  2. 2 KB = 2 × 1024 × 8 = 16,384 bits. In the decimal convention, 2 MB would be 2,000,000 bytes.

Example 2 (conversions). Convert 100 (decimal) to binary, octal and hexadecimal.

  1. Divide by 2: 100 → 50 r0 → 25 r0 → 12 r1 → 6 r0 → 3 r0 → 1 r1 → 0 r1. Remainders bottom to top: 1100100.
  2. Octal: groups of three from the right, 1 | 100 | 100 → 144 (64 + 32 + 4 = 100).
  3. Hexadecimal: groups of four, 110 | 0100 → 64 (6 × 16 + 4 = 100).

Example 3 (binary addition and hexadecimal). Find (1101)₂ + (1011)₂, and convert (2F)₁₆ to decimal.

    1 1 0 1     (13)
  + 1 0 1 1     (11)
  ---------
  1 1 0 0 0     (24)
  1. From the right: 1 + 1 = 10 (write 0, carry 1); 0 + 1 + 1 = 10; 1 + 0 + 1 = 10; 1 + 1 + 1 = 11. Result 11000 = 24 = 13 + 11.
  2. (2F)₁₆ = 2 × 16 + 15 = 47.

Example 4 (download time). A 250 MB video is downloaded over a 20 Mbps link. Using decimal units and ignoring overheads, how long does it take?

  1. 250 MB × 8 = 2000 megabits.
  2. 2000 ÷ 20 = 100 seconds. The trap answer 12.5 s forgets that speeds are in bits.

Example 5 (how many bits). What is the smallest number of bits that gives 100 students different codes?

  1. 26 = 64 is too few; 27 = 128 is enough. Answer: 7 bits, the same reason ASCII has 128 codes.

Concepts in depth: ICT abbreviations and terminology

The syllabus names “general abbreviations and terminology” first in Unit 8, and NET usually tests them as a match-the-list or a “which expansion is correct” question. Learn them in families.

FamilyAbbreviation and expansion
HardwareCPU Central Processing Unit; ALU Arithmetic Logic Unit; RAM Random Access Memory; ROM Read-Only Memory; BIOS Basic Input/Output System; USB Universal Serial Bus; SSD Solid-State Drive; HDD Hard Disk Drive; GPU Graphics Processing Unit; LED Light-Emitting Diode; LCD Liquid Crystal Display; DVD Digital Versatile Disc
NetworksLAN Local Area Network; WAN Wide Area Network; ISP Internet Service Provider; IP Internet Protocol; TCP Transmission Control Protocol; DNS Domain Name System; VPN Virtual Private Network; VoIP Voice over Internet Protocol; MAC Media Access Control
Web and e-mailWWW World Wide Web; URL Uniform Resource Locator; HTML HyperText Markup Language; HTTP(S) HyperText Transfer Protocol (Secure); FTP File Transfer Protocol; SMTP Simple Mail Transfer Protocol; POP3 Post Office Protocol version 3; IMAP Internet Message Access Protocol; CC carbon copy; BCC blind carbon copy
Files and codesPDF Portable Document Format; JPEG Joint Photographic Experts Group; GIF Graphics Interchange Format; PNG Portable Network Graphics; MPEG Moving Picture Experts Group; ASCII American Standard Code for Information Interchange
SecurityOTP One-Time Password; CAPTCHA Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart; SSL Secure Sockets Layer; TLS Transport Layer Security; 2FA two-factor authentication
Newer and education termsIoT Internet of Things; AI Artificial Intelligence; AR Augmented Reality; VR Virtual Reality; RFID Radio Frequency Identification; NFC Near Field Communication; GPS Global Positioning System; LMS Learning Management System; MOOC Massive Open Online Course; OER Open Educational Resources

Terms often confused. Bandwidth is how much data a link can carry per second; latency is the delay before data arrive. A cookie is a small file a website stores in your browser; a cache keeps copies of data for faster reuse. Freeware is free to use, shareware is free for a trial, and open-source software makes its source code available. Phishing tricks users into revealing passwords; malware is any harmful software. Cloud computing supplies computing resources over the internet on demand.

NTA traps: URL is Uniform (not Universal) Resource Locator; USB is Universal Serial Bus; the M in IMAP is Message; DVD is Digital Versatile Disc. Books often expand Wi-Fi as “Wireless Fidelity”, but the Wi-Fi Alliance treats Wi-Fi as a brand name for IEEE 802.11 wireless LANs; choose “Wireless Fidelity” only if it is the one sensible option.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Bit, nibble, byte1 nibble = 4 bits; 1 byte = 8 bits
Unit ladderKB, MB, GB, TB, PB, EB, ZB, YB (then RB, QB); × 1024 (binary) or × 1000 (SI)
n bits2n values; largest 2n − 1 (8 bits: 255)
Groupingbinary ↔ octal: 3 bits; binary ↔ hex: 4 bits
Download timesize in bytes × 8 ÷ speed in bits per second
AddressesIPv4 32-bit; IPv6 128-bit; MAC 48-bit
E-mailSMTP sends; POP3 downloads; IMAP synchronises
HistoryARPANET 1969; first e-mail 1971; WWW proposed 1989 (Berners-Lee, CERN)
VolatileRegisters, cache, RAM. Non-volatile: ROM family, flash, HDD
Recognition devicesOCR (Optical Character), OMR (Optical Mark), MICR (Magnetic Ink Character)
Web and network termsHTML, HTTP(S), FTP (File Transfer Protocol), URL, DNS, ISP, TCP/IP, VoIP, LAN/MAN/WAN/PAN
File formatsPDF (Portable Document Format), JPEG, PNG, GIF, MP3, MPEG, ASCII
Newer termsIoT, AI, AR/VR, RFID, NFC, MOOC, LMS (Learning Management System)
Easily confused expansionsURL Uniform Resource Locator; USB Universal Serial Bus; IMAP Internet Message Access Protocol; DVD Digital Versatile Disc; CAPTCHA Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart

NTA traps

  • 1000 versus 1024. Wrong: “1 GB = 1,000,000 KB.” Fix: in the binary convention it is 1024 × 1024 = 1,048,576 KB. Use 1000 only for SI units or network speeds.
  • Bits versus bytes. Wrong: a 100 MB file at 100 Mbps takes 1 second. Fix: 100 MB = 800 Mb, so it takes 8 seconds.
  • Internet versus WWW. Wrong: “they are the same.” Fix: the internet is the network; the WWW is one service on it.
  • Browser versus search engine. Wrong: “Google is a browser.” Fix: Chrome is the browser; Google Search is a website.
  • CC versus BCC. Wrong: “CC hides addresses.” Fix: only BCC hides.
  • Sending versus reading mail. Wrong: “POP3 sends mail.” Fix: SMTP sends; POP3 and IMAP retrieve.
  • Count versus largest value. Wrong: “8 bits store numbers up to 256.” Fix: 256 values, largest 255.

How NTA asks this

  • Match: abbreviations against meanings, devices against uses, networks against coverage.
  • Order: storage units by size, or events in chronological order.
  • Numerical: a small conversion, unit or download-time question.
  • Statements / Assertion–Reason: definitions of intranet, extranet, BCC, volatile memory, IPv4/IPv6.

Mini-example (A-R). A: RAM is called volatile memory. R: The contents of RAM are lost when the power is switched off. Both are true and R is exactly why RAM is called volatile: option 1. If R had said “RAM is faster than a hard disk”, it would be true but not the explanation: option 2.

Elimination trick: in a storage-unit question, write k-M-G-T-P-E-Z-Y in the margin first. Most wrong options swap one neighbouring pair, such as tera and peta.
Watch out: an option that pairs two real terms can still be wrong, such as “HTTP is used to send e-mail”.

terms.definition: Information and Communication Technology: computers, software, networks and telecommunication used together to handle information.
A group of 8 bits, the basic unit of storage. A nibble is 4 bits.
1024 bytes in the traditional binary convention (2¹⁰). The SI kilobyte (kB) is 1000 bytes; the IEC name for 1024 bytes is kibibyte (KiB).
Memory that loses its contents when power is switched off, such as RAM and cache. ROM and flash are non-volatile.
A private network inside an organisation that uses internet technology (TCP/IP, web browsers) but is closed to outsiders.
Part of an intranet opened, with controlled access, to selected outsiders such as suppliers, partners or customers.
Simple Mail Transfer Protocol: used to send and relay e-mail between servers.
Internet Message Access Protocol: reads mail while keeping it on the server, so every device sees the same folders. POP3 usually downloads and removes it.
Blind Carbon Copy: recipients get the mail, but their addresses are hidden from everyone else.
Voice over Internet Protocol: carrying voice calls as data packets over an IP network.

lessons.examTip: For every storage-unit question, first decide the convention: in the binary convention each step (KB → MB → GB → TB → PB) multiplies by 1024 = 2¹⁰. Network speeds (Mbps) always use decimal units, and speeds are in bits, not bytes: divide by 8.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. For every conversion, write the place values or bit groups you used before choosing an option.
Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (1000 versus 1024, bits versus bytes, count versus largest value, CC versus BCC).
From memory, write the unit ladder from bit to quettabyte and 30 abbreviations with full forms; check them against the fact sheet.
Convert five random numbers from 20 to 255 into binary, octal and hexadecimal, and check each by converting back to decimal.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 45–60 seconds per question.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 15 problems finished within 20 minutes.
Any two-digit hexadecimal or six-bit binary number converted to decimal in under 30 seconds.
The e-mail protocol roles (SMTP, POP3, IMAP) and the CC/BCC/Reply All rules stated without hesitation.

quiz.question: In the binary convention (1 KB = 1024 bytes), how many kilobytes make one gigabyte?
quiz.explanation: 1 GB = 1024 MB and 1 MB = 1024 KB, so 1 GB = 1024 × 1024 = 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 KB. 1,073,741,824 = 2³⁰ is the number of bytes in 1 GB, 1024 is the number of MB, and 1,000,000 uses the decimal convention.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is a web address (II). HTTP (HyperText Transfer Protocol) carries web pages between server and browser (IV). SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends e-mail (I). An ISP (Internet Service Provider) sells internet access (III). The first option swaps HTTP and SMTP, the usual confusion between the two transfer protocols.

b: I. Protocol used to send e-mail
II. Address of a resource on the web
III. Company that gives users access to the internet
IV. Protocol used to transfer web pages

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)

stmts: Assertion (A): IPv4 can provide only about 4.3 billion distinct addresses, which is why IPv6 was introduced.

quiz.question: Which of the following is volatile memory?
quiz.explanation: RAM (Random Access Memory) loses its contents when power is switched off. ROM, flash memory (pen drives, SSDs) and hard disks keep their data without power.

quiz.question: Which language translator converts the whole high-level program into object code in one go before it is run?
quiz.explanation: A compiler translates the complete program and reports errors together, producing object code that runs later. An interpreter translates and executes one statement at a time. An assembler translates assembly language, not a high-level language, and a loader places a ready program in memory.

quiz.question: A teacher reads her college e-mail on a laptop, a phone and a lab computer, and wants read/unread status and folders to stay the same on all three. Which protocol should her mail app use to read mail?
quiz.explanation: IMAP keeps messages on the server and synchronises folders and flags, so all devices show the same mailbox. POP3 usually downloads mail to one device (often deleting it from the server). SMTP only sends mail, and FTP transfers files.

lessons.title: Digital initiatives and ICT in governance
lessons.summaryHtml: India runs a large set of digital platforms for higher education, and NTA asks about them in almost every Paper 1. This lesson sorts them into families so they stop blurring together: learning platforms (SWAYAM, SWAYAM Plus, SWAYAM PRABHA, e-PG Pathshala, NDLI), research and library services from INFLIBNET (Shodhganga, Shodhgangotri, ShodhShuddhi, Vidwan and the One Nation One Subscription scheme), and academic-record systems (NAD, DigiLocker, the Academic Bank of Credits and APAAR). It then covers ICT in governance: what e-governance is, its models (G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E) and stages, the National e-Governance Plan, e-Kranti and Digital India, and key public platforms. It ends with cyber security basics: the CIA triad, common attacks, safe practices, and India’s legal and institutional framework (IT Act 2000, CERT-In, I4C and the 1930 helpline, and the DPDP Act 2023). For every platform, learn three things: what it does, who runs it and one key number or date.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Over the last two decades India has built a chain of free digital services for education and for government. A student can take a credit course on SWAYAM, watch lectures on SWAYAM PRABHA television, read a thesis on Shodhganga, keep a degree certificate in DigiLocker and carry credits in the Academic Bank of Credits. A citizen can pay taxes, get certificates and report cyber fraud online. This lesson maps these services, e-governance and the cyber security that protects them.

Why it matters for NET

Digital initiatives appear in Paper 1 almost every cycle, and they also turn up inside teaching-aptitude and higher-education questions. The favourite formats are match-the-list (initiative ↔ purpose or owner), chronology, and statement questions that swap two similar names. Cyber security and e-governance give one or two further questions. The facts are few but precise: purpose, owner, and one date or number for each service.

Watch out: schemes change. The facts here were checked on official sources (swayam.gov.in, onos.gov.in, pib.gov.in, inflibnet.ac.in) in September 2026. Recheck current counts on the official sites before the exam.

Concepts in depth: the umbrella programmes

  • NMEICT (National Mission on Education through ICT, 2009, Ministry of Education) funded most higher-education e-content: e-PG Pathshala, NDLI, Virtual Labs, Spoken Tutorial and more.
  • Digital India (launched 1 July 2015, led by MeitY) has three vision areas (digital infrastructure as a utility for every citizen, governance and services on demand, digital empowerment of citizens) and nine pillars (see below).
  • PM eVIDYA (May 2020) brought all modes of digital and TV education together during the pandemic; DIKSHA became “One Nation, One Digital Platform” for school education.

Concepts in depth: learning platforms

PlatformWhat it doesRun by / anchor fact
SWAYAMNational MOOC platform, Class 9 to postgraduateMinistry of Education; launched 9 July 2017
SWAYAM PlusIndustry-linked, job-oriented coursesIIT Madras; launched February 2024
SWAYAM PRABHAFree 24×7 educational DTH channels32 channels at launch (July 2017), GSAT-15; portal by INFLIBNET, uplink from BISAG-N
NPTELEngineering and science courses by IITs and IIScSWAYAM coordinator for engineering
e-PG PathshalaPostgraduate e-content in about 70 subjectsUGC, under NME-ICT; hosted by INFLIBNET
NDLISingle-window search over millions of learning resourcesIIT Kharagpur, under NMEICT; dedicated to the nation June 2018
DIKSHASchool content and teacher trainingNCERT; launched 5 September 2017 (Teachers’ Day)

SWAYAM in detail. The name expands to “Study Webs of Active-Learning for Young Aspiring Minds”, and its aim is the three cardinal principles of education policy: access, equity and quality. Every course has four quadrants: (1) video lectures (e-tutorial), (2) specially prepared reading material that can be downloaded (e-content), (3) self-assessment through tests and quizzes, and (4) an online discussion forum. Learning is free; a certificate needs a proctored exam, for which a fee is charged. National coordinators: AICTE (self-paced and international courses), NPTEL (engineering), UGC (non-technical postgraduate), CEC (undergraduate), NCERT and NIOS (school), IGNOU (out-of-school students), IIM Bangalore (management) and NITTTR (teacher training); the portal now also lists Institutes of National Importance. Credit transfer: the UGC credit-framework regulations for SWAYAM of 2016 allowed up to 20% of courses in a semester through SWAYAM; the 2021 regulations raised this to 40%.

SWAYAM PRABHA in detail. Each channel telecasts at least four hours of fresh content a day, shown six times, so learners can pick a slot. It reaches homes without internet through an ordinary DTH dish. The channel count has grown since the original 32 (PM eVIDYA school channels share the platform), so check the current figure on the portal.

Concepts in depth: research and library services (INFLIBNET)

The INFLIBNET Centre (Information and Library Network), Gandhinagar, is an inter-university centre of UGC. Its services form one family:

  • Shodhganga: open-access repository of full-text PhD theses, built on DSpace. UGC regulations since 2009 require universities to deposit electronic theses with INFLIBNET.
  • Shodhgangotri: repository of synopses and research proposals (“research in progress”). Gangotri is the source of the Ganga: the synopsis comes before the thesis.
  • ShodhShuddhi: plagiarism-detection software for universities, funded by the Ministry of Education, started September 2019 with URKUND/Ouriginal and switched to DrillBit from 1 October 2023.
  • Vidwan: a database of experts and faculty profiles.
  • e-ShodhSindhu (earlier) and now ONOS for journal access.

One Nation One Subscription (ONOS). Approved by the Union Cabinet on 25 November 2024 and operational from 1 January 2025, for calendar years 2025–2027, with an outlay of about ₹6,000 crore. It gives all central and state government higher-education institutions and central government R&D institutions access to journals of about 30 major international publishers (over 13,000 journals; the portal describes it as 30+ publishers and 6,500+ member institutions), for roughly 1.8 crore students, teachers and researchers. INFLIBNET is the implementing agency, and access is through one national portal, onos.gov.in.

Concepts in depth: academic records

  • NAD (National Academic Depository): a 24×7 online store of degrees, diplomas and mark sheets, approved by the Cabinet in October 2016 and launched with SWAYAM on 9 July 2017. UGC is its authorised body and DigiLocker (MeitY) is the depository.
  • ABC (Academic Bank of Credits): created under the UGC ABC Regulations, 2021 and launched in July 2021, a year after NEP 2020. Students open an academic bank account; credits earned anywhere are deposited, accumulated, transferred and redeemed, which makes multiple entry and exit possible. Credits have a shelf life: at most 7 years, or as the discipline prescribes.
  • APAAR (Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry): a 12-digit “One Nation, One Student ID” that links a learner’s records from school onwards, accessible through DigiLocker and ABC.
Remember: NAD stores documents, ABC stores credits, APAAR is the ID that ties them to one student, and DigiLocker is the locker underneath.

Concepts in depth: ICT in governance

E-governance uses ICT to deliver government services and information and to run government processes. Its goals are the SMART ideals: simple, moral, accountable, responsive and transparent government, with lower cost and less corruption because fewer steps need a human intermediary.

ModelBetweenExample
G2CGovernment and citizensCertificates, taxes, DigiLocker, UMANG
G2BGovernment and businessesGovernment e-Marketplace (GeM, 2016), GST filing
G2GGovernment departmentsData sharing between ministries and states
G2EGovernment and employeesSalary slips, service records, training

Stages of e-governance (the usual maturity model): information/presence → interaction → transaction → transformation.

Plans. The National e-Governance Plan (NeGP) was approved in May 2006 with Mission Mode Projects (27 at first, later 31) and common infrastructure: State Wide Area Networks, State Data Centres and Common Service Centres (CSCs). e-Kranti, “NeGP 2.0”, was approved on 25 March 2015 with principles such as “transformation, not translation”, “cloud by default” and “mobile first”. Digital India’s nine pillars are broadband highways, universal access to mobile connectivity, public internet access, e-governance, e-Kranti, information for all, electronics manufacturing, IT for jobs and early harvest programmes.

Key platforms: Aadhaar (UIDAI, 12-digit identity), DigiLocker (documents), UMANG (one app for many services, 2017), MyGov (citizen participation, 2014), GeM (procurement), UPI (payments, NPCI, 2016), BharatNet (rural broadband) and Common Service Centres (assisted access in villages).

Concepts in depth: cyber security basics

Security aims at the CIA triad: confidentiality (only authorised people see data: encryption, access control), integrity (data is not altered: hashes, digital signatures) and availability (systems stay usable: backups, protection against denial of service). Authentication (passwords, OTPs, biometrics) and non-repudiation support them.

ThreatWhat it does
VirusAttaches to a host file and spreads when the file runs
WormSelf-replicates across networks without a host file
Trojan horseLooks useful but carries hidden malicious code
RansomwareEncrypts data and demands payment
Spyware / keyloggerSecretly records activity or keystrokes
Phishing (vishing by voice, smishing by SMS)Fake messages that steal passwords, OTPs or money
DoS / DDoSFloods a server so genuine users cannot reach it

Good practice: strong, unique passwords with a password manager; two-factor authentication; prompt updates; antivirus and firewall; HTTPS sites only for payments; offline backups; never sharing OTPs.

Law and institutions: the IT Act, 2000 gave legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures; the 2008 amendment added offences such as 66C (identity theft), 66D (cheating by personation) and 66F (cyber terrorism). Section 66A was struck down by the Supreme Court in Shreya Singhal (2015). CERT-In (2004, MeitY, Section 70B) handles incident response; NCIIPC (Section 70A) protects critical infrastructure; the National Cyber Security Policy dates from 2013; I4C (Ministry of Home Affairs, 2020) runs cybercrime.gov.in and the 1930 helpline. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs personal data; its Rules were notified in November 2025 with phased compliance.

Worked examples

Example 1 (which platform?). A rural learner without internet wants to follow lectures; a PhD scholar wants to check a draft for plagiarism; a teacher needs a certified online course that counts for credit. Match each need.

  1. No internet → television → SWAYAM PRABHA.
  2. Plagiarism check → ShodhShuddhi (DrillBit), not Shodhganga.
  3. Credit course → SWAYAM, with credits transferred under UGC regulations.

Example 2 (chronology). Order: SWAYAM, IT Act, ONOS, NeGP, Digital India.

  1. Attach the anchor year: IT Act 2000, NeGP 2006, Digital India 2015, SWAYAM 2017, ONOS 2025.
  2. Order: IT Act → NeGP → Digital India → SWAYAM → ONOS.

Example 3 (credit arithmetic). A semester has 15 courses. How many may be taken on SWAYAM?

  1. Current limit (2021 regulations): 40% of 15 = 6.
  2. Trap: the old 20% limit gives 3. With 10 courses, the answers are 4 (now) and 2 (old).

Example 4 (spot the attack). A message says “Your scholarship is on hold; update your bank details at scholarship-gov.in-verify.co within 24 hours.”

  1. Urgency, a request for secret details, and a look-alike address are the three signs of phishing.
  2. Response: do not click; check on the official portal; report at cybercrime.gov.in or call 1930 if money is lost.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
SWAYAM9 July 2017; Class 9 to PG; 4 quadrants; credit limit 40% (2021 regulations; 20% in 2016)
SWAYAM PRABHADTH, 32 channels at launch; GSAT-15; 4 hours fresh, telecast 6 times a day
SWAYAM PlusIIT Madras, February 2024, job-oriented courses
NDLIIIT Kharagpur, NMEICT
e-PG PathshalaUGC, NME-ICT, about 70 PG subjects
INFLIBNET familyShodhganga (theses), Shodhgangotri (synopses), ShodhShuddhi (plagiarism, DrillBit), Vidwan (experts), ONOS
ONOSFrom 1 Jan 2025; 2025–2027; about ₹6,000 crore; about 30 publishers, 13,000+ journals
RecordsNAD (documents, DigiLocker), ABC (credits, 2021, 7-year shelf life), APAAR (12-digit ID)
SchoolDIKSHA (NCERT, 2017), PM eVIDYA (2020)
GovernanceNeGP 2006; e-Kranti 2015; Digital India 1 July 2015 (9 pillars)
CyberIT Act 2000 (amended 2008); CERT-In 2004 (70B); NCSP 2013; I4C 2020 and 1930; DPDP Act 2023

NTA traps

  • SWAYAM versus SWAYAM PRABHA. Wrong: “SWAYAM telecasts on DTH.” Fix: SWAYAM is online; PRABHA is television.
  • Shodh names. Wrong: “Shodhgangotri stores theses.” Fix: -ganga theses, -gangotri synopses, -shuddhi plagiarism, -sindhu journals.
  • Owners. Wrong: “NDLI is INFLIBNET’s.” Fix: NDLI is IIT Kharagpur; INFLIBNET runs Shodhganga, ShodhShuddhi, Vidwan and ONOS.
  • NAD, ABC, APAAR. Wrong: “ABC stores degree certificates.” Fix: NAD stores awards, ABC credits, APAAR is the ID.
  • Credit limit. Wrong: 20%. Fix: 40% under the 2021 regulations.
  • Ministries. Wrong: “CERT-In is under the Home Ministry.” Fix: CERT-In is MeitY; I4C is Home Affairs.
  • Section 66A. Wrong: it is in force. Fix: struck down in 2015.

How NTA asks this

  • Match: initiative ↔ purpose, owner or coordinator.
  • Order: launch years of schemes or laws.
  • Statements / Assertion–Reason: one statement swaps an owner or a number.
  • Multiple correct: “which are INFLIBNET services”, “which are Digital India pillars”.

Mini-example (A-R). A: SWAYAM PRABHA helps learners without internet. R: It telecasts on DTH channels through satellite. Both true, and R explains A: option 1. If R had said “it has four quadrants”, R would be false for SWAYAM PRABHA (the quadrants belong to SWAYAM courses): option 3.

Elimination trick: in a match, fix the pair you are surest of (DIKSHA–NCERT, NDLI–IIT Kharagpur, Shodhganga–theses) and strike every option that contradicts it; one or two options survive.

terms.definition: The national MOOC platform (launched July 2017) for courses from Class 9 to postgraduate level, built on four quadrants: video, reading material, self-assessment and a discussion forum.
Free 24×7 educational DTH television channels (32 at launch in 2017, expanded since) for learners without reliable internet.
National Digital Library of India: a single-window search platform for learning resources, developed by IIT Kharagpur under the Ministry of Education’s NMEICT.
INFLIBNET’s open-access repository of full-text Indian PhD theses; Shodhgangotri holds synopses of research in progress.

One Nation One Subscription: a central scheme (from 1 January 2025) giving government higher-education and R&D institutions access to journals of about 30 major international publishers, through INFLIBNET.
Academic Bank of Credits: a UGC-regulated digital bank where students’ earned credits are stored and transferred, supporting multiple entry and exit.
Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry: a 12-digit “One Nation, One Student ID” linked to ABC and DigiLocker.
Using ICT to deliver government services and information, and to run government processes, in a faster, more transparent way (G2C, G2B, G2G, G2E).
Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, the national agency for responding to cyber security incidents, under MeitY (Section 70B, IT Act).
A fraud in which a message pretending to come from a trusted source tricks the user into revealing passwords, OTPs or bank details.

lessons.examTip: Learn each platform as a triple: purpose, owner and one anchor fact. SWAYAM (MOOCs, MoE, 2017), SWAYAM PRABHA (DTH TV, 32 channels at launch), NDLI (library, IIT Kharagpur), Shodhganga (theses, INFLIBNET), ShodhShuddhi (plagiarism, INFLIBNET), ABC (credits, UGC), APAAR (12-digit student ID), ONOS (journals, INFLIBNET, from 2025).

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. In every match question, fix one certain pair first and strike out the options that contradict it.

Check every answer with solutions.md. Write each mistake in your error log with the trap you fell for (SWAYAM versus SWAYAM PRABHA, Shodhganga versus Shodhgangotri, NAD versus ABC versus APAAR, CERT-In versus I4C).
From memory, write a table of 15 platforms with purpose, owner and one anchor date or number; check it against the fact sheet.
Write a 10-event timeline from the IT Act (2000) to ONOS (2025) and practise ordering any five events in under a minute.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions at 45–60 seconds per question.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 15 problems finished within 20 minutes.
Owner and purpose of every platform in the fact sheet stated without hesitation.
Any five events from the timeline put in order correctly on the first attempt.

NDLI, developed by IIT Kharagpur, is a single-window library (II). The first option swaps SWAYAM and SWAYAM PRABHA, the most common confusion.

options: All-India Portal for Academic Achievement Records

quiz.explanation: APAAR is the Automated Permanent Academic Account Registry, a 12-digit ID that links a learner’s records across schools and colleges, accessible through DigiLocker and the ABC platform.

quiz.question: Which agency is the national nodal agency for responding to cyber security incidents in India under Section 70B of the IT Act, 2000?
quiz.explanation: CERT-In (under MeitY) handles incident response under Section 70B. NCIIPC protects critical information infrastructure under Section 70A, I4C (under the Ministry of Home Affairs) coordinates action against cybercrime, and UIDAI issues Aadhaar.

quiz.question: A citizen pays property tax to the municipality through an online portal. Which e-governance model is this?
quiz.explanation: Government-to-Citizen (G2C) covers services between government and individual citizens: taxes, certificates, utility bills. G2B involves businesses (e-procurement, GST), G2G is between government departments, and G2E is between government and its employees.

quiz.question: A college office finds that all its files have been encrypted and a message demands payment in cryptocurrency to unlock them. This is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Ransomware encrypts or locks data and demands a ransom. Phishing tricks people into giving away credentials, spyware secretly watches the user, and a denial-of-service attack floods a server so that it cannot serve users.

domains.name: People, Development and Environment
domains.blurb: Development goals, pollution, resources, disasters, laws and international agreements.

lessons.title: Development, environment and human interaction
lessons.summaryHtml: Development means improving human well-being, not just raising income, and sustainable development asks that this happen without using up the options of future generations (the Brundtland definition of 1987). The UN turned this idea into goal lists: eight Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) for 2000–2015, followed by seventeen Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) with 169 targets for 2016–2030. Human activity changes the environment through farming, mining, industry, urbanisation and energy use, and the size of that impact can be read through ideas such as I = P × A × T, carrying capacity and the ecological footprint. Environmental problems are best classified by scale: local (a town’s garbage or noise), regional (acid rain, river pollution, crop-residue smoke) and global (climate change, ozone depletion, biodiversity loss). NET asks for SDG numbers and names, MDG–SDG contrasts, the chronology of conferences, thinkers and their books, and the scale of a given issue.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Development is the process of improving people’s lives: better income, health, education, freedom and security. Economic growth is narrower: a rise in output or income. A country can grow while its forests, rivers and air get worse, and that growth may not last. Sustainable development joins the two concerns. The Brundtland Report, “Our Common Future” (1987), defined it as development that “meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs”. It rests on three pillars: economic, social and environmental. This lesson covers how the UN turned that idea into goals (MDGs and SDGs), how human activities change the environment, and how to classify environmental problems as local, regional or global.

Why it matters for NET

Unit 9 usually gives a small but steady group of questions in Paper 1, and this lesson is the conceptual base for the other two lessons of the unit. The questions are short and factual, so they are quick marks if you have memorised the right facts and costly if you mix up near-identical numbers. The recurring patterns are: the number and names of the SDGs and MDGs; matching SDG numbers with goals; statements contrasting MDGs and SDGs; chronology of conferences from Stockholm to the 2030 Agenda; thinkers and their books; and deciding whether a given problem is local, regional or global. Anthropogenic impacts of agriculture, mining and urbanisation also appear as “which are correct” questions.

Concepts in depth: the road to sustainable development

YearEventWhat to remember
1962Rachel Carson’s Silent SpringExposed the harm of pesticides such as DDT; often called the start of the modern environmental movement
1968Hardin, “The Tragedy of the Commons”; Ehrlich, The Population BombOver-use of shared resources; fears of population growth
1972UN Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm (5–16 June)First UN conference on the environment; led to UNEP (Nairobi); 5 June became World Environment Day. Same year: Club of Rome’s The Limits to Growth
1973E. F. Schumacher’s Small Is BeautifulEconomics “as if people mattered”; appropriate technology
1987Brundtland Report, Our Common FutureWorld Commission on Environment and Development; the classic definition of sustainable development
1992Earth Summit, Rio de Janeiro (UNCED)Agenda 21, Rio Declaration (27 principles), Forest Principles; UNFCCC and CBD opened for signature
2000Millennium Summit, New York (September)Millennium Declaration, from which the eight MDGs were drawn (deadline 2015)
2002World Summit on Sustainable Development, Johannesburg (Rio+10)Johannesburg Plan of Implementation
2012UN Conference on Sustainable Development, Rio de Janeiro (Rio+20)“The Future We Want”; started the process that produced the SDGs
2015UN Sustainable Development Summit, New York (25–27 September)2030 Agenda: 17 SDGs, 169 targets; in effect from 1 January 2016

Sustainable development is often drawn as three overlapping circles (economy, society, environment). Weak sustainability allows natural capital to be replaced by human-made capital as long as total capital does not fall; strong sustainability says some natural capital (a stable climate, the ozone layer) cannot be replaced and must be kept intact.

Concepts in depth: the Millennium Development Goals

World leaders met at UN Headquarters in September 2000 and adopted the Millennium Declaration. From it came eight time-bound goals with a deadline of 2015, with targets and indicators to track them. They were aimed mainly at developing countries, with rich countries as donors.

MDGGoal
1Eradicate extreme poverty and hunger
2Achieve universal primary education
3Promote gender equality and empower women
4Reduce child mortality
5Improve maternal health
6Combat HIV/AIDS, malaria and other diseases
7Ensure environmental sustainability
8Develop a global partnership for development

Concepts in depth: the Sustainable Development Goals

The 2030 Agenda, “Transforming our world”, was adopted at the UN summit of 25–27 September 2015. It has 17 goals and 169 targets, came into effect on 1 January 2016, and runs to 2030. It is organised around the five Ps: People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership. Global follow-up is led by the High-Level Political Forum (HLPF), where countries present Voluntary National Reviews. Progress is tracked with a global indicator framework of roughly 230 indicators that the UN Statistical Commission revises from time to time. In India, NITI Aayog coordinates the SDGs and publishes the SDG India Index for states and union territories; its fourth edition (2023–24) gave India a composite score of 71, up from 66 in the previous edition. MoSPI maintains the National Indicator Framework.

SDGGoalSDGGoal
1No poverty10Reduced inequalities
2Zero hunger11Sustainable cities and communities
3Good health and well-being12Responsible consumption and production
4Quality education13Climate action
5Gender equality14Life below water
6Clean water and sanitation15Life on land
7Affordable and clean energy16Peace, justice and strong institutions
8Decent work and economic growth17Partnerships for the goals
9Industry, innovation and infrastructure
FeatureMDGsSDGs
Period2000–20152016–2030
Goals / targets8 goals (21 targets after revision)17 goals, 169 targets
CoverageMainly developing countriesUniversal: all countries
How madeDrafted largely by experts after the summitNegotiated openly by member states after Rio+20 (Open Working Group)
EnvironmentOne goal (MDG 7)Several goals (6, 7, 12, 13, 14, 15) and integrated across others
Motto–“Leave no one behind”

Concepts in depth: human–environment interaction

Geographers have explained the relation in three ways. Environmental determinism (Ratzel, Semple) says nature controls human life. Possibilism (Vidal de la Blache) says nature offers possibilities and people choose among them. Neo-determinism or “stop-and-go determinism” (Griffith Taylor) takes a middle path: people can hasten or slow development, but within limits set by nature.

The main anthropogenic activities and their impacts:

  • Agriculture: land clearing, over-use of fertilisers and pesticides (eutrophication, nitrate in groundwater, biomagnification), over-irrigation (waterlogging and salinisation), groundwater depletion; methane from paddy and livestock. The Green Revolution belt of north-west India shows most of these.
  • Mining: deforestation, loss of topsoil, acid mine drainage, heavy-metal pollution, displacement of communities.
  • Industry and energy: air pollutants (SO₂, NOₓ, particulates), greenhouse gases, hazardous waste, thermal pollution of rivers.
  • Urbanisation: loss of wetlands, urban flooding, the urban heat island (concrete and asphalt absorb heat and there is little vegetation), solid waste and sewage, vehicle pollution and noise.
  • Dams and big projects: submergence of forests, changed river flows, sediment trapping, displacement.

Three tools help measure human pressure. I = P × A × T (Ehrlich and Holdren) splits impact into population, affluence and technology; a cleaner technology (lower T) can offset growth in P and A. Carrying capacity is the population an area can support indefinitely; for humans it is not fixed because trade and technology change it. The ecological footprint compares demand with biocapacity; when footprint exceeds biocapacity there is overshoot. The Environmental Kuznets Curve suggests some pollutants first rise then fall as income grows, but this does not hold reliably for CO₂. Hardin’s tragedy of the commons explains over-fishing and groundwater over-pumping. Indian people’s movements show the local response: Chipko (1973, Uttarakhand, then Uttar Pradesh), Appiko (1983, Karnataka), Silent Valley (Kerala; declared a national park in 1984) and the Narmada Bachao Andolan (Narmada valley).

Concepts in depth: local, regional and global issues

ScaleMeaningExamples
LocalCause and effect stay within a town, village or wardGarbage dumping, local noise, a polluted pond, urban waterlogging, indoor smoke from chulhas
RegionalEffects cross district, state or national boundaries within a regionAcid rain, river-basin pollution (Ganga, Yamuna), crop-residue smoke over north India, groundwater decline in north-west India, desertification, regional haze
GlobalCauses are spread worldwide and effects are planetaryClimate change, stratospheric ozone depletion, biodiversity loss, ocean acidification, marine plastic

The scale of an issue decides the level of response: municipal rules for local issues, inter-state or river-basin plans for regional ones, and international treaties (Lesson 9.3) for global ones.

Worked examples

Example 1 (I = P × A × T). P = 1.4 billion, A = US$ 2,500 per person, T = 0.5 kg CO₂ per US$. Step 1: P × A = 1.4 × 10⁹ × 2,500 = 3.5 × 10¹² US$. Step 2: × T = 3.5 × 10¹² × 0.5 = 1.75 × 10¹² kg. Step 3: divide by 1,000 to get tonnes: 1.75 × 10⁹ t = 1.75 billion tonnes. If T falls by 20% (to 0.4) while A rises by 25% (to 3,125), impact is 1.4 × 10⁹ × 3,125 × 0.4 kg = 1.75 billion tonnes again: a 20% cut in T exactly offsets a 25% rise in A, because 0.8 × 1.25 = 1.

Example 2 (Human Development Index). The UNDP’s HDI is the geometric mean of three dimension indices. With health 0.80, education 0.60 and income 0.70: product = 0.80 × 0.60 × 0.70 = 0.336; cube root = 0.695. The arithmetic mean, 0.700, is the trap option. The geometric mean punishes a low score in any one dimension.

Example 3 (ecological footprint and doubling time). A region has a footprint of 2.4 global hectares per person and a biocapacity of 1.6 gha per person. Ratio = 2.4 ÷ 1.6 = 1.5: it uses resources 1.5 times as fast as its ecosystems regenerate them. If its population grows at 1.4% a year, the rule of 70 gives a doubling time of 70 ÷ 1.4 = 50 years (exactly, ln 2 ÷ ln 1.014 ≈ 49.9 years).

Example 4 (classifying by scale). Items: (i) SO₂ from a thermal plant causing acid rain 500 km away; (ii) a blocked drain in a colony; (iii) CFC release; (iv) smoke from crop burning covering three states. Step 1: ask how far the effect travels. (ii) stays in the colony: local. (i) and (iv) cross state or national borders within a region: regional. (iii) thins the ozone layer worldwide: global.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
Brundtland Report“Our Common Future”, 1987, World Commission on Environment and Development
MDGs8 goals, Millennium Declaration September 2000, deadline 2015; MDG 7 = environmental sustainability
SDGs17 goals, 169 targets; adopted 25–27 September 2015; in effect 1 January 2016; end 2030
Five PsPeople, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership
Key SDG numbers6 water, 7 energy, 11 cities, 12 consumption, 13 climate, 14 below water, 15 on land, 16 peace and institutions, 17 partnerships
SDG India IndexNITI Aayog; 4th edition 2023–24: India 71 (up from 66)
Impact identityI = P × A × T
HDIGeometric mean of health, education and income indices
Doubling time≈ 70 ÷ growth rate (%)
Overshoot ratioFootprint ÷ biocapacity (> 1 means overshoot)
ThinkersCarson (Silent Spring, 1962), Hardin (commons, 1968), Ehrlich (Population Bomb, 1968), Meadows et al. for Club of Rome (Limits to Growth, 1972), Schumacher (Small Is Beautiful, 1973)

NTA traps

  • Counting goals wrongly. Wrong: “MDGs had 17 goals.” Fix: 8 MDGs (2000–2015), 17 SDGs (2016–2030), 169 targets.
  • Swapping SDG 14 and 15. Fix: 14 life below water, then 15 life on land.
  • “SDGs are for developing countries.” Fix: they are universal; that description fits the MDGs.
  • Adoption date versus start date. Fix: adopted September 2015; effective 1 January 2016.
  • Poverty as a “P”. Fix: the five Ps are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace, Partnership.
  • Brundtland and Rio mixed up. Fix: the definition is 1987 (Brundtland); Agenda 21 is 1992 (Rio).
  • Arithmetic mean for HDI. Fix: HDI uses the geometric mean.
  • Scale by cause instead of effect. Fix: acid rain is regional even though each chimney is local, because the deposition crosses borders.

How NTA asks this

  • Direct MCQ: which report gave the definition; which SDG is a given theme; which is not one of the five Ps.
  • Match the following: SDG numbers with goals; conferences with outcomes; thinkers with books; movements with states.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: MDG versus SDG features; why an issue is regional; what the Kuznets curve claims.
  • Chronology: Stockholm, Brundtland, Rio, Millennium Summit, Johannesburg, Rio+20, 2030 Agenda.
  • Multiple select: which issues are global; which were MDGs; which are consequences of intensive farming.

Mini-example (match). List I: A. Stockholm 1972, B. Rio 1992, C. Johannesburg 2002, D. Rio+20 2012. List II: I. “The Future We Want”, II. Agenda 21, III. creation of UNEP, IV. Johannesburg Plan of Implementation. Answer: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I. Fix the easiest pair first (Johannesburg gives its own name away), then eliminate.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The SDGs are universal. R: They apply to all countries, unlike the MDGs, which were aimed mainly at developing countries. Both are true and R explains A: option 1.

Elimination trick: in chronology questions, find the earliest and the latest item first. Only one or two options usually start and end correctly; then check a single middle pair.
Watch out: numbers of SDG indicators are revised by the UN Statistical Commission, so NTA rarely asks them. Goals (17) and targets (169) are stable and are asked often. For anything recent, check ugcnet.nta.ac.in and official UN or NITI Aayog pages.

terms.definition: Development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs (Brundtland Report, “Our Common Future”, 1987).
Eight time-bound goals drawn from the UN Millennium Declaration of September 2000, with a deadline of 2015; aimed mainly at developing countries.
Seventeen goals and 169 targets of the 2030 Agenda, adopted at the UN summit of 25–27 September 2015 and in effect from 1 January 2016; universal for all countries.
People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership: the five themes around which the 2030 Agenda is organised.
Environmental impact = Population × Affluence (consumption per person) × Technology (impact per unit of consumption); proposed by Ehrlich and Holdren in the early 1970s.
The largest population an environment can support indefinitely with its resources; for humans it shifts with technology and trade.
The area of biologically productive land and water (in global hectares) needed to supply what a population consumes and absorb its wastes; overshoot occurs when footprint exceeds biocapacity.
Caused or produced by human activity, for example anthropogenic CO₂ from burning fossil fuels.
The hypothesis that some pollution first rises and then falls as income per person grows (an inverted U). It holds for some local pollutants, not reliably for CO₂.
Garrett Hardin’s 1968 argument that a shared, open-access resource tends to be over-used because each user gains the full benefit of extra use but bears only part of the cost.

lessons.examTip: For SDG questions, learn the 17 goals as numbered pairs (6 water, 7 energy, 13 climate, 14 life below water, 15 life on land, 17 partnerships). For chronology questions, anchor on 1972 (Stockholm), 1987 (Brundtland), 1992 (Rio), 2000 (MDGs), 2002 (Johannesburg), 2012 (Rio+20) and 2015 (SDGs), then slot everything else between them.

steps: Write the 17 SDGs with their numbers from memory in 5 minutes, then check against the lesson table.
Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes (about 75 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes. In every chronology problem, write the year next to each item before choosing.
Check with solutions.md. Log each mistake with its trap (MDG and SDG counts mixed, SDG 14/15 swapped, arithmetic mean used for HDI, scale judged by the source instead of the effect).
Draw a one-page timeline from 1962 (Silent Spring) to 2016 (SDGs in effect) with one output per event.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the quiz and bank questions at 45–60 seconds each.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
All 17 SDGs written with correct numbers in under 5 minutes.
Every chronology problem solved in under 60 seconds.
Local, regional and global examples classified without error.

quiz.question: The most widely quoted definition of sustainable development, “development that meets the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own needs”, comes from which report?
quiz.explanation: The definition is from “Our Common Future” (1987), the report of the World Commission on Environment and Development chaired by Gro Harlem Brundtland, hence the Brundtland Report. The Limits to Growth (1972) was the Club of Rome study on growth limits; Agenda 21 was the action plan of the 1992 Rio Earth Summit; The Future We Want was the outcome document of Rio+20 (2012).

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: SDG 6 is clean water and sanitation (II), SDG 13 is climate action (IV), SDG 14 is life below water (I) and SDG 15 is life on land (III). The first distractor swaps 14 and 15, the most common slip: “below water” comes before “on land”.

b: I. Life below water
II. Clean water and sanitation
III. Life on land
IV. Climate action

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: Statement I is true: the MDGs were eight time-bound goals with 2015 as the deadline. Statement II is false: the SDGs are universal and apply to all countries, developed and developing. Being aimed mainly at developing countries was a feature of the MDGs.

stmts: Statement I: The Millennium Development Goals were eight goals with a deadline of 2015.
Statement II: The Sustainable Development Goals apply only to developing countries.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

quiz.question: Arrange the following events in chronological order (earliest first).
quiz.explanation: Stockholm (B) was in June 1972; the Brundtland Report (C) in 1987; the Rio Earth Summit (A) in June 1992; the Millennium Summit (E) in September 2000; the 2030 Agenda (D) in September 2015. So B, C, A, E, D.

stmts: A. Rio Earth Summit (UN Conference on Environment and Development)
B. UN Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm
C. Publication of the Brundtland Report
D. Adoption of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development

quiz.question: A country has a population of 1.4 billion, consumption (affluence) of US$ 2,500 per person per year, and a technology factor of 0.5 kg CO₂ per US$ of consumption. Using I = P × A × T, its annual CO₂ impact is:
quiz.explanation: I = 1.4 × 10⁹ × 2,500 × 0.5 kg = 1.75 × 10¹² kg. Since 1 tonne = 1,000 kg, this is 1.75 × 10⁹ tonnes = 1.75 billion tonnes. Forgetting to divide by 1,000 inflates the answer; 3.5 billion tonnes comes from dropping the factor 0.5.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: An issue is regional when its effects cross administrative boundaries within a region. The smoke travels to neighbouring states and the national capital region, which is exactly why the issue is regional. So both are true and R explains A.

stmts: Assertion (A): Crop-residue (stubble) burning in Punjab and Haryana is a regional environmental issue rather than a purely local one.
Reason (R): Its smoke is carried across state boundaries and adds to the winter smog of the Delhi–NCR region.

quiz.question: Which of the following are global-level environmental issues?
options: A, B, C and D only
quiz.explanation: Ozone depletion (A), ocean acidification (B) and climate change (D) are caused by emissions from everywhere and affect the whole planet. Construction noise in one colony (C) and garbage in a ward (E) are local issues whose effects stay near the source.

stmts: A. Stratospheric ozone depletion
B. Ocean acidification
C. Noise from a construction site in one colony
D. Climate change
E. Garbage dumping in a municipal ward
