quiz.question: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development is built around five themes known as the “five Ps”. Which of the following is NOT one of them?
quiz.explanation: The five Ps are People, Planet, Prosperity, Peace and Partnership. Ending poverty is the first goal (SDG 1) and falls under “People”, but “Poverty” itself is not one of the five Ps.

quiz.question: “Affordable and clean energy” is which Sustainable Development Goal?
quiz.explanation: SDG 7 is affordable and clean energy. SDG 5 is gender equality, SDG 9 is industry, innovation and infrastructure, and SDG 11 is sustainable cities and communities.

quiz.question: The idea of “stop-and-go determinism” (neo-determinism), a middle path between environmental determinism and possibilism, was proposed by:
quiz.explanation: Griffith Taylor compared human choice to traffic at a signal: people can speed up or slow down development, but nature sets the lights. Ratzel and Semple are associated with environmental determinism (nature controls human life); Vidal de la Blache with possibilism (nature offers possibilities and humans choose).

lessons.title: Pollution, resources and disasters
lessons.summaryHtml: Pollution is the addition of substances or energy (noise, heat) to air, water or soil faster than the environment can disperse, break down or store them harmlessly. India measures air quality with the National Air Quality Index (six categories from Good to Severe, eight pollutants) and regulates waste through separate rules for solid, plastic, bio-medical, hazardous and electronic waste. Many pollutants have signature health effects that NET loves to match: mercury with Minamata disease, cadmium with itai-itai, nitrate with blue-baby syndrome, fluoride with fluorosis. Climate change is driven by greenhouse gases, compared through global warming potential; 2024 was the first calendar year about 1.55 °C above pre-industrial levels. The lesson also covers renewable and non-renewable energy (solar, wind, hydro, geothermal, biomass, nuclear), forests and soil, and disasters: the hazard–vulnerability–risk idea, the disaster management cycle, India’s Disaster Management Act and the Sendai Framework. Several small numericals (AQI sub-index, decibels, BOD, CO₂-equivalent, wind and hydro power) appear in the exam and are worked here.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Pollution happens when people add substances or energy to air, water or soil faster than nature can dilute, break down or store them safely. Some pollutants act fast and near the source (smoke, noise); others build up slowly and spread worldwide (CO₂, mercury). Natural resources are what we take from nature: energy sources, water, soil and forests. Some renew themselves (sunlight, wind), others are finite (coal, uranium). Disasters happen when a natural or human-made hazard strikes people who cannot cope. This lesson connects all three: how pollution harms health, how we manage waste, what drives climate change, which energy sources India uses, and how disasters are managed.

Why it matters for NET

This is the broadest lesson of Unit 9, and NET draws on it every cycle. Typical questions match pollutants with diseases, waste categories with colour codes or rules, energy sources with sites, and disaster bodies with their chairpersons. Statement questions test ground-level versus stratospheric ozone, primary versus secondary pollutants and renewable versus non-renewable resources. A few short numericals appear: decibel addition, AQI sub-index, BOD, CO₂-equivalent and power formulas. The facts are fixed pairs, so a one-page sheet revised often wins most of these marks.

Concepts in depth: air pollution

Sources: vehicles, thermal power, industry, construction dust, crop-residue and waste burning, household fuels (chulhas). Primary pollutants are emitted directly (CO, SO₂, NOₓ, particulates, lead). Secondary pollutants form in the air: ground-level ozone and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN) in photochemical smog (NOₓ + hydrocarbons + strong sunlight), and sulphate and nitrate aerosols. Classical (London) smog is a reducing mixture of smoke and SO₂ in cold, damp air. A temperature inversion, warm air lying over cooler surface air, stops vertical mixing and traps pollution, which is why north Indian winters are so bad.

Standards and programmes. India’s National Ambient Air Quality Standards (2009) cover 12 pollutants; the annual PM2.5 standard is 40 µg/m³ and the annual PM10 standard 60 µg/m³. The WHO guidelines of 2021 are stricter (annual PM2.5 5 µg/m³, PM10 15 µg/m³). The National AQI was launched on 17 October 2014 (“one number, one colour, one description”). It uses eight pollutants (PM10, PM2.5, NO₂, SO₂, CO, O₃, NH₃, Pb); the overall AQI is the highest sub-index and needs data for at least three pollutants, one of them PM2.5 or PM10. The National Clean Air Programme (NCAP), launched in January 2019, first aimed at a 20–30% cut in PM10 by 2024–25 (base 2017–18) and now aims at up to 40% by 2025–26 in 131 non-attainment and million-plus cities.

AQI categoryAQIPM10 (24-h, µg/m³)PM2.5 (24-h, µg/m³)
Good0–500–500–30
Satisfactory51–10051–10031–60
Moderately polluted101–200101–25061–90
Poor201–300251–35091–120
Very poor301–400351–430121–250
Severe401–500430+250+

Concepts in depth: water, soil and noise pollution

Water. Point sources (a drain, a factory outfall) are easier to control than non-point sources (farm run-off, urban storm water). Key measures: dissolved oxygen (DO, healthy water holds several mg/L), BOD (oxygen microbes need to break down organic matter; BOD₅ = (DOinitial − DOfinal) ÷ dilution fraction) and COD (chemical oxygen demand, always ≥ BOD). Nutrients cause eutrophication: algal blooms, oxygen loss and fish kills. Persistent chemicals show biomagnification. The Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act of 1974 created the pollution control boards; Namami Gange targets the Ganga.

Soil. Over-use of fertilisers and pesticides, industrial effluents, mining wastes, plastics and saline irrigation water degrade soil. Salinisation and waterlogging follow poor drainage.

Noise. Sound level L = 10 log₁₀(I ÷ I₀) dB. +10 dB is 10 times the intensity, +20 dB is 100 times. The Noise Pollution (Regulation and Control) Rules, 2000 set limits in dB(A): industrial 75 by day / 70 by night, commercial 65/55, residential 55/45, silence zone 50/40 (day is 6 a.m. to 10 p.m.).

PollutantMain health effect
Methyl mercuryMinamata disease (nervous system), Japan 1950s
CadmiumItai-itai disease (bones, kidneys)
Arsenic (groundwater)Arsenicosis, skin lesions, “black-foot” disease, cancers
Fluoride (excess)Dental and skeletal fluorosis
Nitrate (excess)Methaemoglobinaemia, “blue-baby” syndrome
LeadDamage to brain and nerves, especially in children; anaemia
Carbon monoxideCarboxyhaemoglobin, oxygen starvation of tissues
SO₂, NO₂, ozoneIrritation of airways, asthma, bronchitis
PM2.5Enters deep lungs and blood; heart and lung disease
Asbestos / silica dustAsbestosis and mesothelioma / silicosis
BenzeneLeukaemia

Concepts in depth: waste

WasteCurrent rules (India)Key points
Municipal solid wasteSolid Waste Management Rules, 2026 (in force 1 April 2026, replacing the 2016 rules)Four-stream segregation at source: wet, dry, sanitary, special-care; duties for bulk waste generators; environmental compensation for violations
PlasticPlastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (amended)Identified single-use plastic items banned from 1 July 2022; carry bags at least 120 microns from 31 December 2022; EPR for producers
Bio-medicalBio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016Colour codes: yellow (anatomical, soiled, expired medicines), red (contaminated recyclable plastics), white translucent (sharps), blue (glass, metallic implants)
HazardousHazardous and Other Wastes Rules, 2016Authorisation, storage, transboundary movement (links to the Basel Convention)
ElectronicE-Waste (Management) Rules, 2022 (in force 1 April 2023)EPR targets and an online EPR portal for producers and recyclers
LiquidWater Act, 1974; sewage treatmentPrimary (physical), secondary (biological) and tertiary (advanced) treatment

The waste hierarchy, from most to least preferred: reduce, reuse, recycle, recover (energy), dispose (sanitary landfill).

Concepts in depth: climate change

Greenhouse gases (water vapour, CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, ozone, fluorinated gases) absorb outgoing infrared radiation and warm the surface. N₂, O₂ and argon are not greenhouse gases. The WMO reports that 2024 was likely the first calendar year about 1.55 °C above the 1850–1900 average, and that CO₂ reached about 420 ppm in 2023, 151% of the pre-industrial level. Gases are compared by GWP: over 100 years, CH₄ is roughly 28 and N₂O roughly 265 in the IPCC Fifth Assessment values (the Sixth Assessment gives slightly different numbers), so emissions are summed as CO₂-equivalent. The IPCC was set up in 1988 by WMO and UNEP. Impacts include heat waves, glacier retreat, sea-level rise, erratic monsoons, coral bleaching and new disease patterns. Ground-level ozone is a pollutant; stratospheric ozone is protective (Lesson 9.3 covers the Montreal Protocol).

Concepts in depth: natural and energy resources

ResourceKey ideaIndia example
SolarPhotovoltaic (light to electricity) or solar thermal; output = area × irradiance × efficiencyNational Solar Mission; rooftop programmes
WindP = ½ρAv³: power rises with the cube of speedTamil Nadu, Gujarat; offshore potential
HydroP = ρgQHη (flow × head × efficiency)Tehri, Bhakra; small hydro
GeothermalHeat from the Earth’s interiorPuga Valley (Ladakh)
Tidal and waveRise and fall of tidesGulf of Khambhat, Gulf of Kutch, Sundarbans (potential)
BiomassCrop residues, biogas, bio-fuels; renewable if regrownBiogas plants, ethanol blending
NuclearFission of uranium or plutonium; low-carbon but not renewable; radioactive wasteKudankulam, Tarapur; three-stage programme: PHWR (natural uranium), fast breeder (plutonium), thorium
ForestsTimber, fuel, water regulation, carbon sink, biodiversityIndia State of Forest Report 2023: forest and tree cover 25.17% of the area (forest 21.76% + tree 3.41%); the National Forest Policy, 1988 aims at one-third
SoilForms very slowly, so effectively non-renewable; lost through erosion and salinitySoil Health Card scheme

India reached 50% of its installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources on 30 June 2025, five years ahead of its 2030 target (Lesson 9.3).

Concepts in depth: natural hazards and disasters

A hazard (earthquake, cyclone, flood, drought, landslide, tsunami, heat wave; or industrial accident) becomes a disaster when it strikes a vulnerable community that cannot cope with its own resources. In words: risk rises with hazard and vulnerability and falls with capacity. The disaster management cycle runs: response, recovery, mitigation, preparedness, and round again. Structural mitigation changes the physical world (embankments, earthquake-resistant buildings, cyclone shelters, check dams); non-structural mitigation changes behaviour and rules (land-use zoning, building codes, early warning, awareness, insurance). Mangroves and coastal forests are natural buffers against storm surges. Earthquake size is measured on a logarithmic magnitude scale: one unit is 10 times the wave amplitude and about 31.6 times the energy.

India’s framework. The Disaster Management Act, 2005 set up the National Disaster Management Authority (chaired by the Prime Minister), State Authorities (Chief Minister) and District Authorities (District Collector or Magistrate), a National Executive Committee (Union Home Secretary), the NDRF and NIDM. The Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 received assent on 29 March 2025; among other things it enables urban disaster management authorities. Globally: the Yokohama Strategy (1994), the Hyogo Framework (2005–2015) and the Sendai Framework (2015–2030), adopted in March 2015 with seven targets and four priorities: understanding risk, strengthening risk governance, investing in resilience, and enhancing preparedness to “build back better”.

Worked examples

Example 1 (AQI sub-index). PM2.5 = 75 µg/m³ lies in 61–90, the band for AQI 101–200. Sub-index = 101 + (200 − 101) ÷ (90 − 61) × (75 − 61) = 101 + 3.414 × 14 = 148.8 ≈ 149. If the PM10 sub-index is 120 and NO₂ is 60, the overall AQI is the highest, 149: Moderately polluted.

Example 2 (decibels). Two machines of 80 dB: intensities 10⁸ I₀ each, total 2 × 10⁸ I₀, so L = 80 + 10 log₁₀ 2 = 83.0 dB. Three such machines: 80 + 10 log₁₀ 3 = 84.8 dB. Going from 60 dB to 80 dB multiplies intensity by 10² = 100.

Example 3 (BOD). A sample is diluted to 2% (P = 0.02). DO falls from 8.4 mg/L to 4.8 mg/L in 5 days. BOD₅ = (8.4 − 4.8) ÷ 0.02 = 3.6 ÷ 0.02 = 180 mg/L. Forgetting to divide by P gives 3.6 mg/L, the trap.

Example 4 (CO₂-equivalent). A farm emits 100 t CO₂, 2 t CH₄ and 1 t N₂O. With GWP CH₄ = 28 and N₂O = 265: 100 + 2 × 28 + 1 × 265 = 100 + 56 + 265 = 421 t CO₂e.

Example 5 (energy). Hydro: Q = 20 m³/s, H = 50 m, η = 0.9: P = 1000 × 9.81 × 20 × 50 × 0.9 = 8,829,000 W ≈ 8.83 MW. Solar: 10 m² of 18%-efficient panels under 1,000 W/m² give 1.8 kW; with 5 peak-sun hours a day, 9 kWh per day. Wind: doubling speed gives 2³ = 8 times the power.

Concepts in depth: soil pollution, liquid waste and hazardous waste

Soil pollution and degradation. Soil is polluted when harmful substances build up in it faster than natural processes remove them, and it is degraded when its fertility or structure declines. The main causes are excess chemical fertilisers and pesticides, industrial effluents and sludge, mining and smelting wastes carrying heavy metals, plastics and dumped solid waste, e-waste burnt in the open, and irrigation with untreated sewage. Degradation also comes from water and wind erosion of bare topsoil, salinisation and alkalinisation where irrigation has poor drainage, waterlogging, acidification, loss of organic carbon and compaction by heavy machines. The effects are lower yields, heavy metals such as cadmium entering the food chain, and nitrate leaching into groundwater. Remedies match the problem: lime for acidic soils, gypsum for alkaline (sodic) soils, terracing, contour bunding, strip cropping and shelter belts against erosion, balanced fertiliser use guided by soil testing, organic matter and bio-fertilisers, and bioremediation or phytoremediation (microbes or plants that take up or break down contaminants). The Soil Health Card scheme was launched on 19 February 2015 at Suratgarh, Rajasthan. A card reports 12 parameters: N, P, K and S (macronutrients); Zn, Fe, Cu, Mn and B (micronutrients); and pH, electrical conductivity and organic carbon.

Liquid waste. Domestic sewage has two parts: blackwater from toilets and greywater from kitchens, bathing and laundry. Greywater carries a much smaller pathogen and organic load, so it is easier to treat and reuse (for gardening or flushing). Industries discharge effluents that may carry chemicals and heavy metals. A sewage treatment plant works in stages: preliminary treatment (screens and grit chambers), primary treatment (sedimentation of settleable solids), secondary treatment (biological: activated sludge, trickling filters or oxidation ponds, where microbes consume organic matter and cut BOD sharply) and tertiary treatment (nutrient removal, filtration and disinfection by chlorine, ultraviolet light or ozone). The settled sludge is often digested anaerobically, which yields biogas (mainly methane). Where there are no sewers, septic tanks and faecal sludge treatment plants do the job. Performance is judged by BOD removal efficiency = (BODin − BODout) ÷ BODin × 100.

Example: BOD removal. A plant receives sewage with a BOD of 250 mg/L and discharges effluent with a BOD of 20 mg/L. Removal efficiency = (250 − 20) ÷ 250 × 100 = 230 ÷ 250 × 100 = 92%. Trap: dividing by the outlet value (230 ÷ 20) gives a meaningless 1150%.

Hazardous waste. The Hazardous and Other Wastes (Management and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2016, notified on 4 April 2016, replaced the 2008 rules. They define hazardous waste as waste that, because of physical, chemical, biological, reactive, toxic, flammable, explosive or corrosive characteristics, causes danger to health or the environment. Examples are used oil, spent solvents, acid and paint sludge, spent catalysts and heavy-metal residues. “Other wastes” include waste tyres, paper waste, metal scrap and used electronic items. Rule 4 fixes the order of management: prevention, minimisation, reuse, recycling, recovery (including co-processing) and, last, safe disposal. Occupiers need authorisation from the State Pollution Control Board, and waste that cannot be recovered goes to a treatment, storage and disposal facility (TSDF) with a secured landfill or incinerator. The rules do not apply to waste-water and exhaust gases (covered by the Water and Air Acts), radioactive wastes (covered by the atomic energy law), bio-medical waste or municipal solid waste, which have their own rules. Movement across borders follows the Basel Convention, adopted on 22 March 1989 and in force since 5 May 1992.

NTA trap: bio-medical waste, e-waste and radioactive waste are not managed under the hazardous waste rules; each has its own regime. And the Basel Convention is about hazardous waste, not ozone (Montreal) or chemicals trade (Rotterdam).

NTA traps

  • Adding decibels. Wrong: 80 dB + 80 dB = 160 dB. Fix: add intensities; the result is 83 dB.
  • Ozone reversed. Wrong: “stratospheric ozone is a pollutant”. Fix: ground-level ozone is a secondary pollutant; stratospheric ozone shields us from UV-B.
  • PM sizes reversed. Fix: PM2.5 is smaller and more dangerous than PM10.
  • Nuclear as renewable. Fix: low-carbon but non-renewable (finite uranium).
  • Mixing the Japanese diseases. Fix: Minamata = mercury, itai-itai = cadmium.
  • Nitrate versus fluoride. Fix: blue-baby syndrome is nitrate; fluorosis is fluoride.
  • Colour codes. Fix: yellow anatomical, red recyclable plastics, white sharps, blue glass.
  • AQI as an average. Fix: the overall AQI is the worst (highest) sub-index.
  • Mitigation versus preparedness. Fix: mitigation reduces the impact itself (embankments, codes); preparedness readies the response (drills, warnings, stockpiles).
  • Wind power linear in speed. Fix: it grows as v³.

How NTA asks this

  • Match the following: pollutant–disease, waste–colour code, energy source–site, authority–chairperson, rule–year.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: ozone at two levels, primary and secondary pollutants, inversion and smog, biomagnification, renewable versus non-renewable.
  • Multiple select: AQI pollutants, greenhouse gases, structural mitigation measures, renewable sources.
  • Order: disaster management cycle, waste hierarchy, noise limits, AQI bands.
  • Numerical: decibel addition, sub-index, BOD, CO₂e, wind or hydro power.

Mini-example (match). A. NDMA, B. SDMA, C. DDMA, D. National Executive Committee; I. Chief Minister, II. Union Home Secretary, III. Prime Minister, IV. District Collector. Answer: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II.

Mini-example (A-R). A: Winter smog is worse in Delhi than in summer. R: Temperature inversions and low wind speeds in winter trap pollutants near the ground. Both true, and R explains A: option 1.

Elimination trick: in pollutant–disease matches, lock the two Japanese diseases first (mercury and cadmium). That usually leaves only one option standing.
Watch out: waste rules are amended often, and the Solid Waste Management Rules were replaced in 2026. For the latest version of any rule, check the MoEFCC or CPCB website before the exam.

terms.definition: A primary pollutant is emitted directly (CO, SO₂, soot); a secondary pollutant forms in the air by reactions among others (ground-level ozone, PAN, sulphate aerosols).
Launched on 17 October 2014; six categories (Good 0–50 to Severe 401–500) based on eight pollutants; the overall AQI is the worst sub-index.
Biochemical oxygen demand: oxygen used by microbes to break down organic matter in water, usually over 5 days at 20 °C; high BOD means heavy organic pollution.
Increase in the concentration of a persistent, fat-soluble pollutant (DDT, methyl mercury) at each higher level of a food chain.
A logarithmic unit of sound level: +10 dB means 10 times the intensity; two equal sources together are about 3 dB louder than one.
Warming caused by 1 tonne of a gas over a period (usually 100 years) relative to 1 tonne of CO₂; used to express emissions as CO₂-equivalent.
The duty of producers to manage their products at end of life; central to India’s plastic, e-waste and battery waste rules.
A hazard is a potentially damaging event; vulnerability is how easily people and assets are harmed; disaster risk grows with hazard and vulnerability and falls with coping capacity.
Measures taken before a disaster to reduce its impact; structural (embankments, resistant buildings, shelters) or non-structural (zoning, codes, awareness, insurance).
UN framework for disaster risk reduction 2015–2030, adopted at Sendai, Japan, in March 2015: seven global targets and four priorities for action.

lessons.examTip: Match pollutants to diseases and waste types to their rules as fixed pairs, and learn the AQI bands (50, 100, 200, 300, 400, 500) and the noise limits (75/65/55/50 dB by day). For numericals, remember three rules: power from wind grows as v³, two equal noise sources add 3 dB, and the AQI sub-index is a straight-line interpolation inside a band.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 12 minutes without notes (about 90 seconds each).
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 12 minutes. Write the formula (dB, sub-index, BOD, P ∝ v³, ρgQHη) before substituting numbers.
Check with solutions.md and log each mistake with its trap (decibels added directly, wrong AQI band, GWP forgotten, dilution not divided, colour codes swapped).
Write the pollutant–disease pairs, the waste rules and years, and the AQI and noise tables from memory; compare with the fact sheet.
Draw the disaster management cycle and list two structural and two non-structural measures each for floods, cyclones and earthquakes.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the quiz and bank at 60–90 seconds per question.
check: At least 12 of 15 practice problems correct.
Every numerical (problems 1, 2, 5, 7, 10, 14) solved within 90 seconds.
All eight AQI pollutants and all six AQI bands written from memory.
Pollutant–disease and waste–colour matches answered without error.

quiz.question: Under India’s National Air Quality Index, the category “Poor” corresponds to which AQI range?
quiz.explanation: The six bands are Good 0–50, Satisfactory 51–100, Moderately polluted 101–200, Poor 201–300, Very poor 301–400 and Severe 401–500. 101–200 is Moderately polluted and 301–400 is Very poor; 151–200 is a band of the US index, not India’s.

quiz.question: The 24-hour average PM2.5 concentration at a station is 75 µg/m³. In India’s AQI, PM2.5 of 61–90 µg/m³ corresponds to sub-index 101–200, found by linear interpolation. The PM2.5 sub-index (rounded) is:
quiz.explanation: Sub-index = I_lo + (I_hi − I_lo) ÷ (C_hi − C_lo) × (C − C_lo) = 101 + (200 − 101) ÷ (90 − 61) × (75 − 61) = 101 + 99 ÷ 29 × 14 = 101 + 47.8 = 148.8 ≈ 149 (Moderately polluted). Using 100 and 60 as the lower ends gives about 150–151, a common slip.

quiz.question: Match List I with List II
quiz.explanation: Methyl mercury in fish at Minamata Bay, Japan, caused Minamata disease (IV). Cadmium in rice fields of Japan caused itai-itai (“ouch-ouch”) disease (I). Nitrate converts haemoglobin to methaemoglobin in infants (II). Excess fluoride causes fluorosis (III).

b: I. Itai-itai disease
II. Methaemoglobinaemia (blue-baby syndrome)
III. Skeletal and dental fluorosis
IV. Minamata disease

quiz.question: Two identical machines each produce a sound level of 80 dB at a point. When both run together, the sound level at that point is about:
quiz.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic, so intensities add, not decibels. L = 10 log₁₀(10⁸ + 10⁸) = 10 log₁₀(2 × 10⁸) = 80 + 10 log₁₀ 2 = 80 + 3.01 ≈ 83 dB. Adding the numbers (160 dB) is the trap.

quiz.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
quiz.explanation: CO forms carboxyhaemoglobin with an affinity about 200 times that of oxygen, so Statement I is true. PM2.5 means particles of 2.5 µm or less, which are smaller than PM10 (10 µm or less) and go deeper into the lungs; Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Carbon monoxide binds with haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does, reducing the blood’s capacity to carry oxygen.
Statement II: PM2.5 particles are larger than PM10 particles.

B. Tidal

quiz.explanation: Immediately after impact comes response (rescue, relief). Then recovery (rehabilitation and reconstruction). Then mitigation, reducing future impact, and preparedness (plans, drills, warnings) before the next event. So B, C, D, A.

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
quiz.explanation: Persistent, fat-soluble chemicals stay in body fat. Each predator eats many prey, so the concentration multiplies up the chain (biomagnification). R is exactly the mechanism behind A.

stmts: Assertion (A): The concentration of DDT is highest in top carnivores such as fish-eating birds.
Reason (R): DDT is fat-soluble and is not easily broken down or excreted, so it accumulates at each step of the food chain.

quiz.question: Under the Bio-Medical Waste Management Rules, 2016, human anatomical waste is to be put in a container of which colour?
quiz.explanation: Yellow is for human and animal anatomical waste, soiled waste and expired medicines, mostly sent for incineration. Red is for contaminated recyclable plastics (tubing, bottles), white (translucent, puncture-proof) for sharps, and blue for glassware and metallic implants.

quiz.question: The power available from wind is proportional to the cube of wind speed. If the wind speed at a site rises from 5 m/s to 10 m/s, the power available rises by a factor of:
quiz.explanation: P = ½ρAv³, so P ∝ v³. The ratio is (10 ÷ 5)³ = 2³ = 8. Choosing 2 or 4 treats power as proportional to v or v².

lessons.title: Environmental protection acts and international agreements
lessons.summaryHtml: India’s environmental law rests on the Constitution (Articles 48A, 51A(g) and 253) and a set of Acts, of which the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 is the umbrella law: passed after the Bhopal gas tragedy, in force from 19 November 1986, and the source of the EIA, coastal zone and waste rules. Climate policy runs through the National Action Plan on Climate Change (30 June 2008) and its eight missions, and through India’s Nationally Determined Contributions: 33–35% (2015), 45% (2022) and, for 2031–2035, a 47% cut in emissions intensity of GDP from 2005 levels. Internationally, the ozone regime (Vienna 1985, Montreal 1987, Kigali 2016) is the success story; the climate regime runs from the UNFCCC (1992) through Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015) to annual COPs, most recently Baku (2024) and Belém (2025); biodiversity runs from the CBD (1992) to the Kunming–Montreal framework (2022). The International Solar Alliance, launched by India and France at COP21 in 2015, is headquartered in Gurugram. NET tests this unit mostly through dates, chronology, matching and statement questions, so exact years matter.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Environmental problems need rules. Inside India, rules come from the Constitution and from Acts of Parliament, and the most important is the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986, an “umbrella” law that lets the Central Government fill any gap. Across borders, countries sign conventions (framework treaties), then protocols and amendments that add binding details, and meet every year at a Conference of the Parties (COP). India connects the two levels through national plans such as the National Action Plan on Climate Change and through its Nationally Determined Contributions under the Paris Agreement. This lesson gives you the dates and details NET asks, organised so that chronology questions become easy.

Why it matters for NET

Almost every NET cycle has at least one question from this lesson, and the formats are predictable: arranging treaties or Acts in order, matching conventions with their subjects or years, statement questions on the Paris Agreement or the Kyoto Protocol, NAPCC missions and ministries, and India’s climate targets. Because many figures are close (33–35%, 45%, 47%; 40%, 50%, 60%), NTA uses them as distractors. Recent events (COP28 to COP30, India’s NDC for 2031–2035) are also likely in the December 2026 cycle.

Concepts in depth: constitutional base and Indian Acts

Article 48A (a Directive Principle) asks the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife; Article 51A(g) makes it a fundamental duty of every citizen to protect the natural environment. Both were inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976). Courts read the right to a clean environment into Article 21 (right to life). Article 253 lets Parliament make laws to implement international agreements, which is the basis of the EPA.

1974Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) ActCreated the Central and State Pollution Control Boards

Concepts in depth: the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986

The Act followed the Bhopal gas tragedy (December 1984). It received assent in May 1986 and came into force on 19 November 1986. It has 26 sections in 4 chapters. “Environment” includes water, air and land and the inter-relationships among them and human beings, other living creatures, plants, micro-organisms and property.

SectionContent
2Definitions: environment, environmental pollutant, pollution, hazardous substance
3Wide powers of the Central Government to protect and improve the environment; 3(3) lets it constitute authorities
5Power to give directions, including closure, prohibition or regulation of any industry and stopping or regulating electricity, water or any other service
6Rules to regulate environmental pollution (standards for air, water, soil; limits on pollutants)
7No person carrying on an industry shall discharge pollutants in excess of the standards
8Handling of hazardous substances only as per procedure and safeguards
10–12Powers of entry and inspection; taking samples; environmental laboratories
15Penalties for contravention
16–17Offences by companies and by government departments
19Cognizance of offences: on complaint by the government or by any person after giving at least 60 days’ notice
25Power to make rules

Penalties. Originally, Section 15 provided imprisonment of up to five years, or a fine of up to one lakh rupees, or both, with more for continuing and long-running offences. The Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2023 decriminalised many contraventions: Section 15 now provides a monetary penalty of not less than ten thousand rupees, which may extend to fifteen lakh rupees, plus up to ten thousand rupees a day for a continuing contravention. Penalties are imposed by an adjudicating officer (not below Joint Secretary to the Government of India or Secretary to a State Government), appeals lie to the National Green Tribunal, and penalties go into an Environment Protection Fund.

Instruments made under the EPA: the Environment (Protection) Rules, 1986; the EIA notifications (1994, 2006); Coastal Regulation Zone notifications (1991, 2011, 2019); Noise Rules (2000); Ozone Depleting Substances Rules (2000); and the waste rules of Lesson 9.2.

Concepts in depth: NAPCC and India’s climate pledges

The National Action Plan on Climate Change was released by the Prime Minister on 30 June 2008. States prepare State Action Plans on Climate Change (SAPCCs) in line with it.

At COP26 in Glasgow (2021) India announced the Panchamrit: 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030; 50% of energy requirements from renewables by 2030; a one-billion-tonne cut in projected emissions by 2030; a 45% cut in carbon intensity by 2030; and net zero by 2070. India submitted its Long-Term Low-Emission Development Strategy at COP27 (2022). Progress: non-fossil sources reached 50% of installed capacity on 30 June 2025, five years early; the government reports that emissions intensity fell by 36% between 2005 and 2020. Mission LiFE was launched at Kevadia (Ekta Nagar), Gujarat, on 20 October 2022.

Concepts in depth: the ozone regime

The Vienna Convention (1985) was a framework; the Montreal Protocol, adopted on 16 September 1987 (now International Ozone Day) and in force from 1 January 1989, set phase-out schedules for CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform, HCFCs and methyl bromide. Amendments: London 1990, Copenhagen 1992, Montreal 1997, Beijing 1999, and Kigali 2016, which added HFCs (not ozone-depleting but powerful greenhouse gases), in force from 1 January 2019, aiming at an 80–85% cut by the late 2040s. It is one of the rare treaties with universal ratification. India became a Party on 19 June 1992 and approved ratification of Kigali in August 2021; India’s HFC schedule is a freeze by 2028, then cuts of 10% (2032), 20% (2037), 30% (2042) and 85% (2047) from its baseline.

Concepts in depth: the climate regime

The UNFCCC was adopted on 9 May 1992, opened for signature at Rio and entered into force on 21 March 1994; it has 198 Parties. Its objective (Article 2) is to stabilise greenhouse gas concentrations at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate. Annex I lists industrialised and transition economies; Annex II the richer ones that must provide finance.

FeatureKyoto ProtocolParis Agreement
Adopted / in force11 December 1997 (COP3) / 16 February 200512 December 2015 (COP21) / 4 November 2016
ApproachTop-down, binding targets for Annex I onlyBottom-up NDCs from all parties, updated every 5 years
TargetsAverage 5% below 1990 in 2008–2012; Doha Amendment: at least 18% below 1990 in 2013–2020 (in force 31 December 2020)Well below 2 °C, pursue 1.5 °C; global stocktake every 5 years (first in 2023)
Entry condition55 parties including Annex I parties with 55% of Annex I CO₂ (1990)55 parties with 55% of global emissions
MarketsCDM, Joint Implementation, International Emissions TradingArticle 6 cooperation; rules completed at COP29

India ratified Kyoto in 2002 and the Paris Agreement on 2 October 2016. The United States never ratified Kyoto; its withdrawal from the Paris Agreement, notified in January 2025, took effect on 27 January 2026 (a withdrawal takes effect one year after notification).

COP31 (2026) is to be hosted by Türkiye in Antalya, with Australia leading the negotiations.

Concepts in depth: International Solar Alliance

Launched by India and France on 30 November 2015 at COP21, first for solar-rich countries lying fully or partly between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn. Its Framework Agreement opened for signature at COP22, Marrakech (15 November 2016), and after Guinea became the 15th country to ratify, the ISA became a treaty-based international intergovernmental organisation on 6 December 2017, the first such body headquartered in India (Gurugram, Haryana). A 2020 amendment opened membership to all UN member states; it now counts more than 120 member and signatory countries. Its aims include mobilising about USD 1 trillion of solar investment by 2030; the Green Grids Initiative–One Sun One World One Grid was launched with the UK at COP26.

Concepts in depth: biodiversity and other conventions

The Convention on Biological Diversity opened for signature at Rio on 5 June 1992 and entered into force on 29 December 1993. Its three objectives are conservation, sustainable use and fair and equitable sharing of benefits from genetic resources. The Cartagena Protocol on biosafety (living modified organisms) was adopted in 2000 (in force 2003); the Nagoya Protocol on access and benefit-sharing in 2010 (in force 2014), when the 20 Aichi targets were also set. The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (COP15, 19 December 2022) has 4 goals and 23 targets, including protecting 30% of land and sea by 2030. COP16 in Cali, Colombia (2024) set up the Cali Fund for benefits from digital sequence information. The United States is the only UN member that is not a party to the CBD.

Worked examples

Example 1 (chronology). Arrange: Kigali Amendment, Kyoto Protocol entering into force, Paris Agreement adopted, Montreal Protocol adopted, UNFCCC entering into force. Step 1: write years: Kigali 2016, Kyoto in force 2005, Paris adopted 2015, Montreal 1987, UNFCCC in force 1994. Step 2: sort: Montreal (1987), UNFCCC (1994), Kyoto in force (2005), Paris (2015), Kigali (2016). Note that “entered into force” and “adopted” give different years for the same treaty.

Example 2 (Kigali arithmetic). Baseline 120 Mt CO₂e. Allowed consumption = baseline × (1 − cut): 2032: 120 × 0.90 = 108; 2037: 120 × 0.80 = 96; 2042: 120 × 0.70 = 84; 2047: 120 × 0.15 = 18 Mt. The cuts are measured from the baseline each time, not from the previous step.

Example 3 (NDC arithmetic). Take India’s 2005 emissions intensity as 100. The targets allow 55 in 2030 (45% cut) and 53 in 2035 (47% cut). The government reports a 36% fall by 2020, so intensity was 64. To reach 53 by 2035, the 2020 level must fall by a further (64 − 53) ÷ 64 = 17.2%. Percentages of different bases cannot simply be subtracted (47 − 36 = 11 is wrong).

Example 4 (ISA entry into force). The 15th ratification (Guinea) came on 6 November 2017 and the Agreement entered into force on 6 December 2017: 30 days later. For NCQG: USD 300 billion is 300 ÷ 1,300 ≈ 23% of the USD 1.3 trillion scale-up call, and three times the old USD 100 billion goal.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact

NTA traps

  • Adoption versus entry into force. Kyoto: 1997 versus 2005; Paris: 2015 versus 2016; Montreal: 1987 versus 1989. Read which one the question asks.
  • Mixing India’s NDC numbers. 33–35% (2015), 45% (2022), 47% (2035 target, 2026); non-fossil 40%, 50%, 60%. The base year is 2005 in every case.
  • Kyoto features on Paris. Binding top-down targets for developed countries only belong to Kyoto; Paris has NDCs for all.
  • Montreal and climate. Montreal controls ozone-depleting substances (and HFCs via Kigali), not CO₂ or methane; Kyoto does not control CFCs.
  • Wrong ISA meeting. Launched at COP21 (2015), agreement opened at COP22 (2016), in force December 2017.
  • Nodal ministries. Energy efficiency is the Ministry of Power, not MNRE; the Himalayan mission is DST, not MoEFCC.
  • EPA date. In force 19 November 1986, not 5 June.
  • “Rio” questions. Kyoto was not a Rio outcome; the UNFCCC and CBD were opened for signature there.

How NTA asks this

  • Chronology (order): treaties, amendments, COPs, Indian Acts, India’s pledges.
  • Match the following: conventions with subjects or years, missions with ministries, COPs with outcomes, EPA sections with contents.
  • Statement I/II and Assertion–Reason: Kyoto versus Paris, why Montreal succeeded, EPA dates and constitutional basis.
  • Multiple select: Rio outcomes, NAPCC missions, Kyoto gases or mechanisms, CBD objectives.

Mini-example (order). Air Act, Water Act, EPA, Wildlife Act, Biological Diversity Act: 1981, 1974, 1986, 1972, 2002, so Wildlife, Water, Air, EPA, Biological Diversity.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The Paris Agreement follows a bottom-up approach. R: Each party sets its own NDC and updates it every five years. Both true; R explains A: option 1.

Elimination trick: in a chronology question, first fix the earliest item (often Ramsar 1971, Stockholm 1972 or the Wildlife Act 1972) and the latest (Kigali, KMGBF or a recent COP). Most options fail at one end.
Watch out: climate pledges, COP hosts and treaty memberships change. Figures here are as reported by PIB, UNFCCC, UNEP and the CBD up to early 2026; check unfccc.int, pib.gov.in and moef.gov.in for anything newer before the exam.

Nationally Determined Contribution: the climate pledge each party communicates under the Paris Agreement, updated every five years.
The five climate commitments India announced at COP26, Glasgow (2021), including 500 GW of non-fossil capacity by 2030 and net zero by 2070.
Treaty adopted on 16 September 1987 to phase out ozone-depleting substances; universally ratified; the Kigali Amendment (2016) added HFCs.
Adopted at COP3 on 11 December 1997, in force on 16 February 2005; binding targets for industrialised (Annex I) countries; flexible mechanisms (CDM, JI, emissions trading).
Adopted at COP21 on 12 December 2015, in force on 4 November 2016; aims to keep warming well below 2 °C and to pursue 1.5 °C; works through NDCs and five-yearly global stocktakes.

The principle that all countries share responsibility for the global environment but developed countries carry more of it because of their historical emissions and greater capacity.
Adopted at CBD COP15 on 19 December 2022: four goals for 2050 and 23 targets for 2030, including “30 by 30”.

domains.name: Higher Education System
domains.blurb: Ancient and modern higher education, value education, policies and regulatory bodies.

lessons.title: Higher education in India: history and institutions
lessons.summaryHtml: India’s higher education has three layers of history. Ancient centres such as Takshashila, Nalanda, Vikramashila and Valabhi taught through a residential guru–shishya system, supported by royal and community endowments. Colonial rule brought examining universities on the London model (Calcutta, Bombay and Madras, 1857) and a string of despatches, commissions and Acts that NTA loves to put in chronological order. After independence, the University Education Commission (1948–49), the UGC (inaugurated 1953, statutory under the UGC Act 1956), the Kothari Commission (1964–66) and the national policies of 1968, 1986 and 2020 shaped a large system of central, state, deemed and private universities, institutes of national importance and research councils. The syllabus also asks you to tell oriental programmes (Sanskrit, Pali, Arabic, Persian learning), conventional campus programmes and non-conventional ones (correspondence, open, online, MOOCs) apart.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

This lesson tells the story of how India has organised higher learning, from the ancient mahaviharas to today’s universities, and names the institutions that carry that story. There are three eras. In the ancient era, learning was residential and personal: a pupil lived with a teacher (guru–shishya), and large Buddhist monasteries such as Nalanda grew into centres that drew students from across Asia. In the colonial era, the British first debated whether to support Indian classical learning or English education, chose English, and then created universities that mainly held examinations. In the post-independence era, a series of commissions and national policies built a very large system with a national grants body (the UGC), technical institutes, research councils, open universities and, most recently, flexible and online routes. “Oriental, conventional and non-conventional programmes” classify programmes by content (classical knowledge) and by delivery (campus or distance/online).

Why it matters for NET

Unit 10 is small, but its questions are pure recall: a prepared candidate answers them in seconds and saves time for reasoning and data questions. The recurring patterns are: chronology of commissions, Acts and institutions; matching an ancient centre with its founder, dynasty or location; matching a commission with its chair; statements about the UGC’s origin (1953 inauguration versus the 1956 Act); and classifying programmes as conventional or non-conventional. Dates that sit close together (1953/1956, 1982/1985, 1917/1929) are where marks are lost.

Concepts in depth: learning in ancient India

Vedic education took place in the teacher’s household (gurukula) or hermitage (ashrama); knowledge was passed on orally, memorised and tested in debate (shastrartha) and scholarly assemblies (parishads). Subjects grew from the Vedas and Vedangas to logic, medicine, law, statecraft and the arts. Teaching was generally free: kings and communities gave land grants and villages, and in the south, ghatikas and agraharas attached to temples supported Brahmanical learning (Kanchi under the Pallavas is the best-known ghatika). Buddhist and Jain monasteries became the first large institutions, with a head, rules of admission and libraries.

Centre (where)Founder / patron and periodRemember it for
Takshashila (Taxila)
Gandhara; now near Rawalpindi, Pakistan		Flourished from about the 6th–5th century BCE; declined after the Huna invasions of the 5th century CENo central administration: independent teachers, pupils usually entered at about 16; traditionally linked with Panini (grammar), Kautilya (statecraft) and Jivaka (medicine)
Nalanda
Near Rajgir, Bihar		Kumaragupta I (Gupta), 5th century CE; later Harshavardhana and the PalasResidential Buddhist mahavihara; admission test by gatekeeper-scholars (dvarapandita); library called Dharmaganja; Xuanzang and Yijing studied here in the 7th century
Valabhi
Saurashtra, Gujarat		Maitraka kings, from about the 6th century CERival of Nalanda in western India; Yijing names the two together
Vikramashila
Bhagalpur district, Bihar		Dharmapala (Pala), late 8th or early 9th centuryVajrayana (tantric) Buddhism; Atisha Dipankara went from here to Tibet
Odantapuri
Bihar Sharif, Bihar		Traditionally Gopala, founder of the Pala dynasty, 8th centuryModel for Tibetan monastery building (Samye)
Somapura Mahavihara
Paharpur, Bangladesh		Dharmapala (Pala)One of the largest viharas south of the Himalayas; UNESCO site
Jagaddala
North Bengal (now Bangladesh)		Ramapala (Pala), late 11th centuryLast of the great Pala mahaviharas

Nalanda and Vikramashila were ruined around 1200 CE during the raids of Bakhtiyar Khalji’s forces. The ruins of Nalanda Mahavihara became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016. A new Nalanda University was created by the Nalanda University Act 2010 as an international university with East Asia Summit partners, and its campus at Rajgir was inaugurated on 19 June 2024. In the medieval period, Islamic education ran through maktabs (elementary) and madrasas (higher learning in Arabic, Persian, theology, law and sciences); the Madrasa of Mahmud Gawan (1472) at Bidar, built under the Bahmanis, is the famous example.

Concepts in depth: the colonial foundation

The East India Company first supported oriental learning: Warren Hastings founded the Calcutta Madrasa (1781), William Jones founded the Asiatic Society (1784) and Jonathan Duncan founded the Benares Sanskrit College (1791). The Charter Act (1813) required the Company to set aside at least one lakh rupees a year for education, which started the Orientalist–Anglicist debate over how to spend it. Macaulay’s Minute (1835) argued for English education and the “downward filtration” of knowledge, and Governor-General Bentinck’s resolution of 1835 settled the matter in favour of English.

YearEventKey point
1813Charter ActAt least ₹1 lakh a year for education
1835Macaulay’s Minute; Bentinck’s resolutionEnglish education and downward filtration
1854Wood’s Despatch“Magna Carta of English education”; universities, grants-in-aid, departments of public instruction
1857Universities of Calcutta, Bombay, MadrasAffiliating and examining bodies on the London model
1882Hunter CommissionFirst Indian Education Commission; mainly primary and secondary education
1902Indian Universities Commission (Thomas Raleigh)Appointed under Curzon
1904Indian Universities ActTightened government control; universities could also teach
1917–19Sadler Commission (Calcutta University Commission)Intermediate stage separated, unitary teaching universities
1929Hartog CommitteeQuality over expansion (“wastage and stagnation”)
1944Sargent Report (CABE)Post-war plan; proposed a University Grants Committee
1945University Grants CommitteeGrants to Aligarh, Banaras and Delhi; extended to all universities in 1947

Concepts in depth: evolution after independence

The University Education Commission (1948–49, Dr S. Radhakrishnan) recommended reconstituting the grants committee as a full-time University Grants Commission. The UGC was formally inaugurated by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad on 28 December 1953 and became a statutory body under the UGC Act of November 1956. The Secondary Education Commission (Mudaliar, 1952–53) and the Education Commission (Kothari, 1964–66) followed; Kothari’s report (“The destiny of India is now being shaped in her classrooms”) led to the first National Policy on Education, 1968. The NPE 1986, revised through the Programme of Action 1992 after the Ramamurti Committee (1990) review, gave us open universities, autonomous colleges and the accreditation council (NAAC, 1994). The National Knowledge Commission (2005–09, Sam Pitroda) and the Yash Pal Committee (2009) both proposed a single higher-education regulator, an idea taken up by NEP 2020.

Technical and research capacity grew in parallel: IIT Kharagpur (1951) was the first IIT, and the Institutes of Technology Act 1961 declared the IITs institutes of national importance; the IIMs at Calcutta and Ahmedabad followed in 1961. Research councils were added for the social sciences (ICSSR, 1969), history (ICHR, 1972) and philosophy (ICPR, 1977), and INFLIBNET (1991), an inter-university centre of the UGC, networks university libraries and runs Shodhganga. Lesson 10.3 covers the newest milestones (NEP 2020, ANRF, the 2025 regulator Bill).

Type of institutionCreated byExample
Central universityAct of Parliament (most under the Central Universities Act 2009 or their own Acts)University of Delhi, BHU, JNU
State universityAct of the state legislatureUniversity of Calicut
State private universityState Act; must meet UGC normsVarious private universities
Deemed-to-be universityCentral Government notification on UGC advice, Section 3 of the UGC ActIISc Bengaluru, TISS Mumbai
Institute of national importanceAct of ParliamentIITs, NITs, AIIMS, IIMs
Affiliated / autonomous collegeAffiliated to a university; autonomy granted under UGC rulesMost colleges

Concepts in depth: oriental, conventional and non-conventional programmes

Oriental programmes teach classical languages and Indian knowledge systems in the traditional way: Sanskrit pathshalas and tols, Arabic and Persian madrasas, and Sanskrit universities with titles such as Shastri (graduate) and Acharya (postgraduate). The Central Sanskrit Universities Act 2020 converted three deemed universities (Rashtriya Sanskrit Sansthan, New Delhi; Shri Lal Bahadur Shastri Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, New Delhi; and Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeeth, Tirupati) into central universities. Conventional programmes are the face-to-face, fixed-duration, campus-based degrees of affiliating and unitary universities. Non-conventional programmes relax place, pace or entry: correspondence courses (started by the University of Delhi in 1962), open universities (Andhra Pradesh Open University, 1982; IGNOU, 1985), online degrees under the UGC (Open and Distance Learning Programmes and Online Programmes) Regulations 2020, MOOCs on SWAYAM (launched in 2017; up to 40% of a semester’s courses can be taken there), the UGC’s 2022 permission to pursue two academic programmes simultaneously, and the Academic Bank of Credits (launched in 2021) that supports multiple entry and exit.

Worked examples

Example 1 (chronology). Arrange: A. Sargent Report, B. Hartog Committee, C. Sadler Commission, D. University Education Commission.

Step 1: write the years: A 1944, B 1929, C 1917–19, D 1948–49. Step 2: sort: C (1917), B (1929), A (1944), D (1948). Answer: C, B, A, D. The trap is placing Hartog before Sadler because both concern universities.

Example 2 (match). A. Nalanda, B. Vikramashila, C. Odantapuri, D. Jagaddala with I. Ramapala, II. Kumaragupta I, III. Gopala, IV. Dharmapala.

Fix the non-Pala centre first: Nalanda is Gupta, so A-II. Among the Palas, Gopala founded the dynasty and Odantapuri (C-III), Dharmapala founded Vikramashila (B-IV), and Ramapala is the latest king and Jagaddala the latest vihara (D-I). Answer: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I.

Example 3 (classification). Classify: (i) a Shastri course at a Sanskrit university, (ii) a B.Sc. with daily classes, (iii) an IGNOU M.A., (iv) a SWAYAM course counted for credit.

(i) is oriental in content and conventional in delivery; (ii) is conventional; (iii) and (iv) are non-conventional. Note that “oriental” describes the content, while “conventional/non-conventional” describes the mode, so one programme can carry two labels.

Example 4 (A-R). A: The universities founded in 1857 did little teaching. R: They were modelled on the University of London, which was then an examining body.

Both are true, and R explains A: the London model made them affiliating and examining bodies, while colleges did the teaching. The 1904 Act later allowed universities to teach. Answer: option 1.

NTA traps

  • 1953 or 1956? Wrong: “UGC was established in 1953 as a statutory body.” Fix: inaugurated in 1953, statutory only from the UGC Act 1956.
  • Pala or Gupta? Wrong: “Nalanda was founded by Dharmapala.” Fix: Nalanda is Gupta (Kumaragupta I); Dharmapala founded Vikramashila and Somapura.
  • First IIT. Wrong: Kanpur or Bombay. Fix: Kharagpur, 1951.
  • First open university. Wrong: IGNOU. Fix: Andhra Pradesh Open University (1982); IGNOU is the national one (1985).
  • Hunter was about universities. Wrong. Fix: Hunter (1882) dealt mainly with primary and secondary education; the university commissions are 1902 (Raleigh) and 1917–19 (Sadler).
  • SWAYAM limit. Wrong: 20%. Fix: 40% since the 2021 regulations.

How NTA asks this

  • Chronology (order): four or five commissions, Acts or institutions. Write the year beside each statement, then check only the first and last positions of each option to eliminate fast.
  • Match: centre with founder or location; commission with chair; institution with year. Fix the one pair you are surest of and strike out options that disagree.
  • Statement I/II and A-R: one true statement paired with a year swap (1857/1882, 1953/1956).
  • Multi-select: “which of these are non-conventional modes” or “which features describe ancient Indian education”.

Mini-example (match). A. University Education Commission, B. Secondary Education Commission, C. Education Commission 1964–66, D. National Knowledge Commission with I. D. S. Kothari, II. Sam Pitroda, III. S. Radhakrishnan, IV. A. L. Mudaliar. Answer: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Remember: the three presidency universities (1857) came three years after Wood’s Despatch (1854); the UGC Act (1956) came three years after the UGC’s inauguration (1953).
Watch out: the syllabus word “oriental” refers to the content (classical Indian and West Asian learning), not to a delivery mode. Do not tick “oriental” in a question about distance or online programmes.

terms.definition: Ancient centre in Gandhara (now near Rawalpindi, Pakistan). Independent teachers taught pupils of their choice; there was no central administration or degree.
Buddhist residential centre near Rajgir, Bihar, founded under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I in the 5th century CE; ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016).
Pala-era mahavihara in Bhagalpur district, Bihar, founded by Dharmapala; known for Vajrayana (tantric) Buddhism and the scholar Atisha Dipankara.
Charles Wood’s despatch called the “Magna Carta of English education in India”; it proposed universities at the three presidency towns.
First commission of free India, chaired by Dr S. Radhakrishnan; recommended a University Grants Commission on the UK model.
An institution declared by the Central Government, on UGC advice, under Section 3 of the UGC Act 1956 to have the status of a university.
An institution (IITs, NITs, AIIMS, IIMs and others) given this status by an Act of Parliament; it awards its own degrees.
Traditional higher learning in classical languages and knowledge systems (Sanskrit, Pali, Prakrit, Arabic, Persian) in tols, pathshalas, madrasas and Sanskrit universities.
A programme that does not require regular campus attendance: correspondence, open and distance learning (ODL), online degrees and MOOCs.
A university that teaches mainly at a distance with flexible entry; the first in India was the Andhra Pradesh Open University (1982), and IGNOU followed in 1985.

lessons.title: Professional, technical, skill, value and environmental education
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers five kinds of education that the syllabus names together. Professional education prepares people for regulated professions (medicine, law, teaching, architecture) and is overseen by statutory councils; technical education (engineering, technology, management, pharmacy and related fields) is overseen by AICTE and delivered by bodies such as the IITs and NITs. Skill and vocational education is organised through the Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, NSDC, the NSQF levels and the regulator NCVET, and NEP 2020 wants it integrated into mainstream schooling and higher education. Value education builds personal, social, professional and constitutional values; the UGC’s Mulya Pravah guidelines (2019, revised as Mulya Pravah 2.0 in 2023) are the current reference. Environmental education grew out of Stockholm (1972), Belgrade (1975) and Tbilisi (1977), and in India it became compulsory for undergraduates after a 1991 Supreme Court direction.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Not all higher education is about general degrees. Professional education trains doctors, lawyers, teachers, architects and pharmacists: people whose work is licensed and whose conduct is policed by a council. Technical education trains engineers, technologists and managers. Skill (vocational) education gives job-ready competencies, usually certified by level. Value education shapes character and ethics, and environmental education shapes how people understand and treat nature. The exam asks which body regulates which field, when key frameworks came, what NEP 2020 says about vocational integration, and the international milestones of environmental education.

Why it matters for NET

Questions here are short and factual. Expect a regulator matched with its Act, a skill milestone placed in time, a statement about NEP’s vocational targets, an environmental education conference matched with its outcome, or a simple credit calculation. Most errors come from confusing look-alike bodies (NSDC and NCVET, AICTE and NBA, Belgrade and Tbilisi).

Concepts in depth: professional and technical education

A profession has four marks: a specialised body of knowledge, long formal training, entry by licence or registration, and a code of ethics enforced by peers. Professional education is therefore regulated by statutory councils, each created by its own Act. Technical education is defined in the AICTE Act 1987 to cover engineering, technology, architecture, town planning, management, pharmacy, applied arts and crafts and other notified fields.

FieldRegulatorLaw
Technical educationAICTE (advisory from 1945)AICTE Act 1987
Teacher educationNCTENCTE Act 1993 (in force from 17 August 1995)
Medical educationNational Medical Commission (replaced MCI)NMC Act 2019; NMC constituted in September 2020
Legal educationBar Council of IndiaAdvocates Act 1961
ArchitectureCouncil of ArchitectureArchitects Act 1972
Pharmacy / DentistryPharmacy Council of India / Dental Council of IndiaPharmacy Act 1948 / Dentists Act 1948
Nursing and midwiferyNational Nursing and Midwifery CommissionNational Nursing and Midwifery Commission Act 2023
Veterinary scienceVeterinary Council of IndiaIndian Veterinary Council Act 1984
Rehabilitation professionalsRehabilitation Council of IndiaRehabilitation Council of India Act 1992
AgricultureICAR (set up 1929; accredits agricultural universities)Registered society

History to remember: the Thomason College (1847) at Roorkee was the first engineering college (it became IIT Roorkee in 2001), the Indian Institute of Science came in 1909, and the Sarkar Committee (1945) proposed the higher technical institutes that became the IITs. IIT Kharagpur opened in 1951 and the Institutes of Technology Act 1961 made the IITs institutes of national importance. The Regional Engineering Colleges became NITs under the NIT Act 2007, and the IIM Act 2017 let the IIMs award degrees instead of diplomas. The National Board of Accreditation (NBA), started by AICTE in 1994 and independent since 2010, accredits technical programmes, while NAAC accredits institutions.

Concepts in depth: skill and vocational education

Vocational education gives competencies for a particular occupation, is assessed by what the learner can do, and is certified by level. NEP 2020 notes that less than 5% of India’s workforce aged 19–24 had formal vocational education, far below countries such as Germany or South Korea, and sets the goal that by 2025 at least 50% of learners in school and higher education have exposure to vocational education. It removes hard separations between academic and vocational streams, starts vocational exposure from Grade 6 with internships (including a 10-day bagless period), brings Indian crafts knowledge (“Lok Vidya”) into courses, and asks for a higher education qualification framework in sync with NSQF.

Body or frameworkYearRole
Apprentices Act1961Legal basis for apprenticeship training
NSDC (set up 2008)2008Not-for-profit public–private partnership company that funds and builds skill-training capacity
NSQF (notified 2013)2013; revised 2023Level-based, competency-based qualification framework; the 2023 version has levels 1–8 with half-levels
Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (2014)2014Nodal ministry for skilling
Skill India Mission (launched 2015)15 July 2015Launched with the National Skill Development Mission, the national skills policy 2015, PMKVY and a skill loan scheme
NCVET (notified 2018)5 December 2018Regulator for VET; subsumed NSDA and NCVT; recognises awarding and assessment bodies
National Credit Framework (2023)April 2023One credit system for school, higher and vocational learning

In higher education, the UGC introduced B.Voc degrees and community colleges aligned with NSQF, and the UGC curriculum framework for four-year UG programmes awards a certificate after 40 credits, a diploma after 80, a degree after 120 and an honours degree after 160; a student leaving after the first or second year must also complete a 4-credit vocational course in the summer. In that framework one lecture credit means one hour a week, or 15 hours in a semester, and one practical credit means 30 hours.

Concepts in depth: value education

Values are lasting beliefs about what is worth doing. Value education develops the ability to recognise, choose and act on them. Common groupings are personal (honesty, self-discipline), social (cooperation, service), moral and spiritual, professional (integrity, accountability) and constitutional or democratic (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity, secularism). Approaches are direct (separate value lessons), integrated or indirect (values woven into subjects), incidental (using events as they happen) and co-curricular (NSS, NCC, clubs, community work). Values are largely “caught” from teachers and institutional culture, not only “taught”.

Every major commission (Radhakrishnan, Kothari) stressed moral and spiritual values, and NPE 1986 called for value education to fight obscurantism and fanaticism. The Chavan Committee (1999), a parliamentary committee on value-based education, identified truth, righteous conduct, peace, love and non-violence as core universal values. The UGC’s first Mulya Pravah (2019) and Mulya Pravah 2.0 (May 2023) restate these values (satya, dharma, shanti, prema, ahimsa) and ask HEIs to model integrity, trusteeship, accountability, inclusiveness, respect, sustainability and constitutional values in governance, teaching and campus life. NEP 2020 lists ethical and moral reasoning, constitutional values and Indian knowledge systems among the aims of holistic education.

Concepts in depth: environmental education

Environmental education (EE) is often described as education about the environment (knowledge), in or through the environment (field experience), and for the environment (values and action to protect it). Its objectives are awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation (Tbilisi); the Belgrade Charter had listed six, adding evaluation ability.

YearMilestoneContribution to EE
1972Stockholm Conference (UN Conference on the Human Environment)Principle 19 called for education in environmental matters; UNEP created
1975Belgrade Charter; UNESCO–UNEP International Environmental Education ProgrammeFirst global framework: goal and six objectives
1977Tbilisi ConferenceFirst intergovernmental conference; objectives, principles
1992Rio Earth Summit (Agenda 21, Chapter 36)Reorienting education towards sustainable development
2005–2014UN Decade of Education for Sustainable DevelopmentESD mainstreamed; now SDG target 4.7

In India, the Centre for Environment Education (1984, Ahmedabad) was set up as a centre of excellence of the environment ministry. After M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court directed compulsory environmental education, and the UGC framed a six-month core module syllabus (2003) for all undergraduates, then an eight-unit Ability Enhancement Compulsory Course (AECC) in 2017, and a draft curriculum framework in 2023. NEP 2020 includes environment education (climate change, pollution, waste management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable living) in the curriculum, and Article 51A(g) makes protecting the environment a fundamental duty.

Worked examples

Example 1 (credits from hours). A skill course has 450 notional learning hours. Under NCrF, credits = 450 ÷ 30 = 15. A full year of 1,200 hours gives 1,200 ÷ 30 = 40 credits.

Example 2 (exit awards). A student has earned 84 credits under the UGC four-year UG framework and leaves. The diploma needs 80 credits (plus the 4-credit summer vocational course), the degree 120. So she qualifies for the UG diploma, and needs 120 − 84 = 36 more credits for the three-year degree.

Example 3 (chronology). Arrange: A. Tbilisi, B. Stockholm, C. Agenda 21, D. Belgrade. Years: 1977, 1972, 1992, 1975. Order: B, D, A, C.

Example 4 (regulator match). A law college, a B.Arch. college, an engineering college and a B.Ed. college need approval. Law: Bar Council of India. B.Arch.: Council of Architecture. Engineering: AICTE. B.Ed.: NCTE. Remember that a university still awards the degree; the council approves the programme.

Formula and fact sheet

ItemFact
CreditsNCrF: 30 hours = 1 credit; 1,200 hours = 40 credits a year. UGC UG: 40 / 80 / 120 / 160 credits for certificate / diploma / degree / honours
SkillingNSDC 2008; NSQF 2013 (revised 2023); MSDE 2014; Skill India 15 July 2015; NCVET 5 Dec 2018; NCrF 2023
NEP vocational≥50% exposure by 2025; from Grade 6 with internships; under 5% of workers aged 19–24 had formal VE
CouncilsAICTE 1987, NCTE 1993, BCI 1961, CoA 1972, PCI 1948, NMC 2019, NNMC 2023
ValuesChavan Committee 1999; Mulya Pravah 2019; Mulya Pravah 2.0 (May 2023): satya, dharma, shanti, prema, ahimsa
EEStockholm 1972, Belgrade 1975, Tbilisi 1977, Rio 1992, DESD 2005–14; M. C. Mehta 1991; UGC module 2003; AECC 2017

NTA traps

  • NSDC is the regulator. Wrong. Fix: NSDC funds and builds training capacity; NCVET regulates.
  • Evaluation ability is a Tbilisi category. Wrong. Fix: it is one of Belgrade’s six objectives; Tbilisi lists five.
  • AICTE regulates medicine or law. Wrong. Fix: those have their own councils (NMC, BCI).
  • NBA and NAAC do the same job. Wrong. Fix: NBA accredits programmes (mainly technical); NAAC accredits institutions.
  • Skill India was launched on World Environment Day. Wrong. Fix: on World Youth Skills Day, 15 July 2015.
  • NEP separates vocational and academic streams. Wrong. Fix: it removes hard separations and integrates them.

How NTA asks this

  • Match: council with Act, conference with outcome, body with role.
  • Chronology: skilling milestones or EE conferences.
  • Multi-select: Tbilisi objectives, NEP vocational provisions, statutory councils.
  • Numerical: hours to credits, or credits to an exit award.

Mini-example (A-R). A: The Belgrade Charter lists six objectives of EE. R: It was adopted at the Rio Earth Summit. A is true; R is false (Belgrade is 1975, Rio 1992). Answer: option 3.

Remember: “SKiLL” order: NSDC (2008), NSQF (2013), MSDE (2014), Skill India (2015), NCVET (2018), NCrF (2023).
Watch out: NEP’s 50% target is for exposure to vocational education by 2025; its 50% GER target is for higher education by 2035. Do not swap the years.

terms.definition: Education that prepares for a profession with a specialised body of knowledge, entry through licence or registration, and a code of ethics enforced by a statutory council.
Programmes in engineering, technology, architecture, town planning, management, pharmacy, applied arts and crafts and similar fields as defined in the AICTE Act 1987.
National Skills Qualifications Framework, a competency-based framework that arranges qualifications by levels; notified on 27 December 2013 and revised on 6 June 2023.
National Council for Vocational Education and Training, notified on 5 December 2018 as the regulator for vocational education and training; it subsumed NSDA and NCVT.
The 2023 framework that lets credits be earned across school, higher and vocational education; 30 notional learning hours make 1 credit, so 1,200 hours a year give 40 credits.
Education that develops the ability to choose and act on good values: personal, social, moral, professional and constitutional.
UGC guidelines (May 2023) for inculcating human values and professional ethics in higher education institutions, revising the 2019 Mulya Pravah.
Education about, in and for the environment that builds awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation (the Tbilisi categories).
Outcome of the first intergovernmental conference on environmental education (UNESCO–UNEP), which set its goals, objectives and guiding principles.

lessons.examTip: Link every regulator to its Act and year (AICTE 1987, NCTE 1993, BCI 1961, CoA 1972, NMC 2019, NCVET 2018), and keep the environmental education chain Stockholm 1972 → Belgrade 1975 → Tbilisi 1977 → Rio 1992 in one line of memory.

Recompute the credit problems (hours to credits, credits to exit award) without a calculator.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions.
