lessons.title: Policies, governance and administration
lessons.summaryHtml: This lesson covers how higher education is governed in India. The Constitution places education in the Concurrent List (since the 42nd Amendment, 1976) but reserves coordination and standards in higher education for the Union (List I, Entry 66), and it guarantees rights such as free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 (Article 21A) and the minorities’ right to run their own institutions (Article 30). Policy has moved from the National Policies on Education of 1968 and 1986 (revised 1992) to the National Education Policy 2020, which targets a 50% GER by 2035, multiple entry and exit, the Academic Bank of Credits, the phasing out of affiliation and a single regulator. Today the UGC, AICTE and NCTE regulate, NAAC and NBA accredit, and NIRF ranks; the single regulator proposed by NEP (HECI) has been introduced as the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025, which was referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee and has not become law at the time of writing.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Governance answers three questions: who makes the rules, who pays, and who checks quality. In India the Constitution splits law-making power between the Union and the states; national policies (1968, 1986, 2020) set the direction; the Ministry of Education and statutory regulators (UGC, AICTE, NCTE and professional councils) set norms and release grants; NAAC and NBA accredit; NIRF ranks; and each university runs itself through a Vice-Chancellor, an Executive Council and an Academic Council. NEP 2020 wants to replace the many regulators with one, “light but tight”, and the Bill for that is now before Parliament.

Why it matters for NET

This is the most tested part of Unit 10. Expect NEP 2020 numbers (50% GER by 2035, 15 years for affiliation, certificate after one year), the four HECI verticals, the constitutional articles on education, UGC Act sections, NAAC and NIRF facts, and a chronology of laws. The newest trap is the status of HECI.

Concepts in depth: constitutional provisions

ProvisionContent
Article 21AFree and compulsory education for all children aged 6–14 (86th Amendment 2002; RTE Act 2009 in force from 1 April 2010)
Article 45Early childhood care and education for children below six
Article 51A(k)Duty of a parent or guardian to provide education to a child aged 6–14
Article 15(4), 15(5), 15(6)Special provisions for backward classes, SCs and STs; 15(5) (93rd Amendment 2005) covers admission, including private institutions except minority ones; 15(6) (103rd Amendment 2019) allows up to 10% for economically weaker sections
Article 28No religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by the State
Article 29Protection of the language, script and culture of minorities; no denial of admission to State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language
Article 30Right of religious and linguistic minorities to establish and administer educational institutions
Article 46Promotion of the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections
Article 350AInstruction in the mother tongue at the primary stage for linguistic minorities

In the Seventh Schedule, Entry 25 of the Concurrent List covers education, including technical and medical education and universities, subject to Union List Entries 63–66. Entry 63 covers BHU, AMU, Delhi and other universities of national importance; Entry 64 covers scientific or technical institutions financed by the Government of India and declared institutions of national importance; Entry 65 covers Union agencies for professional, vocational or technical training and research; and Entry 66, the source of the UGC’s power, covers the coordination and determination of standards in higher education, research and scientific and technical institutions. The 42nd Amendment (1976) moved education from the State List to the Concurrent List.

Concepts in depth: policies

The first National Policy on Education (1968) followed the Kothari Commission and aimed at a common school structure (10+2+3) and 6% of national income for education. The NPE 1986, modified through the Programme of Action (1992), brought open universities, autonomous colleges, the accreditation council and value education. NEP 2020 was approved on 29 July 2020, and the Ministry of Human Resource Development was renamed the Ministry of Education the same year.

NEP 2020 higher education provisionDetail
GER50% by 2035 (from 26.3% in 2018); 3.5 crore new seats
Undergraduate structure3 or 4 years with multiple exits: certificate after 1 year, diploma after 2, bachelor’s after 3, bachelor’s with research after 4
CreditsAcademic Bank of Credits to store and transfer credits
InstitutionsResearch-intensive universities, teaching-intensive universities and autonomous degree-granting colleges; MERUs at par with IITs and IIMs
ScaleBy 2030 a large multidisciplinary HEI in or near every district; by 2040 all HEIs multidisciplinary with 3,000+ students
AffiliationPhased out in 15 years through graded autonomy
DegreesM.Phil. discontinued (the UGC’s 2022 Ph.D. regulations bar it)
RegulationHECI with four verticals (NHERC, NAC, HEGC, GEC); medical and legal education excluded; “light but tight”
Research and technologyNational Research Foundation (now ANRF under the ANRF Act 2023); National Educational Technology Forum (NETF)
Teachers and funding4-year integrated B.Ed. as the minimum teaching qualification by 2030; public spending on education to reach 6% of GDP
EquityGender Inclusion Fund and Special Education Zones for disadvantaged groups and regions

Concepts in depth: governance and administration

The Ministry of Education works through its Department of Higher Education; the Central Advisory Board of Education (CABE) advises the Union and states; State Councils of Higher Education plan at state level. Funding comes through UGC grants, schemes such as RUSA (2013) and loans from the Higher Education Financing Agency (HEFA), a joint venture of the Ministry and Canara Bank. Inside a university, the Visitor (the President, for central universities) has powers of inspection; the Chancellor (usually the Governor, for state universities) presides over convocations; the Vice-Chancellor is the principal executive and academic officer; the Court/Senate is the large policy body, the Executive Council/Syndicate the executive body, the Academic Council the principal academic body, and the Boards of Studies design syllabi. An Internal Quality Assurance Cell (IQAC) sustains quality after accreditation.

BodyBasis and yearMain role
UGCInaugurated 1953; UGC Act 1956Coordination and standards; grants (Section 12B); recognition (Section 2(f)); deemed status advice (Section 3)
AICTEAdvisory 1945; AICTE Act 1987Approval and norms for technical institutions
NCTENCTE Act 1993; statutory from 17 August 1995Teacher education norms and recognition
NAACNAAC was set up by the UGC in 1994, BengaluruInstitutional accreditation for five years on seven criteria
NBAStarted by AICTE 1994; independent from 7 January 2010Programme accreditation (engineering, management, pharmacy and others)
NIRFLaunched 29 September 2015; rankings every year since 2016Ranking on TLR 0.30, RP 0.30, GO 0.20, OI 0.10, PR 0.10 (Overall)
NTA (set up 2017)Autonomous testing agencyConducts UGC NET, CUET, NEET and others

NAAC’s seven criteria are curricular aspects; teaching–learning and evaluation; research, innovations and extension; infrastructure and learning resources; student support and progression; governance, leadership and management; and institutional values and best practices. Its familiar letter grades run from A++ down to C, with D meaning not accredited. After the Dr K. Radhakrishnan committee, NAAC announced in January 2024 a shift to binary accreditation (accredited or not) followed by Maturity-Based Graded Levels 1–5; the rollout is phased, so check naac.gov.in for the current position. NIRF 2025 added a deduction for retracted publications and citations within the research parameter.

Concepts in depth: HECI, from policy to Bill

The idea of one regulator came from the National Knowledge Commission (2005–09) and the Yash Pal Committee (2009). A draft HECI Act (2018), which would have repealed the UGC Act, was put out for comment but not passed. NEP 2020 then designed HECI with four verticals. The Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan Bill, 2025 (Cabinet approval 12 December 2025; introduced on 15 December 2025; referred to a 31-member Joint Parliamentary Committee on 16 December 2025) proposes an apex body with three councils: the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Viniyaman Parishad (regulation), the Gunvatta Parishad (accreditation) and the Manak Parishad (standards). It would replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE; medical and legal education stay outside, and funding of centrally funded HEIs stays with the Ministry of Education. At the time of writing the Bill has not been passed, so the existing regulators continue.

Worked examples

Example 1 (NIRF score). Scores: TLR 72, RP 45, GO 88, OI 64, PR 30. Weighted total = 0.30 × 72 + 0.30 × 45 + 0.20 × 88 + 0.10 × 64 + 0.10 × 30 = 21.6 + 13.5 + 17.6 + 6.4 + 3.0 = 62.1.

Example 2 (GER). A state has 36 lakh students in higher education and 1.2 crore people aged 18–23. GER = 36 ÷ 120 × 100 = 30%. To reach 50% with the same population it needs 60 lakh students, an increase of 24 lakh, or 24 ÷ 36 × 100 ≈ 66.7%.

Example 3 (A-R). A: NEP 2020 keeps medical education outside HECI. R: NEP 2020 makes HECI the single regulator for all higher education without exception. A is true; R is false because of the medical and legal exclusions. Answer: option 3.

Example 4 (chronology). Arrange: A. draft HECI Act, B. Yash Pal Committee report, C. VBSA Bill, D. NEP 2020. Years: 2018, 2009, 2025, 2020. Order: B, A, D, C.

NTA traps

  • HECI is in force. Wrong. Fix: the 2025 Bill is pending; the UGC, AICTE and NCTE still function.
  • The Bill copies NEP’s four verticals. Wrong. Fix: it has three councils; funding stays with the Ministry.
  • GER target by 2030. Wrong. Fix: 50% by 2035.
  • Article 29 gives minorities the right to run institutions. Wrong. Fix: that is Article 30; Article 29 protects culture and admission.
  • Section 2(f) means central grants. Wrong. Fix: grants need Section 12B; 2(f) is recognition.
  • NAAC ranks and NIRF accredits. Wrong. Fix: NAAC accredits (quality threshold), NIRF ranks (comparison).

How NTA asks this

  • Match: HECI vertical with function; article with content; UGC Act section with purpose.
  • Chronology: Acts, policies and amendments.
  • Statement I/II: one NEP fact with a year swap, or a claim about HECI’s status.
  • Numerical: NIRF weighted score or GER.

Mini-example (match). A. Article 21A, B. Article 30, C. Article 45, D. Article 350A with I. early childhood care below six, II. mother tongue at the primary stage, III. free and compulsory education 6–14, IV. minority institutions. Answer: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.

Remember: NEP 2020 = 29 July 2020; HECI verticals spell “R-A-F-S”: Regulation (NHERC), Accreditation (NAC), Funding (HEGC), Standards (GEC).
Watch out: policy facts change. Before the exam, check ugc.gov.in, education.gov.in and pib.gov.in for the status of the Adhishthan Bill and NAAC’s new accreditation system.

terms.definition: National Education Policy approved by the Union Cabinet on 29 July 2020; replaced the NPE 1986 (as modified in 1992).
Higher Education Commission of India proposed by NEP 2020 with four verticals: NHERC (regulation), NAC (accreditation), HEGC (funding) and GEC (standard setting).
Bill introduced in the Lok Sabha on 15 December 2025 to replace the UGC, AICTE and NCTE with one apex body and three councils; referred to a Joint Parliamentary Committee on 16 December 2025.
Gross Enrolment Ratio: enrolment in higher education (any age) as a percentage of the population aged 18–23.
Makes an institution eligible for central grants; Section 2(f) covers recognition and Section 3 deemed universities.
National Assessment and Accreditation Council, set up by the UGC in September 1994 at Bengaluru; accredits institutions for five years.
National Institutional Ranking Framework, launched on 29 September 2015; ranks on five parameters (TLR, RP, GO, OI, PR).
Freedom from regulatory approvals that grows with an institution’s accreditation or ranking; NEP uses it to phase out affiliation in 15 years.
Education, including technical and medical education and universities, subject to Entries 63–66 of the Union List.

lessons.examTip: For HECI, keep two lists apart: NEP 2020’s four verticals (NHERC, NAC, HEGC, GEC) and the 2025 Bill’s three councils (regulatory, accreditation, standards) with funding left to the Ministry. Never mark HECI as “established”: the Bill is still pending.

steps: Attempt problems 1–8 of practice-set.md in 10 minutes without notes.
Attempt problems 9–15 in the next 10 minutes, writing the NIRF and GER working in full.
Check with solutions.md and log each mistake with its trap (HECI enacted?, 2030 vs 2035, 2(f) vs 12B, Article 29 vs 30, NAAC vs NIRF).
Write the NEP 2020 higher education table from memory, then the HECI verticals and the Bill’s three councils side by side.
Look up the current status of the Adhishthan Bill and NAAC accreditation on pib.gov.in and naac.gov.in and note any change.
Redo the wrong problems after 24 hours, then take the lesson quiz and bank questions.
check: At least 13 of 15 practice problems correct.
All NIRF and GER numericals correct with working shown.
Both match problems correct on the first attempt.
HECI verticals and the Bill’s councils written from memory without mixing them up.

D. Psychomotor domain with five levels (Imitation to Naturalisation)

II. E. J. Simpson

questionBank.question: An objective reads: “The student will design a normalised schema for a new hostel-management system.” Which level of the revised cognitive domain does it target?
questionBank.explanation: “Design” something new that did not exist before is the Create level (planning and producing). Apply would be using a known procedure, such as decomposing a given relation to 3NF; Analyse would be differentiating or organising parts of a given schema; Evaluate would be judging a given schema against criteria.

questionBank.question: In the revised (2001) Bloom’s taxonomy, the cognitive process “classifying” belongs to which category?
questionBank.explanation: Anderson and Krathwohl list interpreting, exemplifying, classifying, summarising, inferring, comparing and explaining under Understand. Classifying means placing an example in a category, which shows comprehension. It is a trap because it sounds analytical; Analyse covers differentiating, organising and attributing.

questionBank.question: Which of the following belong to the knowledge dimension of the revised Bloom’s taxonomy?
options: A, B, C and D only
A, C, D and E only
B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: The knowledge dimension has exactly four types: factual, conceptual, procedural and metacognitive (awareness of one’s own thinking). “Evaluative” is invented: Evaluate is a cognitive process, not a knowledge type.

stmts: A. Factual knowledge
B. Conceptual knowledge
C. Procedural knowledge
D. Metacognitive knowledge
E. Evaluative knowledge

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: The levels form a ladder: memory → understanding → reflective. A learner cannot reason about a problem without understanding the concepts involved, so R gives exactly the reason why understanding comes first.

stmts: Assertion (A): Understanding-level teaching should normally precede reflective-level teaching.
Reason (R): Reflective thinking needs insight into facts, concepts and their relationships, which is developed at the understanding level.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true. But memory-level teaching is called thoughtless because it needs no insight or reasoning from the learner, only retention and reproduction. Presenting facts in an organised sequence is a feature of the model, not the reason it is thoughtless.

stmts: Assertion (A): Memory-level teaching is often described as “thoughtless” teaching.
Reason (R): At the memory level, the teacher presents facts in a well-organised, sequential way.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is Mager’s three-part objective: performance, condition, criterion. R is false: “know”, “understand” and “appreciate” describe inner states that cannot be observed, so behavioural objectives replace them with action verbs such as list, compute, compare or design.

stmts: Assertion (A): In Mager’s approach, a behavioural objective states the observable performance, the conditions of performance and the criterion of acceptable performance.
Reason (R): A good behavioural objective uses verbs such as “know”, “understand” and “appreciate”.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: the group produced the cognitive (1956) and affective (1964) handbooks; the psychomotor domain was developed later by others such as Simpson, Dave and Harrow. Statement II is false: the lowest affective level is Receiving (attending); Responding is the second.

stmts: Statement I: Bloom’s original committee published complete handbooks for all three domains, including the psychomotor domain, by 1964.
Statement II: The lowest level of the affective domain is Responding.

options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I describes the opposite of reflective teaching; it is learner-centred and the learners themselves solve the problem. Statement II is the correct description: open, democratic climate, learner most active, teacher as guide.

stmts: Statement I: Reflective-level teaching is teacher-centred, with the teacher solving problems in front of a passive class.
Statement II: At the reflective level, the classroom climate is open and democratic and the learner’s role is primary.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT a step of Morrison’s understanding-level model of teaching?
questionBank.explanation: Morrison’s steps are exploration, presentation, assimilation, organisation and recitation. Formulating and testing hypotheses belongs to the reflective-level (Hunt) model, which is why it is the distractor here.

questionBank.question: Arrange the steps of Morrison’s understanding-level model in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: Exploration (B) finds out what learners already know; Presentation (D) introduces the unit; Assimilation (E) lets learners absorb it through study and practice; Organisation (A) has learners arrange what they learned; Recitation (C) is learners presenting it orally or in writing.

stmts: A. Organisation
B. Exploration
C. Recitation
D. Presentation
E. Assimilation

questionBank.question: Which evaluation device is most appropriate for reflective-level teaching?
options: True/false items testing recall of definitions
Matching items on names and dates
Open-ended problems and essay tasks requiring hypotheses and justification
questionBank.explanation: Reflective teaching develops problem-solving and critical thinking, so its evaluation must ask learners to analyse a problem, propose and test ideas and justify a conclusion. The first three options only test recall, which suits the memory level.

questionBank.question: Teaching is said to be a science because:
options: it depends entirely on the teacher’s inborn talent
it can be observed, analysed, measured and systematically improved
it cannot be taught to others
it has no connection with feelings and values
questionBank.explanation: The scientific side of teaching is that its behaviours can be observed, measured (for example by interaction analysis), analysed and improved through training such as microteaching. Talent and creativity are the “art” side, and teaching certainly involves feelings and values.

questionBank.explanation: Building on students’ existing Wi-Fi experience is known to unknown (A-III). A physical chip before symbolic algebra is concrete to abstract (B-IV). Several particular examples before the rule is particular to general, the inductive approach (C-I). The whole site before its parts is whole to part (D-II).

II. Showing a complete working website before studying HTML, CSS and JavaScript separately
III. Starting a networking lesson from the hostel Wi-Fi students already use

questionBank.question: Which of the following are characteristics of a well-written behavioural (specific) objective?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A behavioural objective is learner-centred (A), observable and measurable (B) and specific to one outcome (D). It states what the learner will do, not the teacher (C is wrong). “Appreciate” and “realise” cannot be observed (E is wrong).

stmts: A. It is stated in terms of the learner’s behaviour
B. The behaviour is observable and measurable
C. It describes what the teacher will do in class
D. It focuses on a single learning outcome
E. It uses verbs such as “appreciate” and “realise”

questionBank.question: According to Philip W. Jackson, which activity belongs to the post-active phase of teaching?
options: Deciding the objectives of the lesson
Asking questions and reinforcing answers during the lesson
Evaluating achievement and revising the teaching strategy
questionBank.explanation: The post-active phase follows the lesson: evaluating what was learned, giving feedback and modifying the strategy. Fixing objectives and diagnosing entry behaviour are pre-active; questioning and reinforcing are interactive.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following teacher activities in the order in which they occur across the phases of teaching.
questionBank.explanation: Pre-active: first fix objectives (C), then select and sequence content to meet them (B). Interactive: present and question (D). Post-active: test achievement (A), then revise the plan (E). Content is chosen to serve objectives, so C comes before B.

stmts: A. Testing students’ achievement
B. Selecting and sequencing content
C. Fixing the instructional objectives
D. Presenting content and questioning the class
E. Revising the plan for the next class

questionBank.question: In the widely used Indian model of microteaching, the phases are teach 6 minutes, feedback 6 minutes, replan 12 minutes, reteach 6 minutes and re-feedback 6 minutes. What is the total duration of one cycle?
questionBank.explanation: 6 + 6 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 36 minutes. Replanning takes the largest share (12 of 36 minutes, one-third). 30 forgets the replan doubling; 42 and 45 come from adding a phase twice.

questionBank.question: In the revised Bloom’s taxonomy, any objective can be placed in a two-dimensional taxonomy table formed by the knowledge dimension and the cognitive process dimension. How many cells does this table have?
questionBank.explanation: There are 4 knowledge types (factual, conceptual, procedural, metacognitive) and 6 cognitive processes (remember to create). 4 × 6 = 24 cells. 18 or 30 come from using 3 or 5 knowledge types.

questionBank.question: A student, without being asked, joins a campus club promoting open-source software, argues for its benefits in debates and regularly contributes. At which affective level is this behaviour best placed?
questionBank.explanation: Voluntary commitment to a value, expressed in consistent action and advocacy, is Valuing. Responding is participation, often on request, with some satisfaction. Receiving is only attending. Characterisation would require an integrated value system that governs the student’s whole lifestyle, which the description does not show.

questionBank.question: A trainee now types at a steady speed without looking at the keyboard, automatically and with ease. In Dave’s psychomotor domain this is:
questionBank.explanation: Naturalisation is the top level of Dave’s scale: the skill is performed automatically, with minimal mental effort. Precision is accurate performance that still needs attention; Manipulation is performing from instructions; Imitation is copying a demonstration.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both are correct. Indoctrination instils beliefs without regard to evidence; genuine teaching gives reasons and allows questioning. Conditioning links responses to stimuli through reinforcement and does not depend on understanding.

stmts: Statement I: Teaching differs from indoctrination because it respects the learner’s reason and invites evidence and questioning.
Statement II: Conditioning shapes behaviour mainly through reinforcement, with little appeal to the learner’s understanding.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Thorndike’s law of readiness implies that, as a basic requirement of teaching, the teacher should:
options: cover the whole syllabus as fast as possible
ensure learners are physically and mentally prepared and motivated before new learning
repeat the same content until it is memorised
questionBank.explanation: The law of readiness says learning is satisfying when the learner is prepared to act and frustrating when forced. So teaching should start by creating readiness and motivation. Repetition relates to the law of exercise; speed and punishment are not requirements.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about the memory level of teaching are correct?
questionBank.explanation: Memory level: recall and recognition (A), a dominant teacher (B), recall-type testing (D). Insight (C) is the goal of the understanding level, and problem-solving (E) belongs to the reflective level.

stmts: A. The emphasis is on recall and recognition of facts
B. The teacher’s role is dominant
C. Development of insight is the main goal
D. Evaluation mainly uses recall-type items
E. Problem-solving is the central activity
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: R correctly defines analysis and synthesis. A is false: the maxim says to begin by breaking the problem into parts (analysis) and then combine them into a solution (synthesis). It does not ask the teacher to avoid analysis.

stmts: Assertion (A): The maxim “from analysis to synthesis” asks the teacher to avoid breaking a problem into its parts.
Reason (R): Analysis breaks a whole into its parts, and synthesis combines parts into a meaningful whole.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: The maxim “from psychological to logical” means that the teacher should:
options: begin with the learners’ interests, needs and experiences and move towards the logical organisation of the subject
teach the logical structure of the subject first and consider learners later
use psychological tests before every lesson
questionBank.explanation: Psychological order is the order that suits the learner’s mind (interest, experience, readiness); logical order is the structure of the subject. The maxim starts with the learner and ends with the subject’s logic. It does not reject logic, it postpones it.

questionBank.question: Which action verb best fits an objective at the Analyse level of the revised taxonomy?
questionBank.explanation: Differentiate (distinguishing relevant from irrelevant or important from unimportant parts) is an Analyse process. Recall is Remember, summarise is Understand, and critique is Evaluate.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Training develops skills through guided practice (A-III). Conditioning shapes responses through reinforcement (B-IV). Instruction is the systematic delivery of knowledge (C-I). Indoctrination instils beliefs without regard to evidence (D-II). Option 2 swaps training and conditioning, the pair most often confused.

b: I. Systematic delivery of knowledge and information
II. Instilling beliefs without regard to evidence or reasons
III. Developing skills through guided practice
IV. Shaping responses through reinforcement

stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which evaluation approach best suits the understanding level of teaching?
options: Questions that ask learners to explain, compare, give new examples and apply principles to unfamiliar cases
Oral repetition of definitions exactly as dictated
Only true/false items on names and dates
No evaluation, since understanding cannot be measured
questionBank.explanation: Understanding-level teaching aims at insight into relationships and principles, so evaluation uses objective and essay items that require explanation, comparison, fresh examples and application. Pure recall (options 2 and 3) suits the memory level, and understanding certainly can be measured.

questionBank.question: Which of the following best explains why Dewey’s view of teaching is called tripolar rather than bipolar?
options: It adds the principal as a third party
It adds the social environment (curriculum) as the third pole alongside teacher and learner
It divides teaching into three phases
It recognises three levels of teaching
questionBank.explanation: Dewey added the social environment, through which educational aims and content are set, as the third pole. Three phases (Jackson) and three levels (memory, understanding, reflective) are different ideas that share the number three, which is what the distractors exploit.

The common confusion is between facilities and support material.

questionBank.question: Arrange Piaget’s stages of cognitive development in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: Sensorimotor (0–2, B), preoperational (2–7, D), concrete operational (7–11, A), formal operational (11 onwards, C). Higher-education learners should be at the formal operational stage, able to reason abstractly.

stmts: A. Concrete operational
B. Sensorimotor
C. Formal operational
D. Preoperational

questionBank.question: A child aged 8 years 4 months has a mental age of 10 years. What is the ratio IQ?
questionBank.explanation: Use months: CA = 8 × 12 + 4 = 100 months, MA = 10 × 12 = 120 months. IQ = 120 ÷ 100 × 100 = 120. 119 comes from wrongly writing 8 years 4 months as 8.4 years (10 ÷ 8.4 × 100 ≈ 119); 84 inverts the ratio.

questionBank.question: A 10-year-old student has a ratio IQ of 90. What is the student’s mental age?
questionBank.explanation: MA = IQ × CA ÷ 100 = 90 × 10 ÷ 100 = 9 years. An IQ below 100 means the mental age is below the chronological age.

questionBank.question: On a deviation-IQ scale with mean 100 and standard deviation 15, what IQ corresponds to a score 2 standard deviations above the mean?
questionBank.explanation: IQ = 100 + 15 × 2 = 130. 115 is only one SD above; 145 is three SD above.

questionBank.question: In a Flanders observation of 200 tallies, categories 1–7 total 120, categories 8–9 total 60 and category 10 totals 20. What is the teacher talk ratio?
questionBank.explanation: Teacher talk ratio = (sum of categories 1–7) ÷ N × 100 = 120 ÷ 200 × 100 = 60%. 30% is the pupil talk ratio (60 ÷ 200) and 10% the silence ratio. 66.7% wrongly divides by 180, leaving out silence.

questionBank.question: Flanders tallies: category 1 = 4, 2 = 16, 3 = 10, 4 = 30, 5 = 150, 6 = 12, 7 = 3. What is the revised i/d ratio, (1 + 2 + 3) ÷ (6 + 7)?
questionBank.explanation: Numerator = 4 + 16 + 10 = 30; denominator = 12 + 3 = 15. i/d = 30 ÷ 15 = 2.0. The revised ratio leaves out questions (4) and lecturing (5), so it measures how the teacher reacts to pupils: here mainly with acceptance and praise. Including category 4 gives 60 ÷ 15 = 4, and using D = 5 + 6 + 7 gives 60 ÷ 165 ≈ 0.36, both wrong formulas.

questionBank.question: A teacher records Flanders categories for a 20-minute lesson, coding every 3 seconds. How many tallies will be recorded?
questionBank.explanation: 20 minutes = 1,200 seconds. One tally every 3 seconds gives 1,200 ÷ 3 = 400 tallies. 600 assumes a 2-second interval; 200 a 6-second interval.

questionBank.question: The term “scaffolding”, describing temporary support that is withdrawn as a learner gains competence, was introduced by:
questionBank.explanation: David Wood, Jerome Bruner and Gail Ross introduced the term in 1976. It is closely linked to Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, but Vygotsky himself did not use the word, which makes “Vygotsky” a tempting wrong answer when it appears.

questionBank.question: Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development refers to:
options: the stage at which abstract thinking begins
the gap between what a learner can do alone and what he or she can do with guidance
the difference between mental age and chronological age
the period of storm and stress in adolescence
questionBank.explanation: The ZPD is the range of tasks a learner cannot yet do alone but can do with help from a teacher or a more capable peer. Teaching aimed inside this zone produces the most growth. The other options describe Piaget, IQ and Hall.

questionBank.question: Which statement about Edgar Dale’s cone of experience is correct?
options: It shows that people remember 10% of what they read and 90% of what they do
It arranges experiences from concrete at the base to abstract at the top
It ranks media by their cost
It places verbal symbols at the base
questionBank.explanation: Dale’s cone is a scale of concreteness: direct purposeful experience at the base, verbal symbols at the top. The retention percentages were attached to the cone later by others and are not supported by Dale’s work or by research. It is not about cost.

questionBank.question: According to the Yerkes–Dodson law, a learner’s performance on a demanding task is best when arousal (anxiety, pressure) is:
questionBank.explanation: The law describes an inverted U: performance rises with arousal up to an optimum and falls beyond it, and the optimum is lower for difficult tasks. Teachers should create moderate challenge, avoiding both boredom and panic.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is an institution-related factor affecting teaching?
options: The college’s teacher–student ratio and academic calendar
questionBank.explanation: Teacher–student ratio and the academic calendar are set by the institution. Prior knowledge and motivation are learner factors; voice and clarity are teacher factors.

questionBank.question: An adult learner says: “I would like to join the evening course, but my night-shift job and my children leave me no time.” In K. Patricia Cross’s classification, this is a:
questionBank.explanation: Situational barriers arise from a person’s life situation (job, family, time, money). Institutional barriers come from the provider (timings, fees, rules); dispositional barriers are attitudes and self-perceptions, such as “I am too old to learn”. “Cognitive barrier” is not one of Cross’s three.

questionBank.question: Which of the following best describes the concrete operational stage in Piaget’s theory?
options: Learning mainly through senses and movement
Logical thinking about concrete objects, conservation and reversibility, but difficulty with abstractions
Symbolic play with egocentric thinking and no conservation
questionBank.explanation: The concrete operational stage (about 7–11) brings conservation, reversibility and classification, but reasoning stays tied to concrete objects. Option 1 is sensorimotor, option 3 formal operational and option 4 preoperational.

questionBank.question: An IQ of 85 on a deviation scale (mean 100, SD 15) corresponds to what z-score?
questionBank.explanation: z = (IQ − 100) ÷ 15 = (85 − 100) ÷ 15 = −15 ÷ 15 = −1. The score is one standard deviation below the mean.

questionBank.question: SWAYAM stands for

questionBank.explanation: The INFLIBNET Centre maintains the SWAYAM PRABHA web portal (and its app). BISAG-N uplinks the channels; NPTEL and CEC are content providers.

questionBank.question: On a SWAYAM PRABHA channel, every new programme is telecast once and then repeated 5 more times in the day. How many times in all is a new programme aired in a day?
questionBank.explanation: One first telecast + 5 repeats = 6 airings. With at least 4 hours of new content, 4 × 6 = 24 hours fills the day. 5 counts only the repeats; 24 is the hours, not the airings.

questionBank.question: In the Indian (NCERT) model of microteaching, the phases take teach 6, feedback 6, re-plan 12, re-teach 6 and re-feedback 6 minutes. What is the duration of one complete cycle?
questionBank.explanation: 6 + 6 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 36 minutes. The answer 30 comes from taking re-plan as 6 minutes; in fact it is the longest phase, at 12 minutes.

questionBank.question: A programme offers 7 courses in a semester. Under the UGC SWAYAM credit regulations of 2021 (up to 40% of courses per semester), what is the maximum number of courses a student may take through SWAYAM?
questionBank.explanation: 40% of 7 = 2.8. Since the rule is “up to 40%”, the number cannot exceed 2.8, so the maximum whole number is 2. Rounding up to 3 would be 42.9%, which is over the limit.

questionBank.question: In Flanders’ Interaction Analysis an observer records one category every 3 seconds. How many tallies are recorded during a 30-minute class?
questionBank.explanation: 30 minutes = 1,800 seconds; 1,800 ÷ 3 = 600 tallies. 900 would be a tally every 2 seconds; 300 a tally every 6 seconds.

questionBank.question: The branching type of programmed instruction is associated with

questionBank.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the four quadrants of a SWAYAM course?

questionBank.question: A live webinar, in which the teacher and learners meet online at the same time, is an example of

questionBank.question: In Edgar Dale’s Cone of Experience, which experience lies at the base of the cone?
questionBank.explanation: The base is the most concrete: direct, purposeful, first-hand experience. The cone rises towards abstraction, with verbal symbols at the top.

questionBank.question: The Dalton plan of instruction is best described as
options: Monthly assignments done by each learner at his or her own pace in subject laboratories
A lecture followed by a whole-class recitation

A discussion led by a panel of experts
questionBank.explanation: Helen Parkhurst’s Dalton plan (1920) gives each learner assignments (contracts) to complete at his or her own pace, using subject laboratories and teacher guidance. The other options describe recitation, the project method and a panel discussion.

questionBank.question: Four semesters carry 20, 22, 24 and 22 credits, and a student’s SGPAs in them are 7.2, 8.1, 6.9 and 7.6. What is the CGPA?
questionBank.explanation: CGPA = Σ(credits × SGPA) ÷ Σ credits = (144.0 + 178.2 + 165.6 + 167.2) ÷ 88 = 655.0 ÷ 88 = 7.443 → 7.44. 7.45 is the unweighted mean of the four SGPAs, the standard trap.

questionBank.question: An item is answered correctly by 60 of the 150 students who attempted it. What is its difficulty index?
questionBank.explanation: P = number correct ÷ number attempted = 60 ÷ 150 = 0.40 (40%). A higher P would mean an easier item. 2.50 inverts the fraction; 0.60 is the proportion who got it wrong.

questionBank.question: With upper and lower groups of 30 students each, an item is answered correctly by 6 students of the upper group and 12 of the lower group. What is its discrimination index, and what does it suggest?
options: −0.20; the item or its key is faulty
questionBank.explanation: D = (R_U − R_L) ÷ n = (6 − 12) ÷ 30 = −0.20. A negative D means the weaker students did better than the stronger ones, so the item is ambiguous or wrongly keyed and must be revised or dropped.

questionBank.question: In a test with mean 60 and standard deviation 8, a student scores 72. What is the student’s T-score?

In an NTA session, 2,000 candidates appeared. For a candidate, 1,640 candidates of the session (including the candidate) had a raw score equal to or less than the candidate’s. What is the candidate’s percentile score?
questionBank.explanation: Percentile = 100 × (candidates with a raw score ≤ the candidate’s) ÷ (total in the session) = 100 × 1,640 ÷ 2,000 = 82.0. 18.0 is the percentage above the candidate.

questionBank.question: Under UGC’s Curriculum and Credit Framework for Undergraduate Programmes, how many contact hours in a semester does a 3-credit theory course with an additional 1-credit practicum carry?
questionBank.explanation: One theory credit = 15 hours and one practicum credit = 30 hours per semester. 3 × 15 + 1 × 30 = 45 + 30 = 75 hours. 60 treats the practicum credit like a theory credit (4 × 15).

questionBank.question: A student takes courses of 4, 4, 4 and 2 credits and earns A, F, B+ and O respectively on the UGC 10-point scale. What is the SGPA?
questionBank.explanation: Credit points = 4×8 + 4×0 + 4×7 + 2×10 = 32 + 0 + 28 + 20 = 80. Credits taken = 14, including the failed course. SGPA = 80 ÷ 14 = 5.714 → 5.71. 8.00 wrongly drops the F course (80 ÷ 10); 6.25 is the unweighted mean (25 ÷ 4).

questionBank.question: The correlation between the odd-item and even-item halves of a test is 0.80. What is the reliability of the full test by the Spearman–Brown formula?
questionBank.explanation: r = 2 × 0.80 ÷ (1 + 0.80) = 1.60 ÷ 1.80 = 0.889 ≈ 0.89. 1.60 forgets the denominator (a reliability can never exceed 1); 0.64 squares r.

questionBank.question: According to Auguste Comte’s law of three stages, human thought passes through which sequence?
questionBank.explanation: Comte held that thought first explains events by gods or supernatural agents (theological), then by abstract forces or essences (metaphysical), and finally by observed facts and laws (positive, or scientific). The positive stage is the last, which rules out options 3 and 4, and the theological stage is the first.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I states the positivist view of knowledge (observation and verification). Statement II states the interpretivist view (Weber’s Verstehen: understand action through its meaning to the actor). Both are standard definitions, so both are true.

stmts: Statement I: Positivism treats only knowledge that can be verified through observation and experience as genuine knowledge.
Statement II: Interpretivism holds that social action should be understood through the meanings that actors attach to it.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true, and R explains A. Because falsifiability is Popper’s demarcation criterion (R), a theory that cannot be refuted by any possible observation fails the criterion and is not scientific (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): For Karl Popper, a theory that no conceivable observation could refute is not a scientific theory.
Reason (R): Popper made falsifiability the criterion that separates science from non-science.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true. But R does not explain A: historians prefer primary sources because they are closest to the events, not because sources are criticised. Criticism is applied to primary and secondary sources alike. So option 2.

stmts: Assertion (A): Historical research relies heavily on primary sources such as original documents and eyewitness accounts.
Reason (R): In historical research every source is subjected to external and internal criticism.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: grounded theory is inductive and uses constant comparison to let categories emerge from data. R is also true (The Discovery of Grounded Theory, 1967). But who proposed the method does not explain why it is inductive, so R is not the explanation of A.

stmts: Assertion (A): Grounded theory builds theory from the data rather than testing a hypothesis fixed in advance.
Reason (R): Grounded theory was proposed by Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A describes the strength of the case study. R is false: one case is not a random sample, so statistical generalisation is not possible. A case study can support analytical generalisation (to theory), not statistical generalisation (to a population).

stmts: Assertion (A): A case study gives an in-depth, holistic understanding of a single unit in its real-life context.
Reason (R): Findings of a single case study can normally be generalised statistically to a large population.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is false: action research arose in social psychology and education to solve practical, local problems with the people concerned, not to discover universal physical laws. R is true: Lewin used the term in the 1940s, and Stephen Corey later popularised it in schools.

stmts: Assertion (A): Action research was first developed as a method for discovering universal laws in physics.
Reason (R): The social psychologist Kurt Lewin introduced the term “action research” in the 1940s.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: R is the defining feature of ethnography: long immersion in a culture, participant observation and informal interviews. A describes a mail survey, the opposite approach, so A is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): Ethnography relies mainly on structured questionnaires mailed to a large random sample.
Reason (R): Ethnography involves prolonged fieldwork and participant observation within a cultural group.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:

Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both are standard definitions. A cross-sectional study is a snapshot of different units at one time. A panel study is the longitudinal design that measures the same individuals repeatedly; a trend study samples different people from the same population each time, and a cohort study follows a group defined by a shared event (such as birth year).

stmts: Statement I: In a cross-sectional study, data are collected from different groups at a single point in time.
Statement II: A panel study follows the same individuals over a period of time.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Both descriptions are reversed. Qualitative research uses small purposive samples and aims at depth, not statistical generalisation. It is in qualitative research that the researcher is the main instrument; quantitative research relies on standardised tests and structured instruments and tries to keep the researcher detached.

stmts: Statement I: Qualitative research typically uses large random samples so that its findings can be generalised statistically.
Statement II: In quantitative research, the researcher’s own subjectivity is treated as the main research instrument.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I describes fundamental research, not applied research; applied research exists precisely to solve practical problems. Statement II is the standard definition of evaluation research (formative during a programme, summative at its end).

Statement II: Evaluation research judges the worth or effectiveness of a programme, policy or intervention.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I defines external validity, not internal validity (internal validity asks whether the treatment really caused the effect). Statement II is also wrong: random assignment equalises groups and so protects internal validity; random selection from the population supports external validity.

stmts: Statement I: Internal validity is the extent to which the results of a study can be generalised to other settings and populations.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Induction goes from particular cases to a general pattern (Statement II, true). Deduction goes the other way, from a general premise or theory to a specific conclusion or prediction, so Statement I is false.

stmts: Statement I: Deductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion.
Statement II: Inductive reasoning moves from specific observations to a general conclusion.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Pragmatism judges methods by what answers the question, which justifies mixing them, so Statement I is true. In the explanatory sequential design the quantitative phase comes first and the qualitative phase explains its results; qualitative-first is the exploratory sequential design. Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Mixed methods research is commonly associated with the pragmatist paradigm.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are features of the positivist paradigm?

B, C, D and E only

questionBank.explanation: History (outside events), maturation (natural change in participants), statistical regression (extreme scorers drifting towards the mean) and experimental mortality (drop-out) are all threats. questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of reflective thinking, as described by John Dewey, in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: Dewey’s sequence: a felt difficulty (B), its location and definition (D), a suggested solution, that is, a hypothesis (A), reasoning out its implications (E), and testing it by observation or experiment (C). Option 2 proposes a solution before the problem is defined, and option 4 reasons out a solution before suggesting it.

questionBank.explanation: Explanatory sequential means quantitative first: collect (B) and analyse (D) the numbers, pick out the surprising results and plan the follow-up (E), collect and analyse qualitative data (A), and finally interpret the two together (C). Option 1 is the exploratory design’s qualitative-first order.

questionBank.explanation: Comte’s Course appeared in volumes from 1830 to 1842 (B); Popper’s Logik der Forschung in 1934 (D); Kuhn in 1962 (A); Glaser and Strauss in 1967 (C); Bhaskar in 1975 (E). A common slip is to date Popper by the 1959 English translation, which still comes before Kuhn.

stmts: A. Kuhn, The Structure of Scientific Revolutions
B. Comte, Course of Positive Philosophy
C. Glaser and Strauss, The Discovery of Grounded Theory

questionBank.question: A researcher takes the state-wise Gross Enrolment Ratio figures already published by the government and critically evaluates them to explain regional differences. According to Kothari’s classification, this is mainly:
questionBank.explanation: Kothari separates descriptive research, which describes the state of affairs as it exists (often by collecting new data), from analytical research, which uses facts or information already available and analyses them to make a critical evaluation. Nothing is manipulated, so it is not experimental, and the researcher is not improving her own practice.

questionBank.question: Which feature distinguishes a quasi-experimental design from a true experimental design?
options: There is no manipulation of the independent variable.
Participants are not randomly assigned to groups.
No data are collected after the treatment.
questionBank.explanation: In a quasi-experiment the researcher still manipulates the treatment and measures the outcome, but uses intact groups (for example existing sections) instead of random assignment. No manipulation at all would make the study ex post facto or descriptive.

questionBank.question: Workers in a factory improved their output whenever the lighting was changed, whether it was made brighter or dimmer, apparently because they knew they were being studied. This is known as the:
questionBank.explanation: The Hawthorne effect, named after the Western Electric Hawthorne works studies, is a change in behaviour caused by the awareness of being observed. The Pygmalion effect is the effect of expectations on performance, the John Henry effect is a control group working harder to compete, and the halo effect is a rater’s overall impression colouring specific judgements.

questionBank.question: In the Solomon four-group design, how many of the four groups take the pretest?
questionBank.explanation: The four randomly formed groups are: pretest–treatment–posttest, pretest–posttest, treatment–posttest and posttest only. So 2 groups are pretested, 2 receive the treatment and all 4 are post-tested. Comparing the pretested and unpretested treatment groups isolates the effect of the pretest itself.

questionBank.question: A study that intensively examines one exceptional village school over two years in order to understand its unique features is best described as:
options: Longitudinal survey of a random sample
questionBank.explanation: Idiographic study aims to understand a particular case in depth, which is what an intensive case study of one school does. Nomothetic study seeks general laws across many cases. The study does run over two years, but it is one case, not a survey of a random sample, and it is not a one-time snapshot.

questionBank.question: Research that relies on experience or observation alone, and whose conclusions can be verified by observation or experiment, is called:
questionBank.explanation: Kothari’s pair: conceptual research deals with abstract ideas and theory (used by philosophers and thinkers to develop concepts), while empirical research is data-based and yields conclusions that can be verified by observation or experiment.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).

Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. Cluster sampling is cheaper because the selected units are concentrated in a few places (less travel and no full list of individuals is needed). R states the ideal composition of a cluster, which affects precision, not cost. So R does not explain A.

questionBank.question: A college has 600 arts, 300 science and 100 commerce students. A proportionate stratified sample of 80 students is drawn. How many science students are in the sample?
questionBank.explanation: Sampling fraction = 80 ÷ 1,000 = 0.08. Science: 300 × 0.08 = 24. (Arts 48 and commerce 8 are the other strata; 27 is 80 ÷ 3, an equal allocation.)

questionBank.question: A 4-item scale has a sum of item variances equal to 6 and a total-score variance of 16. Cronbach’s alpha is approximately:
Using Cochran’s formula with 95% confidence (z = 1.96), a margin of error of ±5% and p = 0.5, the minimum sample size for estimating a proportion in a very large population is:
questionBank.explanation: n₀ = z²p(1 − p) ÷ e² = 1.96² × 0.25 ÷ 0.0025 = 3.8416 × 100 = 384.16, rounded up to 385. 400 uses z = 2, 196 forgets to square z, and 1,537 uses a 2.5% margin.

questionBank.question: Two observers classify 100 episodes. Both say “on task” in 40 and “off task” in 30; they disagree in the other 30 (observer A says “on” in 20 of these). Cohen’s kappa is:
With a sample of 100, the standard error of the mean is 4. Other things equal, what sample size makes the standard error 2?
questionBank.explanation: SE = σ ÷ √n, so SE halves when √n doubles, that is when n is multiplied by 4: 100 × 4 = 400. Doubling n to 200 only reduces SE to 4 ÷ √2 ≈ 2.83.

questionBank.question: Cochran’s initial estimate n₀ = 384.16 is corrected for a finite population of N = 2,000 using n = n₀ ÷ (1 + (n₀ − 1) ÷ N). The required sample (rounded up) is:
questionBank.explanation: (n₀ − 1) ÷ N = 383.16 ÷ 2,000 = 0.1916. n = 384.16 ÷ 1.1916 = 322.4, rounded up to 323. For a small population the correction lowers the required sample.

questionBank.question: A journal published 120 citable items in 2022 and 130 in 2023. In 2024, these items received 300 and 450 citations respectively. What is the journal’s 2024 Impact Factor?
questionBank.explanation: Impact Factor 2024 = citations in 2024 to 2022–23 items ÷ citable items of 2022–23 = (300 + 450) ÷ (120 + 130) = 750 ÷ 250 = 3.0. 2.5 uses 300 ÷ 120 only, 3.75 uses 450 ÷ 120, and 6.0 adds the two yearly ratios.

questionBank.question: A researcher’s seven papers have 42, 15, 11, 10, 9, 4 and 2 citations. Her h-index and i10-index are, respectively:
questionBank.explanation: h-index: rank 5 has 9 citations (9 ≥ 5) and rank 6 has 4 (4 < 6), so h = 5. i10-index: papers with at least 10 citations are 42, 15, 11 and 10, so i10 = 4 (a paper with exactly 10 counts). “5 and 3” wrongly excludes the paper with 10.

questionBank.question: A researcher’s ten papers have 30, 17, 10, 6, 4, 2, 1, 0, 0 and 0 citations. What is the g-index?
questionBank.explanation: The g-index is the largest g such that the top g papers together have at least g² citations. Running totals: 30, 47, 57, 63, 67, 69, 70, 70, 70, 70. At g = 8, 70 ≥ 64; at g = 9, 70 < 81. So g = 8. 4 is the h-index.

questionBank.question: Which of the following is the most suitable title for the passage?
options: Why cities are more dishonest than villages
From acquaintance to institutions: how trust works among strangers
The case for stricter surveillance of professionals
questionBank.explanation: The passage traces trust from personal (village, reputation) to institutional (rules, licences, courts) forms, and then discusses the strengths and fragility of institutional trust. Option 3 captures that journey. Option 1 is too narrow and slightly off (the village is only the starting contrast). Option 2 is unsupported: the passage never says cities are more dishonest. Option 4 contradicts the last paragraph, which warns about the hidden cost of more surveillance.

stem.passage:
For most of human history, people lived among those they knew. A villager could judge the honesty of a trader because she had watched him for years, and the trader behaved well partly because a single act of cheating would be remembered by everyone whose goodwill he needed. Trust, in such settings, was personal: it rested on reputation built slowly through repeated face-to-face contact.

The modern city dissolves this arrangement. A resident of a large metropolis may pass thousands of people in a day and never see most of them again. She buys food from shops whose owners she does not know, sends her children to schools run by strangers and deposits her savings with institutions whose officers she will never meet. If trust still depended on personal acquaintance, such a life would be impossible. What makes it possible is a different kind of trust, which sociologists call impersonal or institutional trust. We rely less on the character of particular individuals than on the rules, licences, courts, auditors and professional bodies that stand behind them. I trust the pharmacist not because I know her but because I believe that the system which trained, certified and inspects her works.

This shift has brought enormous gains. Institutional trust allows cooperation on a scale that personal trust could never support; markets, bureaucracies and scientific communities all depend on it. But it is also fragile in a particular way. Personal trust is damaged one relationship at a time, whereas institutional trust can collapse all at once. When a single well-publicised scandal reveals that inspectors were bribed or auditors looked away, people do not merely distrust the individuals involved; they begin to doubt the entire system, and with it everyone who works inside it.

The response to such a crisis is often to demand more rules and more surveillance. Some of this is necessary, yet it carries a hidden cost. Rules cannot anticipate every situation, and people who feel that they are constantly monitored tend to do exactly what the rules require and nothing more. The willingness to act in good faith where no rule applies, which no inspector can compel, is precisely what institutions need most. A society that tries to replace trustworthiness with checking may find that it has less of both.

stem.passage:
For most of human history, people lived among those they knew. A villager could judge the honesty of a trader because she had watched him for years, and the trader behaved well partly because a single act of cheating would be remembered by everyone whose goodwill he needed. Trust, in such settings, was personal: it rested on reputation built slowly through repeated face-to-face contact.

The modern city dissolves this arrangement. A resident of a large metropolis may pass thousands of people in a day and never see most of them again. She buys food from shops whose owners she does not know, sends her children to schools run by strangers and deposits her savings with institutions whose officers she will never meet. If trust still depended on personal acquaintance, such a life would be impossible. What makes it possible is a different kind of trust, which sociologists call impersonal or institutional trust. We rely less on the character of particular individuals than on the rules, licences, courts, auditors and professional bodies that stand behind them. I trust the pharmacist not because I know her but because I believe that the system which trained, certified and inspects her works.

This shift has brought enormous gains. Institutional trust allows cooperation on a scale that personal trust could never support; markets, bureaucracies and scientific communities all depend on it. But it is also fragile in a particular way. Personal trust is damaged one relationship at a time, whereas institutional trust can collapse all at once. When a single well-publicised scandal reveals that inspectors were bribed or auditors looked away, people do not merely distrust the individuals involved; they begin to doubt the entire system, and with it everyone who works inside it.

The response to such a crisis is often to demand more rules and more surveillance. Some of this is necessary, yet it carries a hidden cost. Rules cannot anticipate every situation, and people who feel that they are constantly monitored tend to do exactly what the rules require and nothing more. The willingness to act in good faith where no rule applies, which no inspector can compel, is precisely what institutions need most. A society that tries to replace trustworthiness with checking may find that it has less of both.

questionBank.question: The author compares a healthy wetland to a sponge in order to show that it:
options: absorbs water in wet periods and releases it slowly in dry periods, reducing both floods and shortages
is soft and difficult to build on
absorbs pollutants permanently so that they never reach rivers
needs to be squeezed dry before it can be useful
questionBank.explanation: The sentence after the image explains it: “it absorbs rainwater during storms and releases it slowly during dry months, reducing both floods downstream and water shortages later in the year.” Option 2 uses a literal property of sponges, not the author’s point. Option 3 adds “permanently” and “never” (extreme). Option 4 reverses the argument.

stem.passage:
For centuries, wetlands were treated as wasteland. Marshes, swamps and floodplains were difficult to farm, bred mosquitoes and stood in the way of roads and housing, so draining them was regarded as a mark of progress. Across much of the world, a large share of the wetlands that existed a few centuries ago has been drained or filled, and the loss continues in many places today.

Ecologists now describe wetlands in very different terms. A healthy wetland behaves like a sponge: it absorbs rainwater during storms and releases it slowly during dry months, reducing both floods downstream and water shortages later in the year. Its plants and sediments trap pollutants, so that water leaving a marsh is often cleaner than the water that entered it. Wetlands shelter fish nurseries and migratory birds, and peat wetlands store vast quantities of carbon that would enter the atmosphere if they were drained and allowed to dry.

Why, then, were these services ignored for so long? Part of the answer lies in how societies keep accounts. When a wetland is drained to build a housing colony, the value of the houses appears in the economic record at once. The value of the flood protection that has been lost does not; it appears years later, if at all, as the cost of repairing flooded homes, and it is rarely traced back to the vanished marsh. Services that are free and diffuse are easily treated as though they were worthless.

Some economists therefore propose that nature be given a price, so that the services of a wetland can be compared directly with the profits of developing it. Supporters argue that decision-makers pay attention only to numbers and that a figure, however rough, is better than an implied value of zero. Critics reply that some things cannot sensibly be priced, and that attaching a figure to a marsh invites the conclusion that it may be destroyed whenever someone offers more. Both sides agree on one point: a decision that ignores what a wetland does is not an economic decision at all, but a failure of accounting.

The practical lesson is modest but important. Before a wetland is drained, the question to ask is not only what could be built on it, but also what the wetland is already doing for free, and who will pay when it stops.

questionBank.question: According to the passage, in what respect did Socrates consider himself wiser than others?
options: He had studied more subjects than the people he questioned.
He could prove that nothing can be known.
He was aware of his own ignorance, while others wrongly believed they had knowledge.
questionBank.explanation: Paragraph 2: “he knew that he did not know, whereas the people he questioned believed that they knew what they did not.” Option 2 confuses Socrates with the universal sceptic. Options 1 and 3 are not in the passage, and option 3 is the opposite of the inquiring spirit described.

stem.passage:
Doubt has a poor reputation. In ordinary speech, to doubt someone is to insult them, and a person who is unsure of their beliefs is often thought weak or indecisive. Yet much of the history of philosophy can be read as a defence of doubt, not as an end in itself, but as the beginning of knowledge.

Socrates, as Plato portrays him, claimed to be wiser than others in only one respect: he knew that he did not know, whereas the people he questioned believed that they knew what they did not. His method of patient questioning was designed to expose this false confidence. It often left his partners confused and irritated, but the confusion was useful. A person who believes that he already knows has no reason to inquire; only someone who recognises a gap in his understanding will look for ways to fill it.

Centuries later, Descartes turned doubt into a deliberate method. He resolved to set aside every belief that could possibly be false, in the hope of finding something that could not be doubted at all. The project was more radical than the questioning of Socrates, and later philosophers disputed whether it succeeded. But it established the idea that the strength of a belief depends on how well it survives serious attempts to challenge it.

It is important to distinguish this kind of doubt from mere scepticism. The universal sceptic, who doubts everything equally, is as lazy in his own way as the dogmatist who doubts nothing, for both have excused themselves from the labour of weighing evidence. Productive doubt is selective and proportionate. It asks which beliefs deserve more scrutiny, what would count as evidence against them, and whether that evidence has been honestly sought. Many modern philosophers call this attitude fallibilism: the view that we may hold beliefs with reasonable confidence while admitting that any of them could, in principle, turn out to be mistaken.

Such an attitude has practical value far beyond philosophy. A physician who considers that her first diagnosis may be wrong orders the test that catches the rarer disease; a judge who keeps an open mind hears the witness whose testimony changes the case. The confident are not always wrong, and the doubtful are not always right. But those who have never learned to doubt themselves have lost the means by which mistakes are found.

The project was more radical than the questioning of Socrates, and later philosophers disputed whether it succeeded. But it established the idea that the strength of a belief depends on how well it survives serious attempts to challenge it.

It is important to distinguish this kind of doubt from mere scepticism. The universal sceptic, who doubts everything equally, is as lazy in his own way as the dogmatist who doubts nothing, for both have excused themselves from the labour of weighing evidence. Productive doubt is selective and proportionate. It asks which beliefs deserve more scrutiny, what would count as evidence against them, and whether that evidence has been honestly sought. Many modern philosophers call this attitude fallibilism: the view that we may hold beliefs with reasonable confidence while admitting that any of them could, in principle, turn out to be mistaken.

Such an attitude has practical value far beyond philosophy. A physician who considers that her first diagnosis may be wrong orders the test that catches the rarer disease; a judge who keeps an open mind hears the witness whose testimony changes the case. The confident are not always wrong, and the doubtful are not always right. But those who have never learned to doubt themselves have lost the means by which mistakes are found.

stem.passage:
Science is often presented as a collection of established facts, but working scientists tend to describe it differently: as a method for discovering which of our current ideas are wrong. Its reputation for reliability rests less on the brilliance of individual researchers than on a set of social arrangements that make errors likely to be caught.

The first of these is publication. A result that stays in a laboratory notebook cannot be tested by anyone else; a result that is published, with a description of the methods used, can be. Before publication, most journals send a manuscript to other experts in the field, who examine it for flaws in design, analysis or reasoning. This process, known as peer review, is valuable, but it is widely misunderstood. Reviewers usually see only what the authors choose to report. They rarely repeat the experiment themselves, and they cannot detect every error, let alone deliberate fraud. Peer review is a filter, not a guarantee.

The stronger safeguard is replication. If a finding is genuine, other researchers following the same procedure should observe it again. When they do, confidence grows; when repeated attempts fail, the original claim is weakened, however prestigious the journal that printed it. In recent years, large coordinated efforts to repeat published studies in several fields, notably psychology and biomedicine, have found that a worrying proportion of results could not be reproduced. Some commentators called this a crisis. Others pointed out that the discovery itself was science doing its job: the errors were found by scientists, using scientific methods.

The episode nonetheless exposed weaknesses in how research is rewarded. Journals and funding bodies have tended to favour new and surprising findings over careful repetitions, and researchers under pressure to publish may be tempted to analyse their data in many ways until something appears significant. Reforms now being tried include registering a study's hypotheses and methods before the data are collected, sharing data openly and publishing well-designed studies whether or not their results are striking.

The lesson for the non-scientist is not that science cannot be trusted. It is that a single study, however widely reported, is only the beginning of a conversation. Confidence is earned by findings that many independent groups have tested and failed to overturn.

B. It is irreversible.
C. It is always intentional.
D. It takes place in a context.
E. In the presence of others, it is possible not to communicate at all.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are among the “7 Cs” of effective communication, as commonly listed in business-communication texts?
options: A, B, C and E only
A, B, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: The 7 Cs are clear, concise, concrete, correct, coherent, complete and courteous. Complexity is the opposite of what the checklist aims for.

stmts: A. Clarity
B. Conciseness
C. Complexity
D. Courtesy
E. Correctness

options: A, B, D and E only
A, B, C and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: Paralanguage is vocal but not verbal: pitch, pauses, rate, tone, volume, fillers. Posture is a body cue and belongs to kinesics.

B. Pauses
C. Posture
D. Rate of speech
E. Tone

questionBank.question: Which of the following help to overcome communication barriers in a classroom?
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A reduces semantic distance, C creates feedback, D removes physical barriers. Speaking faster (B) overloads the receiver, and unexplained jargon (E) is itself a semantic barrier.

stmts: A. Using examples from the students’ own context
B. Speaking faster to cover more content
C. Checking understanding through questions
D. Reducing noise and arranging seating so that everyone can see and hear

questionBank.explanation: The sender first forms the idea (B), encodes it (E), transmits it (C); the receiver decodes it (A) and responds with feedback (D). Encoding must come after ideation and before transmission.

stmts: A. Decoding by the receiver
B. Ideation by the sender
C. Transmission through a channel
D. Feedback

questionBank.question: Arrange Hall’s proxemic zones in increasing order of distance.
questionBank.explanation: Intimate (up to about 18 in) < personal (about 1.5–4 ft) < social (about 4–12 ft) < public (about 12 ft and beyond): B, D, A, C.

C. Public
