questionBank.question: A researcher uses systematic sampling to draw 60 colleges from a numbered list of 1,800 colleges. The random start chosen from the first interval is 17. What is the serial number of the 12th college in the sample?
questionBank.explanation:
Sampling interval k = N ÷ n = 1800 ÷ 60 = 30.
The selected serial numbers are 17, 47, 77, … , i.e. 17 + (i − 1) × 30.
For i = 12: 17 + 11 × 30 = 17 + 330 = 347.
Trap: 377 uses 12 × 30 (counting one interval too many); 360 is simply 12 × 30; 330 forgets to add the random start.

questionBank.question:
Read the passage and answer the question that follows.
Which of the following best states the central argument of the passage?
options: Consumers have become careless and wasteful, and they must be persuaded to feel guilty about replacing devices.
Traditional repair streets were ideal workplaces and should be restored exactly as they were.
The decline of repair is driven mainly by product design and pricing, so the remedy lies in rules on parts, information and repairable design rather than in appeals to individual conscience.
Electronic waste can be solved only by recycling minerals in large, centralised factories.
questionBank.explanation: The second and third paragraphs locate the cause in design (glued batteries, locked software) and in parts pricing, and state that the movement treats the problem as “structural rather than moral”, asking governments for rules. The carelessness option is the very view the author rejects (“not simply that people have grown … careless”). The romantic option is contradicted by the last paragraph. Centralised recycling is never proposed; the passage praises local repair.

stem.passage:
A generation ago, most Indian towns had a street where almost nothing was thrown away. Radios, pressure cookers, wristwatches and bicycles went there to be opened, diagnosed and returned to work. The repairer’s knowledge was rarely written down; it lived in the hands and passed from master to apprentice through years of watching and doing. Today many of those streets are thinning. The reason is not simply that people have grown richer or more careless. The products themselves have changed.
Modern devices are increasingly designed to be replaced rather than mended. Batteries are glued in rather than screwed down, components are soldered onto a single board, and diagnostic software is locked so that only the manufacturer’s authorised centres can read the fault codes. Spare parts, where they exist at all, are often priced so close to the cost of a new unit that repair stops making economic sense. A consumer who is told that fixing a two-year-old phone will cost two-thirds of the price of a new one is not being wasteful when she buys the new one; she is responding rationally to a price that someone else has set.
This is why the growing “right to repair” movement insists that the problem is structural rather than moral. Its campaigners do not mainly ask individuals to feel guilty. They ask governments to require that manuals, tools and parts be made available on fair terms, and that products be designed so that a competent independent technician can open them. Several jurisdictions have begun to move in this direction, and some manufacturers have responded, often grudgingly, with self-repair programmes.
The environmental case is obvious: every repaired device is one less item in the swelling stream of electronic waste, and the energy and minerals already embedded in it are not squandered. The social case is made less often but is just as strong. Repair work is local, skilled and hard to automate. A town that repairs keeps money and livelihoods within its own economy instead of sending both to distant factories.
Yet it would be naive to romanticise the old repair street. Not every repair was safe, and informal workshops seldom offered warranties or fair wages. The task is not to return to the past but to rebuild repair as a recognised trade, with training, standards and access to information. Skill that once survived by accident must now be protected by design.

questionBank.question:

questionBank.explanation: The sentence ends: she “is responding rationally to a price that someone else has set.” The example moves the blame from the consumer to the pricing of parts and repair. A certified training course and published standards for independent repair technicians, backed by access to manuals and parts

questionBank.question:
What is the next term of the series?
2, 3, 8, 27, 112, ?
questionBank.explanation:
Each term is the previous term multiplied by k and then increased by k, for k = 1, 2, 3, …:
2×1 + 1 = 3; 3×2 + 2 = 8; 8×3 + 3 = 27; 27×4 + 4 = 112; 112×5 + 5 = 565.
Trap: 560 is 112 × 5 without adding 5; 453 treats the rule as ×4 + 5 again.

questionBank.question: In a certain code, each letter of a word is first replaced by its “mirror” letter in the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, C↔X, and so on), and then the resulting letters are written in reverse order. In this code PAPER is written as IVKZK. How is MARKS written in that code?
questionBank.explanation:
Mirror letter: position p becomes 27 − p.
Check with PAPER: P→K, A→Z, P→K, E→V, R→I gives KZKVI; reversed, IVKZK. ✓
MARKS: M(13)→N(14), A→Z, R(18)→I(9), K(11)→P(16), S(19)→H(8), giving NZIPH; reversed, HPIZN.
Trap: NZIPH forgets the reversal; HPZIN reverses wrongly; GPIZN takes M’s mirror as G.

questionBank.question: Ravi walks 12 m towards the north, turns right and walks 5 m, turns right again and walks 20 m, and then turns left and walks 10 m. How far is he from his starting point, and in which direction?
questionBank.explanation:
Take the start as (0, 0) with north as +y and east as +x.
12 m north → (0, 12). Right turn faces east; 5 m → (5, 12). Right turn faces south; 20 m → (5, −8). Left turn from south faces east; 10 m → (15, −8).
Distance = √(15² + 8²) = √(225 + 64) = √289 = 17 m. He is east and south of the start, so the direction is south-east.
Trap: 23 m adds the 15 and 8 without Pythagoras; 13 m uses only the first east leg (5, −12); north-east ignores the net southward displacement.

questionBank.question: Two trains, 180 m and 220 m long, run on parallel tracks at 54 km/h and 90 km/h. How many seconds longer do they take to cross each other completely when running in the same direction than when running in opposite directions?
questionBank.explanation:
Total distance to be covered = 180 + 220 = 400 m.
Opposite directions: relative speed = 54 + 90 = 144 km/h = 144 × 5/18 = 40 m/s; time = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 s.
Same direction: relative speed = 90 − 54 = 36 km/h = 10 m/s; time = 400 ÷ 10 = 40 s.
Difference = 40 − 10 = 30 s.
Trap: 40 is the same-direction time itself and 10 is the opposite-direction time.

D-III: anupalabdhi is non-perception, the Bhatta Mimamsa and Advaita source of knowing absence. Arthapatti and anupalabdhi are the pair most often swapped because both are accepted only by Mimamsa and Vedanta.

b: I. Knowledge of a thing through its similarity to something already known
II. Postulating a fact without which an observed fact cannot be explained
III. Knowledge of the absence of a thing from its non-perception
IV. Knowledge arising from contact of the senses with the object

questionBank.question: If the proposition “Some scholars are not idealists” is false, which of the following must be true? (Assume, as in the traditional square of opposition, that the classes are non-empty.)
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: The given O proposition is false, so its contradictory, the A proposition “All scholars are idealists” (A), is true. By subalternation the I proposition “Some scholars are idealists” (C) is then true, and an I proposition converts simply, so “Some idealists are scholars” (D) is true. B is the E proposition, the contrary of a true A, so it is false. E (“Some idealists are not scholars”) is undetermined: the idealist class may or may not extend beyond scholars. Hence A, C and D only.

stmts: A. All scholars are idealists.
B. No scholars are idealists.
C. Some scholars are idealists.
D. Some idealists are scholars.
E. Some idealists are not scholars.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question:
Statements:
All poets are dreamers.
No dreamer is a banker.
Some bankers are singers.
Conclusions:
I. No poet is a banker.
II. Some singers are not dreamers.
III. Some singers are poets.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
options: All of I, II and III follow
questionBank.explanation:
I: All poets are dreamers + No dreamer is a banker gives No poet is a banker (AEE, valid). I follows.
II: Some bankers are singers converts to Some singers are bankers; with No banker is a dreamer this gives Some singers are not dreamers (IEO, valid). II follows.
III: Poets lie inside dreamers, which do not overlap bankers; singers are only known to overlap bankers. Nothing links singers with poets, so III is not certain (a model where no singer is a poet satisfies every statement).
Hence only I and II follow.

questionBank.question:
Identify the mood and figure of the following categorical syllogism.
No rational being is cruel.
All philosophers are rational beings.
Therefore, no philosopher is cruel.
questionBank.explanation:
Terms: minor S = philosopher (subject of the conclusion), major P = cruel (predicate of the conclusion), middle M = rational being.
Major premise (contains P): No M is P, an E proposition. Minor premise (contains S): All S is M, an A proposition. Conclusion: No S is P, an E proposition. Mood = EAE.
The middle term is the subject of the major premise and the predicate of the minor premise, which is Figure 1. So the form is EAE-1 (Celarent), a valid form.
AEE-1 lists the premises in the order they are written without first identifying the major premise; EAE-2 would need M as predicate in both premises.

questionBank.question: A pen drive has a usable capacity of 64 GiB. How many complete video files of 700 MiB each can be stored on it?
questionBank.explanation:
1 GiB = 1024 MiB, so 64 GiB = 64 × 1024 = 65,536 MiB.
65,536 ÷ 700 = 93.6…, so 93 complete files fit.
Trap: 91 comes from taking 1 GiB = 1000 MiB (64,000 ÷ 700 = 91.4); 94 rounds up, which would leave the last file incomplete.

questionBank.question: What is the value of (2F)₁₆ + (57)₈, expressed in decimal?
questionBank.explanation:
(2F)₁₆ = 2 × 16 + 15 = 47.
(57)₈ = 5 × 8 + 7 = 47.
Sum = 47 + 47 = 94 (binary 1011110).
Trap: 104 reads 57 as a decimal number (47 + 57); 96 and 86 come from taking F as 16 or 57₈ as 39.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both statements are true. A password is “something you know”; 2FA adds a second factor of a different kind, such as a one-time code on the user’s phone (“something you have”) or a fingerprint (“something you are”). An attacker who has stolen only the password still lacks the second factor, and that is exactly why the risk falls. So (R) correctly explains (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): Enabling two-factor authentication greatly reduces the damage an attacker can do with a stolen password.
Reason (R): Two-factor authentication requires two independent factors from different categories, such as something the user knows and something the user has.

questionBank.question: Two identical machines each produce a sound level of 80 dB at a point. What is the approximate sound level at that point when both run together?
questionBank.explanation:
Decibels are logarithmic, so intensities (not decibel values) add.
L = 10 log₁₀(2 × 10⁸) = 10 × (8 + log₁₀ 2) = 80 + 10 × 0.301 ≈ 83 dB.
Doubling the intensity adds about 3 dB. Trap: 160 dB adds the decibel numbers; 86 dB would need four such machines.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: a norm-referenced score (a percentile or rank, for example) only has meaning relative to how a norm group performed. Statement II is false: choosing items so that scores spread widely (items of moderate difficulty and high discrimination) is the logic of NORM-referenced tests. A criterion-referenced test chooses items that match the stated learning objectives, and interprets each score against a fixed standard of mastery, for example "can solve 80% of linear equations". In a criterion-referenced test, it is quite acceptable for every learner to reach the criterion.

stmts: Statement I: A norm-referenced test interprets a learner’s score by comparing it with the performance of a defined reference group.
Statement II: In a criterion-referenced test, items are chosen mainly so as to spread candidates’ scores as widely as possible.

questionBank.question: Under the UGC’s CBCS guidelines, SGPA = Σ(Cᵢ × Gᵢ) ÷ ΣCᵢ, where Cᵢ is the credit and Gᵢ the grade point of course i. A student’s five courses in a semester carry 4, 4, 3, 3 and 2 credits, and she earns grade points 9, 7, 8, 6 and 10 in them, in that order. Her SGPA, rounded to two decimal places, is:
questionBank.explanation: Credit points: 4×9 = 36, 4×7 = 28, 3×8 = 24, 3×6 = 18, 2×10 = 20. Total = 126. Total credits = 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 16. SGPA = 126 ÷ 16 = 7.875, which is 7.88 to two decimals. Trap 1: 8.00 is the plain average of the five grade points (40 ÷ 5), which ignores credits. SGPA is a CREDIT-WEIGHTED average. Trap 2: 7.41 comes from dividing by 17, a miscount of the credits. Trap 3: 6.30 comes from dividing by 20, as if every course carried 4 credits. CGPA uses the same formula across semesters: it is Σ(credits of semester × SGPA) ÷ total credits.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true. Of the three levels (memory, understanding and reflective), the reflective level is the highest. It is problem-centred and learner-centred, and it develops critical and original thinking. It includes the understanding level, which in turn includes the memory level. (R) is false. A dominant teacher and passive learners who receive facts describe the MEMORY level (Herbart). At the reflective level (Hunt and Bigge), learners are active: they identify problems, frame hypotheses and test them, and the teacher mainly creates the problem situation. So the answer is: (A) is true but (R) is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): The reflective level of teaching is regarded as the highest level of teaching.
Reason (R): At the reflective level, the teacher dominates the class and learners are mainly passive receivers of facts.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Malcolm Knowles based andragogy on a set of assumptions about adult learners. Which of the following are among those assumptions?
questionBank.explanation: A is true: the "need to know" assumption. B is true: readiness to learn comes from what adults must do in their roles as workers, parents and so on. D is true: an adult’s experience is a resource, and it also shapes the adult’s self-identity. C is false: Knowles held that adults are life-centred, task-centred or problem-centred in their orientation. A SUBJECT-centred orientation is the pedagogical assumption about children. E is false: Knowles held that adults respond to some external motivators, but that the most potent motivators are internal ones such as self-esteem, job satisfaction and quality of life. So the correct set is A, B and D. Every distractor includes C or E.

stmts: A. Adults need to know why they should learn something before they commit to learning it.
B. Adults’ readiness to learn is closely tied to the tasks of their social and occupational roles.
C. Adults’ orientation to learning is mainly subject-centred rather than problem-centred.
D. Adults bring a larger and more varied pool of experience, which is itself a resource for learning.
E. Adults are motivated mainly by external rewards rather than internal ones.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Historical research relies on documents and relics. External criticism tests whether a source is genuine; internal criticism tests whether its content is accurate and credible (A-III). Experimental research is defined by manipulating the independent variable and controlling other variables (B-IV). Ethnography, from anthropology, means long-term fieldwork and participant observation inside the culture being studied (C-I). Ex post facto ("after the fact"), or causal-comparative, research starts from an effect that has already happened and looks back for probable causes, because the variables cannot be manipulated (D-II). Option 2 swaps experimental and ex post facto, the classic trap, since both are about cause and effect.

b: I. Prolonged immersion in a community through participant observation
II. Studies presumed causes after the effect has already occurred, with no manipulation of variables
III. Subjects its sources to external and internal criticism
IV. Deliberately manipulates an independent variable under controlled conditions

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false. Post-positivism (associated with Popper’s falsifiability and critical realism) does the opposite: it accepts that observation is theory-laden, that all knowledge claims are fallible, and that objectivity is an ideal to approach through criticism and replication, not something achieved with certainty. Statement II is false. Comte’s three stages are theological, then metaphysical, then positive (scientific). The positive stage, in which knowledge rests on observation and verification, is the final and highest one; the metaphysical stage is only transitional. So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: Post-positivism holds that a careful researcher can reach knowledge that is completely certain and free of the researcher’s theoretical assumptions.
Statement II: In Auguste Comte’s law of three stages, the metaphysical stage is the final and highest stage of human thought.

questionBank.question: A researcher wants a systematic sample of 60 teachers from a numbered list of 2,400 teachers in a district. The random start chosen within the first interval is 17. What is the serial number of the 5th teacher selected?
questionBank.explanation: Sampling interval k = N ÷ n = 2400 ÷ 60 = 40. The units selected are 17, 17 + 40, 17 + 2×40, …, so the r-th unit is 17 + (r − 1)×40. For r = 5 it is 17 + 4×40 = 17 + 160 = 177. The sequence runs 17, 57, 97, 137, 177. Trap 1: 217 = 17 + 5×40 uses r instead of r − 1, which gives the 6th unit. Trap 2: 160 forgets the random start. Trap 3: 200 = 5×40 makes both errors. Note that systematic sampling is a probability method only because the start is chosen at random.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of a research study in their usual logical sequence.
questionBank.explanation: A study begins by identifying and defining the problem (D). A literature review (B) then sharpens the problem and shows what is already known. Hypotheses (A) are framed in the light of that review, data are collected (E), and finally the data are analysed and interpreted (C) to test the hypotheses. Correct order: D, B, A, E, C. Option 1 starts with the review; a preliminary reading may come first in practice, but the formal sequence starts with the problem. Option 3 frames hypotheses before reviewing the literature, which gives uninformed hypotheses. Option 4 collects data before stating hypotheses, which reverses hypothesis-testing research.

stmts: A. Formulating hypotheses
B. Reviewing the related literature
C. Analysing and interpreting data
D. Identifying the research problem
E. Collecting data
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about referencing styles are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
A, B, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is true: APA is an author–date system. B is true: APA 7 (2020) dropped the older rule of listing up to five authors in the first citation; for three or more authors it uses "et al." from the first citation. C is false: APA calls the list "References", and it contains only works cited in the text. "Works Cited" is the MLA term, and "Bibliography" is used in Chicago notes–bibliography style. D is true: MLA puts author and page, with no comma and no year. E is true: Chicago has two systems, notes–bibliography (common in the humanities) and author–date (common in the sciences). So the answer is A, B, D and E.

stmts: A. APA style uses author–date in-text citations, for example (Rao, 2023).
B. In APA 7th edition, a work with three or more authors is cited in text by the first author’s surname followed by “et al.” from the very first citation.
C. In APA style, the list of sources at the end of a paper is titled “Bibliography”.
D. MLA style uses author–page in-text citations, for example (Rao 45).
E. The Chicago Manual of Style offers both a notes–bibliography system and an author–date system.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Knowledge in old manuscripts survives only as long as people keep reading, copying and using it, whatever the medium
Digitisation has permanently solved the problem of preserving palm-leaf manuscripts
Palm-leaf manuscripts are more durable than stone inscriptions in humid climates
The spread of printing deliberately destroyed the manuscript traditions of South Asia
questionBank.explanation: The passage builds towards its last paragraph: manuscripts outlived their material "because communities kept using them", and digital copies will last "only if someone keeps using them too". Option 1 states this central idea. Option 2 is the view the passage explicitly rejects ("It is tempting to conclude that the problem has been solved. Two difficulties suggest otherwise."). Option 3 contradicts the second paragraph, which says a palm leaf is NOT durable in the way stone is. Option 4 distorts the passage: printing led to a decline in copying and an "unnoticed" decay, not deliberate destruction.

stem.passage:
For nearly two thousand years, much of what South Asia knew about medicine, astronomy, law and poetry was written not on paper but on the dried leaves of the palmyra and talipot palms. A scribe incised the letters with an iron stylus and then rubbed the leaf with a paste of lamp-black and oil, so that the grooves turned dark while the surface stayed pale. Bundled between wooden boards and tied with cord, such a manuscript could be carried, copied and consulted for generations.

Yet a palm leaf is not a durable object in the way a stone inscription is. In a warm and humid climate it becomes brittle, insects bore through it, and the ink fades as the oil dries. A text survived, therefore, not because any single copy lasted but because families of scribes, temple libraries and physicians kept recopying it, usually every few generations. Preservation was an activity rather than a thing. When the practice of copying declined in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, as printing spread, the existing bundles began a slow and largely unnoticed decay in attics and prayer rooms.

Recent decades have brought a rush to digitise these collections. High-resolution imaging can recover letters invisible to the naked eye, and a scan, once made, can be shared with scholars on another continent. It is tempting to conclude that the problem has been solved. Two difficulties suggest otherwise. First, digital files are themselves fragile: storage formats become obsolete, servers are decommissioned when funding ends, and a folder of images without a catalogue is nearly as inaccessible as a locked cupboard. Second, an image is not a reading. Many of the scripts involved are known to only a handful of people, and the technical vocabulary of an Ayurvedic or astronomical text can defeat even a fluent reader of the script.

The lesson that emerges is an old one in a new form. The manuscripts outlived their material because communities kept using them; digital copies will outlive their servers only if someone keeps using them too. Funding agencies that pay for scanning but not for cataloguing, training in scripts and periodic migration of files are, in effect, paying for a single copy and hoping it will last. A sustainable programme would treat readers as part of the infrastructure, supporting young scholars who can transcribe, translate and annotate what has been imaged, so that the texts re-enter teaching and research rather than sitting in a well-organised silence.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Theodore Newcomb’s 1953 model is the A–B–X model: two communicators, A and B, and their orientations towards an object X; communication restores balance or symmetry (A-III). Frank Dance’s helical model (1967) shows communication as a spiral that keeps growing, with each stage drawing on earlier ones (B-I). Westley and MacLean (1957) adapted Newcomb’s model to mass communication by adding C, the channel role or gatekeeper who selects messages, together with feedback (C-IV). David Berlo’s SMCR model (1960) lists factors in the source and the receiver: communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture (D-II). Options 1 and 3 swap one pair each, and option 2 swaps Newcomb and Dance.

b: I. Communication as an ever-widening helix that builds on what went before
II. Source–Message–Channel–Receiver, each shaped by skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture
III. An A–B–X model of the co-orientation of two persons towards an object
IV. Adds a gatekeeping role (C) between events and the audience in mass communication

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true. It is the core idea of agenda-setting, based on Bernard Cohen’s 1963 remark: by choosing what to cover and how prominently, the media shape which issues the public treats as important (salience), even if they do not decide people’s opinions. (R) is true. McCombs and Shaw compared the issues undecided Chapel Hill voters rated as important with the issues the media emphasised in the 1968 campaign, and published the study in 1972. But (R) gives the historical origin of the theory. It does not explain WHY the media influence salience; that comes from selection, repetition and prominence of coverage. So both are true, but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A).

stmts: Assertion (A): The agenda-setting function of the mass media means that the media may not succeed in telling people what to think, but they are very successful in telling people what to think about.
Reason (R): Maxwell McCombs and Donald Shaw developed the agenda-setting hypothesis from a study of voters in Chapel Hill during the 1968 US presidential election.

questionBank.question: According to Edward T. Hall, in a high-context culture the meaning of a message is carried mainly by:
options: the shared situation, relationships and non-verbal cues that surround the words
the explicit words of the message, stated as precisely as possible
written documents rather than face-to-face conversation
the formal grammar of the language used
questionBank.explanation: Hall (Beyond Culture, 1976) distinguished high-context from low-context cultures. In a high-context culture (for example Japan, China and much of India and the Arab world), much of the meaning lies in the context: the relationship between speakers, their status, shared history, tone and silence. Relatively little is spelt out. In a low-context culture (for example Germany, Switzerland and the USA), meaning is carried mainly by explicit words, so option 2 describes low context. Options 3 and 4 are not part of Hall’s distinction. In intercultural classrooms and meetings, a mismatch of context levels is a common cultural barrier to communication.

questionBank.question: Find the next term in the series: 4, 9, 25, 64, 169, ?
questionBank.explanation: Every term is a perfect square: 2², 3², 5², 8², 13². The bases 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 are consecutive Fibonacci numbers, each the sum of the previous two. The next base is 8 + 13 = 21, so the next term is 21² = 441. The distractors 361 (19²), 400 (20²) and 484 (22²) come from guessing the next base instead of finding the rule. The differences of the bases (1, 2, 3, 5) are themselves Fibonacci numbers, which confirms the rule.

questionBank.question: From the college gate, Anil walks 10 km north, turns right and walks 6 km, turns right again and walks 18 km, then turns left and walks 9 km. How far is he from the gate, and in which direction?
questionBank.explanation: Put the gate at (0, 0), with north as +y and east as +x. 10 km north takes him to (0, 10). Turning right from north means facing east: 6 km takes him to (6, 10). Turning right from east means facing south: 18 km takes him to (6, −8). Turning left from south means facing east: 9 km takes him to (15, −8). The distance is √(15² + 8²) = √(225 + 64) = √289 = 17 km. He is 15 km east and 8 km south, so he is south-east of the gate. Trap 1: 23 km adds the east and south displacements (15 + 8) instead of using Pythagoras. Trap 2: 15 km gives only the east displacement. Trap 3: north-east comes from forgetting that 18 km south takes him past the starting latitude.

questionBank.question: A trader claims to sell rice at 8% below cost price, but he uses a false weight of 800 g in place of 1 kg. What is his actual gain or loss per cent?
questionBank.explanation: Let the cost price be ₹100 per kg. He charges 92% of it, which is ₹92, for what he calls 1 kg, but he gives only 800 g. The cost of 800 g is ₹80. Gain = 92 − 80 = ₹12 on a cost of ₹80, which is 12 ÷ 80 × 100 = 15%. In formula form: (1 − 0.08) ÷ 0.8 = 1.15. Trap 1: "8% loss" ignores the false weight. Trap 2: 10% is 12 ÷ 120, the gain on the wrong base. Trap 3: "8% gain" simply flips the sign of the stated discount. Gain per cent is always taken on the cost of the goods actually given.

questionBank.question: A research assistant can transcribe a set of interviews alone in 12 days, and a second assistant can do it alone in 18 days. They start together, but the second assistant leaves 3 days before the work is finished. In how many days is the whole work completed?
questionBank.explanation: Let the work take T days. The first assistant works all T days, and the second works T − 3 days. T/12 + (T − 3)/18 = 1. Multiplying by 36 gives 3T + 2(T − 3) = 36, so 5T − 6 = 36, 5T = 42 and T = 8.4 days. Check: 8.4/12 = 0.7 and 5.4/18 = 0.3, and 0.7 + 0.3 = 1. Trap 1: 7.2 days is the time if both work throughout: 1 ÷ (1/12 + 1/18) = 36/5. Trap 2: 10.2 days adds 3 days to 7.2. Trap 3: 9 days fails the check, since 9/12 + 6/18 ≈ 1.08, which is more than the whole work.

questionBank.question: A sum of money invested at compound interest (compounded annually) amounts to ₹5,618 after 2 years and ₹5,955.08 after 3 years. The sum invested was:
questionBank.explanation: The amount in year 3 ÷ the amount in year 2 = 1 + r. So 1 + r = 5955.08 ÷ 5618 = 1.06, and r = 6% per annum. The principal = 5618 ÷ 1.06² = 5618 ÷ 1.1236 = ₹5,000. Check: 5000 × 1.06³ = 5955.08. Trap 1: ₹5,300 = 5618 ÷ 1.06 goes back only one year, which gives the amount after 1 year. ₹5,100 and ₹4,800 fail the check: 5100 × 1.06² = 5730.36 and 4800 × 1.06² = 5393.28, not 5618. The interest in year 3 (₹337.08) is 6% of ₹5,618, not of the principal.

questionBank.question: Using the traditional square of opposition, suppose the proposition “Some teachers are researchers” is FALSE. Which of the following can then be validly concluded?
questionBank.explanation: The given proposition is an I proposition, and it is false. B: E ("No teachers are researchers") is the contradictory of I, so it is TRUE. A: A ("All teachers are researchers") is the superaltern of I; if the subaltern is false, the superaltern must be false. (Equivalently, A and E are contraries and E is true.) C: O ("Some teachers are not researchers") is the subaltern of E, which is true, so on the traditional square with existential import O is TRUE. (O is also the subcontrary of I, and subcontraries cannot both be false.) D: the I proposition converts simply, so "Some researchers are teachers" is logically equivalent to the given one and is also FALSE. All four conclusions follow. Option 3 is the usual trap: forgetting that conversion also applies to I.

stmts: A. “All teachers are researchers” is false.
B. “No teachers are researchers” is true.
C. “Some teachers are not researchers” is true.
D. “Some researchers are teachers” is false.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Ad verecundiam is an appeal to an inappropriate authority: a film actor is no authority on pedagogy (A-III). Post hoc ergo propter hoc ("after this, therefore because of this") treats a sequence in time as cause and effect (B-II). Tu quoque ("you too") dismisses a criticism by pointing to the critic’s own faults, a kind of ad hominem; the critic’s errors do not make the data sound (C-I). Petitio principii, or begging the question, assumes what it sets out to prove; here the argument is circular (D-IV). Option 2 swaps tu quoque and petitio principii. Option 4 swaps post hoc and tu quoque.

a: B. Post hoc ergo propter hoc
b: I. “Your criticism of my data is worthless; you made errors in your own thesis too.”
II. “Enrolment rose after we repainted the corridors, so the new paint attracted students.”
III. “This teaching method must work, because a famous film actor recommends it.”
IV. “The report is reliable because it is trustworthy, and it is trustworthy because it is reliable.”

questionBank.question:
Statements:
1. All mentors are scholars.
2. No scholar is careless.
3. Some careless persons are teachers.

Conclusions:
I. No mentor is careless.
II. Some teachers are not scholars.
III. Some teachers are not mentors.

Which conclusion(s) logically follow from the statements?
options: All of I, II and III follow
questionBank.explanation: I: All mentors are scholars, and no scholar is careless, so no mentor is careless (the valid form Celarent: All M are S, No S is C, therefore No M is C). I follows. II: Some careless persons are teachers, so there is at least one teacher who is careless. That teacher cannot be a scholar, because no scholar is careless. So some teachers are not scholars. II follows. III: the same careless teacher cannot be a mentor either, because every mentor is a scholar and no scholar is careless. So some teachers are not mentors. III follows. In a Venn diagram, the careless-and-teacher region lies wholly outside the scholar circle, and the mentor circle lies inside the scholar circle. All three conclusions follow. The trap is to assume that "Some … are not" can never be drawn from a negative premise; here the particular premise supplies the existence.

questionBank.question: In a survey of 150 research scholars, 80 use SPSS, 65 use R and 50 use Python. 30 use both SPSS and R, 25 use both R and Python, 20 use both SPSS and Python, and 10 use all three. How many scholars use exactly one of the three tools?
questionBank.explanation: SPSS only = 80 − 30 − 20 + 10 = 40. R only = 65 − 30 − 25 + 10 = 20. Python only = 50 − 25 − 20 + 10 = 15. Exactly one = 40 + 20 + 15 = 75. Check with the whole diagram: exactly two = (30 − 10) + (25 − 10) + (20 − 10) = 45; all three = 10; at least one = 75 + 45 + 10 = 130 (the same as 80 + 65 + 50 − 30 − 25 − 20 + 10); none = 150 − 130 = 20. The distractors are the other regions: 45 is exactly two, 20 is none, and 130 is at least one. Draw the three circles and fill the centre first.

questionBank.question: In Nyāya philosophy, the five-membered inference (pañcāvayava anumāna) for others (parārthānumāna) has the members listed below. Arrange them in their proper order.
questionBank.explanation: The classic example runs as follows. Pratijñā: "The hill has fire." Hetu: "Because it has smoke." Udāharaṇa: "Wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen." Upanaya: "This hill has smoke, which is invariably accompanied by fire." Nigamana: "Therefore the hill has fire." So the order is B, D, E, A, C. The udāharaṇa states the vyāpti (invariable concomitance) with an example, and the upanaya applies it to the case at hand. That is why the example must come before the application. Option 2 swaps hetu and example, and option 4 swaps example and application.

stmts: A. Upanaya (application)
B. Pratijñā (proposition)
C. Nigamana (conclusion)
D. Hetu (reason)
E. Udāharaṇa (example)

questionBank.question: By what percentage did the total research grant of the five departments increase from 2021 to 2025?
questionBank.explanation: Totals: 2021 = 120 + 90 + 60 + 45 + 30 = 345, and 2025 = 180 + 135 + 84 + 72 + 39 = 510. Increase = 165. Percentage increase = 165 ÷ 345 × 100 = 47.83%, which is 47.8%. Trap 1: 32.4% divides by the 2025 total (165 ÷ 510). The base of a percentage change is always the earlier value. Trap 2: 46.0% is the simple average of the five departmental growth rates (50, 50, 40, 60 and 30), which ignores their different sizes. Trap 3: 50.0% is the growth of Physics alone.

questionBank.question: The binary number (1101101.101)₂ is equal to which decimal number?
questionBank.explanation: Integer part: 1101101 = 64 + 32 + 8 + 4 + 1 = 109. Fractional part: .101 = 1×2⁻¹ + 0×2⁻² + 1×2⁻³ = 0.5 + 0.125 = 0.625. So the number is 109.625. Trap 1: 109.525 reads the fraction as if it were decimal. Trap 2: 109.375 reverses the fractional bits (.011 = 0.25 + 0.125). Trap 3: 108.625 drops the units bit. Fractional places carry weights 1/2, 1/4, 1/8 and so on, from left to right after the binary point.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about e-mail are correct?
options: A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: A is true: Cc (carbon copy) recipients are visible to everyone. B is false: Bcc (blind carbon copy) recipients are hidden from all other recipients. That is the whole purpose of Bcc, for example when writing to many students without revealing their addresses. C is true: POP3 is a download-and-delete protocol by default (port 110). D is true: IMAP (port 143) leaves mail on the server and keeps several devices in sync. E is false: SMTP SENDS mail; POP3 and IMAP retrieve it. So the answer is A, C and D.

stmts: A. Addresses in the Cc field are visible to all recipients of the message.
B. Addresses in the Bcc field are visible to the recipients in the To field.
C. By default, POP3 downloads messages to one device and usually removes them from the server.
D. IMAP keeps messages on the server and synchronises folders across several devices.
E. SMTP is the protocol a mail client uses to retrieve messages from its mailbox.

questionBank.question: Two identical machines in a workshop each produce a sound level of 70 dB at a point when running alone. Approximately what sound level is produced at that point when both run together?
questionBank.explanation: Decibels are logarithmic: L = 10 log₁₀(I/I₀). Two equal, uncorrelated sources double the intensity, so the combined level is L = 70 + 10 log₁₀2 = 70 + 3.01, which is about 73 dB. Trap 1: 140 dB adds the decibel values arithmetically, which is never valid. Trap 2: 70 dB assumes nothing changes. Trap 3: 76 dB is the level from FOUR such machines (70 + 10 log₁₀4 = 76.0). Rule of thumb: every doubling of equal sources adds about 3 dB, and a 10-fold increase in intensity adds 10 dB.

questionBank.question: The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015–2030 is built around:
options: 4 priorities for action and 7 global targets
3 priorities for action and 5 global targets
5 priorities for action and 7 global targets
4 priorities for action and 17 global targets
questionBank.explanation: The Sendai Framework was adopted at the Third UN World Conference on Disaster Risk Reduction in Sendai, Japan, in March 2015. It has 4 priorities for action: (1) understanding disaster risk; (2) strengthening disaster risk governance; (3) investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience; (4) enhancing preparedness for effective response and to "Build Back Better". It also has 7 global targets, such as reducing disaster mortality and increasing early-warning coverage. Trap 1: 5 priorities belonged to its predecessor, the Hyogo Framework for Action 2005–2015. Trap 2: 17 is the number of SDGs.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following reports and policies on education in India in chronological order.
questionBank.explanation: C: the University Education Commission, chaired by S. Radhakrishnan, was appointed in 1948 and reported in 1949; it was the first commission of independent India. E: the Yash Pal Committee reported in 2009 and recommended a single overarching higher-education regulator. D: NEP 2020 was approved on 29 July 2020. So the order is C, B, A, E, D. questionBank.question: The National Skills Qualifications Framework (NSQF), notified by the Government of India in December 2013, organises qualifications into how many levels?
questionBank.explanation: The NSQF, notified on 27 December 2013, arranges qualifications into 10 levels. Each level is defined by learning outcomes: process, professional knowledge, professional skill, core skill and responsibility. Level 1 is the entry level, and level 10 is the highest. The framework allows vertical and horizontal mobility between vocational and general education, and recognition of prior learning. It is now implemented through the National Council for Vocational Education and Training (NCVET), and NEP 2020 asks for vocational education to be aligned with it. Trap: 8 is the number of levels in the European Qualifications Framework, not the NSQF.

questionBank.question: Arrange the Herbartian formal steps of a lesson in the order in which a teacher uses them.
questionBank.explanation: The five formal steps developed by Herbart’s followers run: Preparation (B: link to what learners already know and state the aim) → Presentation (D: the new material) → Association or comparison (E: relate the new ideas to old ones and to each other) → Generalisation (A: draw out the rule or principle) → Application (C: use the rule on new examples, which also checks learning). So B, D, E, A, C. The distractors swap Presentation with Association (you cannot compare material before it is presented), put Presentation before Preparation, or apply the rule before it has been generalised.

stmts: A. Generalisation
B. Preparation
C. Application
D. Presentation
E. Association (comparison)

The distractors swap Gardner and Vygotsky, Knowles and Kolb (both write about adults and experience), or Vygotsky and Kolb.

IV. Multiple intelligences

questionBank.question: The term “action research”, for research done by practitioners to improve their own practice through cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting, is most closely associated with:
questionBank.explanation: Kurt Lewin used the term action research in the 1940s and described its spiral of planning, action and fact-finding about the result of the action; Stephen Corey later popularised it in education. Popper is associated with falsifiability, Comte with positivism, and Guba (with Lincoln) with naturalistic and constructivist inquiry, not with action research.

questionBank.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Local solar time was scientifically inaccurate, so scientists replaced it with standard time.
Common time standards spread because networks such as the railways made disagreement costly, and law followed later.
The British Parliament created railway time in 1880 and the railways then adopted it.
India adopted a standard time earlier and more smoothly than Britain and North America.
questionBank.explanation: The passage traces how the railways (and later other networks) forced towns onto a single time, and ends with the general lesson that standards follow the cost of disagreement, with law confirming them later. The passage never says local time was inaccurate; it was correct for each town. The 1880 Act came long after railways had adopted London time, so the order in that option is reversed. India’s path is called “similar but slower”, not earlier or smoother.

stem.passage:
Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every town set its clocks by its own sky. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local church or temple, and because the Earth turns through one degree of longitude every four minutes, a town lying a little to the east kept a time slightly ahead of its western neighbour. Nobody minded. A journey between the two took most of a day on horseback, and a difference of a few minutes vanished in the dust of the road.

The railway ended this comfortable disorder. A train that left one town at a published hour and arrived at another had to be timetabled in a single time, or passengers would miss connections and, far worse, two trains could be sent onto the same single track. British companies began to run their services on London time in the 1840s, and station clocks soon showed it even where the town hall clock disagreed. For some years a few towns displayed two minute hands, one for the local sun and one for the railway. Parliament made Greenwich time the legal time of Great Britain only in 1880, long after the railways had made it the practical one.

North America faced a larger version of the same problem, with dozens of local times along a single line. On a November day in 1883 its railway companies, acting on their own authority, divided the continent into broad zones an hour apart. A year later an international conference in Washington chose the meridian through Greenwich as the zero of longitude, giving the world a common reference from which such zones could be counted.

India followed a similar but slower path. The railways ran on Madras time, while Bombay and Calcutta kept their own. Indian Standard Time, based on the meridian of 82.5° east, was introduced in 1906, yet Calcutta retained its local time until after independence, and Bombay held on to its own for some years more. Clocks, it turned out, were not only instruments but symbols of civic identity, and people gave them up reluctantly.

The lesson reaches beyond clocks. Standards are rarely adopted because they are elegant; they are adopted when some network, whether of rails, telegraph wires or today’s digital systems, makes the cost of disagreement too high to bear. Law usually arrives later, to confirm what the network has already decided.

questionBank.question: Following the reasoning in the first paragraph, what would be the difference in local time between two towns whose longitudes differ by 7.5°?
questionBank.explanation: The passage says the Earth turns through one degree of longitude every four minutes. So 7.5° × 4 minutes = 30 minutes. (Check: 360° × 4 minutes = 1,440 minutes = 24 hours.) 7.5 minutes forgets to multiply by 4; 15 minutes uses 2 minutes per degree; 45 minutes uses 6.

stem.passage:
Until the middle of the nineteenth century, every town set its clocks by its own sky. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local church or temple, and because the Earth turns through one degree of longitude every four minutes, a town lying a little to the east kept a time slightly ahead of its western neighbour. Nobody minded. A journey between the two took most of a day on horseback, and a difference of a few minutes vanished in the dust of the road.

The railway ended this comfortable disorder. A train that left one town at a published hour and arrived at another had to be timetabled in a single time, or passengers would miss connections and, far worse, two trains could be sent onto the same single track. British companies began to run their services on London time in the 1840s, and station clocks soon showed it even where the town hall clock disagreed. For some years a few towns displayed two minute hands, one for the local sun and one for the railway. Parliament made Greenwich time the legal time of Great Britain only in 1880, long after the railways had made it the practical one.

North America faced a larger version of the same problem, with dozens of local times along a single line. On a November day in 1883 its railway companies, acting on their own authority, divided the continent into broad zones an hour apart. A year later an international conference in Washington chose the meridian through Greenwich as the zero of longitude, giving the world a common reference from which such zones could be counted.

India followed a similar but slower path. The railways ran on Madras time, while Bombay and Calcutta kept their own. Indian Standard Time, based on the meridian of 82.5° east, was introduced in 1906, yet Calcutta retained its local time until after independence, and Bombay held on to its own for some years more. Clocks, it turned out, were not only instruments but symbols of civic identity, and people gave them up reluctantly.

The lesson reaches beyond clocks. Standards are rarely adopted because they are elegant; they are adopted when some network, whether of rails, telegraph wires or today’s digital systems, makes the cost of disagreement too high to bear. Law usually arrives later, to confirm what the network has already decided.

questionBank.question: The author’s attitude towards cities that kept their own local time after a standard time had been introduced is best described as:
options: contemptuous, because the author sees the cities as backward
celebratory, because the author wants local times restored
indifferent, because the author does not comment on it
understanding, because the author sees clocks as symbols of civic identity
questionBank.explanation: The author explains the reluctance: clocks “were not only instruments but symbols of civic identity, and people gave them up reluctantly”. That is sympathetic understanding. There is no scorn (so not contemptuous), no call to restore local times (so not celebratory), and the author does comment on it (so not indifferent).

Hall’s distinction says that in high-context cultures (for example Japan or much of India) meaning depends heavily on shared context, status and non-verbal cues, while low-context cultures (for example Germany or the USA) spell meaning out in words. (R) is true: proxemics, a term also from Hall, is the study of the use of personal space. questionBank.question:
What comes next in the series?
2, 6, 15, 31, 56, ?
questionBank.explanation: Differences: 6 − 2 = 4, 15 − 6 = 9, 31 − 15 = 16, 56 − 31 = 25. These are 2², 3², 4², 5², so the next difference is 6² = 36 and the next term is 56 + 36 = 92. 81 adds 5² again (repeating the last difference); 91 and 93 are one-off arithmetic slips (adding 35 or 37).

questionBank.question: In a certain code, NET is written as VGP. Using the same rule, how is CLOUD written?
questionBank.explanation: Find the rule from NET → VGP. Reverse NET to get TEN, then move each letter 2 places forward: T+2 = V, E+2 = G, N+2 = P, giving VGP. Apply it to CLOUD: reversed it is DUOLC; +2 gives D→F, U→W, O→Q, L→N, C→E, so FWQNE. ENQWF shifts by 2 but forgets to reverse; EVPMD reverses but shifts by 1; FWQNF slips on the last letter (C+2 is E, not F).

questionBank.question: Pointing to a boy, Anjali says, “He is the son of the only child of my mother.” How is the boy related to Anjali?
questionBank.explanation: The only child of Anjali’s mother is Anjali herself (she is her mother’s child, and the mother has only one). So the boy is the son of Anjali, that is, her son. “Nephew” would need Anjali to have a sibling, which “only child” rules out; “brother” would be the son of her mother, not of her mother’s child.

questionBank.question: A train 240 m long, running at 72 km/h, crosses a platform completely in 30 seconds. What is the length of the platform?
questionBank.explanation: Speed = 72 km/h = 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s. In 30 s the train covers 20 × 30 = 600 m. To cross the platform completely it must cover its own length plus the platform: 240 + platform = 600, so the platform is 360 m. 600 m forgets to subtract the train’s length; 840 m adds the train’s length instead of subtracting it; 120 m converts 72 km/h wrongly to 12 m/s (12 × 30 − 240).
questionBank.topic: Time and distance: train and platform

questionBank.question: The average of 11 observations is 60. The average of the first 6 is 58 and the average of the last 6 is 63. What is the sixth observation?
questionBank.explanation: The 6th observation is counted in both groups. Sum of first 6 = 6 × 58 = 348; sum of last 6 = 6 × 63 = 378; sum of all 11 = 11 × 60 = 660. So 6th = 348 + 378 − 660 = 66. 60, 63 and 58 are simply the three given averages, which is what one guesses without working with sums.

questionBank.question:
Statements:
All servers are computers.
Some computers are routers.
No router is a printer.
Conclusions:
I. Some servers are routers.
II. Some computers are not printers.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questionBank.explanation: II follows: some computers are routers, and no router is a printer, so those computers (the ones that are routers) are not printers. I does not follow: the computers that are routers need not be servers; servers are only known to lie inside computers, and a Venn diagram can keep the server circle completely apart from the router circle. So only II follows. The trap is to link servers to routers through the middle term “computers”, which is undistributed in “Some computers are routers”.

questionBank.question: Which Sustainable Development Goal is “Life below water”, on conserving and sustainably using the oceans, seas and marine resources?
questionBank.explanation: SDG 14 is Life below water. SDG 6 is Clean water and sanitation, SDG 13 is Climate action, and SDG 15 is Life on land (forests, desertification, biodiversity). The traps are SDG 6, because of the word “water”, and SDG 15, the land counterpart of SDG 14.

questionBank.question: The National Medical Commission (NMC), constituted in 2020 under the National Medical Commission Act, 2019, replaced which body as the regulator of medical education in India?
questionBank.explanation: The NMC Act, 2019 dissolved the Medical Council of India (set up under the Indian Medical Council Act, 1956), and the NMC was constituted in September 2020 as the regulator of medical education and practice. The National Board of Examinations conducts exams such as NEET-PG, ICMR is the apex body for biomedical research, and the Dental Council of India still regulates dental education separately. None of them was replaced.

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about value, environmental and vocational education in India are correct?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: A is correct: in the 1991 Environmental Education case the Supreme Court directed that environment be taught as a compulsory subject. B is correct: the Court asked the UGC to take steps requiring universities to prescribe a course on the environment; UGC later introduced a compulsory Environmental Studies course for undergraduates. C is correct: NEP 2020 says that by 2025 at least 50% of learners through the school and higher education system shall have exposure to vocational education. D is false: Nai Talim was Mahatma Gandhi’s scheme, presented at the Wardha conference of 1937. E is false: value education develops ethical, social and democratic values and is broader than any religious doctrine. So A, B and C only.

stmts: A. In M. C. Mehta v. Union of India (1991), the Supreme Court directed that environmental education be made compulsory in schools and colleges.
B. The same judgment asked the UGC to take steps requiring universities to prescribe a course on the environment.
C. NEP 2020 aims that by 2025 at least 50% of learners in school and higher education should have exposure to vocational education.
D. The idea of Nai Talim (basic education) was put forward by Rabindranath Tagore.
E. Value education is concerned only with teaching the doctrines of particular religions.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: NAAC was set up by the UGC in 1994 as an autonomous institution, registered as a society, with its headquarters in Bengaluru. It was not created by an Act of Parliament. Statement II is false: NIRF was launched by the then MHRD (now the Ministry of Education) on 29 September 2015, and the first rankings came out in 2016. So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: The National Assessment and Accreditation Council (NAAC) is a statutory body created by an Act of Parliament.
Statement II: The National Institutional Ranking Framework (NIRF) was launched in 2018.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true: the 42nd Amendment, 1976 moved education (as Entry 25) to the Concurrent List, so both the Union and the States can legislate on it. (R) is true: Article 21A was inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002 and is implemented through the RTE Act, 2009. But (R) does not explain (A): they are separate amendments made 26 years apart for different purposes. So both are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): The Forty-second Amendment (1976) moved education from the State List to the Concurrent List.
Reason (R): Article 21A, inserted by the Eighty-sixth Amendment (2002), makes free and compulsory education a fundamental right of children aged 6 to 14 years.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: NEP 2020 sets which target for the gross enrolment ratio (GER) in higher education, including vocational education?
questionBank.explanation: NEP 2020 aims to raise the GER in higher education, including vocational education, from 26.3% (2018) to 50% by 2035. The 100% GER target is for school education (preschool to secondary) by 2030, which gives the “100%” and “2030” traps; 35% is roughly where the GER stood at the time, not a target.

questionBank.question: A teacher prepares three versions of the same assignment, each with a different reading level and amount of support, so that every learner in a mixed-ability class can reach the same objective. This practice is called:
questionBank.explanation: Differentiated instruction keeps one common objective but varies content, process or product to suit learners’ readiness, interests and learning profiles, which is exactly what the teacher does. Streaming (option 2) separates learners into different classes by ability. Programmed instruction (option 3) is Skinner’s self-paced sequence of small frames with immediate feedback. Remedial teaching (option 4) is corrective help after a diagnosed weakness, given only to those who need it.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-III: the project method (purposeful activity in a social setting) was developed by W. H. Kilpatrick, following Dewey. B-I: the heuristic method (the learner finds things out as a discoverer) is H. E. Armstrong’s. C-IV: programmed instruction grew out of B. F. Skinner’s operant conditioning. D-II: the Dalton plan (individual assignments or ‘contracts’, laboratories instead of classrooms) was devised by Helen Parkhurst. Option 1 swaps Skinner and Parkhurst, option 2 swaps Kilpatrick and Armstrong, option 4 swaps Armstrong and Skinner.

b: I. H. E. Armstrong
II. Helen Parkhurst
III. W. H. Kilpatrick
IV. B. F. Skinner

questionBank.question: In a flipped classroom, learners typically:
options: watch recorded lectures in class and do exercises at home
study the lecture material before class and use class time for discussion and problem-solving
learn only through MOOCs with no face-to-face contact
are taught entirely by their peers instead of the teacher
questionBank.explanation: ‘Flipping’ reverses the traditional order: the input (videos, readings) is studied at home before class, and the contact hour is used for active work such as discussion, problem-solving and projects, with the teacher as facilitator. Option 1 describes the traditional arrangement, not the flipped one. Option 3 is fully online learning, and a flipped class still has face-to-face sessions. Option 4 describes peer teaching, which may be used in class but is not the defining feature.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: Knowles’s andragogy assumes that adults are self-directed, bring a reservoir of experience, are ready to learn what their life roles need and are problem-centred. Statement II is false: the concrete operational stage (about 7 to 11 years) is limited to logical thinking about concrete objects; abstract and hypothetical reasoning belongs to the formal operational stage, which begins around 11 to 12 years, in adolescence. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: Adult learners, as described by Malcolm Knowles in andragogy, tend to be self-directed and use their own experience as a resource for learning.
Statement II: In Piaget’s theory, the concrete operational stage marks adolescence, when learners first reason about abstract and hypothetical ideas.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: A test that reports whether each student has reached a fixed standard of mastery, whatever the scores of the other students, is a:
questionBank.explanation: A criterion-referenced test compares each performance with a pre-set criterion (for example ‘can solve 8 of 10 linear equations’), so everyone can pass or everyone can fail. A norm-referenced test (option 1) ranks a student against the group, as in percentiles. A diagnostic test (option 2) identifies specific learning difficulties. An aptitude test (option 3) predicts future ability to learn. The trap is option 1: ‘whatever the scores of the other students’ rules out any comparison with the group.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: in a double-blind study neither the participants nor the people collecting the data know who is in the treatment group, so expectations cannot colour the results. R is also true: deliberate manipulation of the independent variable is what makes a study experimental. But R does not explain A; manipulation is present in single-blind and open experiments too, and the bias control comes from the blinding, not from the manipulation. So both are true but R is not the correct explanation.

stmts: Assertion (A): A double-blind design reduces experimenter bias in experimental research.
Reason (R): In experimental research, the investigator deliberately manipulates the independent variable.
stem.after: In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-II: Popper argued that a theory is scientific only if it can in principle be proved false, a key post-positivist idea. B-IV: Kuhn (The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, 1962) described normal science within a paradigm and paradigm shifts. C-I: Glaser and Strauss (1967) proposed grounded theory, where theory is built up from qualitative data. Option 1 swaps Popper and Kuhn, option 2 swaps Comte and Glaser–Strauss, option 3 swaps Kuhn and Glaser–Strauss.

a: A. Falsifiability as the test of a scientific theory
D. Law of three stages and positivism
b: I. Barney Glaser and Anselm Strauss
II. Karl Popper
III. Auguste Comte
IV. Thomas Kuhn

questionBank.question: In APA style (7th edition), a journal article by four authors, Rao, Menon, Iyer and Das (2023), is cited in the text, from the very first citation, as:
options: (Rao, Menon, Iyer, & Das, 2023) the first time, and (Rao et al., 2023) afterwards
questionBank.explanation: APA 7 uses ‘first author et al.’ for every work with three or more authors, from the first citation onwards: (Rao et al., 2023). Option 1 is the older APA 6 rule, which listed three to five authors in full the first time; that change is the usual trap. ‘and others’ is not APA wording, and ‘et al.’ always comes straight after the first author’s surname, never after the year. In the reference list, APA 7 gives up to 20 authors in full.

questionBank.question: Under the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018, a PhD thesis whose similarity (excluding permitted exclusions) is found to be 45% falls in:
questionBank.explanation: For theses and dissertations the 2018 regulations define: Level 0, up to 10% (minor, no penalty); Level 1, above 10% to 40% (submit a revised script within a stipulated period of up to six months); Level 2, above 40% to 60% (debarred from submitting a revised script for one year); Level 3, above 60% (registration for the programme is cancelled). 45% lies in the band above 40% up to 60%, so it is Level 2.

questionBank.question: From a list of 2,000 students, a researcher picks a random number between 1 and 20 (say 7) and then selects the 7th, 27th, 47th and so on. The sampling method and the sample size are:
questionBank.explanation: Selecting every k-th unit after a random start is systematic sampling. The interval is k = 20, so the sample size is 2,000 ÷ 20 = 100 (7, 27, …, 1,987). It is not simple random sampling, because after the first pick every other selection is fixed. Stratified sampling divides the population into strata first, and cluster sampling selects whole groups. Options with 20 confuse the interval with the sample size.

questionBank.question: Which one of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Malcom McLean was the most important inventor of the twentieth century
The container transformed trade mainly because of the standardised system built around it
Break-bulk shipping ended because dockworkers demanded higher wages
Globalisation was caused mainly by falling fuel costs for ocean shipping
questionBank.explanation: Paragraph 3 states the thesis directly: ‘The value of the container lay less in the object than in the system that grew up around it’, and the last paragraph generalises it to innovation. Option 1 contradicts the passage, which says the box was not a clever invention and warns against celebrating individuals. Wages (option 3) and fuel costs (option 4) are never mentioned.

stem.passage:
In April 1956 a converted wartime tanker, the Ideal X, sailed from Newark to Houston with fifty-eight metal boxes lashed to its deck. The boxes were truck trailers with the wheels taken off, and the man behind the voyage, a trucking entrepreneur named Malcom McLean, wanted nothing grander than a cheaper way to move freight along the coast. Few observers thought the experiment mattered.

Before the container, cargo moved as ‘break-bulk’: sacks, barrels, crates and bales were carried aboard one at a time by gangs of dockworkers and fitted into the hold like pieces of a puzzle. A ship could spend as long tied up in port as it spent at sea, and theft and damage were routine. Loading costs, not ocean distance, made up much of the price of shipping, so it often made little sense to manufacture goods far from the people who would buy them.

The box itself was not a clever invention; wooden and steel boxes had been used on railways and ships for decades. What changed the world was agreement. Once shipping lines, port authorities and governments accepted a small set of standard sizes and corner fittings, the same box could be lifted by any crane, stacked on any ship and carried away by any truck or train without anyone opening it. The value of the container lay less in the object than in the system that grew up around it.

That system had costs as well as benefits. Ports moved out of old city centres to places with room for vast stacking yards, and tens of thousands of dockworkers found their skills no longer needed. Waterfront neighbourhoods that had lived off the docks declined. At the same time, because moving a box across an ocean became cheap and predictable, firms could split production across continents, making a component in one country, assembling it in another and selling it in a third. Much of what is now called globalisation rests on this dull steel rectangle.

The history holds a lesson for anyone who studies innovation. We tend to celebrate striking inventions and the individuals linked to them, yet the changes that matter most are often unglamorous and collective: a standard that everyone agrees to follow, a practice that removes friction from thousands of small transactions. Such changes are easy to overlook precisely because, once they succeed, they become invisible.

questionBank.question: According to the passage, why did it often make little sense to produce goods far from their buyers before containers?
options: Handling cargo in port was slow and costly, so loading rather than distance drove shipping prices
Ocean voyages were too long for the ships of that period
Governments banned imports of manufactured goods
Trucks could not reach the ports
questionBank.explanation: Paragraph 2: ‘Loading costs, not ocean distance, made up much of the price of shipping, so it often made little sense to manufacture goods far from the people who would buy them.’ Option 2 contradicts this (distance was not the main cost). Options 3 and 4 are not in the passage.

questionBank.question: Which one of the following is NOT supported by the passage?
options: Standard sizes let the same box be handled by different cranes, ships, trucks and trains
Moving ports away from city centres hurt some waterfront communities
Theft and damage were common under break-bulk handling
The steel box was a new invention first patented by McLean in 1956

questionBank.question: The author calls the container a ‘dull steel rectangle’ in order to:

stress that a plain, unremarkable object had very large consequences
suggest that containers should be replaced by better designs
argue that globalisation has been harmful overall

Standards slow innovation and should be avoided

questionBank.question: A lecturer’s heavy use of technical jargon leaves first-year students unable to follow the lecture. This is mainly a:
questionBank.explanation: Semantic barriers arise from language: jargon, ambiguous words and symbols that sender and receiver decode differently. Physical barriers are noise, distance or poor acoustics; psychological barriers are emotions, prejudice or lack of attention; organisational barriers come from hierarchy, rules and long chains of command. The problem here is the words themselves, so it is semantic.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-III: proxemics (E. T. Hall) studies space and distance, such as intimate, personal, social and public zones. B-IV: chronemics studies time, such as punctuality and waiting. C-I: haptics studies touch. D-II: paralanguage covers the vocal cues that go with words: pitch, tone, pace, pauses and volume. Option 2 swaps space and time, option 3 swaps touch and voice, option 4 swaps time and touch.

b: I. Use of touch
II. Pitch, tone and pace of the voice
III. Use of personal space and distance
IV. Use and perception of time

questionBank.question: The concept of ‘noise’, meaning anything that distorts a signal between the sender and the receiver, entered communication models through the work of:
questionBank.explanation: Shannon and Weaver’s mathematical model (1948–49) has an information source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination, with a noise source acting on the channel. Lasswell’s verbal formula (‘Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect’) has no noise element; Aristotle’s rhetorical model has speaker, speech and audience; Berlo’s SMCR model (1960) focuses on source, message, channel and receiver characteristics.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: agenda-setting theory (McCombs and Shaw, 1972 Chapel Hill study) holds that the media are not very successful in telling people what to think but are very successful in telling them what to think ABOUT, by deciding which issues get attention. Statement II is true: McLuhan (Understanding Media, 1964) stressed that each medium changes human perception and social organisation regardless of its content. So Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: According to agenda-setting theory (McCombs and Shaw), the mass media mainly tell people what to think.
Statement II: Marshall McLuhan argued that ‘the medium is the message’, meaning that the form of a medium shapes society as much as its content does.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: A is true: on social media any user can reach many others, and many users interact with one another at the same time. R is true and explains A: because new media are digital, networked and interactive, the audience is no longer only a receiver; users create, share and respond to content (‘prosumers’). This two-way, user-generated character is exactly what turns one-to-many broadcasting into many-to-many communication.

stmts: Assertion (A): Social media platforms support many-to-many communication.
Reason (R): New media are digital and interactive, and they let users be both producers and consumers of content.

questionBank.question:
What number comes next in the series?
2, 6, 15, 31, 56, ?
questionBank.explanation: Differences: 6 − 2 = 4, 15 − 6 = 9, 31 − 15 = 16, 56 − 31 = 25. These are 2², 3², 4², 5², so the next difference is 6² = 36 and the next term is 56 + 36 = 92. The other options (86, 88, 90) come from adding a wrong difference of 30, 32 or 34.

questionBank.question: In a certain code, GARDEN is written as FZQCDM. How is MARKET written in that code?
questionBank.explanation: Each letter moves one place back: G→F, A→Z, R→Q, D→C, E→D, N→M. So M→L, A→Z, R→Q, K→J, E→D, T→S, giving LZQJDS. NBSLFU moves each letter forward instead. LZQKDS leaves K unchanged, and LZRJDS leaves R unchanged.

questionBank.question: Asha walks 6 km towards the north, turns right and walks 8 km, then turns right again and walks 12 km. How far is she from her starting point, and in which direction?
questionBank.explanation: Take the start as (0, 0). North 6 km gives (0, 6). A right turn from north faces east: 8 km gives (8, 6). A right turn from east faces south: 12 km gives (8, −6). Distance = √(8² + 6²) = √100 = 10 km, and the point is east and south of the start, so south-east. North-east forgets that 12 km south overshoots the starting line; 14 km adds 8 + 6 instead of using Pythagoras.

questionBank.question: A shopkeeper marks an article 25% above its cost price and then allows a discount of 12% on the marked price. His profit per cent is:
questionBank.explanation: Let CP = 100. Marked price = 125. Selling price = 125 × 0.88 = 110. Profit = 10%. Shortcut: net effect = 25 − 12 − (25 × 12)/100 = 13 − 3 = 10%. 13% is the trap of simply subtracting 25 − 12.

questionBank.question: A train 180 m long crosses a platform 270 m long in 27 seconds. The speed of the train is:
questionBank.explanation: To cross a platform the train covers its own length plus the platform’s: 180 + 270 = 450 m in 27 s, i.e. 450 ÷ 27 = 50/3 m/s. In km/h: 50/3 × 18/5 = 60 km/h. 24 km/h is the trap of using only the train’s length (180 ÷ 27 × 18/5).

questionBank.question: In the inference ‘The lake is warm, because it is knowable’, the hetu (knowability) is found both where warmth is present and where it is absent. The hetvābhāsa committed is:
questionBank.explanation: Savyabhicāra (the ‘erratic’ or inconclusive middle) occurs when the hetu is not invariably connected with the sādhya: knowability occurs in warm and in non-warm things, so it proves nothing (its sādhāraṇa form). Viruddha is a hetu that proves the opposite of the sādhya; asiddha is a hetu that is itself unestablished (for example not present in the pakṣa); bādhita is an inference whose conclusion is contradicted by a stronger pramāṇa such as perception.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-IV: Cārvāka accepts only pratyakṣa (perception). B-III: Sāṅkhya accepts three: pratyakṣa, anumāna and śabda. C-II: Nyāya accepts four, adding upamāna (comparison). D-I: Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā (Kumārila) accepts six, adding arthāpatti (postulation) and anupalabdhi (non-apprehension); Advaita Vedānta also accepts six. Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā accepts five (no anupalabdhi), and Vaiśeṣika and the Buddhists accept two.

b: I. Six
II. Four
III. Three
IV. One
