questionBank.question: If the proposition ‘Some poets are not critics’ is false, which one of the following must be true?
options: It is false that some poets are critics
questionBank.explanation: ‘Some poets are not critics’ is an O proposition. Its contradictory is the A proposition ‘All poets are critics’, and contradictories always have opposite truth values, so A must be true. Then the E proposition ‘No poets are critics’ is false (A and E are contraries) and ‘Some poets are critics’ (I) is true by subalternation, so option 4 is false. ‘Some critics are not poets’ is not determined by the given information.

questionBank.question: A speaker argues: “No one has ever proved that this herbal tonic does not improve memory, so it must improve memory.” The fallacy committed is:
questionBank.explanation: Treating the absence of disproof as proof is the appeal to ignorance. Ad hominem attacks the person instead of the argument; petitio principii assumes the conclusion in a premise; hasty generalisation draws a general rule from too few cases. None of those fits an argument whose only support is ‘not proved false’.

questionBank.question:
Statements: All pens are erasers. No eraser is a ruler.
Conclusions:
I. No pen is a ruler.
II. Some erasers are pens.
Which conclusion(s) follow(s)?
questionBank.explanation: Pens lie inside erasers, and erasers are entirely outside rulers, so no pen can be a ruler: I follows (the valid form Celarent, AEE-1). ‘All pens are erasers’ converts by limitation to ‘Some erasers are pens’, so II also follows (with the usual assumption, used in NET syllogisms, that the class of pens is not empty). So both follow.

questionBank.question: Which e-mail protocol lets a user read mail while it stays on the server, so that folders and read/unread status stay the same on every device?
questionBank.explanation: IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol, port 143, or 993 over TLS) keeps messages and folders on the server and synchronises their state across devices. POP3 usually downloads messages to one device and removes them from the server. SMTP is for sending and relaying mail, not reading it. FTP transfers files.

questionBank.question: The binary number (110101)₂ is equal to the decimal number:
questionBank.explanation: (110101)₂ = 32 + 16 + 0 + 4 + 0 + 1 = 53. 43 comes from reading the digits in reverse (101011₂). 106 is 110101 followed by a 0, i.e. double the value (a one-place left shift). 45 is 101101₂.

C-IV: a firewall allows or blocks traffic according to security rules. D-I: a cookie is a small text file a website saves in the browser to remember sessions and preferences. questionBank.question: Which Government of India platform gives citizens a single mobile app for services of many central and state government departments?
questionBank.explanation: UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance), launched in 2017, brings services of many central and state departments into one app. DigiLocker is a cloud wallet for issued documents and certificates; e-Sanjeevani is the national telemedicine service; MyGov is a citizen-engagement platform for participation in governance, not a single-window service app.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following international environmental events in chronological order, from the earliest to the latest.
questionBank.explanation: Ramsar Convention: 1971 (B). Stockholm Conference: 1972 (C). Vienna Convention: 1985 (E). Montreal Protocol: 1987 (A). Rio Earth Summit: 1992 (D). So B, C, E, A, D. Option 1 puts Stockholm before Ramsar; option 3 puts the Montreal Protocol before the Vienna Convention, but the protocol was made under the convention two years later.

stmts: A. Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer
B. Ramsar Convention on Wetlands
C. United Nations Conference on the Human Environment, Stockholm
D. United Nations Conference on Environment and Development (Earth Summit), Rio de Janeiro
E. Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer

questionBank.question: How many national missions were laid down in India’s National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC), released in 2008?
questionBank.explanation: The NAPCC (released on 30 June 2008) set out eight national missions: Solar; Enhanced Energy Efficiency; Sustainable Habitat; Water; Sustaining the Himalayan Ecosystem; Green India; Sustainable Agriculture; and Strategic Knowledge for Climate Change. Remember ‘eight missions, 2008’.

questionBank.question: The 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, adopted by the UN General Assembly in 2015, contains:
questionBank.explanation: The SDGs are 17 goals with 169 targets. 8 goals belong to the Millennium Development Goals (2000–2015), which had 21 targets after the 2007 revision. 231 is the number of unique indicators in the global indicator framework, not the number of targets, and that is the trap in option 3.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: there were 8 MDGs (2000–2015); 17 is the number of SDGs. Statement II is false: the SDGs are the 2030 Agenda, with 2030 as the target year. (2035 is the NEP 2020 target year for 50% GER in higher education, a common mix-up.) So both statements are false.

stmts: Statement I: The Millennium Development Goals were 17 goals with 2015 as the target year.
Statement II: The Sustainable Development Goals have 2035 as their target year.

questionBank.question: ‘Blue baby syndrome’ (methaemoglobinaemia) in infants is mainly associated with an excess of which of the following in drinking water?
questionBank.explanation: Nitrate from fertilisers and sewage is converted to nitrite, which turns haemoglobin into methaemoglobin that cannot carry oxygen, so the infant’s skin looks bluish. Excess fluoride causes dental and skeletal fluorosis; arsenic causes skin lesions and cancers (arsenicosis); mercury causes Minamata disease.

questionBank.question: Which one of the following is an example of a non-conventional learning programme in Indian higher education?
options: A regular full-time B.A. in an affiliated college
A Shastri course in a traditional Sanskrit pathshala
A full-time M.Sc. in a university department
An open and distance learning degree from IGNOU
questionBank.explanation: Non-conventional programmes break with the full-time, campus-based model: open and distance learning (IGNOU, state open universities), correspondence courses and online degrees. Regular full-time degrees in colleges and university departments (options 1 and 3) are conventional programmes. A Shastri course in a pathshala (option 2) belongs to oriental learning, the traditional Sanskrit, Pali, Arabic and Persian stream.

D-II: legal education by the Bar Council of India (Advocates Act, 1961). Option 1 swaps NCTE and PCI, option 2 swaps CoA and PCI, option 3 swaps NCTE and BCI.

h: List II (Statutory council that regulates its standards)
b: I. National Council for Teacher Education

questionBank.question: The National Education Policy 2020 aims to raise the Gross Enrolment Ratio in higher education (including vocational education) to:
questionBank.explanation: NEP 2020 targets a GER of 50% in higher education by 2035 (from 26.3% in 2018). 100% by 2030 is its GER target for school education from preschool to secondary, which is the usual trap; 50% by 2030 mixes the two.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: the four verticals of HECI are the National Higher Education Regulatory Council (NHERC), the National Accreditation Council (NAC), the Higher Education Grants Council (HEGC) and the General Education Council (GEC). Statement II is false: NEP 2020 makes HECI the single umbrella body for higher education EXCLUDING medical and legal education. So Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: NEP 2020 proposes a Higher Education Commission of India (HECI) with four independent verticals: NHERC for regulation, NAC for accreditation, HEGC for funding and GEC for standard setting.
Statement II: Under NEP 2020, medical and legal education are also brought under the HECI.

questionBank.question: The first Intergovernmental Conference on Environmental Education, organised by UNESCO and UNEP, whose declaration set out the objectives of environmental education (awareness, knowledge, attitudes, skills and participation), was held at:
questionBank.explanation: The Tbilisi Declaration (1977) of the first Intergovernmental Conference on Environmental Education set its goals and its five objective categories. The Belgrade Charter (1975) came out of an earlier international workshop, not an intergovernmental conference. Stockholm (1972) was the UN Conference on the Human Environment, and Rio (1992) was the Earth Summit that adopted Agenda 21.

questionBank.question: Under a credit-based grading system, a student earns the following in one semester (credits, grade point): Course 1 (4, 9), Course 2 (3, 6), Course 3 (2, 10), Course 4 (3, 7), Course 5 (2, 8). The student’s SGPA, correct to two decimal places, is:
questionBank.explanation: SGPA is the credit-weighted mean of grade points: Σ(Cᵢ × Gᵢ) ÷ ΣCᵢ. Credit points = 4×9 + 3×6 + 2×10 + 3×7 + 2×8 = 36 + 18 + 20 + 21 + 16 = 111. Total credits = 4 + 3 + 2 + 3 + 2 = 14. SGPA = 111 ÷ 14 = 7.928… ≈ 7.93. The trap 8.00 is the simple average of the five grade points (40 ÷ 5), which ignores credits; 7.40 is 111 ÷ 15 (a miscounted credit total); 8.15 has no valid basis.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II

C-III: placement evaluation comes before instruction and checks entry behaviour and prerequisite skills. D-IV: formative evaluation runs during instruction; its feedback is used to improve teaching and learning, not to grade. Option 1 swaps diagnostic and formative, option 3 swaps summative and placement, option 4 swaps summative and diagnostic.

b: I. Finding the underlying causes of learning difficulties that persist despite corrective help
II. Certifying or grading achievement at the end of a course
III. Determining the entry behaviour of learners before instruction begins
IV. Monitoring progress during instruction to give feedback and adjust teaching

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about SWAYAM and SWAYAM Prabha are correct?

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is false. In the revised taxonomy the order is Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analysing, Evaluating, Creating; ‘Creating’ (roughly the old ‘Synthesis’) moved to the top and ‘Evaluating’ is now fifth. The trap is the original 1956 order, where Evaluation was the highest level. (R) is true: the revision changed the nouns (Knowledge, Comprehension, …) into verbs (Remembering, Understanding, …). So (A) is false but (R) is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): In the revised Bloom’s taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001), ‘Evaluating’ is the highest level of the cognitive domain.
Reason (R): The revision renamed the categories of the cognitive domain from nouns to verbs.

questionBank.question: In a ‘flipped classroom’, which of the following is the essential change from a conventional lecture course?
options: Students take turns teaching the whole class while the teacher sits with the learners
Class time is used only for tests, and all teaching happens through printed modules
First exposure to new content happens before class, through videos or readings, and class time is used for application, discussion and problem-solving
The teacher gives the summary first and the detailed lecture at the end of each period
questionBank.explanation: Flipping swaps where the two activities happen: content transmission moves out of class (pre-recorded videos, readings), and the ‘homework’ of applying ideas moves into class, where the teacher can support it. Option 1 describes learning-by-teaching or peer tutoring, not flipping. Option 2 confuses it with correspondence study plus testing. Option 4 only reorders the parts of a lecture; the teacher is still transmitting content in class.

questionBank.question: A researcher concludes that a new reading programme raises comprehension scores, but in reality the programme has no effect. The researcher has committed:
options: A Type II error, whose probability is denoted by β
A Type I error, whose probability is denoted by β
A Type II error, whose probability is denoted by α
A Type I error, whose probability is denoted by α
questionBank.explanation: The null hypothesis here is ‘the programme has no effect’. It is actually true, but the researcher rejected it: that is a Type I error (a false positive), and its probability is the level of significance α. A Type II error is the opposite, failing to reject a false null (missing a real effect), with probability β; power = 1 − β. The distractors pair the right error with the wrong symbol or the wrong error with the right symbol.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following steps of a research study in the correct order.
questionBank.explanation: A study begins by identifying the problem (D). The literature is then reviewed (B) to sharpen the problem and to ground the hypotheses, which are formulated next (A). Data are collected (C) and finally analysed and interpreted (E). So D, B, A, C, E. Option 1 puts the review before the problem is identified (the review needs a problem to focus it); option 2 frames hypotheses before reviewing the literature; option 4 collects data before hypotheses exist.

stmts: A. Formulating hypotheses
B. Reviewing the related literature
C. Collecting data with the chosen tools
D. Identifying and defining the research problem
E. Analysing and interpreting the data

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-II: historical research tests sources by external criticism (is the document genuine?) and internal criticism (is its content credible?). B-IV: ethnography relies on prolonged immersion and participant observation in a culture. C-III: in ex post facto (causal-comparative) research the independent variable has already acted, so the researcher can only compare groups after the fact. D-I: action research is done by practitioners (for example teachers) to solve a local, immediate problem. Option 2 swaps historical and ethnographic; option 3 swaps ex post facto and action research; option 4 swaps ethnographic and ex post facto.

b: I. A practitioner studies and solves an immediate problem in his or her own setting
II. Evidence is judged through external and internal criticism of sources

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: Comte coined ‘positivism’, the view that science should rest on observable, verifiable facts. Statement II is also true: post-positivism (influenced by Popper’s falsification) keeps the aim of objectivity but holds that observations are fallible and shaped by theory, so claims are tested and provisionally accepted, never finally proved. The trap is to treat post-positivism as a rejection of objectivity; that is closer to interpretivism.

stmts: Statement I: Positivism, associated with Auguste Comte, holds that genuine knowledge must rest on what can be observed and verified.
Statement II: Post-positivism accepts that all observation is fallible and theory-laden, so research can at best reject or provisionally support claims rather than prove them conclusively.

questionBank.question: A university has 2,400 undergraduates, 1,500 postgraduates and 600 doctoral scholars. A sample of 300 is drawn by proportionate stratified random sampling. How many doctoral scholars will be in the sample?
questionBank.explanation: Population N = 2,400 + 1,500 + 600 = 4,500. Sampling fraction = 300 ÷ 4,500 = 1/15. Doctoral scholars in the sample = 600 × 1/15 = 40 (undergraduates 160, postgraduates 100, total 300). The trap 100 is equal allocation (300 ÷ 3), which is not proportionate; 60 is 10% of 600; 20 has no valid basis.

questionBank.question: Which of the following best states the central idea of the passage?
options: Placebos contain a hidden healing force that doctors should learn to use more widely
Improvement after an intervention does not by itself show that the intervention caused it; a fair comparison is needed
Surgery is an unreliable way to treat chest pain and should be replaced by medicines
Symptoms such as pain and fatigue cannot be measured reliably and should not be studied
questionBank.explanation: The passage uses the sham-surgery story to argue that improvement can come from regression to the mean, changed reporting and expectation, so a treatment is shown to work only when it beats a comparable control; the last paragraph extends this to reforms and policies. Option 1 is the popular view the author explicitly rejects (‘less mysterious’). Option 3 over-generalises from one abandoned operation. Option 4 distorts the point about subjective symptoms, which are said to be measured by asking, not to be unmeasurable.

stem.passage:
In the late 1950s a surgical operation for chest pain enjoyed a brief popularity. Surgeons tied off two arteries inside the chest wall, reasoning that more blood would then be diverted to the heart, and patients reported striking relief. Then two small trials did something that now seems obvious. In some patients the surgeon made the skin incisions but tied nothing. Those who had the sham operation improved about as much as those who had the real one, and the procedure was soon abandoned.

Stories like this are usually told as evidence of the power of the placebo, as though a sugar pill or a fake operation contained some hidden healing force. The truth is less mysterious and more useful. Part of the improvement seen in any group of patients would have happened anyway. Many illnesses wax and wane, and people tend to seek treatment when they feel worst, so on average they will feel better later whatever is done; statisticians call this regression to the mean. Part of it lies in reporting: patients who have been examined, cared for and reassured describe their symptoms differently, especially when the symptom, like pain or fatigue, can only be measured by asking. Only what remains after these effects are set aside is a genuine response to expectation, and that response, though real, is largest for subjective complaints and smallest for measures such as tumour size or blood sugar.

This is why the controlled trial matters. A treatment is not shown to work because patients who receive it improve. It is shown to work when they improve more than comparable patients who receive something that looks the same but lacks the supposed active ingredient. Without that comparison, a physician’s experience, however long, is a record of what happened after treatment, not of what happened because of it.

None of this means that expectation should be ignored. Clinicians who explain, listen and show confidence may genuinely reduce the distress their patients feel, and some researchers report that even placebos given openly, with patients told exactly what they are, can ease certain symptoms. The ethical difficulty lies elsewhere: deceiving a patient in order to harness the effect undermines the very trust on which the effect depends.

The lesson reaches well beyond medicine. Whenever we judge a reform, a teaching method or a policy by whether things improved afterwards, we risk mistaking the ordinary drift of events, and the enthusiasm of those involved, for the effect of the intervention itself.

questionBank.question: According to the passage, ‘regression to the mean’ explains part of the improvement because:
options: patients who are reassured describe their symptoms more favourably
people tend to seek treatment when they feel worst, so on average they will feel better later whatever is done
doctors with long experience learn to predict which patients will recover
expectation produces real changes in subjective complaints
questionBank.explanation: The passage defines it directly: illnesses wax and wane, people come for treatment at their worst, so on average they improve later regardless of treatment. Option 1 is the separate ‘reporting’ effect; option 4 is the genuine expectation response; option 3 is not mentioned. The trap is that all four ideas appear near each other in the second paragraph.

questionBank.question:
Which of the following can be inferred from the passage?
A. A placebo would be expected to show a larger effect on reported pain than on measured blood sugar.
B. Sham-operation trials show that the arteries tied off in the chest operation were harmful.
C. A physician’s long experience cannot, on its own, establish that a treatment works.
D. An openly given placebo can never ease any symptom.
Choose the correct answer:
questionBank.explanation: A follows: the expectation response is said to be largest for subjective complaints and smallest for measures such as blood sugar. C follows: experience without a comparison is ‘a record of what happened after treatment, not … because of it’. B does not follow: the trials showed the real operation was no better than the sham, not that it was harmful. D contradicts the passage, which reports that open placebos can ease certain symptoms. Hence A and C only.

stem.passage:
In the late 1950s a surgical operation for chest pain enjoyed a brief popularity. Surgeons tied off two arteries inside the chest wall, reasoning that more blood would then be diverted to the heart, and patients reported striking relief. Then two small trials did something that now seems obvious. In some patients the surgeon made the skin incisions but tied nothing. Those who had the sham operation improved about as much as those who had the real one, and the procedure was soon abandoned.

Stories like this are usually told as evidence of the power of the placebo, as though a sugar pill or a fake operation contained some hidden healing force. The truth is less mysterious and more useful. Part of the improvement seen in any group of patients would have happened anyway. Many illnesses wax and wane, and people tend to seek treatment when they feel worst, so on average they will feel better later whatever is done; statisticians call this regression to the mean. Part of it lies in reporting: patients who have been examined, cared for and reassured describe their symptoms differently, especially when the symptom, like pain or fatigue, can only be measured by asking. Only what remains after these effects are set aside is a genuine response to expectation, and that response, though real, is largest for subjective complaints and smallest for measures such as tumour size or blood sugar.

This is why the controlled trial matters. A treatment is not shown to work because patients who receive it improve. It is shown to work when they improve more than comparable patients who receive something that looks the same but lacks the supposed active ingredient. Without that comparison, a physician’s experience, however long, is a record of what happened after treatment, not of what happened because of it.

None of this means that expectation should be ignored. Clinicians who explain, listen and show confidence may genuinely reduce the distress their patients feel, and some researchers report that even placebos given openly, with patients told exactly what they are, can ease certain symptoms. The ethical difficulty lies elsewhere: deceiving a patient in order to harness the effect undermines the very trust on which the effect depends.

The lesson reaches well beyond medicine. Whenever we judge a reform, a teaching method or a policy by whether things improved afterwards, we risk mistaking the ordinary drift of events, and the enthusiasm of those involved, for the effect of the intervention itself.

Using placebos is forbidden by law in most countries

questionBank.question: A school adopts a new timetable in the year after its worst-ever examination results, and the next year’s results improve. On the reasoning of the passage, which conclusion is most justified?
options: The timetable clearly caused the improvement, since results rose after it was introduced
The improvement proves that the teachers’ enthusiasm, not the timetable, raised the results
The timetable should be abandoned because the improvement was only a placebo effect
The improvement may partly be a return from an unusually bad year, so a comparison with similar schools that did not change is needed before crediting the timetable
questionBank.explanation: The last paragraph warns that judging a reform by whether things improved afterwards risks mistaking ‘the ordinary drift of events’ (here, a rebound from a worst-ever year, i.e. regression to the mean) and enthusiasm for the effect of the change. The justified response is to ask for a comparison group. Option 1 is exactly the error the passage describes. Options 2 and 3 overclaim in the other direction: the passage says such factors may contribute, not that they alone explain the change or that the reform failed.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-II: Harold Lasswell (1948) described communication by the questions who, says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect. B-IV: Shannon and Weaver’s mathematical model has an information source, transmitter, channel, receiver and destination, and introduced ‘noise’. D-III: Berlo’s SMCR model lists factors such as communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture for source and receiver. Option 1 swaps the circular and SMCR models; option 3 swaps Lasswell and Shannon–Weaver; option 4 swaps Shannon–Weaver and Osgood–Schramm.

b: I. A circular model in which both parties encode, decode and interpret in turn
II. A verbal formula: who says what, in which channel, to whom, with what effect
III. Source, message, channel and receiver, each shaped by skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture
IV. A transmitter, a signal and a receiver, with noise that can distort the signal

B. Poor acoustics in a large lecture hall

So (A) is true but (R) is false.

questionBank.question: A student concludes that a professor who regularly keeps visitors waiting for twenty minutes is signalling his high status. This inference about the use of time as a message belongs to the study of:
questionBank.explanation: Chronemics studies how time is used and read as communication: punctuality, waiting time and pacing often signal status and respect. Proxemics is the use of space and distance (Edward T. Hall); haptics is touch; kinesics is body movement, gestures and facial expression. The trap is proxemics, because Hall’s cultural work also discussed time.

questionBank.question:
What comes next in the series?
3, 7, 16, 35, 74, ?
questionBank.explanation: Each term is twice the previous one plus an increasing addend: 3×2+1 = 7, 7×2+2 = 16, 16×2+3 = 35, 35×2+4 = 74, so the next is 74×2+5 = 153. The differences 4, 9, 19, 39 double plus one each time (next difference 79), which confirms 153. 148 (plain doubling) and 149 (adding 1 again) are the traps.

questionBank.question: In a certain code, CLASS is written as HHZOX. How is TEACH written in that code?
questionBank.explanation: Each letter is replaced by its mirror letter in the alphabet (A↔Z, B↔Y, …, i.e. position p becomes 27 − p), and then the word is written backwards. CLASS → X O Z H H → reversed HHZOX. TEACH → T→G, E→V, A→Z, C→X, H→S gives GVZXS; reversed, SXZVG. GVZXS forgets the reversal; SXZVH mirrors H wrongly; TXZVG leaves T unchanged.

questionBank.question: Pointing to a man in a photograph, Meera says, “His mother is the only daughter of my mother’s father.” How is the man related to Meera?
questionBank.explanation: Meera’s mother’s father is Meera’s maternal grandfather. His only daughter must be Meera’s own mother (Meera’s mother is certainly his daughter, and he has only one). So the man’s mother is Meera’s mother, and the man is Meera’s brother. ‘Maternal cousin’ is the trap for those who read ‘only daughter’ as an aunt; an aunt on the mother’s side would be another daughter of the same father, which ‘only’ rules out.

questionBank.question: A shopkeeper marks an article 40% above its cost price and then allows two successive discounts of 10% each. His profit per cent is:
questionBank.explanation: Let the cost price be 100. Marked price = 140. After the first 10% discount: 140 × 0.9 = 126. After the second: 126 × 0.9 = 113.4. Profit = 13.4 on 100, i.e. 13.4%. The trap 20% subtracts the discounts from the mark-up (40 − 10 − 10); successive discounts of 10% and 10% equal a single discount of 19%, not 20%, and 140 × 0.81 = 113.4.

questionBank.question: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a sum for 3 years at 10% per annum is ₹93. The sum is:
questionBank.explanation: For 3 years, CI − SI = P[(1 + r)³ − 1 − 3r] = P[1.331 − 1 − 0.30] = 0.031P. So 0.031P = 93 and P = ₹3,000. Check: SI = ₹900, CI = 3,000 × 0.331 = ₹993, difference ₹93. The trap ₹9,300 uses the 2-year formula P(r)² = 0.01P; ₹3,100 divides 93 by 0.03.

D-II: hasty generalisation leaps from two cases to all officials. Option 2 swaps post hoc and begging the question; option 3 swaps ad hominem and hasty generalisation; option 4 swaps begging the question and hasty generalisation.

b: I. “This book is reliable because it says it is true, and a true book never lies.”
II. “I met two rude officials in this city, so its officials are rude.”
III. “His proposal on exam reform should be rejected; he failed his own exams.”
IV. “The college won the tournament after the new flag was hoisted, so the flag brought the win.”

questionBank.question: If the proposition ‘Some politicians are honest’ is false, then according to the traditional square of opposition:
options: ‘No politicians are honest’ is true; ‘All politicians are honest’ is false; ‘Some politicians are not honest’ is undetermined
‘No politicians are honest’ is true; ‘All politicians are honest’ is undetermined; ‘Some politicians are not honest’ is true
‘No politicians are honest’ is false; ‘All politicians are honest’ is false; ‘Some politicians are not honest’ is true
‘No politicians are honest’ is true; ‘All politicians are honest’ is false; ‘Some politicians are not honest’ is true
questionBank.explanation: The false proposition is an I. Its contradictory E (‘No politicians are honest’) must be true. Falsity passes down from the particular to its universal by subalternation, so A (‘All politicians are honest’) is false. I and O are subcontraries and cannot both be false, so O (‘Some politicians are not honest’) is true (it also follows from E by subalternation, given existential import). Option 1 is the trap of treating O as undetermined; option 2 forgets that a false I makes A false.

questionBank.question:
Statements:
1. All pens are erasers.
2. Some erasers are sharpeners.
3. No sharpener is a scale.
Conclusions:
I. Some pens are sharpeners.
II. Some erasers are not scales.
III. No pen is a scale.
Which conclusion(s) follow?
questionBank.explanation: II follows: the erasers that are sharpeners (statement 2) cannot be scales (statement 3), so some erasers are not scales. I does not follow: the pens lie inside the erasers, but the erasers that are sharpeners may be entirely outside the pens. III does not follow: nothing links pens to scales; a pen that is not a sharpener may well be a scale. A Venn test with a diagram where pens and sharpeners do not overlap, and some pen is a scale, satisfies all three statements, which refutes I and III. Hence only II.

questionBank.question: ACEG : ZXVT :: BDFH : ?
questionBank.explanation: Each letter is paired with its mirror letter (position p ↦ 27 − p): A↔Z, C↔X, E↔V, G↔T. Applying the same rule to BDFH: B→Y, D→W, F→U, H→S, giving YWUS. YXVT copies the answer to the first pair after changing only the first letter; XWUS and YWVS each mirror one letter wrongly.

questionBank.question: “Fire is cold, because it is a substance.” In Nyāya logic, the reason (hetu) here is set aside because perception directly shows that fire is hot. This fallacy of inference (hetvābhāsa) is called:
questionBank.explanation: Bādhita (also kālātyayāpadiṣṭa, the ‘sublated’ reason) is a reason whose conclusion is already contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge, here perception (fire is felt to be hot). Viruddha (the trap) is a reason that proves the opposite of the conclusion because it is pervaded by the absence of the sādhya. Savyabhicāra is an inconclusive or irregular reason found with and without the sādhya. Satpratipakṣa is a reason counterbalanced by another reason of equal strength proving the opposite.

questionBank.question: The sum of (10110)₂ and (17)₈, expressed in hexadecimal, is:
questionBank.explanation: (10110)₂ = 16 + 4 + 2 = 22. (17)₈ = 8 + 7 = 15. Sum = 37 in decimal. 37 = 2 × 16 + 5, so the answer is (25)₁₆. questionBank.question:
In a CBCS semester, a student takes five courses with the credits and grade points shown below.
Course 1: 4 credits, grade point 9
Course 2: 4 credits, grade point 7
Course 3: 3 credits, grade point 8
Course 4: 3 credits, grade point 6
Course 5: 2 credits, grade point 10
What is the student’s SGPA (rounded to two decimal places)?
questionBank.explanation:
SGPA is the credit-weighted mean of grade points: SGPA = Σ(credits × grade points) ÷ Σ credits.
Σ(C × G) = 4×9 + 4×7 + 3×8 + 3×6 + 2×10 = 36 + 28 + 24 + 18 + 20 = 126.
Σ C = 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 16.
SGPA = 126 ÷ 16 = 7.875 ≈ 7.88.
The trap 8.00 is the simple average of the five grade points (40 ÷ 5), which ignores credits. 7.50 and 7.94 come from arithmetic slips.

questionBank.question: A researcher wants to know whether growing up bilingual influences the career choices of adults. She compares the careers of adults who were raised bilingually with those of adults who were not, without manipulating anything herself. Which research method is she using?
questionBank.explanation: In ex post facto (“after the fact”) research the independent variable (here, bilingual upbringing) has already occurred and cannot be manipulated or randomly assigned by the researcher; she can only compare groups that already differ and look back for possible causes. Experimental research requires the researcher to manipulate the independent variable and control other variables. Action research is done by practitioners to solve an immediate problem in their own setting. Historical research reconstructs past events from records and relics; it does not compare present groups on an existing variable.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are probability sampling methods?
questionBank.explanation: In probability sampling every unit of the population has a known, non-zero chance of selection. Simple random sampling (A), stratified random sampling (C: random selection within each stratum) and cluster sampling (D: random selection of whole groups) all qualify. Snowball sampling (B) grows through referrals from existing participants, and quota sampling (E) fills fixed quotas by the researcher’s convenience or judgment; both are non-probability methods. The quota-versus-stratified confusion is the usual trap: both divide the population into groups, but only stratified sampling selects randomly within each group.

stmts: A. Simple random sampling
B. Snowball sampling
C. Stratified random sampling
D. Cluster sampling
E. Quota sampling

questionBank.question:
Read the passage and answer the question.
Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The alphabetical index made careful reading unnecessary and was therefore opposed by teachers.
Printing, not the needs of scholars, was the real origin of the book index.
The index changed how people read rather than ending careful reading, but it quietly carries its compiler’s judgments.
Readers should avoid indexes because they are compiled by people with fixed beliefs.
questionBank.explanation: The passage traces the index from medieval concordances to printed books and concludes that “searching and reading are not rivals”: the index “changed its rhythm” of study, while the real danger is that every index reflects its compiler’s choices. Option 3 captures both halves. Option 1 contradicts the conclusion (every generation “goes on reading”). Option 2 is wrong because the passage says the index grew out of the needs of preachers and teachers; printing only added stability. Option 4 overstates the warning: the author cautions against trusting an index completely, not against using one.

stem.passage:
Before the printed page settled into fixed shapes, finding a particular idea in a book was a labour of memory. A reader who wanted to return to a passage in a manuscript had to remember roughly where it lay, or read again from the beginning. Two copies of the same text rarely matched page for page, because each scribe wrote at his own size and pace. A note that said “see folio forty” was useful only to the owner of one particular copy.

The alphabetical index grew out of the needs of thirteenth-century preachers and teachers, who had to find, quickly, every passage in scripture and in the writings of earlier authorities that touched on the theme of a sermon or a lecture. Friars compiled concordances in which each word was followed by the places where it occurred, and university masters divided texts into chapters and numbered sections so that a reference could survive the copying of a book. The alphabet, an order with no meaning of its own, was adopted precisely because it was arbitrary: anyone who knew their letters could use it, whatever they believed about the relative importance of the subjects listed.

Not everyone welcomed the tool. Some teachers worried that students who could leap directly to the sentence they needed would never read the whole argument, and would quote authorities without understanding them. The complaint has a familiar ring. Every generation that gains a faster way of finding information hears the warning that it will lose the patience to read, and every generation, on the whole, goes on reading.

What printing added was stability. Once hundreds of identical copies left the press, a page number meant the same thing in every library, and the index became a map that strangers could share. By the eighteenth century a serious book without an index was widely thought to be incomplete, and some authors grumbled that readers now consulted the index instead of the book.

The history suggests that searching and reading are not rivals. The index did not replace careful study; it changed its rhythm, allowing scholars to move back and forth between the whole and its parts. The real danger lay elsewhere. Every index reflects the judgment of whoever compiled it: someone decided which words mattered, which ideas deserved an entry and which could be left out. A reader who trusts an index completely inherits those choices without ever noticing that they were made.

Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement II is false: agenda-setting theory, from the 1968 Chapel Hill study published in 1972, holds that the media are not very successful in telling people WHAT to think but are very successful in telling them what to think ABOUT, that is, the media shape the salience of issues rather than the opinions held on them.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are examples of non-verbal communication in a classroom?
questionBank.explanation: Verbal communication uses words, whether spoken or written; non-verbal communication uses everything else. Eye contact and deliberate pauses (A, oculesics and chronemics), the use of space and seating (C, proxemics) and the tone, pitch and pace of the voice (D, paralanguage) are non-verbal. B is written words and E is spoken words, so both are verbal. Paralanguage is the common trap: it accompanies speech but is classed as non-verbal because it carries meaning apart from the words themselves.

stmts: A. A teacher pausing and making eye contact to regain attention
B. A written assignment sheet handed out to students
C. The arrangement of desks in a circle for a seminar
D. The tone and pitch of the teacher’s voice while reading aloud
E. A teacher explaining a rule through a spoken example

options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true and R explains A. Traditional broadcasting is largely one-to-many and one-way: feedback is delayed and indirect (ratings, letters). New media are digital, networked and participatory; users can comment, share, remix and publish, which makes communication many-to-many and highly interactive. That participatory structure is precisely the reason for the greater interactivity stated in A.

stmts: Assertion (A): Communication through new media such as social networking platforms is generally more interactive than communication through traditional broadcast television.
Reason (R): New media allow many-to-many communication in which receivers can respond, share and create content themselves.

questionBank.question:
What number comes next in the series?
3, 7, 16, 35, 74, ?
questionBank.explanation: Each term is twice the previous term plus an increasing number: 3×2+1 = 7, 7×2+2 = 16, 16×2+3 = 35, 35×2+4 = 74, so the next term is 74×2+5 = 153. The option 149 comes from using “×2+1” every time (74×2+1), 148 from simple doubling, and 151 from “×2+3”.

questionBank.question: Pointing to a girl in a photograph, Ravi says, “She is the daughter of the only son of my father’s father.” Ravi’s father has no brothers. How is the girl related to Ravi?
questionBank.explanation: “My father’s father” is Ravi’s paternal grandfather. His only son must be Ravi’s father (the question confirms Ravi’s father has no brothers). The daughter of Ravi’s father is Ravi’s sister. Cousin is the trap for readers who assume the “only son” is an uncle; niece and aunt belong to other generations.

questionBank.question: A grocer buys 25 kg of rice at ₹48 per kg and 15 kg of another variety at ₹56 per kg. He mixes the two and sells the whole mixture at ₹60 per kg. What is his profit percentage (to two decimal places)?
questionBank.explanation:
Cost price = 25 × 48 + 15 × 56 = 1,200 + 840 = ₹2,040 for 40 kg.
Selling price = 40 × 60 = ₹2,400.
Profit = 2,400 − 2,040 = ₹360.
Profit % = 360 ÷ 2,040 × 100 = 17.647… ≈ 17.65%.
The trap 15.38% uses the simple average of the two prices, (48 + 56) ÷ 2 = 52, ignoring that the quantities are unequal; the true average cost is 2,040 ÷ 40 = ₹51 per kg, and (60 − 51) ÷ 51 = 17.65%. 20.00% is the wrong-base slip of dividing by a cost of 50.

questionBank.question: The difference between the compound interest (compounded annually) and the simple interest on a certain sum for 2 years at 8% per annum is ₹96. What is the sum?
questionBank.explanation:
For 2 years, CI − SI = P × (r/100)², because the only extra amount in CI is the interest earned in the second year on the first year’s interest.
96 = P × (0.08)² = P × 0.0064 → P = 96 ÷ 0.0064 = 15,000.
Check: SI = 15000 × 0.08 × 2 = 1,200; amount with CI = 15000 × 1.08² = 17,496, so CI = 2,496 and CI − SI = 96. ₹12,000 would give a difference of 76.80.

questionBank.question: A cyclist rides from town A to town B at 12 km/h and returns along the same road at 18 km/h. The whole journey takes 5 hours. What is the distance between A and B?
questionBank.explanation:
Let the distance be d. Time = d/12 + d/18 = (3d + 2d)/36 = 5d/36 = 5 hours, so d = 36 km.
Check with average speed: for equal distances the average speed is the harmonic mean 2×12×18/(12+18) = 14.4 km/h; total distance 2d = 14.4 × 5 = 72 km, so d = 36 km.
The trap 37.5 km uses the arithmetic mean 15 km/h (15 × 5 ÷ 2).

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Contraries (A: All S are P; E: No S is P) cannot both be true but CAN both be false, for example “All students are graduates” and “No student is a graduate” are both false when some students are graduates and some are not. So Statement II is true. Subcontraries (I: Some S are P; O: Some S are not P) are the mirror image: they can both be true but CANNOT both be false, so Statement I is false. Contradictories (A–O, E–I) always take opposite truth values.

stmts: Statement I: In the traditional square of opposition, two subcontrary propositions (I and O) can both be false at the same time.
Statement II: In the traditional square of opposition, two contrary propositions (A and E) can both be false at the same time.

questionBank.question:
Statements:
All pens are books.
Some books are bags.
No bag is a chair.
Which of the following conclusions follow logically from the statements?
options: B, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: B follows: some books are bags, and no bag is a chair, so those books are not chairs (I + E gives O). C follows by converting “Some books are bags” (I converts simply). E follows by converting “All pens are books” by limitation (A → I), since the terms are taken to be non-empty. A does not follow: pens are inside books, but the bags may lie in a part of books that contains no pen. D does not follow: nothing links pens to chairs, since the pens may be books that are not bags, and such books may well be chairs. So only B, C and E follow.

stmts: A. Some pens are bags.
B. Some books are not chairs.
C. Some bags are books.
D. No pen is a chair.
E. Some books are pens.
stem.after: Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

questionBank.question: Which of the following best describes the Venn diagram that represents the relationship among Mothers, Women and Doctors?
options: Mothers inside Women, and Doctors overlapping both Women and Mothers
Women inside Mothers, and Doctors inside Women
Doctors inside Mothers, and Mothers inside Women
questionBank.explanation: Every mother is a woman, so the Mothers circle lies inside the Women circle. Some doctors are women and some are not, and some doctors are mothers while some are not, so the Doctors circle overlaps both Women and Mothers and also extends outside Women. Option 3 reverses the subset (not every woman is a mother). Option 4 wrongly puts all doctors inside Mothers. Option 1 ignores the obvious overlaps.

questionBank.question: Arrange the five members (avayavas) of the Nyaya syllogism for others (pararthanumana) in their correct order.

So C, E, A, D, B. Option 1 swaps udaharana and upanaya; option 3 starts with the reason; option 4 puts the example before the reason.

B. Nigamana (conclusion)
C. Pratijna (proposition to be proved)
D. Upanaya (application to the present case)
E. Hetu (reason)

questionBank.question: Arrange the following storage quantities in increasing order of size (use 1 KB = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, and so on).
questionBank.explanation: Convert all to powers of two. 1023 MB is just under 1 GB (2³⁰ bytes). 1 GB = 2³⁰ bytes. 1.5 GB = 1.5 × 2³⁰ bytes. 2³¹ bytes = 2 GB. 0.5 TB = 0.5 × 2⁴⁰ = 2³⁹ bytes = 512 GB. So the order is B (1023 MB) < A (1 GB) < D (1.5 GB) < C (2 GB) < E (512 GB): B, A, D, C, E. Option 2 misreads 2³¹ bytes as smaller than 1.5 GB.

questionBank.question: The binary number 11010110 is equal to which of the following?
questionBank.explanation:
Group the bits in fours from the right: 1101 0110 = D (13) and 6, so the hexadecimal value is D6.
Decimal: 128 + 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 214 (bits set at positions 7, 6, 4, 2, 1). Equivalently 13 × 16 + 6 = 214.
(6D)₁₆ is the trap of reading the nibbles in reverse order; 206 is a decimal slip (adding 8 instead of 16).

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about e-mail and networks are correct?
questionBank.explanation: A is true: blind carbon copy hides those addresses from everyone else. B is true: IMAP (Internet Message Access Protocol) works on the server copy and keeps folders and read status in sync. C is false: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) SENDS and relays mail; retrieval uses POP3 or IMAP. D is true: an intranet uses TCP/IP, web servers and browsers but is restricted to the organisation. Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true and R explains A. This is the pattern of Minamata disease in Japan, where a chemical factory discharged mercury compounds into the bay. Methylmercury is not easily excreted; it builds up in the tissues of organisms (bioaccumulation) and becomes more concentrated at each trophic level (biomagnification). Fish at the top of the marine food chain therefore carried high levels, and people who ate them regularly received large doses even though the water concentration was low.

questionBank.explanation: The affective domain has five categories, from the lowest to the highest: receiving, responding, valuing, organisation and characterisation by a value (or value complex). So A, B, D and E are affective categories. C (evaluating, or evaluation) belongs to the cognitive domain: it is the top level of the original 1956 cognitive taxonomy and the second-highest level of the 2001 revision. Every option that contains C is therefore wrong, which leaves only "A, B, D and E only".

stmts: A. Receiving
B. Valuing
C. Evaluating
D. Organisation
E. Characterisation by a value or value complex

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: Both are true. (A): teachers of adolescents routinely observe that group acceptance shapes participation, dress, speech and even willingness to answer in class. (R): in Erikson's psychosocial theory the central task of adolescence is forming an identity; the alternative is role confusion. (R) explains (A): because the adolescent is building an identity, the peer group becomes the main mirror in which that identity is tested, so its approval matters so much. Hence option 1. A teacher can use this by designing co-operative tasks in which peer approval rewards effort rather than conformity.

stmts: Assertion (A): Adolescent learners are often strongly influenced by the approval of their peer group during classroom activities.
Reason (R): Adolescence is the stage in which a person seeks a stable personal and social identity, the conflict Erikson called identity versus role confusion.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following cognitive processes of the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Anderson and Krathwohl, 2001) from the lowest to the highest order.
questionBank.explanation: The revised taxonomy has six levels: Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create. Leaving out Understand, the given five run C (Remember), B (Apply), E (Analyse), A (Evaluate), D (Create), i.e. C, B, E, A, D. The main trap is "C, B, E, D, A": in the original 1956 taxonomy, Synthesis came below Evaluation, but the 2001 revision renamed Synthesis as Create and placed it at the top. The other options swap the lower rungs (Apply and Analyse, or Remember and Apply).

B. Apply
C. Remember
D. Create

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: formative evaluation (term coined by Scriven) is continuous and diagnostic; quizzes, class questions and assignments during a unit feed back into the teaching. Statement II is false: it describes a criterion-referenced test, which compares performance with a pre-set criterion (e.g. 80% of the objectives mastered). A norm-referenced test places the learner relative to a norm group (percentiles, ranks), so the same raw score can mean different things in different groups. Hence Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-III: historical research works with primary sources (letters, diaries, records) and subjects them to external criticism (is the source genuine?) and internal criticism (is its content credible?). B-II: the defining marks of a true experiment are manipulation of the independent variable, control and random assignment. C-IV: ethnography is qualitative; the researcher lives with the group for a long period and describes its culture from an insider (emic) view. D-I: causal-comparative or ex post facto ("after the fact") research begins after the effect has occurred, and the variables cannot be manipulated. The commonest slip is to swap B and D, since both deal with cause and effect; the difference is whether the researcher manipulates the cause. Correct code: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I.

II. Randomly assigns participants to treatment and control groups and manipulates the independent variable

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is false: post-positivism (associated with Karl Popper's critical rationalism and critical realism) rejects the claim to absolute certainty. It accepts that all observation is fallible and theory-laden, so knowledge is provisional and claims are tested by attempted falsification. Statement II is true: Comte's positivism accepts only what can be observed and verified; metaphysical and speculative claims are set aside. Hence Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

stmts: Statement I: Post-positivism holds that a careful researcher using objective measurement can reach absolute certainty about social reality.
Statement II: Positivism, associated with Auguste Comte, treats knowledge that can be verified through observation and experience as the only genuine knowledge.

questionBank.question: Arrange the elements of a journal-article reference in the APA 7th edition style in the order in which they are written.
questionBank.explanation: APA 7th edition: Author, A. A., & Author, B. B. (Year). Title of the article. Journal Name, volume(issue), pages. https://doi.org/xxxx. So the order is B (authors), D (year in parentheses), A (article title), E (journal, volume, issue, pages), C (DOI): B, D, A, E, C. The year immediately after the authors is the signature of APA (an author–date style). "B, A, D, E, C" is closer to MLA, where the date comes after the container title rather than right after the author. Writing the journal before the article title, or starting with the year, is not used by any of the common styles.

stmts: A. Title of the article
B. Author(s)
C. DOI (written as a URL)
D. Year of publication (in parentheses)
E. Journal name, volume (issue) and page range

questionBank.question: Which of the following statements about the UGC (Promotion of Academic Integrity and Prevention of Plagiarism in Higher Educational Institutions) Regulations, 2018 are correct?
options: A, B, C and E only
B, C, D and E only
A, C, D and E only
questionBank.explanation: The regulations grade similarity in the core work of students and researchers into four levels. Level 0 (up to 10%): minor, no penalty, so A is correct. Level 1 (above 10% to 40%): the student must submit a revised script within a stipulated time not exceeding 6 months. Level 2 (above 40% to 60%): the student is debarred from submitting a revised script for one year. Level 3 (above 60%): the registration for that programme is cancelled, so B is correct and D is wrong (D attaches the Level 1 penalty to Level 2). The regulations exclude from the check: all quoted work reproduced with permission and acknowledgement, references, bibliography, table of contents, preface and acknowledgements, generic terms, laws, standard symbols and equations, and common knowledge or coinage, so C and E are correct. Answer: A, B, C and E only.

B. A research scholar whose thesis shows similarity above 60% (Level 3) has the registration for that programme cancelled.
C. Quoted work used with permission and due acknowledgement is excluded from the similarity check.
D. For similarity above 40% and up to 60% (Level 2), the student is asked to submit a revised script within six months.
E. Common knowledge and generic terms are excluded from the similarity check.

questionBank.question: A researcher studies 6,000 undergraduates of a university: 1,200 in science, 1,800 in commerce and 3,000 in arts. She uses stratified random sampling with proportional allocation to draw a sample of 240 students. How many arts students will be in the sample?
questionBank.explanation: Proportional allocation gives each stratum the same share of the sample as it has in the population. Sampling fraction = 240 ÷ 6,000 = 1/25 = 4%. Arts: 3,000 × 1/25 = 120. (Check: science 1,200 ÷ 25 = 48, commerce 1,800 ÷ 25 = 72, and 48 + 72 + 120 = 240.) 80 is equal allocation (240 ÷ 3), which ignores the stratum sizes; 72 is the commerce share; 150 comes from dividing 3,000 by 20 instead of 25.

questionBank.question: Which of the following best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: Large volumes of volunteer observations have become scientifically valuable despite their errors, but their uneven coverage and participation must be recognised and addressed
Volunteer birdwatchers have become as accurate as trained ornithologists, so expert surveys are no longer needed
Citizen science is mainly a cheap substitute for professional research that funding agencies prefer
Bird populations in India are declining because remote grasslands are poorly surveyed
questionBank.explanation: The passage moves from the value of volunteer data (paragraphs 1–3), to its limits (paragraph 4), to how good projects handle those limits (paragraph 5). Only the first option captures both halves. The second contradicts the passage, which says acceptance came "not [because] volunteers became experts". The third is the view the last paragraph argues against ("more than a cheap way of gathering numbers"). The fourth is never claimed: poor coverage is a problem of the data, not a cause of decline.

stem.passage:
Every winter, on a chosen weekend, thousands of people across India step outside with a notebook and a pair of binoculars and spend a quarter of an hour counting birds. Most of them are not ornithologists. They are schoolteachers, retired bank clerks, college students and farmers, and the lists they upload to a shared online database have quietly become one of the richest records of bird life the country has ever had. This is citizen science: research in which members of the public collect, and sometimes analyse, the data on which scientific conclusions rest.

Professional scientists were once wary of such data, and not without reason. A volunteer may mistake one warbler for another, count the same flock twice or report only the striking species while ignoring the drab ones. A single expert survey, carefully designed, seemed more trustworthy than a thousand casual observations. What changed the argument was not that volunteers became experts but that their numbers became large enough for errors to be measured and corrected. When the same patch of wetland is visited by forty observers over ten years, an improbable sighting stands out against the pattern and can be queried; systematic habits, such as the tendency to record more birds on sunny mornings, can be estimated and removed by statistical models. Scale, in other words, does not eliminate error; it makes error visible.

Citizen science also reaches places and seasons that funded surveys cannot. A research team may visit a forest once a year; a resident birdwatcher sees it every week. Several shifts in the arrival dates of migratory species were first noticed not in a laboratory but in the notebooks of amateurs who had watched the same lake for decades.

Yet the approach has limits that enthusiasm can hide. Volunteers cluster near cities, roads and famous sanctuaries, so remote grasslands and hill tracts remain thinly recorded, and a map of observations can be mistaken for a map of birds. Participation also depends on leisure, smartphones and connectivity, which means that the people who know a landscape best, those who work in it every day, are often the least represented in the data.

The most thoughtful projects therefore treat volunteers not as free labour but as partners. They train observers, share results with the communities that produced them and invite local knowledge into the design of the survey itself. Where this happens, citizen science becomes more than a cheap way of gathering numbers. It becomes a way of widening who is allowed to take part in making knowledge.

questionBank.question: According to the passage, what mainly changed professional scientists' view of volunteer-collected data?
options: Volunteers were trained until they reached expert standards of identification
Smartphones removed the problem of misidentification
The number of observations became large enough for errors and biases to be detected and corrected
Funding agencies began to require public participation in surveys
questionBank.explanation: The second paragraph states it directly: "What changed the argument was not that volunteers became experts but that their numbers became large enough for errors to be measured and corrected." The second option is the very explanation the passage rejects. Smartphones are mentioned only as a condition of participation (paragraph 4), not as a cure for error, and funding requirements are not mentioned at all.

questionBank.question:
Consider the following statements:
A. A map showing where observations were recorded may reflect where observers go rather than where birds live.
B. Long-term observations by amateurs have helped detect changes in the timing of bird migration.
C. Statistical models can remove all errors from volunteer data.
D. People who work in a landscape every day are completely excluded from citizen-science projects.
Which of these can be inferred from the passage?
questionBank.explanation: A is supported: volunteers "cluster near cities, roads and famous sanctuaries", so "a map of observations can be mistaken for a map of birds". B is supported: shifts in arrival dates "were first noticed ... in the notebooks of amateurs". C over-states the passage, which says models can estimate and remove "systematic habits" and that scale "does not eliminate error". D turns "often the least represented" into "completely excluded", an extreme word the passage does not support. Answer: A and B only. Words like "all", "completely" and "always" in an option are a common signal that it goes beyond the text.

questionBank.question: What does the author mean by the statement "Scale, in other words, does not eliminate error; it makes error visible"?
options: Large projects contain more errors than small ones, so their results are less reliable
Errors disappear automatically once enough data have been collected
Only large-scale expert surveys can reveal the mistakes made by volunteers
When many observers record the same places over many years, unusual records and consistent biases can be recognised and corrected
questionBank.explanation: The sentence sums up the preceding lines: with forty observers over ten years, "an improbable sighting stands out against the pattern" and systematic habits "can be estimated and removed". So a large volume of data lets errors be seen and handled; it does not remove them by itself. The second option reverses the argument, the third contradicts "does not eliminate error", and the fourth credits expert surveys with what the passage credits to the scale of volunteer data.

questionBank.question: The author's attitude towards citizen science is best described as:
options: appreciative but critically aware of its limitations
questionBank.explanation: The author praises citizen science as "one of the richest records of bird life" and credits amateurs with real discoveries, but also devotes a paragraph to "limits that enthusiasm can hide" (spatial bias and unequal participation) and ends by saying what good projects must do. questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: A-III: Harold Lasswell (1948) framed communication as the question "Who says what in which channel to whom with what effect?", a linear model popular in mass-media research. B-II: David Berlo (1960) proposed the SMCR model, stressing the communication skills, attitudes, knowledge, social system and culture of source and receiver. C-I: Frank Dance (1967) proposed the helical model: communication grows cumulatively over time like a helix, each exchange building on the earlier ones. D-IV: Osgood and Schramm (1954) described a circular model in which each participant acts as encoder, interpreter and decoder, removing the sender/receiver distinction. Correct code: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

D. Circular model in which both parties encode, decode and interpret
b: I. Frank Dance
II. David Berlo
III. Harold Lasswell
IV. Charles Osgood and Wilbur Schramm

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (A) is true: kinesics (term from Ray Birdwhistell) is the study of body movement: gestures, posture, facial expression and eye movement, all of which carry meaning in the classroom (a nod, folded arms, a raised hand). (R) is false: the study of space and interpersonal distance (intimate, personal, social and public zones) is proxemics, from Edward T. Hall. Other non-verbal channels: haptics (touch), chronemics (time), paralanguage (tone, pitch, pauses) and artefacts (dress, objects). Hence (A) is true but (R) is false.

stmts: Assertion (A): Kinesics is a channel of non-verbal communication in the classroom.
Reason (R): Kinesics is the study of how communicators use space and interpersonal distance.

questionBank.question: Which of the following are semantic barriers to communication?
options: A, B, C and D only
questionBank.explanation: Semantic barriers arise from meaning: words, symbols and their interpretation. A (jargon), B (a word with different meanings for the two parties) and D (an idiom translated word for word, so its meaning is lost) are all semantic. C is a physical or environmental barrier (noise in the channel). E is a psychological barrier (emotion, anxiety, fear affecting reception). Answer: A, B and D only.

stmts: A. Technical jargon that the audience does not know
B. A word that carries different meanings for the sender and the receiver
C. The hum of a faulty projector fan in a lecture hall
D. A literal translation of an idiom from one language into another
E. The anxiety of a student facing a strict examiner

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: McCombs and Shaw's 1968 Chapel Hill study showed that the issues voters rated as important matched the issues the media emphasised; the theory builds on Bernard Cohen's remark that the press is "stunningly successful in telling its readers what to think about". Statement II is true: studies by Lazarsfeld and colleagues (The People's Choice, 1944) and Katz and Lazarsfeld (Personal Influence, 1955) found that media messages flow first to opinion leaders, who pass them on to less attentive people through personal contact. Hence both statements are true.

stmts: Statement I: Agenda-setting theory (McCombs and Shaw) holds that the mass media are more successful in telling people what to think about than in telling them what to think.
Statement II: The two-step flow model (Lazarsfeld and Katz) proposes that media influence reaches much of the public through opinion leaders.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following stages of the communication process in the order in which they occur.
questionBank.explanation: Communication starts with ideation (D): the sender forms the idea. The idea is then encoded (B) into a message, transmitted through a channel (E), decoded by the receiver (A), and the receiver responds with feedback (C), which closes the loop. So the sequence is D, B, E, A, C. The distractors put encoding before the idea exists, decode before transmission, or transmit before encoding.

B. Encoding of the idea into words, symbols or gestures
C. Feedback from the receiver to the sender
D. Ideation (the sender forms the idea to be conveyed)
E. Transmission of the message through a channel

questionBank.question:
What comes next in the series?
5, 11, 24, 51, 106, ?
questionBank.explanation: Each term is double the previous term plus an increasing number: 5 × 2 + 1 = 11, 11 × 2 + 2 = 24, 24 × 2 + 3 = 51, 51 × 2 + 4 = 106, so the next term is 106 × 2 + 5 = 217. 212 is 106 × 2 with the addend forgotten; 213 keeps the addend fixed at 1; 218 adds 6 instead of 5. The differences (6, 13, 27, 55, 111) confirm it: each difference is double the previous one plus 1.

Applying the same rule, GRAPE → G→H, R→S, A→B, P→Q, E→F = HSBQF, not HSBQG (the last letter was shifted twice). So Statement I is false. Statement II: CAT = 3 + 1 + 20 = 24, the sum of alphabetical positions. DOG = 4 + 15 + 7 = 26, not 27. So Statement II is false. Hence both statements are false.

questionBank.question: Meera walks 12 km north from her house, turns right and walks 5 km, turns right again and walks 21 km, and then turns left and walks 7 km. How far is she from her house, and in which direction?
questionBank.explanation: Take the house as (0, 0), with east as +x and north as +y. 12 km north → (0, 12). Facing north, a right turn faces east: 5 km → (5, 12). Facing east, a right turn faces south: 21 km → (5, −9). Facing south, a left turn faces east: 7 km → (12, −9). Distance = √(12² + 9²) = √(144 + 81) = √225 = 15 km. She is 12 km east and 9 km south of the house, so the direction is south-east. North-east forgets that 21 km south overshoots the 12 km north; 13 km comes from √(5² + 12²), the position after the second leg; 21 km adds 12 + 9.

questionBank.question: The monthly incomes of P and Q are in the ratio 5 : 3 and their monthly expenses are in the ratio 9 : 5. If each of them saves ₹2,600 a month, what is P's monthly income?
questionBank.explanation: Let the incomes be 5x and 3x and the expenses 9y and 5y. Savings: 5x − 9y = 2,600 and 3x − 5y = 2,600. Equating: 5x − 9y = 3x − 5y → 2x = 4y → x = 2y. Substituting in the second equation: 6y − 5y = 2,600 → y = 2,600, x = 5,200. P's income = 5x = ₹26,000 (expense 9y = ₹23,400, saving ₹2,600). Q's income = 3x = ₹15,600 (expense ₹13,000, saving ₹2,600). The distractors are Q's income, P's expense and Q's expense.

questionBank.question: Match List I with List II
questionBank.explanation: Nyaya lists five hetvabhasas (fallacies of the reason). A-II: savyabhichara (anaikantika, the "erratic" reason) is too wide, e.g. "the hill has fire because it is knowable": knowability is present both where fire is and where it is not. B-IV: viruddha (contradictory) establishes the opposite, e.g. "sound is eternal because it is produced": whatever is produced is non-eternal. C-I: asiddha (unestablished, also called sadhyasama) rests on a reason that is itself unproven, e.g. "the sky-lotus is fragrant because it is a lotus". D-III: badhita (kalatita, the "contradicted") draws a conclusion refuted by a stronger pramana, e.g. "fire is cold because it is a substance", refuted by perception. The fifth is satpratipaksha, where a counter-reason of equal strength proves the opposite. Correct code: A-II, B-IV, C-I, D-III.

b: I. The reason itself is unestablished; its presence in the subject is not proven
II. The reason is found both where the property to be proved is present and where it is absent, so it is inconclusive
III. The conclusion is contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge such as perception
IV. The reason proves the very opposite of what it is meant to establish

questionBank.question: Arrange the five members (avayavas) of the Nyaya inference-for-others (pararthanumana) in their correct order.
questionBank.explanation: The five-membered Nyaya syllogism runs: 1. Pratijna (B): "The hill has fire." 2. Hetu (D): "Because it has smoke." 3. Udaharana (E): "Wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in a kitchen." 4. Upanaya (A): "The hill has smoke, which is invariably accompanied by fire." 5. Nigamana (C): "Therefore the hill has fire." So B, D, E, A, C. The example with the universal rule (vyapti) must come before the application to the case at hand; the distractors swap these, or put the reason before the thesis.

stmts: A. Upanaya (application)
B. Pratijna (proposition)
C. Nigamana (conclusion)
D. Hetu (reason)
E. Udaharana (example with the universal rule)

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion (A) and the other is labelled as Reason (R).
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A)
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is NOT the correct explanation of (A)
questionBank.explanation: (R) is true: in the traditional square of opposition, A ("All S are P") and E ("No S are P") are contraries: they cannot both be true, but they can both be false. (A) is false: because contraries can both be false, the falsity of the A proposition leaves the E proposition undetermined. If some poets are dreamers and some are not, both "All poets are dreamers" and "No poets are dreamers" are false. The inference "one false, so the other true" holds only for contradictories (A–O, E–I). Hence (A) is false but (R) is true.

stmts: Assertion (A): If the proposition "All poets are dreamers" is false, then the proposition "No poets are dreamers" must be true.
Reason (R): A and E propositions with the same subject and predicate are contraries, which cannot both be true.

questionBank.question:
Statements:
All mentors are readers.
Some readers are singers.
No singer is a critic.
Conclusions:
I. Some readers are not critics.
II. Some mentors are singers.
III. No mentor is a critic.
Which conclusion(s) logically follow?
questionBank.explanation: I follows: "Some readers are singers" and "No singer is a critic" together say that the readers who are singers are not critics, so some readers are not critics (an O conclusion from I + E, valid in the third-figure form). II does not follow: mentors lie inside readers, but the singers among the readers may lie entirely outside the mentors. III does not follow: nothing links mentors to critics; a mentor who is not a singer may be a critic. A Venn diagram (or checking every possible arrangement of the regions) shows a case where I is true and both II and III fail. Hence only I follows.

questionBank.question: Given below are two statements:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questionBank.explanation: Statement I is true: argumentum ad ignorantiam treats the absence of proof against a claim as proof for it (or the reverse). Statement II is false: attacking the person is argumentum ad hominem (abusive or circumstantial). A straw man misrepresents the opponent's argument, usually as a weaker version, and then refutes the distorted version. Both are informal fallacies of relevance. Hence Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

stmts: Statement I: The argument "No one has proved that ghosts do not exist, so ghosts exist" commits the fallacy of appeal to ignorance.
Statement II: Attacking the character or circumstances of the person who makes an argument, instead of the argument itself, is the straw man fallacy.

questionBank.explanation: The 2021 Regulations allow an institution to offer up to 40% of the total courses of a programme in a semester through the online learning courses on SWAYAM, with the credits transferred to the learner’s record. 40% of 15 = 0.40 × 15 = 6 courses. The option 3 comes from the older 2016 limit of 20% (0.20 × 15 = 3), a common trap. 7 exceeds the ceiling, and 5 applies no rule.

questionBank.question: In a CBCS semester a student takes five courses with the following credits and grade points: Course 1 – 4 credits, grade point 9; Course 2 – 4 credits, grade point 8; Course 3 – 3 credits, grade point 7; Course 4 – 3 credits, grade point 10; Course 5 – 2 credits, grade point 6. What is the student’s SGPA (to two decimal places)?
questionBank.explanation:
SGPA = Σ(credits × grade points) ÷ Σ credits.
Credit points: 4 × 9 = 36; 4 × 8 = 32; 3 × 7 = 21; 3 × 10 = 30; 2 × 6 = 12. Total = 131.
Total credits = 4 + 4 + 3 + 3 + 2 = 16.
SGPA = 131 ÷ 16 = 8.1875 ≈ 8.19.
The trap 8.00 is the simple mean of the five grade points (40 ÷ 5), which ignores credit weighting; CBCS always weights grade points by credits.

questionBank.question: Arrange the following levels of the affective domain (Krathwohl’s taxonomy) from the lowest to the highest.
questionBank.explanation: Krathwohl, Bloom and Masia (1964) arranged the affective domain by increasing internalisation: Receiving (willing to attend) → Responding (active participation) → Valuing (attaching worth) → Organisation (bringing different values into a system and resolving conflicts) → Characterisation by a value or value complex (the value system consistently governs behaviour). So the order is B, D, A, E, C. The distractors swap Valuing with Responding or Organisation, the two most frequently confused steps.

stmts: A. Valuing
B. Receiving
C. Characterisation by a value or value complex
D. Responding
E. Organisation
